summary: The frame story opens. The bard Sauti arrives at the forest of Naimisha, where sages are gathered at a long sacrifice, and is asked to tell them the Mahabharata as Vaishampayana first recited it at King Janamejaya's snake sacrifice. He praises its source, tells how Vyasa composed it and how Ganesha wrote it down, and lists what it contains. He then retells, through Dhritarashtra's lament to Sanjaya, the whole course of the war, and Sanjaya consoles the blind king that fate is the work of Time. The chapter ends with the merit of hearing the epic and why it is called the Great Bharata.

The sages ask about the place called Samanta-panchaka and the word Akshauhini. Sauti explains how Parashurama's slaughter of the warrior class created five blood-lakes there, which later became the Kurukshetra battlefield, and he defines an Akshauhini as a vast army unit. He then gives a contents list (Parva-sangraha) of all eighteen books of the epic, with the number of sections and verses in each, and ends by praising the merit of hearing the Bharata.

Sauti begins the Paushya section. King Janamejaya's brothers beat a dog, the son of the divine bitch Sarama, and she curses the family. To cleanse the curse Janamejaya appoints a priest. Then comes a chain of teacher-and-pupil stories about Ayoda-Dhaumya's disciples Aruni, Upamanyu and Veda, and Veda's pupil Utanka. Utanka fetches Queen Paushya's earrings as a gift for his teacher's wife, fights the serpent king Takshaka who steals them, and wins them back. He then urges Janamejaya to avenge his father Parikshit's death by a snake sacrifice, which plants the seed of the whole frame story.
Back in the Naimisha forest, Sauti offers to tell more tales. The sages ask him to wait until their leader Saunaka finishes his rites. Saunaka arrives and sits down to question him.

Saunaka asks Sauti to tell the history of the Bhrigu family. Sauti traces Bhrigu's descendants down to Sunaka and begins the story of why Bhrigu's son was named Chyavana. A demon named Puloma finds Bhrigu's pregnant wife Puloma alone, and the fire god Agni, forced to speak truthfully, confirms that she is Bhrigu's lawful wife.

The Rakshasa turns into a boar and carries Puloma off, but her unborn child drops from the womb with such fiery power that the demon is burnt to ashes. The child is named Chyavana (the one who fell). Her tears become the river Vadhusara. When Bhrigu learns that Agni identified her, he curses Agni to eat everything.

Agni protests the curse, saying he only told the truth and that he carries offerings to gods and ancestors. He withdraws from the world, stopping all rites. The gods and sages go to Brahma, who softens the curse: only the flame in Agni's lowest parts will devour everything, and whatever Agni burns becomes pure. Agni agrees and rites resume.

The line of Bhrigu continues: Chyavana's son Pramati has a son, Ruru. The Apsara Menaka leaves her baby daughter by the river, and the sage Sthulakesa raises her as Pramadvara. Ruru falls in love and is betrothed to her, but days before the wedding she steps on a snake and dies. The sages gather around her and weep, and Ruru withdraws in grief.

Ruru weeps in the forest and offers his own merit to bring Pramadvara back. A heavenly messenger says she can live if Ruru gives her half his lifespan. Dharma, the judge of the dead, agrees, and she revives. They marry, but Ruru, bitter about the snakebite, vows to kill every snake. One day he lifts his staff to kill an old Dundubha snake, which asks why.

Ruru says his wife died of a snakebite so he has sworn to kill all snakes. The Dundubha answers that harmless Dundubhas are snakes only in name and should not be killed. Ruru spares it and asks who it is. The snake says it was once a sage named Sahasrapat and was cursed into this shape.

Sahasrapat explains: as a joke he scared his friend, the ascetic Khagama, with a toy snake made of grass, and Khagama cursed him to become a harmless snake until he met Ruru. Seeing Ruru frees him and he regains his human form. He tells Ruru that sparing life is the highest duty of a Brahmana, that a Brahmana should not take life, and promises the story of the snake sacrifice and Astika.

Ruru asks why Janamejaya wanted to destroy the serpents and how Astika saved them. The sage says Brahmanas will tell him this, then vanishes. Ruru searches for him in vain, faints, recovers and asks his father, who tells him the story.

The Astika section opens. Saunaka asks why Janamejaya wanted to kill snakes and how Astika saved them. Sauti begins with Astika's father, the ascetic Jaratkaru, who finds his ancestors hanging head down over a pit because he has no children. They tell him to marry and have a son. Jaratkaru agrees on the condition that the bride share his name and be offered freely.
Jaratkaru searches for a wife and finds none. In the forest he prays aloud for a bride, and the serpent king Vasuki offers his sister, whose name is also Jaratkaru. The sage accepts and marries her.

The serpents' mother had cursed them to be burnt in Janamejaya's sacrifice, and Vasuki married off his sister to prevent that. Their son Astika grew up wise and later saved the serpents at the sacrifice. Jaratkaru paid his debts to the gods, sages and ancestors, his ancestors went to heaven, and he later died. Sauti asks what to tell next.

Saunaka asks Sauti to retell the Astika story from the beginning. Sauti starts with Kasyapa's two wives, the sisters Kadru and Vinata. Kadru is granted a thousand snake sons and Vinata two stronger sons. After five hundred years, Vinata impatiently breaks one egg and the half-formed son Aruna curses her to become a slave, with the other son Garuda as her eventual rescuer. Aruna becomes the sun's charioteer, and Garuda hatches and flies off in search of food.

The two sisters see the splendid horse Uchchaihsravas, born when the gods churned the ocean. Saunaka asks why the ocean was churned. Sauti begins describing the golden Mount Meru, where the gods met, anxious for the nectar of immortality, and Narayana told Brahma that the gods and Asuras should churn the ocean.

The gods prepare to churn the ocean. Ananta uproots Mount Mandara, a tortoise carries it on his back, and the serpent Vasuki serves as the rope, with Asuras at his head and gods at his tail. Destruction and fire follow, put out by Indra's rain. Tired, the gods ask Narayana for strength. The moon, Lakshmi, Soma, the white horse, the Kaustubha jewel, Dhanwantari with the nectar, and the elephant Airavata rise, then the deadly poison Kalakuta, which Siva swallows and so gets a blue throat. Narayana then takes the form of an enchanting woman and gets the nectar from the Asuras.

The Asuras attack, but Vishnu as the enchantress takes the nectar, and the gods drink it. The demon Rahu drinks among them in disguise, and Vishnu cuts off his head, which is why Rahu's head still swallows the sun and moon in eclipses. A huge battle follows on the sea shore; Vishnu's discus Sudarsana kills thousands, Nara breaks the hurled mountains with arrows, and the Asuras flee into the earth and sea. The gods put Mandara back and give the nectar to Narayana to keep.

Sauti finishes the churning story and returns to the sisters. Kadru and Vinata bet on the colour of the horse Uchchaihsravas: Vinata says it is white, Kadru says its tail is black, and the loser will be a slave. Kadru orders her snake sons to turn into black hairs on the tail, but they refuse, so she curses them to burn in Janamejaya's sacrifice. Brahma approves the curse, since the snakes are poisonous and harm creatures, and tells Kasyapa not to grieve, giving him the knowledge to neutralise poison.

The next morning the sisters set out to see the horse and pass over the ocean. The chapter is a long poetic description of the sea: its depth, creatures, gems, rivers pouring in, its use as Vishnu's bed, and the place where the Asuras hide.
The snakes decide to obey their mother so as not to lose her favour and become hairs on the horse's tail. The sisters fly over the ocean to see the horse, with another description of the sea.

Kadru and Vinata reach the horse. It is white except for black hairs in the tail, so Vinata loses and becomes Kadru's slave. Garuda hatches by himself, blazing so brightly that the gods fear him to be fire. Agni explains he is Vinata's son Garuda. The gods approach and praise Garuda at length as the supreme one, asking him to reduce his brilliance, and he does so.

Garuda shrinks his body, carries his brother Aruna to the east and sets him in front of the sun. Sauti explains why: Surya had been angry at Rahu's enmity after he exposed Rahu, and resolved to burn the world. Brahma arranged for Aruna to be Surya's charioteer and shield the world from his heat.

Garuda goes to his mother Vinata, who is Kadru's slave. Kadru orders Vinata to carry her to a snake island, and Garuda carries the snakes. As he flies up toward the sun, the heat scorches the snakes. Kadru prays to Indra with a long hymn, asking him to save them with rain.
Indra answers Kadru's prayer and sends storm clouds that pour rain, shielding the snakes and cooling the earth. They reach the island of Ramaniyaka safely.

The snakes enjoy the beautiful forested island, then order Garuda to take them to another island. Garuda asks his mother why he must serve the snakes, and Vinata tells him of her wager and enslavement. Garuda asks the snakes what price will free them. They say: bring the nectar of immortality by force.

Garuda tells his mother he will fetch the nectar and asks what to eat on the way. Vinata sends him to the Nishadas (fisher tribe) living by the sea, but warns him never to kill a Brahmana, whom she says is like fire, and gives him signs to recognise one: a Brahmana will burn his throat and not be digested. She blesses him. Garuda attacks the Nishadas, stirring up dust, and swallows thousands of them.

A Brahmana and his Nishada wife are swallowed in Garuda's throat and burn it. Garuda lets them out. He tells his father Kasyapa he is still hungry. Kasyapa shows him a lake where an elephant and a tortoise, who were once brothers named Supritika and Vibhavasu, fight each other because they cursed each other over a quarrel about inheritance. He tells Garuda to eat them and bless him for the fight with the gods. Garuda seizes them and lands on a huge banyan tree, whose branch breaks.

The broken branch holds the Valakhilya sages hanging head down. Garuda catches it in his beak to save them, gets his name for carrying such a load, and flies to Kasyapa on Mount Gandhamadana. Kasyapa persuades the sages to leave the branch and they go to the Himalayas. Garuda drops the branch on a deserted snowy peak and eats the elephant and tortoise. Meanwhile bad omens appear in heaven. Indra's teacher Vrihaspati explains that Garuda is coming for the nectar, and the gods arm and guard it.

Saunaka asks how Garuda came to be born. Sauti tells how Indra, carrying logs for Kasyapa's sacrifice, laughed at the tiny Valakhilya sages struggling with a leaf-stalk. Angered, they performed a rite to create a rival Indra. Indra begged Kasyapa for help, and Kasyapa persuaded the sages to let the new Indra be a lord of birds, Kasyapa's own son. Vinata then bore Aruna and Garuda, and Indra was warned never to insult Brahmanas again.

Garuda fights the gods who guard the nectar. He defeats the craftsman god Viswakarma, blinds the gods with dust, and fights off Indra's attacks with talons and wings, causing them to flee in four directions. He kills several Yaksha guards, drinks rivers with many mouths to put out the fire ringing the nectar, and shrinks to enter.

Garuda passes through a razor-sharp spinning wheel, blinds and kills two fiery guardian snakes, and seizes the nectar without tasting it. Vishnu is pleased by his restraint and grants him the boons of immortality and a seat above him; Garuda becomes Vishnu's mount and emblem on his flag. Indra hurls his thunderbolt, but Garuda is unhurt and sheds a feather in respect, earning the name Suparna. Indra, impressed, asks for friendship and to know his strength.

Garuda and Indra become friends. Garuda boasts that he can carry the earth and all the worlds on a single feather. Indra asks for the nectar back, and Garuda says he will set it down so Indra can take it. As a favour Garuda asks that snakes become his food, which Indra grants. Garuda gives the snakes the nectar on kusa grass and tells them to bathe first; Indra takes it away. The snakes lick the grass and their tongues split. Garuda eats snakes, and Sauti closes with the blessing for hearing this tale.
Saunaka asks for the names of the snakes. Sauti gives a list of the chief ones, starting with Sesha and Vasuki and naming dozens more, and says the rest are too many to name.

Saunaka asks what the snakes did after the curse. Sesha, the eldest, leaves his wicked brothers and performs severe penances. Brahma appears and offers a boon. Sesha asks only for a heart devoted to virtue. Brahma tells him to hold up the earth steady, and Sesha goes under the earth and bears it on his head. Brahma gives him Garuda as a helper.

Vasuki calls a council of snakes to find a way to cancel their mother's curse. Many plans are put forward: disguising themselves as Brahmana advisers, killing the priests, becoming rain clouds to put out the fire, stealing the sacrificial vessels, fouling the food, demanding fees, kidnapping or biting the king. The kinder snakes object that killing Brahmanas is wrong. Vasuki rejects all of them and says only the help of their father Kasyapa can save them.

The snake Elapatra tells the council that the sacrifice cannot be stopped, but he overheard the gods asking Brahma why he allowed the curse. Brahma said only the wicked snakes would die and foretold that a sage named Jaratkaru would have a son Astika by Vasuki's sister, of the same name, and that Astika would stop the sacrifice. Elapatra advises Vasuki to give his sister to that sage when he comes asking.

The snakes cheer Elapatra's advice, and Vasuki raises his sister carefully. After the gods and Asuras churn the ocean using Vasuki as the rope, the gods ask Brahma to relieve his fear. Brahma confirms Elapatra's plan. Vasuki orders the snakes to watch Jaratkaru and report when he asks for a wife.

Saunaka asks the meaning of the name Jaratkaru, and Sauti explains it: the sage wore down his large body by penance. Saunaka then asks how Astika was born. Sauti tells how King Parikshit, hunting a wounded deer, found a silent sage and, angered at his silence, hung a dead snake on his shoulder. The sage Samika did not curse him, but his young son Sringin hears of it from a companion, Krisa, and flares up in anger.

Sringin learns from Krisa what the king did. In rage he curses Parikshit to die within seven nights by Takshaka's bite. He tells his father, the sage Samika, who rebukes him: a king must be forgiven, as kings protect hermits and keep dharma. The king acted from hunger and ignorance of the vow of silence, so the curse was wrong.

Sringin insists the curse cannot be unsaid. Samika advises peace and sends his pupil Gaurmukha to warn the king. Parikshit is sorry and builds a guarded tower on one pillar. On the seventh day, the physician Kasyapa heads to cure him if bitten. Takshaka, disguised as a Brahmana, meets him and says he will bite the king.

Takshaka challenges Kasyapa to revive a banyan tree he burns with a bite. Kasyapa revives it from ashes. Takshaka then asks what Kasyapa wants from the king, offers more wealth, and warns that his skills may fail on a king cursed by a Brahmana. Kasyapa sees that the king's life has run out and takes the payment. Takshaka then sends snakes disguised as ascetics with gifts to the king. The king eats a fruit and finds a small worm in it, jokes that it should be Takshaka and puts it on his neck. It turns into Takshaka and bites him.

The ministers flee as the palace blazes with poison and the king dies. His minor son is crowned Janamejaya. His ministers arrange his marriage to Vapushtama, daughter of the king of Kasi, and the young king lives happily with her.

The wandering sage Jaratkaru sees his ancestors hanging head down in a pit, held only by a thread of roots that a rat gnaws. He offers his merit to save them. They explain: they hang because they have no descendants; the thread is Jaratkaru himself, who practises only penance, and the rat is Time. They ask the stranger to tell Jaratkaru to marry and have a son, and ask who he is.

Jaratkaru identifies himself as their son and asks what to do. He explains he had vowed to remain celibate but, after seeing them, will marry if he finds a bride of his own name who is offered freely and does not need support. He searches in vain, then calls out in the forest. The snakes watching him tell Vasuki, who brings his sister. Jaratkaru hesitates and asks her name and states he will not support her.

Vasuki says his sister bears the same name and he will maintain her. Jaratkaru marries her on the condition that he will leave if she ever does anything he dislikes. She conceives. One evening he sleeps with his head in her lap and sunset nears. Fearing the loss of his evening prayers, she wakes him. He is furious at the insult, says he will leave, and ignores her pleas, but tells her the child in her womb will be a great sage. He departs for more penance.

Jaratkaru's wife tells Vasuki what happened. He asks about the child because the snakes' hopes rest on it. She says her husband told her that a son would be born. Vasuki is relieved and honours her. The boy is born, studies the Vedas with Chyavana, and is named Astika ("there is") for his father's words before leaving.

Saunaka asks to hear again what Janamejaya asked his ministers about his father. Janamejaya asks how his father died. The ministers praise Parikshit as a just king who protected all classes and ruled for sixty years. They then tell how, hunting as an old man, he put a dead snake on a silent sage's shoulders.

The ministers report how the sage Utanka was insulted by King Janamejaya's father, and how the sage's son Sringin cursed the king to die by Takshaka's poison. Takshaka kills the king in his mansion after Kasyapa, sent to save him, is paid off and turns back. Janamejaya hears the whole story from his ministers and resolves to avenge his father, which sets up the snake-sacrifice.

Janamejaya, having heard that Takshaka killed his father, asks his priests for a way to burn the snake and his kin. The chief priest names the snake-sacrifice, a rite said to be known from the Puranas and possible only for the king to perform. Preparations begin with the sacrificial platform, but a builder warns that a Brahmana will obstruct the rite, so the king orders his gatekeepers to admit no one.

The snake-sacrifice begins with priests in black garments pouring butter into the fire while calling out the names of the snakes. Snakes of every kind, young and old, fall into the flames by the hundreds of thousands. The scene shows the terrible effect of the rite on the snake race.

Saunaka asks who served as priests and assembly members at the snake-sacrifice, and Sauti lists the famous sages. As the rite goes on, snakes keep falling into the fire, and Takshaka flees to Indra, who promises to protect him. Vasuki, seeing his family dwindling, sends for his sister so that her son Astika can stop the sacrifice.

Jaratkaru tells her son Astika why she was given to his father: Kadru cursed her sons to burn in Janamejaya's sacrifice, and Brahman foretold that a Brahmana born of Jaratkaru would free the snakes. Astika promises Vasuki he will stop the sacrifice. He then enters the sacrificial compound and praises the king and the priests.

Astika praises Janamejaya's sacrifice by comparing it with the great sacrifices of gods, sages and kings, and he praises the priests and Vyasa. The praise is the opening of his plea to stop the sacrifice. Janamejaya, noticing omens around him, turns to speak to the assembly.

Janamejaya offers Astika a boon, but the priests say Takshaka has not yet come into the sacrifice. The Ritwiks report that Takshaka is hiding with Indra, and when Indra is forced to release him, Takshaka is drawn toward the fire. At that moment Astika asks that the sacrifice end, and the king, unwilling at first, is urged by the assembly to grant the request.

Saunaka asks for the names of the snakes burned in the sacrifice, and Sauti says the number is too great to count. He names the chief snakes of several families, including the lines of Vasuki, Takshaka, Airavata, Kauravya and Dhritarashtra. He adds that their sons and grandsons were burned too, which shows how vast the destruction was.

Janamejaya is puzzled that Takshaka still hangs in the air, though Astika had told him to stay. The king grants Astika's boon, ends the sacrifice, rewards the priests and Lohitaksha, and sends Astika home. The grateful snakes promise protection to anyone who recalls Astika's deed, and Astika later goes to heaven. Sauti closes by saying the recital banishes fear of snakes.

Saunaka asks Sauti to recite the history composed by Vyasa, which Vyasa had recited at Janamejaya's sacrifice. Sauti says the Brahmanas spoke on many Vedic subjects in the intervals, but Vyasa recited the great Bharata. Sauti agrees to tell the Mahabharata from its beginning. This short chapter is the frame that opens the main epic.

Vyasa, the grandfather of the Pandavas, arrives at Janamejaya's sacrifice and is welcomed with honour. Janamejaya asks him why the Kurus and Pandavas fought their great war. Vyasa tells his disciple Vaisampayana to recite the whole history to the king and the assembly.

Vaisampayana begins the history by explaining the quarrel, which started when Duryodhana plotted against the Pandavas after their father's death, using poison, drowning and a lac house. The Pandavas escape, win Draupadi, and settle Khandavaprastha, but a dice game with Duryodhana sends them into exile. The chapter ends with the great war, in which the Kauravas lose their kingdom and Duryodhana is slain.

Janamejaya asks for the full story rather than a summary, and wants to know why the Pandavas endured the Kurus' wrongs without fighting back. Vaisampayana agrees, and before starting he praises the Bharata at length: its size, the merit it brings to those who recite or hear it, and Vyasa's purpose in composing it. He says the work also covers gods, sages and kings, so it is the place to learn about every subject worth knowing.

Vaisampayana traces the origins of the great families, starting with King Vasu, whose seed, carried by a hawk, is swallowed by a fish and produces the twins Matsya and Satyavati. Satyavati later bears Vyasa to the sage Parasara, and Vyasa arranges the Vedas and teaches this history to his disciples. The chapter then lists the births of the heroes of both sides, including Bhishma, Vidura, the Pandavas, the Kauravas and their allies, who meet in the great battle.

Janamejaya asks why these great warriors were born on earth. Vaisampayana explains that after Parasurama cleared the earth of Kshatriyas, a golden age returned, but then Asuras reborn as proud kings oppressed the world. The earth appealed to Brahman, who sent the gods down to be born on earth, and Narayana agreed to descend as well.

Vaisampayana describes the births of gods and other beings, starting with Brahman's sons, Kasyapa, and the daughters of Daksha who became the mothers of most creatures. He names the Adityas, the sons of Diti and Danu who became Asuras, the children of Sinhika, Krodha, Kala, Vinata and Kadru, including Garuda and the Nagas, and the Gandharvas and Apsaras. He ends by saying that reading this account brings long life, progeny and fame.

Vaisampayana continues the genealogy of creation, naming Brahman's sons, the Rudras, the Vasus, Dharma's sons, and Daksha's daughters, who were married to Dharma, Soma and Kasyapa. He traces the Bhrigu line through Sukra, Chyavana, Aurva and Parasurama, and lists the animals and beings born of Tamra, Krodha, Surabhi and others. The chapter closes by saying that hearing this genealogy cleanses sins and brings knowledge.

Vaisampayana lists the earthly rebirths of gods, Asuras and other beings, naming kings such as Jarasandha, Sisupala and Salya, and the heroes of the story, including Bhishma, Drona, Kripa, Sakuni, Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura. He then names the hundred sons of Dhritarashtra and their sister, and describes the Pandavas and Draupadi as portions of gods and goddesses, with Soma's prophecy about Abhimanyu. The chapter closes with the birth of Karna to Kunti and Surya and the births of the Yadu family, so the cast of the story is set.

Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana to tell the Kuru dynasty from its beginning. Vaisampayana starts with King Dushmanta, founder of the Paurava line, who rules the four quarters of the earth. His reign is described as prosperous and virtuous, with no fear of theft, famine or disease.

Janamejaya asks for the story of Bharata's birth, Sakuntala's origin, and how Dushmanta won her. Vaisampayana describes Dushmanta setting out for the forest with a great army, cheered by the women of the city. His hunt there drives away the animals, and the forest is left empty.

After his hunt, Dushmanta crosses a barren plain and reaches a lovely forest beside the river Malini. He finds a hermitage of the sage Kanwa, of the race of Kasyapa, filled with Vedic chanting and learned Brahmanas. He leaves his army at the forest edge and enters with only his minister and priest, which sets up his meeting with Sakuntala.

Dushmanta finds Kanwa's hermitage empty, and a maiden appears who says she is Kanwa's daughter and that her father has gone to fetch fruit. Dushmanta is struck by her beauty, but doubts that a sage who has kept his vows could have a child. Sakuntala replies that she will explain, and begins with the story of her birth, which starts with Indra's fear of the sage Viswamitra and his sending of Menaka.

Sakuntala reports the rest of Kanwa's account. Menaka tempts Viswamitra, and their union produces a daughter, whom Menaka leaves on a river bank. Vultures guard the infant until Kanwa finds her, adopts her, and names her Sakuntala after the birds, and Sakuntala says she regards Kanwa as her father.

Dushmanta proposes marriage to Sakuntala in the Gandharva form, a union by mutual consent, and lists the eight forms of marriage. She agrees on the condition that the son born of their union becomes heir-apparent, and they marry before he returns to his capital. Kanwa, returning, knows all and approves the union, blessing the son to come, and Sakuntala asks for a boon that the Paurava kings stay virtuous and keep their thrones.

Sakuntala brings her grown son to Dushmanta and asks him to keep his promise and install the boy as heir. Dushmanta denies knowing her and insults her birth, and Sakuntala answers with a long speech on the duties of husbands and fathers and on the power of truth, before threatening to leave. A voice from heaven then declares the boy to be Dushmanta's son, the king names him Bharata and installs him, and the Bharata line begins its glory.

Vaisampayana recites the royal genealogy from Daksha through Manu and Pururavas, whose arrogance toward the Brahmanas brings his destruction by their curse. He then tells of Nahusha and his son Yayati, who asks his sons to take his old age, and only the youngest, Puru, agrees. Yayati enjoys Puru's youth but finds his desires unsatisfied, so he returns the youth and names Puru his heir, then retires to the mount of Bhrigu and dies.

Janamejaya asks how Yayati won Sukra's daughter, and Vaisampayana turns to the war between gods and Asuras. The gods send Kacha, son of Vrihaspati, to learn the reviving science from Sukra, and Kacha wins Devayani's affection, but the Danavas kill him three times. After the last killing, Kacha escapes from Sukra's stomach, revives Sukra, and Sukra then curses Brahmanas who drink wine.

Kacha's vow ends and he prepares to return to the gods, but Devayani asks him to marry her. He refuses, saying she is his preceptor's daughter and that he regards her as a sister. Devayani curses that his knowledge will not bear fruit, and he answers that no son of a Rishi will marry her, and that his knowledge will bear fruit only in those he teaches. The gods praise his achievement on his return.

After Kacha brings back his science, Indra, as wind, mixes up the clothes of bathing maidens, and Sarmishtha takes Devayani's garment by mistake. Their quarrel ends with Sarmishtha throwing Devayani into a well, where King Yayati finds her and raises her out. Devayani sends for her father Sukra, who is told of the insult and calms her with words about his own power.

Sukra counsels Devayani that the man who controls his anger and forgives insults is the true victor. Devayani replies that a disciple's insolence should never be forgiven and that she will not live in a land where bad conduct is tolerated. She says the insults burn her like fire, and that for her death would be better than such shame.

Sukra, angered by the mistreatment of his daughter, announces he will leave the Asuras. Vrishaparvan begs him to stay and offers him all the Asura wealth, but Sukra says he cannot bear his daughter's grief. Devayani then demands that Sarmishtha and a thousand maids serve her, and Sarmishtha, though insulted, agrees, so Sukra returns to the Asura capital.

Devayani and Sarmishtha, with a thousand maids, are in the woods when Yayati comes by, tired and thirsty. After the two women tell him who they are, Devayani chooses Yayati as her husband, though he says a Brahmana must be feared more than a snake or fire. Sukra arrives and gives Devayani to Yayati, absolving him of the sin of a mixed marriage and forbidding him to take Sarmishtha to his bed, and the marriage is performed.

Yayati brings Devayani home and sets up Sarmishtha in a separate mansion. When Devayani bears a son, Sarmishtha, anxious to have a child herself, approaches the king. She argues that a lie is excusable in such matters and that Yayati is her husband too, and he, bound by his vow to grant requests, yields, and she bears a son.

Devayani learns that Sarmishtha has a child and is jealous. Sarmishtha claims the father is a Rishi, but Devayani later finds Sarmishtha's three sons playing with Yayati in the woods and learns the truth. Devayani angrily goes to her father Sukra, who curses Yayati with sudden old age, and Yayati begs for relief.

Yayati, aged by Sukra's curse, asks his eldest son Yadu to exchange youth for his decrepitude. Yadu refuses and is cursed, and Turvasu, Drahyu and Anu do the same. Only Puru agrees to take his old age, and Yayati transfers his decrepitude to him.

With Puru's youth, Yayati enjoys life for a thousand years, then realises that desire is never satisfied and returns the youth. The four orders object to passing over the elder sons, but Yayati explains that Puru alone obeyed him, and the people agree to crown Puru. Yayati then retires to the forest, and the peoples descended from his sons are named.

Yayati, having crowned Puru, lives in the forest, ascends to heaven, and is later hurled down by Indra, though he remains in the sky and later returns to the celestials. Janamejaya asks why Yayati fell and how he regained heaven, and Vaisampayana agrees to tell the full story.

Yayati lives in heaven, honoured by the gods, and visits the region of Brahman. When Indra asks what he told Puru on handing over the kingdom, Yayati recites his counsel: rule the land between the Ganga and Yamuna, be forgiving, avoid harsh speech, and follow the wise.

Indra tells Yayati that his virtue has diminished because he disregards his superiors and equals, so he must fall from heaven. Yayati asks to fall among the virtuous, and Indra agrees. As Yayati falls, the royal sage Ashtaka sees him and welcomes him into a gathering of the wise, where he is safe.

Falling from heaven, Yayati introduces himself to the sages and explains that he did not greet them first because he is older. He reflects that destiny rules all, that the wise should neither exult nor grieve, and that all beings return to the Supreme Soul. When Ashtaka, his grandson through a daughter, asks where he has been, Yayati recounts his long stay in the heavens and the celestial warning that brought his fall.

Ashtaka questions Yayati about the afterlife. Yayati says that boasters suffer in the earth-hell, that a fallen being is reborn through the womb from a subtle seed of water, and that the dead keep their memories and enter new forms. He ends by listing the seven gates to heaven, all of which vanity destroys, and says that knowledge without humility does not lead to Brahma.

Ashtaka asks how the four stages of life should be lived, and Yayati outlines the duties of the student, householder, mendicant and forest-dweller. Ashtaka then asks how many kinds of Munis there are, and Yayati explains that a Muni is one who is detached and content, whether he lives in the woods or in a village.

Ashtaka asks whether the ascetic or the man of knowledge first reaches Brahman, and Yayati says the wise attain it first by knowledge. Yayati then says he is falling into the earth-hell, and Ashtaka offers him the heavenly regions he has earned. Yayati refuses to accept gifts he has not earned, and Pratardana then offers his worlds too.

Vasumat and Sivi each offer Yayati the heavenly worlds they have earned, and Yayati refuses to take gifts he has not earned, although Vasumat offers to let him buy them for a straw. Ashtaka and the others then board five golden cars, and the company sets out for heaven, with Sivi ahead as the most generous. Yayati identifies himself and recounts his gifts and truthfulness, and the chapter closes with his ascent, rescued by his descendants.

Janamejaya asks for the histories of the kings descended from Puru, and Vaisampayana traces the line from Puru's sons through Dushmanta and Bharata. The Panchalas defeat the Bharatas and drive Samvarana into exile until the sage Vasishtha restores him. The line then runs through Kuru, Kurukshetra, Pratipa and Santanu.

Janamejaya asks for the full genealogy from Manu, and Vaisampayana recites it from Daksha and Aditi through Yayati, Puru and Janamejaya's own line. The line runs through Dushmanta and his son Bharata, who gave the family its name, to Hastinapura, Kuru and Santanu. The chapter gives Janamejaya a full account of his ancestry.

The chapter traces Santanu's line through his son Bhishma and Satyavati's sons, then through Pandu's curse and the birth of the five Pandavas to Kunti and Madri. It lists the Pandavas' troubles with Duryodhana, their marriages and children, and ends with the rebirth of Parikshit. It then turns to King Mahabhisha, cursed by Brahman for staring at Ganga, who asks to be reborn to Pratipa, while Ganga agrees to bear the Vasus as her children.

Ganga appears to the ascetic-king Pratipa as a maiden and asks him to take her as his wife. Pratipa refuses on grounds of his vow, but offers her as wife to his future son, and she agrees on condition that Santanu never judge her acts. Pratipa later retires to the woods, and Santanu, out hunting by the Ganges, falls in love with Ganga and asks her to marry him.

Ganga agrees to marry Santanu on condition that he never interfere with her acts or speak to her harshly, and he keeps his promise. She drowns each of their first seven sons at birth, and the king's silence breaks only when the eighth is threatened. Ganga reveals that she bore the eight Vasus and freed them from their curse, then leaves, giving the eighth child to Santanu to rear as Gangadatta.

Santanu asks why the Vasus were cursed to be born among men, and Ganga explains that the sage Vasishtha, also called Apava, cursed them after they stole his wish-granting cow Nandini. Dyu, who took the cow to please his wife, must live on earth for a time and remain childless, and the Vasus were freed when Ganga drowned them at birth. Ganga then takes her son away, and Santanu returns home sorrowful.

Santanu's virtuous reign is praised, and Ganga returns his grown son Devavrata, who becomes heir. Santanu falls in love with a fisherman's daughter, but the fisherman demands that her son be made heir, which Santanu cannot promise. Devavrata renounces the throne and vows lifelong celibacy, earns the name Bhishma, and Santanu grants him the power to choose the time of his death.

Santanu marries Satyavati, and their sons Chitrangada and Vichitravirya are born, after which Santanu dies. Chitrangada is later slain in a battle with a Gandharva of the same name, and Bhishma crowns the young Vichitravirya, who obeys him.

Bhishma, acting for his half-brother Vichitravirya, carries off the three princesses of Kasi at their swayamvara, defeating the assembled kings and sparing the defeated Salya. He lets the eldest, Amba, go to the king she had loved, and marries Ambika and Ambalika to Vichitravirya, who dies of disease after seven years. Bhishma then arranges his funeral rites.

Satyavati, grieving for her son, asks Bhishma to raise children on his brother's widows to continue the line. Bhishma refuses, saying he will not give up his vow of truth, and that a Kshatriya must not break truth. He promises to suggest another remedy for the line's extinction.

To persuade Satyavati, Bhishma tells how Parashurama emptied the earth of Kshatriyas, and how Kshatriya women then bore children to Brahmanas. He recounts the story of Dirghatamas, born blind after Brihaspati ignored the unborn child's protest, who was later cast into the Ganges, rescued by King Vali, and fathered sons on Vali's wife and her nurse. Bhishma concludes that the Kshatriya line has often been continued by seed from Brahmanas.

Bhishma proposes that a Brahmana be paid to raise children on Vichitravirya's widows. Satyavati reveals that her son Vyasa, born to the sage Parashara before her marriage, can do it, and Bhishma approves. Vyasa agrees on condition that the women keep a year-long vow, and after Satyavati persuades one of the widows, the princess of Kosala, to accept him, the plan goes ahead.

The princess of Kosala, Vichitravirya's eldest widow, shuts her eyes in fear of Vyasa and bears a blind son, Dhritarashtra. Ambalika turns pale at his sight and bears Pandu, who is pale in complexion. A third widow sends a maidservant, who bears Vidura, a son who is wise and fortunate.

Janamejaya asks what the god of justice did to be cursed to be born in the Sudra caste, and by which Brahmana. Vaisampayana tells of the sage Mandavya, who sat silent under a tree while thieves hid their loot in his hermitage. The officers impaled him as a thief, and the sage survived, and other sages came to him in the form of birds to ask what sin he had committed.

Mandavya, still alive on the stake, forgives the king and is known from then on as Ani-Mandavya, the sage with the stake in him. He goes to the god of justice and asks what sin he committed, and the god says it was pricking an insect as a child. Mandavya rules that a child's offence is no sin, and curses the god of justice to be born a Sudra, which is how Vidura came to be born.

After the three sons are born, the Kuru land prospers in a golden age, with good harvests, honest people and a splendid capital. Bhishma raises Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura as his own sons, and each excels in a different art. Pandu becomes king, since Dhritarashtra is blind and Vidura is born of a Sudra woman, and Bhishma then turns to Vidura for counsel on family matters.

Bhishma proposes marriages for the Kuru princes, naming three noble maidens of pure blood, and Vidura defers to him. Bhishma hears that Gandhari, daughter of Suvala, has a boon of a hundred sons from Siva, and arranges her marriage to the blind Dhritarashtra. Gandhari blindfolds herself out of devotion to her husband, and her brother Sakuni brings her to Hastinapura, where she serves the family faithfully.

Pritha, the daughter of Sura, is given to Kuntibhoja, and Durvasa gives her a mantra to summon any god. Testing it as a maiden, she summons the Sun, who fathers Karna, and she abandons the child in the water. Karna is raised by Radha and her husband, and later gives his natural armour to Indra in disguise, earning the name Karna for cutting it away.

Pritha, now called Kunti, has no suitors, so her father holds an assembly at which she may choose her husband. She chooses Pandu, the Kuru prince, and they are married with the rites and return to Hastinapura.

Bhishma goes to Madra to seek Madri as a second wife for Pandu. King Salya explains his family custom, and Bhishma, accepting it, offers gifts that persuade Salya to give his sister. Pandu marries Madri, conquers many kingdoms, and returns to Hastinapura in triumph.

Pandu shares his conquest wealth with Bhishma, Satyavati and the others, and performs sacrifices with the money. He then retires with Kunti and Madri to the forests of the Himalaya to hunt, and is supplied with comforts at Dhritarashtra's command. Bhishma marries Vidura to Devaka's daughter, who is born of a Sudra wife, and they have many sons.

Gandhari, granted a boon of a hundred sons, goes two years without delivering and in grief strikes her womb, producing a lump of flesh. Vyasa divides it into a hundred and one parts, which grow in pots of butter. Duryodhana is born first, with ominous signs, and Dhritarashtra asks whether his son or the eldest Yudhishthira should be king, and Vidura advises casting off the first son, but Dhritarashtra refuses.

Janamejaya asks how Gandhari came to have a daughter, Duhsala, when Vyasa had divided the lump into only a hundred parts. Vaisampayana explains that Gandhari secretly wished for a daughter, and Vyasa set aside an extra part in its own pot, which became Duhsala. Vaisampayana then offers to tell more.

Janamejaya asks for the names of Dhritarashtra's sons in order of birth. Vaisampayana gives the long list of the hundred sons and names their one sister, Duhsala. He says they were all warriors and scholars, and that Duhsala was given in marriage to Jayadratha, king of Sindhu. This closes the account of the Kaurava side before the story turns to the Pandavas.

Janamejaya asks to hear about the Pandavas from their birth, now that he has heard the Kaurava names. Vaisampayana tells how Pandu, hunting in the Himavat woods, shoots a deer that is actually a sage, Kindama, while the sage is mating with his mate. The dying sage rebukes Pandu and curses him to die at the moment desire rises in him, with his wife following him to the land of the dead. This curse is the reason for Pandu's later renunciation.

After the curse, Pandu weeps and resolves to give up desire, children and worldly life for forest asceticism. His wives insist on going with him, and he sends word to the court that he has retired to the woods. He gives his wealth to Brahmanas, sends his attendants back to Hastinapura, and travels with his wives through the Himalayas toward Satasringa. The chapter begins the forest life of Pandu and his wives.

Pandu's austerities win him the regard of the Siddhas and sages, and when the sages set out for Brahma's gathering he asks to join them, though they warn that the northern heights are too dangerous for his wives. Pandu says a sonless man cannot reach heaven and that his debt to his ancestors remains unpaid. The sages foresee a blessed son, and Pandu urges Kunti to bear children by another man of high standing.

Kunti refuses to take any other man and asks Pandu to father children on her himself. To make her case she tells the old story of King Vyushitaswa, whose widow Bhadra, sonless and grieving, was promised offspring by a voice. The dead king's body is said to have fathered seven children on her, and Kunti urges Pandu to use his ascetic power the same way.

Pandu replies that in ancient times women moved freely and were not bound to one husband, and that the present rule of fidelity was set by Swetaketu out of anger. He cites other precedents, such as Madayanti bearing a son to Vasishtha, and says a wife must obey her husband's command to bear children. Kunti then reveals a mantra Durvasa gave her to summon a god, and Pandu tells her to call upon Dharma, the god of justice.

Kunti calls on Dharma, the god of justice, who fathers Yudhishthira, and then on Vayu, who fathers the strong Bhima. Pandu, wanting a greater son, undertakes a long austerity to win Indra, and Kunti's call to Indra brings forth Arjuna. The gods, sages and celestial singers gather to celebrate, but when Pandu asks for more children Kunti refuses, saying a fourth union is not sanctioned.

Madri asks Pandu for children of her own, and Pandu persuades Kunti to help. Kunti tells Madri to call a god, and Madri bears the twins Nakula and Sahadeva to the Ashvins. The five sons are named and grow up on the mountain, and Kunti later refuses further requests, complaining that Madri has used the mantra to gain twins.

Pandu, roaming a flowering grove with Madri, is overcome by desire, forces himself on her, and dies in the act, as the sage's curse had foretold. Kunti and Madri both claim the right to die with him, and Madri argues that she should be the one to follow him and asks Kunti to raise her sons. Madri then climbs onto the funeral pyre.

The sages on the mountain decide that Pandu's sons, left in their trust, must be taken to Hastinapura, and they set out with Kunti, the boys and the two bodies. At the gate, the court and citizens come out to greet them, and the eldest sage tells the Kurus how each son was born and asks for Pandu's rites to be performed. The sages then vanish from sight.

Dhritarashtra orders a royal funeral for Pandu and Madri, with gifts to all who ask and careful wrapping of Madri's body. Vidura and Bhishma prepare the rites, and the bodies are carried in procession to the Ganga, bathed, dressed and burned. After Kausalya collapses in grief, the Kurus perform the water rite, and the city mourns for twelve days with the Pandavas.

After Pandu's funeral rites are performed and the people return to Hastinapura, Vyasa warns his mother Satyavati that the age is declining, and she goes to the forest and ascends to heaven. Pandu's sons grow up strong, and Bhima outplays the Kaurava boys, which stirs Duryodhana's jealousy. Duryodhana then plots to drown Bhima, who survives the poisoning and the water and is restored among the serpents.

The Kauravas return to Hastinapura without Bhima, and Kunti, fearing that Duryodhana has killed him, asks for help. Vidura counsels her to protect her other sons, and after eight days Bhima wakes in the Naga realm, strengthened, and returns to his brothers. When Duryodhana tries poison again, Yuyutsu warns the Pandavas, and Dhritarashtra has all the princes taught arms by Kripa.

Janamejaya asks how Kripa was born and where he got his weapons. Vaisampayana explains that Gautama's son Saradwat was born skilled in arms, and that after a nymph sent by Indra distracted him, his seed fell on a clump of heath and produced twins. King Santanu adopted the twins, named Kripa and Kripi, and Saradwat later trained Kripa in arms.

Bhishma chooses Drona, son of Bharadwaja, to teach the princes, and they quickly master the arts of war. Vaisampayana explains Drona's birth from Bharadwaja's seed, which was caught in a vessel after he saw a nymph, and tells of Drona's marriage to Kripi and the birth of Aswatthaman. Drona then goes to Rama, Jamadagni's son, who gives away his wealth and his weapons to him.

Drona goes to his old boyhood friend Drupada, king of the Panchalas, and claims their friendship. Drupada, proud of his wealth, rebukes him and says that friendship cannot last between a rich man and a poor one. Drona, filled with anger, leaves for Hastinapura.

Drona lives quietly in Kripa's house, while his son Aswatthaman gives the Kuru princes some lessons. When the princes lose a ball in a well, Drona recovers it with blades of grass and then retrieves a ring with an arrow, and Bhishma recognises him. Drona explains how Drupada, once his boyhood friend, has scorned him, and Bhishma gives him the post of teacher to the princes.

Bhishma gives Drona a house and presents, and Drona takes the Kaurava and Pandava princes as pupils, with Arjuna the most devoted. Refused as a pupil, the tribal prince Ekalavya makes a clay image of Drona and becomes a fine archer on his own; when Drona later demands his right thumb as fee, Ekalavya gives it, and Arjuna is relieved. Drona then tests his pupils by having them aim at a mock bird, and each one reports seeing more than the target and is sent aside.

Drona tests the princes again, and only Arjuna, who sees just the vulture's head, hits the mark, which delights Drona. Later a crocodile seizes Drona in the Ganga, and Arjuna kills it with arrows. Drona then gives Arjuna the Brahmasira weapon, with a strict warning never to use it against a human, and promises that no bowman will surpass him.

Drona asks Dhritarashtra for permission to show the princes' skill in a public tournament, and the king agrees. The arena, stages and galleries are prepared, and on the day the crowd gathers to watch. The princes display archery, horsemanship and swordsmanship, and then Bhima and Duryodhana enter with maces.

The crowd splits between partisans of Duryodhana and of Bhima, and Drona has Aswatthaman restrain the two maces. Drona then presents Arjuna, whose feats with weapons, including conjured fire, water and mountains, delight the spectators and Dhritarashtra. Just as the show winds down, a thunderous sound comes from the gate, and Duryodhana rises with his brothers.

Karna enters the arena and matches Arjuna's feats, and Duryodhana embraces him as a friend. When Arjuna insults him, Karna challenges him, but Kripa asks Karna to name his lineage, since a prince fights only one of royal birth. Duryodhana then makes Karna king of Anga, and the two swear friendship.

Karna's foster father, the charioteer Adhiratha, enters the lists, and Karna bows to him as his father. Bhima mocks Karna as a charioteer's son, and Duryodhana rises to defend him by pointing to the obscure origins of heroes. The sun sets and the crowd disperses, with Kunti pleased to see her son honoured and Duryodhana reassured against Arjuna.

At Drona's demand, the princes attack Drupada's capital to seize him as the fee. After a fierce fight, Drupada is captured by Arjuna, who also stops Bhima from slaughtering the people, and the princes bring him to Drona. Drona humbles his old friend, grants him half his kingdom and asks for friendship, and Drupada, learning that Brahmanical power outmatches his own, begins searching for a son who can defeat Drona.

Dhritarashtra makes Yudhishthira heir apparent for his honesty and patience, and the Pandavas grow strong in their training, with Arjuna excelling in every weapon. Drona reminds Arjuna of the Brahmasira weapon and of his promised fee, and the Pandavas go on to conquer the Sauviras, the Yavanas and kings to the east and south. Dhritarashtra, seeing their power, grows uneasy and cannot sleep.

Dhritarashtra, jealous of the Pandavas' growing might, asks his counsellor Kanika whether he should make peace or war with them. Kanika advises ruthless statecraft: strike foes thoroughly, hide one's own weaknesses, use deceit, gifts and spies, and destroy an enemy's allies as well. He illustrates his advice with a fable of a jackal who tricks his companions out of a deer, and urges the king to act the same way toward the Pandavas.

Duryodhana, Karna and Sakuni, with Dhritarashtra's consent, plot to burn Kunti and her sons in a house of lac, but Vidura reads their intent and arranges a boat for escape. The Pandavas get away, a Nishada woman and her children burn in the house along with the architect Purochana, and the people are told the Pandavas have died. Back in the capital the citizens favour Yudhishthira as king, and Duryodhana, alarmed, presses his father to act before the kingdom passes to Pandu's line.

Duryodhana urges his father to send the Pandavas away to Varanavata. Dhritarashtra hesitates, since Pandu was virtuous and the elders would never sanction such an exile, but Duryodhana argues that Bhishma will stay neutral and that Drona and Kripa will side with his party. The chapter ends with Duryodhana pressing his father to act that very day.

Duryodhana wins the people over with gifts, and Dhritarashtra's councillors lure the Pandavas with tales of a festival of Shiva at Varanavata. Yudhishthira, aware that he is weak and friendless, accepts the king's command, and the elders bless him. The Pandavas then complete their preparations and set out.

Duryodhana, having sent the Pandavas to Varanavata, tells his counsellor Purochana to build a house of lac and inflammable material. Once the Pandavas and Kunti are asleep inside, Purochana is to set it alight so that the deaths look accidental. Purochana obeys and sets off at once.

The Pandavas take leave of Bhishma, Dhritarashtra, Drona, Kripa and Vidura, and citizens lament the injustice of their exile, but Yudhishthira asks them to go home. Vidura warns Yudhishthira in a language only the two of them understand that the house is a trap and that they should keep a way out in mind. Kunti asks what Vidura said, Yudhishthira explains the warning, and the Pandavas reach Varanavata.

The citizens of Varanavata welcome the Pandavas, and Purochana lodges them in the palace he has built. After a while Purochana shows them the house he calls the Blessed Home, and Yudhishthira realises it is a flammable trap set by Duryodhana, as Vidura had warned. Bhima wants to leave, but Yudhishthira counsels calm, disguise and a secret escape route.

A skilled miner sent by Vidura reveals himself to the Pandavas and warns that Purochana will set their house on fire. Yudhishthira trusts him, and the miner digs a secret passage under the house, covered with planks. The Pandavas keep up a show of contentment, sleeping armed and hunting by day, while preparing to escape.

After a year of apparent calm, Yudhishthira decides the time to escape has come. On a night when Kunti feeds Brahmanas and women, a Nishada woman and her sons sleep drunk inside the house. Bhima sets the house alight where Purochana sleeps, and the Pandavas and Kunti flee through the tunnel, with Bhima carrying them through the darkness.

Vidura's trusted agent finds the Pandavas and Kunti in the forest by the Ganga and shows them a sturdy boat, proving his loyalty by repeating Vidura's coded words. He ferries the family across the river, blesses their journey and goes home. The Pandavas send word back to Vidura and hurry on in secret.

At dawn the people of Varanavata find the ashes of the house, with Purochana dead, and blame Duryodhana for the plot. Dhritarashtra, told that the Pandavas have perished, mourns them and orders their funeral rites, while Vidura alone does not weep because he knows the truth. Meanwhile the fugitives cross the Ganga and struggle through a dense forest, until Yudhishthira asks Bhima to carry them on.

Bhima carries his mother and brothers through the forest and rivers until evening, when they reach a wild, waterless place. When Kunti cries out with thirst, Bhima finds a lake and brings water back, then sees his family asleep on the bare ground, laments their fall and rails at Dhritarashtra's sons. He sits up awake to keep watch over them.

A man-eating Rakshasa named Hidimva, perched in a sal tree nearby, smells the sleeping Pandavas and sends his sister to fetch them as food. Instead the Rakshasa woman falls in love with Bhima and offers to help him, and Bhima refuses to abandon his sleeping family. She offers to wake them and save them from her brother.

Hidimva comes down from his tree, sees his sister disguised as a human and infatuated with Bhima, and in rage rushes at her to kill her. Bhima stops him, defends her, and challenges Hidimva to a single combat. The two wrestle fiercely, and the noise wakes the Pandavas, who see Hidimva before them.

Kunti questions Hidimva, who explains that she was sent to kill the family but fell in love with Bhima, and that her brother has now come after them. The brothers wake to see Bhima wrestling the Rakshasa, and Arjuna urges him to finish quickly before dawn. Bhima kills Hidimva, and the family hurries off toward a town, with the Rakshasa woman following them.

Bhima threatens Hidimva's sister, but Yudhishthira forbids him to harm a woman. Hidimva humbly begs Kunti and Yudhishthira to let her marry Bhima, and Yudhishthira agrees on condition that she bring him back each night. After wandering the world with Hidimva, Bhima fathers a son, Ghatotkacha, who is bald and fierce but loyal to the Pandavas, and Hidimva and the boy take their leave.

The Pandavas wander through forests and lands of the Matsyas, Trigartas and Panchalas, living disguised as ascetics and studying the Vedas. They meet their grandfather Vyasa, who tells them their exile is for their good and not to grieve. He leads them to the town of Ekachakra and predicts that Yudhishthira will one day rule the earth, and then he departs.

At Ekachakra the Pandavas live on alms, which Kunti divides among them. One day, when only Bhima is at home with Kunti, they hear a Brahmana family lamenting, and Kunti resolves to help them. The Brahmana laments that he cannot escape the calamity or give up any of his family, and he is ready to die with them.

The Brahmana's wife tells him not to mourn, since all must die, and offers to go to the Rakshasa in his place. She argues that her husband's life and their children's future matter more, and that he may take another wife. The Brahmana embraces her, and the two weep together in silence.

The daughter asks her parents to give her up, arguing that her sacrifice can rescue the family and that she would otherwise be a helpless burden. The little son cheers them with a playful threat to slay the Rakshasa with a blade of grass. Kunti then steps forward, and her words revive the family as nectar revives the dead.

Kunti asks the Brahmana the cause of his grief and offers to remove it. He explains that the Rakshasa Vaka rules the region and is fed in turn by each household with a cart of rice, two buffaloes and a man, and that his family's turn has now come. He has no money to buy a substitute and sees no escape, so he plans to go to the Rakshasa with his whole family.

Kunti offers to send one of her five sons to the Rakshasa in the Brahmana's place, since his son and daughter are too young. The Brahmana refuses to let anyone die in his stead, saying he would rather die himself than sacrifice a Brahmana or a guest. Kunti assures him that her son Bhima is mighty enough to deliver the tribute and save himself, and Bhima agrees to go.

Bhima pledges to take on the task, and Yudhishthira, reading the matter from Bhima's face, asks his mother what has been arranged. Kunti explains that Bhima will go to save the Brahmana and the town. Yudhishthira objects that the plan is reckless and against the Vedas, and that the family depends on Bhima's strength, but Kunti answers that the Brahmana deserves repayment and that Bhima's might has already been proved.

Yudhishthira accepts that Kunti acted from compassion and trusts Bhima to win. That night Bhima carries the Rakshasa's tribute into the forest and eats it in full view of Vaka, who charges in fury. The two fight with trees and wrestle until Bhima bends Vaka double over his knee, and Vaka begins to vomit blood.

Bhima kills Vaka and makes the Rakshasa's kin promise to stop eating men, then leaves the body at the town gate. When the townspeople find it, the host Brahmana says a Brahmana skilled in mantras had taken the food to the forest and done the deed, which keeps the Pandavas hidden. The town marks the event with a festival honouring Brahmanas.

The Pandavas stay on at Ekachakra, and a visiting Brahmana tells them of distant lands, shrines and the wonders of Drupada's sacrifice, including the birth of Draupadi. The Pandavas ask for the full story of how Dhrishtadyumna and Draupadi were born and how Drona and Drupada became enemies. The Brahmana begins to recount Draupadi's birth.

The visiting Brahmana tells how Drona was born from Bharadwaja's seed in a pot and grew up as the boyhood friend of Drupada, son of Prishata. After Drona receives Rama's weapons, Drupada scorns his claim to friendship, and Drona later has the Pandavas capture Drupada as his fee. The humbled Drupada accepts Drona's terms and makes peace, but he never forgets the humiliation.

Drupada, bent on revenge, seeks a sacrifice that will give him a son to kill Drona. After Upayaja refuses, his brother Yaja, promised a large reward, performs the rite, and from the sacrificial fire come a son, Dhrishtadyumna, destined to slay Drona, and a dark, beautiful daughter, Krishna. An unseen voice foretells that Krishna will be the foremost of women and the cause of many Kshatriyas' deaths, and Drona trains Dhrishtadyumna in arms.

The Pandavas are deeply troubled by the Brahmana's tale. Kunti proposes that they leave Ekachakra, since they have seen all its sights and alms are harder to get, and suggests going to Panchala, where King Yajnasena is generous to Brahmanas. Yudhishthira agrees that they must obey, but wonders whether his younger brothers will want to go.

The Pandavas agree to Kunti's plan and leave Ekachakra for Panchala. Before they go, Vyasa visits them and tells of a maiden who, in a past life, prayed to Shiva for a husband and was promised five husbands, so that Draupadi, born in Drupada's line, is to be the wife of all five brothers. Vyasa bids them farewell and departs.

On the way to Panchala the Pandavas reach the Ganga, where the proud Gandharva Angaraparna bars their path, claiming the river at that hour belongs to the Gandharvas and the Rakshasas. Arjuna refuses to yield, and after a fiery weapon burns the Gandharva's chariot, he drags him away, but Yudhishthira spares him at his wife's plea. The grateful Gandharva offers Arjuna a science of illusion and a hundred swift horses, and explains that the Pandavas were rebuked for travelling at night without wives or a priest.

Arjuna asks why the Gandharva calls them Tapatyas, and the Gandharva explains through the story of Tapati, the Sun's daughter, whom no one in the three worlds equals in beauty. The Sun chooses King Samvarana, a devout worshipper, as her husband. When Samvarana's horse dies on a hunt in the hills, he sees Tapati and is struck with desire, and he asks who she is.

Tapati reappears and gently tells the king to rise, and he pours out his passion and begs her to accept him. She replies that she is under her father's control, so he must ask the Sun for her hand with worship and vows. She then names herself as the Sun's daughter and Savitri's younger sister.

Samvarana, revived by his minister, worships the Sun, and his priest Vasishtha asks the Sun for Tapati's hand on his behalf. The Sun consents, and the couple live together on the mountain for twelve years, until a long drought ravages the kingdom and Vasishtha brings the king home to end it. The Gandharva explains that Arjuna is called Tapatya because Samvarana's son Kuru was born of Tapati.

Moved by the story, Arjuna asks about Vasishtha. The Gandharva describes Vasishtha as Brahma's mind-born son and the family priest of Arjuna's forebears, whose ascetic power outmatched even Desire and Wrath. He urges the Pandavas to choose a learned Brahmana as their priest, since a Kshatriya needs one to conquer the earth.

The Gandharva tells the old feud between Vasishtha and the king Viswamitra, who coveted Vasishtha's wish-granting cow Nandini and offered a kingdom for her. When Viswamitra seized the cow, Nandini produced armies of barbarians from her body and routed his troops. Humbled, Viswamitra renounced his kingdom and set out to win Brahmanhood through austerity.

The Gandharva tells of King Kalmashapada, who strikes the sage Shakti, Vasishtha's eldest son, with a whip when neither will yield on a forest path, and is cursed to become a man-eating Rakshasa. Viswamitra, who had wanted the king as his disciple, secretly has a Rakshasa enter him, and the possessed king serves human flesh to a hungry Brahmana, earning a second curse. The king then kills and devours Shakti and his brothers, and Vasishtha, grief-stricken, tries again and again to end his life.

Vasishtha, bereft of his sons, tries to drown himself in rivers, but each current casts him ashore, and the rivers are renamed after his failed attempts. He learns from his daughter-in-law Adrisyanti that she is carrying a child by his son Shakti, and so he gives up his plan to die. He then frees the Rakshasa-possessed King Kalmashapada, who asks for a son to continue his line, and the queen eventually bears Asmaka after twelve years.

Adrisyanti bears a son, Parasara, whom Vasishtha raises as his grandson. When the boy calls Vasishtha father, his mother corrects him, and he resolves to destroy the world. To turn him from this, Vasishtha tells how the Kshatriyas slaughtered the Bhrigus after a hidden treasure was found, and how a Bhrigu woman's unborn son burst from her thigh to avenge them.

The Bhrigu woman tells the blinded Kshatriyas that her unborn son, held in her thigh for a hundred years, blinded them to avenge his slaughtered race, and that they must propitiate him. The thigh-born child, named Aurva, restores their sight, but he resolves to destroy the whole world in revenge. The Pitris come to beg him to restrain his wrath.

Aurva refuses to give up his vow, arguing that kings failed to protect the Bhrigus and that his anger must be satisfied. The Pitris advise him to cast the fire of his wrath into the waters, and he throws it into the ocean, where it becomes the horse-headed fire Vadavamukha that still consumes the sea. Vasishtha then urges Parasara to give up his own plan to destroy the world.

Parasara, persuaded to restrain his wrath toward the worlds, nevertheless begins a Rakshasa sacrifice to avenge his father Shakti, and Vasishtha does not stop him. The sages Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha and Kratu come to halt the rite, and Pulastya says Shakti brought his death on himself and that the Rakshasas are innocent. Parasara ends the sacrifice and casts its fire into the northern forest.

Arjuna asks why King Kalmashapada sent his queen to Vasishtha, and whether Vasishtha sinned in lying with her. The Gandharva explains that the cursed king devoured a Brahmana while his wife wept, and she cursed him to die when he approached his queen and to father a child on her by Vasishtha. Remembering the curse after his queen sent him away, the king repented and asked Vasishtha to beget an heir.

Arjuna asks the Gandharva which learned Brahmana would make a good priest, and the Gandharva names Dhaumya, who lives in a shrine called Utkochaka. Arjuna hands over his fire weapon, and the Gandharva keeps the horses until they are needed. The Pandavas install Dhaumya as their priest and set out for Drupada's Swayamvara.

The Pandavas set out for Panchala and meet Brahmanas bound for Drupada's Swayamvara, a great contest to win Draupadi. The Brahmanas describe the princess and the many kings expected, and invite the Pandavas to come along. Yudhishthira agrees to go with them.

The Pandavas meet Vyasa on the road and enter Panchala, lodging as mendicant Brahmanas in a potter's house, unknown to anyone. Drupada, who secretly hopes Arjuna will be his son-in-law, has a very stiff bow made and a mark set up above a machine, and proclaims that whoever strings the bow and shoots the mark will win his daughter. Kings, sages and crowds gather in a splendid amphitheatre, and on the sixteenth day Draupadi enters and her brother Dhrishtadyumna announces the contest.

Dhrishtadyumna names the many princes who have come to win his sister: Duryodhana and his brothers with Karna, Shakuni, Aswatthaman, a long roll of kings from many lands, and the Yadavas Krishna and Balarama, along with Jarasandha and Shishupala. He says these men will shoot the mark, and that Draupadi should choose whoever succeeds.

The princes rise in jealous desire for Draupadi, while the gods, sages and Yadavas watch and Krishna points out the Pandavas to Balarama. One by one the princes fail to string the stiff bow, and Karna succeeds in drawing it until Draupadi declares she will not choose a charioteer's son, so he sets the bow down. When Shishupala, Jarasandha and Shalya also fail, Arjuna steps forward to try.

When the other kings give up, Arjuna, disguised as a Brahmana, rises amid murmurs from the Brahmanas about a stripling's presumption. He bows to Shiva, strings the bow with ease, and shoots the mark through the machine, to the delight of the gods and the crowd. Krishna greets him with a garland, and Arjuna leaves the hall with Draupadi as his bride.

The rejected kings, angry that Drupada has given his daughter to a Brahmana, resolve to kill him and his son, since the Swayamvara was meant for Kshatriyas. They rush at Drupada, who takes shelter with the Brahmanas, but Bhima and Arjuna step forward to face them. Krishna names the brothers to Balarama and is glad that they escaped the house of lac.

Arjuna and Bhima stand up to the attacking kings: Arjuna duels Karna to a standstill, and Bhima hurls Shalya aside. Impressed, the kings ask who the Brahmanas are, and Krishna persuades them that the maiden was rightly won, so they withdraw. Meanwhile Kunti, anxious at her sons' delay, fears for their lives until Arjuna walks into the potter's house.

The brothers present Draupadi to Kunti as their alms, and Kunti, having told them to share everything, is alarmed. Yudhishthira proposes that Arjuna marry her, but Arjuna insists that the eldest should marry first. Seeing that all five desire her, Yudhishthira declares that Draupadi shall be the common wife of all five, and Krishna and Balarama then visit the potter's house.

Dhrishtadyumna secretly follows the Pandavas and hides in the potter's house. That night he overhears the brothers, while Kunti divides the food and they sleep on kusha grass with Draupadi at their feet. In the morning he reports all this to Drupada, who anxiously asks who has won his daughter.

Dhrishtadyumna tells his father Drupada how the archer won Krishna, and how the winners took refuge at a potter's house where their mother was waiting. Drupada sends his priest to ask who the strangers are, and Yudhishthira answers that the bride's price was paid fairly, so Drupada has no cause to grieve. A messenger then announces that the wedding feast is ready. The chapter sets up the revelation that the strangers are the Pandavas.

A messenger invites the group to the wedding feast, and they ride in golden-lotus chariots to Drupada's palace. Drupada lays out goods of many kinds to judge their caste, and the guests are seated and fed with honour. Their royal bearing and interest in the weapons convince Drupada and his son that they are of royal blood.

Drupada asks who the strangers are, and Yudhishthira reveals that they are Kshatriya sons of Pandu who escaped the lac house. Drupada is overjoyed, vows to help restore Yudhishthira to his throne, and asks Arjuna to take Krishna's hand. Yudhishthira then insists that Krishna be the wife of all five brothers, which Drupada resists, and the family is left to decide the matter when Vyasa arrives.

Vyasa arrives and is welcomed by all, then asks each person for their view of one woman marrying several men. Drupada and Dhrishtadyumna object on grounds of custom and the Vedas, while Yudhishthira cites old precedents and his mother's command. Kunti fears her word may be untrue, and Vyasa promises to explain the custom privately to Drupada, which sets up his defence of polyandry.

Vyasa tells Drupada a story to explain who the Pandavas really are. Yama stopped killing during a sacrifice, and after Indra is humbled by Mahadeva for his pride, he and four other Indras are sent to be born as men, with the goddess Sri as their common wife. Vyasa then identifies the brothers as those Indras and Draupadi as Sri, and grants Drupada divine sight to see them in their former forms.

Drupada accepts the story, saying fate and Mahadeva's decree have settled the matter, and gives his consent. Vyasa names an auspicious day, and the wedding goes ahead with Dhaumya presiding, Yudhishthira going first and the brothers taking Krishna's hand in turn. Drupada sends the couples off with cars, elephants, servants and wealth, and the Pandavas settle in his capital.

Drupada is pleased with the alliance and no longer fears even the gods. Kunti blesses Krishna, comparing her to famous wives of gods and heroes, and asks her to bear strong sons and rule as queen. Hari (Krishna) then sends the Pandavas costly gifts, including ornaments, robes, servants, elephants, horses and gold, which Yudhishthira accepts to please Govinda.

Word reaches the kings that Draupadi has married the Pandavas, that Arjuna won her in disguise, and that the brothers are alive after all. Duhsasana and the others return to Hastinapura dejected, and Dhritarashtra, first thinking his son has won her, then praises the Pandavas and their powerful allies. Vidura leaves, and Duryodhana and Karna urge their father to weaken the Pandavas before they overpower the Kauravas.

With Vidura gone, Dhritarashtra asks his son Duryodhana and Karna to speak openly about how to undo the Pandavas. Duryodhana lists a string of schemes: sowing discord among the brothers, buying off Drupada, luring them away from Panchala, turning Krishna against them, and having Bhima killed. He argues that time is short, because once the brothers win Drupada's trust they will be beyond reach.

Karna argues that Duryodhana's subtle plans cannot work, because the Pandavas are now grown, allied with Drupada, and bound together by their shared wife, and Krishna will not abandon them. He advises an open attack on Drupada before Krishna's Yadava forces arrive. Dhritarashtra praises his courage but wants the elders' advice, and he calls his ministers together.

Bhishma, asked for his opinion, says he will never approve of a quarrel with the Pandavas, who are as near to him as the Kauravas are. He argues that a good name is what keeps a man alive, and that the brothers' survival and Purochana's death should ease the king's reputation. He urges Duryodhana to give them half the kingdom.

Drona agrees with Bhishma and proposes sending a messenger with gifts to Drupada and the Pandavas, then bringing the brothers back to be installed on the throne. Karna mocks both elders as biased and tells the tale of the Magadha king Amvuvicha, whose minister seized power, to argue that kingship depends on fate. Drona rebukes Karna and warns that the Kurus will be destroyed if the good advice is not followed.

Vidura defends Bhishma and Drona as the king's best advisers and calls Karna's counsel malicious. He says the Pandavas are the king's sons as much as Duryodhana is, and argues that they cannot be beaten given their champions and allies. He urges peace with them and an alliance with Drupada, and warns against the counsel of Duryodhana, Karna and Sakuni.

Dhritarashtra accepts the elders' counsel, calls the Pandavas his children by ordinance, and orders them brought home with Kunti and Krishna. Vidura travels to Drupada with gifts, embraces the brothers and greets Vasudeva. He then delivers Dhritarashtra's message that the Kurus are glad of the alliance and ask the Pandavas to return to their ancestral kingdom.

Drupada agrees that the Pandavas may return to their ancestral kingdom if they and Rama and Krishna agree, and the brothers enter Hastinapura to a joyful welcome. Dhritarashtra sends them to Khandavaprastha with half the kingdom, where they build the great city of Indraprastha, which draws Brahmanas, merchants and craftsmen. Krishna then goes back to Dwaravati with Rama.

Janamejaya asks how the Pandavas governed their new kingdom and how they avoided quarrels while sharing one wife. Vaisampayana says they ruled Indraprastha in harmony until the sage Narada visited, honoured him, and warned them to make a rule about Draupadi. Narada cites the brothers Sunda and Upasunda, who killed each other over a woman, and Yudhishthira asks for the full story.

Narada tells the story of the Daitya brothers Sunda and Upasunda, sons of Nikumbha, who were inseparable. Through harsh penance in the Vindhya mountains they resist the gods' temptations and illusions, and Brahma refuses them immortality. He grants them invulnerability except from each other, and the brothers return home to a life of revelry.

Sunda and Upasunda set out with a great army to conquer the three worlds. They overrun heaven and the lower worlds, then turn on the Brahmanas and sacrificers, killing them and destroying sacred sites until ritual and life grind to a halt. They finally settle at Kurukshetra, without a rival.

Distressed by the slaughter, the gods and Rishis go to Brahma, who has Viswakarman create a captivating maiden, Tilottama, and send her to make the brothers quarrel over her. As she walks round the assembly, every eye turns to her, and Mahadeva grows extra faces and eyes to watch her. She departs for the Asuras' city, and the great god First Cause dismisses the gathering.

Narada tells how the Asura brothers, having conquered everything, grew idle and indulged in pleasure. On the Vindhya plateau both claim the apsara-like Tilottama, fight, and kill each other with their maces. Narada urges the Pandavas to make a rule about Draupadi, and they agree that whoever finds a brother with her must spend twelve years as a celibate forest-dweller.

The Pandavas rule well, and Draupadi delights in her five husbands. When robbers steal a Brahmana's cattle, Arjuna must enter the chamber where Yudhishthira is with Draupadi to fetch his weapons, which breaks the rule the brothers made. Yudhishthira says no fault attaches to a younger brother's entry, but Arjuna insists on keeping his vow and leaves for twelve years in the forest.

Arjuna sets out for the forest, followed for a distance by Brahmanas, ascetics and musicians. He journeys through forests, rivers and seas, admiring the scenery. At the source of the Ganga he decides to settle.

At the source of the Ganga, the Naga princess Ulupi drags Arjuna into the river and into her palace, and he agrees to yield to her in spite of his vow. She grants him invincibility in water. Arjuna then visits holy sites across the north, east and coast, and at Manipura he marries Chitrangada, daughter of King Chitravahana, whose son is to carry on the royal line.

Arjuna goes to the sacred waters on the southern ocean, which the ascetics shun because crocodiles lurk there and seize bathers. He bathes in the Saubhadra water, is seized by a crocodile, and drags it ashore. The crocodile turns into the Apsara Varga, who begins to explain that she and her companions were cursed after tempting a Brahmana.

Varga explains that the Brahmana pardoned her and her companions but fixed their punishment at a hundred years, after which a worthy man would free them, and that the waters would be called Nari-tirthas. Narada told them to seek Arjuna at the southern waters, and Arjuna frees all the Apsaras. He then returns to Manipura to see Chitrangada and their son Vabhruvahana, before going on to Gokarna.
