Arjuna tours the sacred places on the western shore and reaches Prabhasa, where Krishna comes to meet him. The two friends talk, feast and enjoy entertainments on Raivataka mountain, and then ride in a golden car to Dwaraka. The Yadava city turns out to welcome Arjuna, who takes up residence with Krishna.

A grand festival of the Vrishnis and Andhakas begins on Raivataka, with Haladhara (Valarama), Ugrasena, Satyaki and many others in attendance. Arjuna sees Bhadra, Vasudeva's daughter and Krishna's sister, and asks Krishna to help him win her. Krishna's side suggests carrying her off by force, which is praised for brave Kshatriyas, and messengers are sent to Yudhishthira, who consents.

Arjuna, with Krishna's assent, drives off in his golden car with Subhadra, and her attendants flee to Dwaraka to raise the alarm. The Vrishnis and Andhakas arm in anger, and Valadeva, wine-flushed, first tells them to wait for Krishna's word, then rages at Arjuna and vows to make the earth empty of Kauravas. The assembly roars its approval.

Vasudeva defends Arjuna's abduction of Subhadra as a proper form of marriage for a warrior, and the Vrishnis are persuaded to bring Arjuna back for a lawful wedding. Krishna and Balarama then come to Indraprastha with rich gifts, and Subhadra bears the son Abhimanyu. Draupadi bears five sons, one to each brother, and all are trained in arms by Arjuna and Dhaumya.

Yudhishthira rules Indraprastha so justly that his subjects, his brothers and other kings prosper in virtue. Arjuna proposes a summer outing on the Yamuna, and he and Krishna go with friends to a pleasant grove for feasting and revelry. While the two heroes talk apart, a radiant Brahmana approaches, and they rise to receive him.

Agni, in the guise of a hungry Brahmana, asks Arjuna and Krishna to help him burn the Khandava forest, which Indra protects because it shelters his friend, the Naga Takshaka. Vaisampayana then tells the story of King Swetaki, whose priests grew weary of his endless sacrifices and left him, and who won Rudra's help after a long penance. Agni fell ill from the butter he drank at that sacrifice, and he must now eat the creatures of Khandava to recover, but the forest's inhabitants put out his fire again and again.

Agni, still ill and frustrated, goes to Brahma, who explains that Arjuna and Vasudeva are the incarnations of the ancient gods Nara and Narayana, and points Agni to them for help. Agni asks them to aid him. Arjuna replies that he needs a worthy bow, inexhaustible quivers and a fitting car to hold back Indra's rain.

Agni calls on Varuna, who gives Arjuna the bow Gandiva, two inexhaustible quivers and a car with an ape banner drawn by white steeds. Agni gives Krishna a fiery discus, and Varuna adds a mace called Kaumodaki. Armed, the two heroes promise to help Agni, who then surrounds the forest with his flames.

Arjuna and Krishna take positions on opposite sides of the forest and cut down creatures trying to escape, while the fire kills others in agony. The gods go to Indra and ask whether the end of the world has come. Indra covers the sky with clouds, but the heat of the fire dries up the rain until he gathers a heavier downpour.

Arjuna blocks Indra's rain with a storm of arrows and his Vayavya weapon while Agni blazes on. When the young Naga Aswasena tries to escape by being swallowed by his mother, Arjuna beheads her, but Indra's wind stuns Arjuna and Aswasena gets away. The gods then join the battle with their weapons, and Arjuna and Krishna repel them, with Arjuna shattering a mountain-peak that Indra hurls at him.

Krishna's discus and Arjuna's arrows cut down the creatures of Khandava, and the gods retreat after an unseen voice tells Indra that Arjuna and Vasudeva are Nara and Narayana and that the forest's fate is sealed. Krishna and Arjuna spare the Asura Maya when he runs to Arjuna for protection, and Agni burns the forest for many days. Only six creatures survive: Aswasena, Maya and four Sarngaka birds.

Janamejaya asks why the Sarngaka birds survived the fire, and Vaisampayana tells how the ascetic Mandapala, refused entry to the realm of the Pitris for want of children, took the form of a Sarngaka and fathered four sons. When he saw Agni coming to burn Khandava, he praised the god at length and asked him to spare his unhatched sons. Agni agreed.

As the fire closes in, the mother bird Jarita weeps, unable to save all of her unfledged chicks. Her young urge her to save herself, since she can have other children, and she suggests hiding them in a mouse's hole until the fire passes. The chicks refuse, arguing that being eaten by the mouse would be more shameful than dying in the fire.

Jarita tells her sons that a hawk has carried off the mouse, so the hole is now safe. The chicks doubt her, pointing out that other mice may remain, and urge her to save herself so she can have other children. She insists she saw the hawk take the mouse, but they still refuse, and she leaves them as the fire closes in.

The four sons of Mandapala speak their last words before the fire reaches them. Jaritari says the wise remain awake facing death, and the others speak of the eldest's duty to protect them and of the fire's threat. Each then sings a hymn of praise to Agni, asking the god to spare them, and Agni agrees to do so, remembering his promise to their father.

Mandapala frets about his sons, and his second wife Lapita answers jealously that he cares more for her rival Jarita. Mandapala replies that he sought children for their sake and leaves Lapita to go her own way. When he reaches the sons, they greet him coldly, and Jarita quarrels with him over Lapita, until he cites the story of Arundhati and the sons finally come forward to worship him.

Mandapala tells his sons that he delayed out of trust in Agni's promise and in their own strength, and asks them to bear no resentment. Agni, having consumed Khandava with Krishna and Arjuna's help and drunk its fat and marrow, shows himself to Arjuna, and Indra offers the heroes boons. Arjuna asks for Indra's weapons and Krishna asks for eternal friendship, and the three then rest on a riverbank.

Maya, a Danava craftsman whom Arjuna has just saved from fire and flood, offers to repay him. Arjuna declines and redirects the offer to Krishna, who asks Maya to build a grand assembly hall for Yudhishthira. Maya is welcomed by Yudhishthira, lays out a large site and begins the work, setting up the palace that will house the Pandavas' court.

Krishna, after staying a while at Khandavaprastha, decides to visit his father in Dwaraka. He takes leave of the Pandavas, Kunti, Subhadra, Draupadi and Dhaumya, and rides out with the brothers and priests following on foot. Krishna reaches Dwaraka, where he is welcomed by his family and the Yadavas, while Yudhishthira returns to his own capital.

Maya leaves Arjuna, promising to return with treasures he had earlier gathered in the north: a great club, the conch Devadatta and a store of gems. He recovers them at the lake Vindu near Mount Kailasa, a sacred site linked to Bhagiratha, Indra and Shiva. He then builds a magnificent palace with gold columns and a crystal-stepped tank, guarded by Rakshasas, and reports its completion to Yudhishthira within fourteen months.

Yudhishthira formally enters the new hall after feeding ten thousand Brahmins and giving them cows, and the day is celebrated with music and entertainments. A long list of sages, Kshatriya kings and Vrishni princes take their seats there and wait on him, and Gandharvas and Kinnaras sing for the assembly. The chapter sets the scene for the court that gathers in the new hall.

The sage Narada arrives at the assembly of the Pandavas, is honoured with a seat and gifts, and blesses Yudhishthira. He then questions the king at length about how he governs: his wealth, officials, spies, army, finances, agriculture, justice and personal discipline. Yudhishthira promises to follow this counsel, and Narada says such a ruler gains the whole earth and goes to heaven. The chapter presents Narada's counsel as the model of good kingship.

After Yudhishthira answers Narada's questions, he asks whether Narada has ever seen an assembly hall finer than his own. Narada says he has not seen one made of gems, but offers to describe the halls of the gods Yama, Varuna, Indra, Kuvera and Brahma. Yudhishthira asks for full details of each hall, which sets up the description of divine assemblies that follows.

Narada describes Indra's assembly hall, called Pushkaramalini, which Indra built as the reward of his own deeds. It is huge, bright and free of age and grief, and Indra sits there with his wife Sachi while gods, sages, musicians and celestial beings attend him. Narada says he has seen this hall and turns next to the hall of Yama.

Narada describes the assembly hall of Yama, the god of death, which Viswakarma built. The hall is free of grief, hunger, thirst and old age, and it is filled with dead royal and Brahmana sages who worship Yama. Narada says the crowd is too large to name in full, and he moves on to describe the hall of Varuna.

Narada describes Varuna's hall, which Viswakarma built beneath the waters and which has white walls and gem trees. Varuna sits there with his queen, served by the Adityas, serpents, Daityas, Danavas, personified rivers and seas, and mountains. Narada then moves on to describe the hall of Kuvera.

Narada describes the assembly hall of Vaisravana, that is Kuvera, which Kuvera built through his own asceticism. The hall seems to float in the sky, and Kuvera sits there with his thousand wives, served by Apsaras, Gandharvas, Yakshas and many others, along with the goddess Lakshmi and Kuvera's son. Narada notes that Shiva is a friend of Kuvera and often sits in the hall, and then announces a description of Brahma's hall.

Narada describes Brahma's assembly hall, which he was able to see only after the sun god Aditya guided him there following a thousand-year vow. The hall is beyond description, free of hunger and discomfort, and attended by sages, gods, planets, goddesses, ancestors and countless other beings. Narada ends his tour of the divine halls by declaring Yudhishthira's hall the finest in the world of men.

Yudhishthira asks why Narada named only one human king, Harishchandra, among the gods in Indra's hall, and what he did to earn that place. Narada explains that Harishchandra won heaven by holding the Rajasuya sacrifice with lavish gifts, and he passes on Pandu's message urging Yudhishthira to hold the same sacrifice, while warning of its dangers. Narada then departs, and Yudhishthira turns his mind to the Rajasuya.

Yudhishthira, stirred by Harishchandra's example, resolves to hold the Rajasuya but wants to be sure it serves his people. His ministers and priests urge him to proceed, and he weighs his own strength and resources. Because he wants a disinterested judge, he sends for Krishna, who arrives at Indraprastha, and Yudhishthira asks for his honest counsel.

Krishna explains why the Rajasuya cannot yet be held: Jarasandha of Magadha has made himself the dominant power over the kings, many of whom side with him or fear him. He recounts how Jarasandha drove the Yadavas out of Mathura, how the Yadavas founded a fortified city in the west, and how Jarasandha has imprisoned kings meaning to sacrifice them. Krishna concludes that the sacrifice cannot succeed unless Jarasandha is defeated and his captives freed, and he asks Yudhishthira to decide.

Yudhishthira admits he is troubled by Jarasandha's power and doubts that the Rajasuya is worth the risk. Bhima answers that a weak king who starts a fight with a strong one perishes, but that Krishna's policy, his own strength and Arjuna's triumphs can bring Jarasandha down. Krishna argues that Jarasandha has already taken eighty-six kings and plans to make the number a hundred, so the fight must be taken up.

Yudhishthira, fearing for Krishna, Bhima and Arjuna, asks that the plan to attack Jarasandha be dropped. Arjuna replies that courage and action, not fear, are what make a king worthy, and he insists that the Pandavas must fight. The chapter sets up the decision to challenge Jarasandha despite the king's reluctance.

Krishna argues that a warrior must fight, and that a secret attack on Jarasandha, who is too strong to face openly, is justified. Yudhishthira asks who Jarasandha is, and Krishna tells his origin: the childless King Vrihadratha of Magadha receives a mango from a sage, his two wives each bear half a child, and a Rakshasa woman named Jara joins the halves into one strong boy. The story explains how Jarasandha came to be so powerful.

Jara reveals herself as a Rakshasa woman who is also the household goddess Grihadevi, and says she gave the child to the king because she was pleased by the worship she received in his house. The king holds the rites of infancy for the boy and names him Jarasandha, meaning united by Jara, after which the boy grows strong.

The sage Chanda-kausika returns and foretells that Jarasandha will become a mighty king whom no weapon can wound and who will see Shiva. Krishna says Hansa, Dimvaka and Kansa are dead, so the time has come to destroy Jarasandha, and he proposes a bare-armed duel in which Bhima will fight. The three set out in disguise as Snataka Brahmanas and travel east toward Magadha.

Jarasandha denies that he has ever wronged the three visitors, but Krishna accuses him of holding many kings captive to be sacrificed to Rudra. Krishna asks Jarasandha which of the three he will fight, and Jarasandha chooses Bhima. Bhima, urged on by Krishna, whirls Jarasandha in the air and breaks his body across his knee, killing him. Krishna frees the imprisoned kings, takes Jarasandha's celestial chariot, and the freed kings pledge to support Yudhishthira's Rajasuya. Krishna installs Jarasandha's son Sahadeva as king of Magadha, returns to Indraprastha, and then takes leave of the family and goes home to Dwarka.

Arjuna asks Yudhishthira for leave to conquer the quarters of the world and collect tribute, so the treasury can be filled, beginning with the northern region of the lord of wealth. The chapter shows the scale of the northern tribute that Arjuna gathers for Yudhishthira.

Arjuna crosses the White Mountains and subdues the Limpurushas and the Guhakas, admiring sacred lakes on the way. He returns with horses, treasure and celestial goods and gives it all to Yudhishthira, who rests in his chambers.

With Yudhishthira's consent, Bhima marches east with a large army and wins over the Panchalas, Gandakas, Videhas and Dasarnas. Yudhishthira's rule has made his kingdom prosperous and his treasury full, and his advisers urge him to hold the Rajasuya sacrifice. Yudhishthira asks the elders to help with the sacrifice and gives each of them a duty, from food and gifts to tribute and treasure. Krishna takes the humble task of washing the feet of the Brahmanas. The chapter adds to Duryodhana's resentment at the Pandavas' rising power.

Sakuni offers to win Yudhishthira's wealth at dice, and Duryodhana presses his father to allow it. Vidura objects to his brother's order, warning that the match will split the sons of Dhritarashtra and destroy the family. Dhritarashtra replies that the world moves under fate, and sends Vidura to bring Yudhishthira. The chapter closes the first step toward the fatal match.

Vidura, sent by Dhritarashtra against his own judgment, goes to Indraprastha and delivers the invitation to a dice match at Hastinapura. Yudhishthira asks who the cheats are, and Vidura names Sakuni and other gamblers, but Yudhishthira says he will play only if summoned, since fate governs all. He sets out with his brothers and Draupadi, is greeted warmly by the Kauravas, and spends a night of revelry before the match.

The Pandavas enter the assembly hall, and Sakuni calls for the dice to be cast. Yudhishthira objects that deceitful gambling is sinful, but Sakuni argues that every contest aims at victory. The kings take their places in the hall, and the match begins. Yudhishthira stakes a precious pearl necklace from the churning of the ocean, and Duryodhana replies that he has great wealth to offer. Sakuni casts the dice and claims the first win.

Yudhishthira keeps staking his riches, from his gold and treasure to chariots, serving-girls, servants, elephants, horses, warriors and jewels, and Sakuni claims each stake in turn. Yudhishthira protests that the wins are unfair but keeps playing. The chapter shows the match growing into a steady loss for the Pandavas.

During the match Vidura warns Dhritarashtra that Duryodhana, who cried like a jackal from birth, will bring ruin on the family. He warns that the Yadavas once rid themselves of a bad son for the good of the whole, and suggests that war with the Pandavas would be disastrous.

Vidura continues his plea that gambling sows dissension and that Duryodhana's intoxication will drive away the family's luck. He calls on Sakuni to go home and urges the king to avoid war with the sons of Pandu.

Duryodhana rounds on Vidura, accusing him of favouring the Pandavas, of speaking harsh words, and of being a parasite who should leave the king's service. Vidura answers that a king who casts off honest counsellors is like a child who quarrels with his friend, and that a man who turns on his wise advisers invites ruin. He then bows to Dhritarashtra and takes his leave, marking a sharp split in the court.

Sakuni keeps pressing Yudhishthira for more stakes, and Yudhishthira stakes his wealth, lands and people, then his brothers one by one, then himself, and finally Draupadi. Sakuni wins each stake in turn. The elders cry out in horror, Vidura sits in grief, Dhritarashtra keeps asking whether the stake has been won, and Karna and Dussasana laugh.

Duryodhana orders Vidura to bring Draupadi into the hall and make her a servant. Vidura warns him sharply that he is tying himself in cords and courting ruin, and argues that Draupadi cannot be enslaved, since Yudhishthira had already lost himself before staking her. He ends with the fable of the goat that swallowed a hook, urging Duryodhana not to swallow the Pandavas' wealth or make them enemies.

Duryodhana sends a messenger to bring Draupadi into the assembly. The chapter is the moral low point of the match and sets up the vows of vengeance that follow.

Draupadi, dragged before the assembly, appeals to the Kurus, recalling that she was seen by the kings only once, at her swayamvara, and asking whether she is a wife or a servant. She challenges the elders to say whether she was won or not, and accepts their verdict. Bhishma replies that dharma is too subtle for him to settle, that the Kurus are ruined by greed and folly, and that Yudhishthira alone can say whether she was won.

Duryodhana taunts Draupadi, telling her that her husbands should answer her question and that Yudhishthira should declare that he is not their lord. Yudhishthira bows to Dhritarashtra and asks for his command. The old king tells him to forget Duryodhana's insults, to return to Indraprastha with his wealth, and to keep to the path of peace and brotherly love. The Pandavas leave with Draupadi for their city.

A royal messenger catches up with Yudhishthira, who has gone some distance, and brings Dhritarashtra's summons back to the dice. Yudhishthira accepts, saying fate rules and he cannot refuse the old king, though he knows the match will ruin him. The defeated Pandavas put on deer-skins, and Dussasana gloats, mocking them and urging Draupadi to choose another husband. After the Pandavas go into the forest, Dhritarashtra is restless, and Sanjaya asks why he grieves now that he has the whole earth. The Pandavas leave Hastinapura after losing at dice, with Draupadi and their attendants, heading north. Citizens angry at Duryodhana and his allies follow them out and beg to go along. Yudhishthira answers that he wants wealth only to support Brahmanas and guests, and Saunaka closes with advice on duty and austerity.

Yudhishthira asks his priest Dhaumya what to do about the Brahmanas who follow him into exile and whom he cannot feed. Dhaumya teaches that the sun sustains all creatures and urges him to worship Surya. Yudhishthira sings a hymn of praise in the Ganges, and the sun grants him an inexhaustible food supply and promises his kingdom back after fourteen years. The Pandavas move through holy places to the Kamyaka forest on the Saraswati, where Munis visit them. Vidura arrives alone, and Yudhishthira, fearing a new dice challenge, asks what he has come for. He applies the lesson to the Kurus and urges Duryodhana to make peace with the Pandavas.

Dhritarashtra asks Vyasa's help, and the sage Maitreya arrives, having seen Yudhishthira at Kamyaka. Maitreya urges Duryodhana to make peace, citing Bhima's feats against Rakshasas and Jarasandha. Duryodhana sneers in silence, so Maitreya curses him that Bhima will break his thigh in the coming war. Maitreya then refuses to say more, sending Dhritarashtra to Vidura for the story of Kirmira.

Dhritarashtra asks Vidura how Bhima killed the Rakshasa Kirmira. Vidura describes how Kirmira, brother of Vaka, blocked the Pandavas at midnight in Kamyaka forest with illusions and vowed to devour Bhima. Bhima fought him with a tree and then wrestled him to death, and the Pandavas moved on to the Dwaita woods. Dhritarashtra sighs and falls into thought at the tale.

Hearing of the Pandavas' exile, Krishna and many allies visit them in the forest, and Krishna vows that the Kauravas will die and Yudhishthira will be restored. Arjuna calms him by recounting Krishna's divine deeds, and Krishna replies that he and Arjuna are one. Draupadi then weeps and recounts the insult in the assembly and the Kauravas' earlier plots, and Dhrishtadyumna and Krishna vow revenge. The chapter turns the exile into a political and personal grievance that the allies take up.

Krishna tells Yudhishthira that had he been at Dwaraka, he would have prevented the dice game by warning of its evils and, if need be, by force. He explains that he learned of the disaster from Yuyudhana and came as fast as he could. He grieves that the brothers now suffer and that he has come to see them.

Yudhishthira asks Krishna where he was while away from Dwaraka. Krishna explains that Salwa, avenging Sisupala, whom Krishna killed at the Rajasuya sacrifice, raided the empty city and killed many young Vrishnis. Krishna chased him to an island in the ocean, and returned to Hastinapura only after hearing of the dice game. The chapter explains why Krishna was absent when the Pandavas needed him.

Yudhishthira asks Krishna to tell him fully how Salwa was slain. Krishna begins with Salwa's siege of Dwaraka and describes the city's preparations in detail. The walls, traps, weapons, watchmen and rules against drinking show how the Vrishnis readied for the attack.

Salwa's army marches on Dwaraka and the young Vrishni princes sally out to meet it. Samva drives off Salwa's commander Kshemavriddhi and kills the demon Vegavat, and Charudeshna kills the demon Vivindhya. Salwa returns to the field in force, and Pradyumna steps forward to rally the Yadavas.

Pradyumna mounts his golden chariot and rides against Salwa, who comes down from his own chariot to fight him. Salwa is struck to the heart by an arrow and falls senseless. He recovers, however, and badly wounds Pradyumna, leaving him insensible on the field.

Pradyumna is carried off the field, senseless, by his charioteer, the son of Daruka. When he wakes, he scolds the charioteer for retreating and orders him to turn back. He insists that a Vrishni warrior never flees, and that the shame of running would be worse than death.

The charioteer answers that he retreated only to protect the wounded warrior, and he now drives back into the enemy host with great skill. Pradyumna again wounds Salwa, who falls senseless. The gods send Narada and the wind god to stop Pradyumna from killing Salwa, since Salwa is fated to die at Krishna's hand, and Salwa flees across the sky.

Krishna, here also called Vasudeva, returns to Dwaraka after the Rajasuya and finds the city mourning Salwa's raid. He vows to kill Salwa, sets out with his army, and follows him to the ocean. There a long battle of arrows and illusions begins, which Krishna meets with counter-illusions and a powerful weapon.

Salwa keeps up his attack, and Krishna's charioteer Daruka is badly wounded. A messenger from Ahuka brings the false report that Salwa has killed Krishna's father Vasudeva in Dwaraka. Krishna is stunned, seeing an illusion of his father falling, and swoons before recovering to fight on.

Krishna fights through Salwa's illusions, including a shower of rocks that buries him, and breaks free with the thunderbolt. Daruka urges him to finish Salwa, and Krishna hurls the Sudarsana discus, which destroys the city of Saubha and Salwa himself. Krishna then takes leave of the Pandavas and returns to Dwaraka, while the allies and Brahmanas go their separate ways.

The Pandavas set out into the forest after giving gifts to Brahmanas, and the people of Kurujangala come to bid them farewell. They lament the king's exile and blame Duryodhana, Dussasana, Karna and Sakuni. Arjuna asks the Brahmanas to plead the Pandavas' cause with the ascetics, and the people go home with heavy hearts.

Yudhishthira tells his brothers they must spend the next twelve years in the forest and asks them to find a suitable place. Arjuna suggests the lake of Dwaitavana, rich in flowers and birds, and Yudhishthira agrees. The Pandavas and their Brahmana companions enter the forest and sit down at the foot of a great tree, welcomed by ascetics.

The Pandavas settle in the Dwaita woods, where Dhaumya performs sacrifices and Yudhishthira honours the ascetics. The sage Markandeya visits and, seeing their plight, recalls Rama's exile. He urges Yudhishthira that no one should act wrongly out of pride in his own might, and predicts that Yudhishthira will win back his fortune. The sage then departs to the north.

The Dwaita woods fill with Brahmanas performing rites, and Vaka of the Dalvya line counsels Yudhishthira that Kshatriya strength needs Brahmanical wisdom. He cites the fall of the demon king Vali, who wronged the Brahmanas, and urges Yudhishthira to keep a learned Brahmana as an adviser. The assembled sages then honour Yudhishthira for his respect towards the Brahmanas.

Draupadi sits with the Pandavas in the forest and grieves for their lost splendour, contrasting their former luxuries with their present hardship. She notes that only four men, Duryodhana, Karna, Sakuni and Dussasana, did not weep at their exile. She asks why Yudhishthira's anger does not blaze up against the Kauravas, and urges him to act, since a Kshatriya who fails to strike back is despised.

Draupadi argues that Yudhishthira should now use his might, citing the old tale of Prahlada's counsel to his grandson Vali. Prahlada teaches that neither constant forgiveness nor constant anger is right, and that the wise must act according to time and place. Draupadi concludes that forgiveness is wasted on the Kauravas and that the time has come for action.

Yudhishthira replies at length that anger destroys people, and that a wise man, strong or weak, should conquer wrath and forgive. He cites Kasyapa's praise of forgiveness and argues that the elders will press for peace, so the kingdom may be returned. He concludes that Duryodhana does not deserve the kingdom and that he himself will hold to forgiveness.

Draupadi challenges Yudhishthira, arguing that virtue has not protected him despite his generosity and great sacrifices, and that he gambled everything away in an evil hour. She argues that God directs all creatures like puppets and then asks how a just God lets the wicked prosper. She ends by asking whether human might, rather than God, is the true cause of action.

Yudhishthira answers Draupadi that he acts out of duty and not for the fruit of his acts, and that doubting virtue is a grave fault. He cites the sages, including Markandeya, who gained lasting merit through virtue, and says that a doubter loses both this world and the next. He urges her to put aside doubt, have faith in God, and honour the Vedas.

Draupadi replies that she has never scorned religion or God, and that her words are the lament of a grieving woman. She argues that every living creature must act, that fate and chance alone bring only ruin, and that human effort, guided by intelligence and by the fruits of past deeds, is the cause of success. She ends by saying that a person must act with confidence and not despair when results are slow, and recalls the teaching she received as a child.

Bhima, angry at the forest life, urges Yudhishthira to give up his pledge and take back the kingdom by force. He says the kingdom was won by Duryodhana's unfair dice and that the Pandavas' patience has only made them look weak. He argues at length that virtue, wealth and pleasure must be pursued together, and that a Kshatriya's duty is to fight with might and stratagem.

Yudhishthira accepts Bhima's anger but explains that Sakuni's trickery won the dice game and that the agreed terms made them exiles for twelve years and a thirteenth year in disguise. He says that breaking a sworn pledge is worse than death, and that the Pandavas must wait for their chance to avenge the wrong. He also reminds Bhima that he once wanted to burn Yudhishthira's hands during the game and was stopped by Arjuna.

Bhima presses Yudhishthira to act at once, arguing that life is short and that waiting thirteen years only brings death closer. He says the Pandavas will be discovered by spies and by the kings they have wronged, and that thirteen months in the forest should be counted as thirteen years. He calls on Yudhishthira to fight, since battle is the Kshatriya's duty.

Yudhishthira weighs Bhima's counsel and warns that rash action will fail against the Kaurava champions and their allied kings. Vyasa arrives, promises to dispel Yudhishthira's fear, and teaches him a sacred science, advising Arjuna to seek weapons from the gods. The Pandavas then leave Dwaitavana for Kamyaka and resume their forest life.

Yudhishthira privately tells Arjuna that Duryodhana's side has the best teachers and weapons, and sends him north to win celestial arms from Indra. He passes on Vyasa's science and sends Arjuna off with blessings from his brothers, Krishna and Draupadi. On the Himalayas, Arjuna is tested by a figure who turns out to be Indra, who urges him to seek the sight of Shiva before he can receive the weapons.

Janamejaya asks for the full tale of how Arjuna won weapons and fought Shiva. Arjuna enters the Himalayan forest and practises harsh austerities, eating less and less until he stands on his toes and lives on air alone. Alarmed by the heat of his penance, the sages go to Shiva, who says he knows Arjuna's wish and will grant it.

Shiva comes to the Himalayas disguised as a Kirata hunter, with Uma and a band of attendants, just as a demon in boar form attacks Arjuna. Both Arjuna and the hunter shoot the boar and quarrel over it, and their duel becomes fierce. Arjuna's weapons fail, the hunter's blows leave him senseless, and Arjuna recovers, makes a clay image of the god, and finds his garland on the hunter's head. Shiva then reveals himself, pardons him and promises a weapon.

Shiva tells Arjuna that he was Nara, the friend of Narayana, and returns the Gandiva bow and inexhaustible quivers that he had taken from him by illusion. Arjuna asks for the Brahmasira weapon so he can win the coming war against Karna, Bhishma, Kripa and Drona. Shiva gives him the Pasupata weapon, warns that it must be used only against a worthy foe, and teaches him its mysteries before departing with Uma.

After Shiva vanishes, the guardians of the world, Varuna, Kubera, Yama and Indra, come to the mountain to see Arjuna. Each gives him a celestial weapon, and Indra promises to take him to heaven to receive his full arms. Arjuna worships the gods, who depart, and he feels that his purpose is fulfilled.

Indra sends his chariot, driven by Matali, to bring Arjuna up to heaven to receive the celestial weapons. Arjuna insists that Matali mount first, bids farewell to Mount Mandara, and rides up through the realms of the virtuous and the heroic dead. He reaches Amaravati, the city of Indra.

Arjuna enters Amaravati, a city of flowers and celestial gardens reserved for the virtuous, and is welcomed by the gods, Gandharvas and sages. Indra embraces him and seats him on his own throne, delighting in his son's splendour while heavenly dancers perform.

Arjuna stays in Indra's palace for five years, receiving the thunderbolt and other celestial weapons. Indra then sends him to learn celestial music and dance from the Gandharva Chitrasena. Arjuna's mind stays restless, troubled by thoughts of his brothers, his mother and the unfair dice game.

Indra notices that Arjuna has looked at the Apsara Urvasi, and sends Chitrasena to ask her to attend Arjuna and teach him the arts of female company. Chitrasena praises Arjuna's virtues in the message, and Urvasi replies that she is already drawn to him and will go to him.

Urvasi dresses richly and goes to Arjuna's palace at night, desiring him. Arjuna honours her as a superior and refuses her advances, calling her like his mother. Urvasi, enraged, curses him to live among women as a dancer, without manhood, for a year. Indra tells Arjuna the curse will serve him in the thirteenth year of exile, when the brothers must remain unknown, and Arjuna is relieved and sports in heaven.

The sage Lomasa visits Indra's heaven and is puzzled to see Arjuna seated beside Indra. Indra explains that Arjuna is his son, that Nara and Narayana have been reborn on earth, and that the demons called Nivatakavachas threaten the gods. He sends Lomasa to Yudhishthira with a message urging him to visit sacred waters and to be guarded against demons on the road.

Janamejaya asks how Dhritarashtra reacted to news of Arjuna's feats. Dhritarashtra, having heard from Vyasa, tells Sanjaya that his sons cannot stand against Arjuna, and he foresees a terrible war that may end the Kuru line. He fears that Arjuna's anger, with Krishna as his ally, will be impossible to calm.

Sanjaya replies that Dhritarashtra's words are true, that the Pandavas are full of rage over Draupadi's humiliation, and that Arjuna has won the favour of the gods, even fighting Shiva as a hunter. He repeats Bhima's vow to smash Duryodhana's thighs. Dhritarashtra laments Karna's cruel words and his sons' folly, and admits that Arjuna, with Krishna as his ally, cannot be conquered.

Janamejaya asks what food the Pandavas lived on in the forest. Vaisampayana says they hunted deer and fed the Brahmanas first, and that Yudhishthira supported thousands of Snataka Brahmanas. Draupadi fed her husbands and the Brahmanas before eating herself, and the brothers spent five years at Kamyaka, anxious for Arjuna's absence yet busy with study and sacrifice.

Dhritarashtra, hearing of the Pandavas' hardy life, is filled with fear and lists their strength, predicting that his army will be destroyed. Sanjaya replies that Krishna visited the forest and promised to restore Yudhishthira and slay Duryodhana and his allies when the exile ends. Dhritarashtra recalls Vidura's warning that the dice game would lead to bloodshed among the Kurus, and fears it is coming true.

Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did while Arjuna was away. Bhima urges Yudhishthira to leave the forest and attack the Kauravas before the term ends, arguing that deceit may be met with deceit and that the thirteen years may be counted loosely. Yudhishthira refuses to break his word, and when he laments his wretched state, the sage Vrihadaswa offers the tale of King Nala, who suffered even more.

Vrihadaswa describes Nala as a virtuous and skilled king of the Nishadhas, and Bhima, king of Vidarbha, who through a sage's boon has a daughter, Damayanti, and three sons. Damayanti is unmatched in beauty, and Nala is peerless too. Hearing of each other from bards, they fall in love, and Nala catches a golden swan that promises to praise him to Damayanti.

Damayanti pines for Nala, and her father Bhima announces a swayamvara, a ceremony at which a bride chooses her husband, inviting all kings. The sages Narada and Parvata tell Indra about the ceremony in heaven. The gods set out for Vidarbha, and on the road they meet Nala, dazzled by his beauty, and ask him to act as their messenger.

Nala agrees to carry the gods' message, reluctantly, and they reveal themselves as Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama. The gods ask him to tell Damayanti to choose one of them as husband. Nala enters the guarded palace by their power and finds Damayanti, who is dazzled by him and asks who he is.

Damayanti tells Nala that she chooses him, pleading with him to love her, and says she would rather die than be refused. Nala warns that refusing the gods is dangerous and urges her to choose one of them. Damayanti refuses, and Nala, bound by his promise, reports back to the gods that she will choose him at the swayamvara in their presence, without blame to him.

At Bhima's swayamvara, Damayanti sees five men who look exactly like Nala and prays that the gods reveal her true husband. The gods reveal their true forms, and she chooses the real Nala by the signs of a mortal, placing a garland on him. The gods grant the couple boons, and Nala and Damayanti rule happily and have children.

On the way home from the swayamvara, the gods meet Kali and Dvapara, who had hoped to win Damayanti. Kali is furious that she chose a mortal and vows to ruin Nala. The gods rebuke Kali for wanting to curse so virtuous a king, but Kali enlists Dvapara to enter the dice and help him possess Nala.

Kali waits for an opening and finds it in the twelfth year, when Nala fails to wash his feet before his evening prayers. Possessed by Kali, Nala is challenged to dice by Pushkara, and he loses his stakes, despite the pleas of his citizens and his wife. The play goes on for months, and Nala is always the loser.

Damayanti sees that Nala is ruined and tries to rouse him through his councillors, and when that fails, she summons the charioteer Varshneya. She sends their children to her kinsfolk in Vidarbha with the charioteer and his horses. Varshneya takes the children to Vidarbha and then leaves for Ayodhya, where he enters the service of King Rituparna.

Pushkara takes Nala's remaining wealth and then taunts him by proposing Damayanti as the next stake. Nala strips off his ornaments and leaves the city with Damayanti, wearing one cloth, but the citizens are forbidden to help them. Starving in the forest, Nala tries to catch golden birds, which are the dice in disguise and steal his cloth, and Damayanti offers to take him to her father's kingdom.

Nala refuses to go to Vidarbha, saying he will not appear in disgrace before the family that once saw him in glory. While Damayanti sleeps in a shelter, Nala, pressed by Kali, decides to desert her. He cuts her garment in half to cover himself, returns in grief, and then leaves her sleeping alone in the forest.

Damayanti wakes alone in the forest and cries out for Nala, who has deserted her. Wandering in grief, she is seized by a huge serpent, and she weeps for Nala even as she is held. A hunter kills the serpent and frees her, but when he tries to force himself on her she curses him, and he falls dead.

Damayanti wanders the wild forest alone in search of Nala, lamenting to beasts, mountains and trees, and describing her royal family. Holy ascetics welcome her, and after predicting that she will find her husband they vanish. She reaches a merchants' caravan led by Suchi, who has not seen Nala, and learns that it is bound for the city of Suvahu in the land of the Chedis.

The merchant caravan camps by a lotus lake, where a herd of wild elephants stampedes through the sleeping men and kills many. The survivors blame the strange woman who joined them, and Damayanti laments her misfortunes as the fruit of sins. She reaches the Chedi capital of Suvahu, where the queen mother takes her in as a companion to her daughter on her own conditions.

Nala sees a fire in the forest and hears a snake, Karkotaka, calling for help. Cursed by the sage Narada, the snake asks Nala to carry him out of the flames, and when Nala sets him down, the snake bites him and changes his appearance so he cannot be recognised. Karkotaka says the poison will torment the one who deceived Nala, gives him two garments that will restore his form, and tells him to go to King Rituparna at Ayodhya.

Nala reaches Ayodhya in disguise as Vahuka, a charioteer and cook, and is taken into the service of King Rituparna as superintendent of the stables. Each evening he recites a verse about his lost wife, and when Jivala asks him about it, he tells the story as if it were another man's. He lives there unknown, remembering Damayanti.

King Bhima sends Brahmanas across the land to find Nala and Damayanti, offering great rewards. The Brahmana Sudeva finds Damayanti in the Chedi palace and recognises her by her beauty, even though she is worn and soiled. He tells her that her parents, brothers and children are alive and searching for her, and the queen mother asks him to tell her Damayanti's story.

Sudeva, a Brahmana searching for Nala, finds Damayanti in the household of the queen-mother and identifies her by a mark on her forehead. The queen-mother recognizes her as a sister's daughter, and Damayanti is sent home to Vidarbha. There she asks her father to have Nala sought, and Brahmanas are dispatched across the lands to find him.

Parnada, a Brahmana, returns from Ayodhya with the report that King Rituparna gave no answer to Damayanti's message, though his charioteer Vahuka spoke to him kindly. Damayanti then arranges a trick: she sends Sudeva to Rituparna with word of a second swayamvara the next day, hoping to bring Nala to Vidarbha. She keeps the plan from her father.

Rituparna decides to reach Vidarbha in a single day for the swayamvara, and Nala, now serving as the charioteer Vahuka, is torn by doubt about whether Damayanti's plan is genuine. Vahuka selects and yokes the horses, and the car rises swiftly into the air. Varshneya, Nala's former charioteer, notices Vahuka's skill and begins to suspect that he is Nala.

On the road Rituparna's upper garment falls, and to show his skill he counts the leaves and fruit of a Vibhitaka tree, which Vahuka fells to check. In exchange for horse-lore, Rituparna teaches Vahuka the science of dice, and as Nala learns it Kali leaves his body and seeks shelter in the tree. Freed, Nala drives on toward Vidarbha, though he has not yet taken back his own form.

Rituparna arrives at Kundina, the Vidarbha capital, and the rattle of his car stirs Damayanti, who half believes it is Nala's. Bhima welcomes the visitor, but Rituparna shows no sign of a swayamvara and says he came only to pay respects, which Bhima doubts. Damayanti, still unsure who the charioteer is, sends a messenger to find out.

Damayanti sends Kesini to question the charioteer Vahuka, who offers a cover story about coming for a second swayamvara and says no one knows where Nala is. When Kesini repeats the words Parnada carried, Nala, still in disguise, is overcome and answers with a speech about the faithfulness of wives, then weeps. Kesini carries his reaction back to Damayanti.

Damayanti, now suspecting that Vahuka is Nala, has Kesini watch him closely, and Kesini reports wonders such as widened passages, vessels filling with water, and fire lit from grass. Damayanti then tests him by tasting his cooking, recognizes Nala's hand in it, and sends her children to him. Nala embraces them in tears but sends Kesini away.

Damayanti tells her mother she will examine Vahuka herself, and with her parents' consent Nala is brought to her apartments. She questions him about his desertion, and Nala blames Kali, the demon Damayanti had cursed, who had lodged in his body and has now left him. The Wind-god vouches for Damayanti, Nala resumes his own form, and the couple are reunited in Bhima's palace some four years after the loss of his kingdom.

The next morning Nala, with Damayanti at his side, pays his respects to Bhima, and the city celebrates his return. Rituparna asks Nala's forgiveness, and Nala gives back the horse-lore he had learned. Rituparna then leaves for his own city with another charioteer, and Nala soon departs from Kundina.

Nala marches back into his own country with a modest army and challenges his brother Pushkara to a new game of dice, with Damayanti and everything else as the stake. Pushkara boasts and mocks him, but Nala wins back his kingdom and his brother's life in a single throw. He then spares Pushkara, blaming the earlier loss on Kali, and rules his restored kingdom to the people's delight.

With the kingdom restored, Damayanti and her children are brought back and Nala rules happily, giving many sacrifices. Vrihadaswa tells Yudhishthira that Nala's story is a comfort in misfortune and offers to teach him the science of dice, so that he will not be caught out by a skilled gambler. Yudhishthira accepts the lore, and Vrihadaswa goes off to bathe.

After Arjuna leaves Kamyaka, the Pandavas live in low spirits, still hunting game to offer to the Brahmanas. Janamejaya asks how his ancestors managed without the hero, and Vaisampayana describes how Draupadi, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva each lament his absence. Sahadeva suggests leaving the forest, since nothing there feels pleasant without Arjuna.

Yudhishthira, saddened by his brothers' and Krishna's grief over Arjuna, greets the sage Narada and asks what merit comes from going round the earth to visit its sacred waters and shrines. Narada replies by recounting what Bhishma once heard from the sage Pulastya. The episode sets up the story of Bhishma's meeting with Pulastya.

The sage Pulastya, pleased with Bhishma's humility and truthfulness, offers to grant him a wish, and Bhishma asks about the merit of visiting sacred bathing places, the tirthas. Pulastya explains that pilgrimage is open even to the poor and is greater than many costly sacrifices, and he singles out the Pushkara tirtha as the foremost. He then leads Bhishma through a long itinerary of holy sites, naming the merit that each one brings.

Pulastya continues his guide to sacred bathing places, starting with Kurukshetra and naming dozens of tirthas, each with the reward it brings in cattle gifts, sacrifices or heavenly regions. The list includes the five lakes that Rama made from the blood of the Kshatriyas he slew, which the Pitris declared holy, and the sacred confluences and springs along the way. The discourse ends by calling Kurukshetra the northern sacrificial altar of the Grandsire.

Pulastya carries on his list of holy bathing places, moving from the tirtha of Dharma and the Saraswati to the Himalayan source of the Ganges and onward to Naimisha, Gaya, and many other sites. Each place is tied to a reward, such as the merit of a horse-sacrifice, the gift of a thousand cows, or passage to a heavenly realm. The catalogue shows pilgrimage as a long, repeated circuit that a devoted person can complete.

Pulastya keeps listing sacred places, ranging from Samvedya and the Kaveri to Gokarna, Dandaka, and Kalanjara, and gives special praise to Prayaga, where the Ganga meets the Yamuna. He says that in the present age the Ganga alone is holy, and that reciting or hearing this account of the tirthas brings sons, wealth, and freedom from sin. Narada then tells Yudhishthira that Bhishma ended his own tour at Prayaga and encourages him to visit these places with the sages, and Yudhishthira begins to recite the merits to the ascetics.

Having heard his brothers and Narada, Yudhishthira tells the sage Dhaumya that he sent Arjuna to win celestial weapons from Indra. He judges the Kaurava champions, especially Karna, to be a grave threat, and says only Arjuna can match them. He asks Dhaumya to name a new forest for the group, since they cannot bear to stay in Kamyaka without Arjuna.

To comfort the grieving Pandavas, the priest Dhaumya begins a survey of holy places, starting with the eastern quarter. He names Naimisha, Gaya, the Ganga, Prayaga, Mahendra and Kundoda, tying many of them to famous sages and kings, including Nala's rest at Kundoda. He promises that visiting these sites brings far greater merit than hearing about them.

Dhaumya turns to the south, naming the Godavari, the Payoshni (where a tale of King Nriga is told), Gokarna, and Agastya's hermitage, and calling the Payoshni's water very cleansing. He then moves to Surashtra, describing Prabhasa, Pindaraka and Mount Ujjayanta. He ends with Dwaravati, where Krishna dwells, as a place of great merit.

Dhaumya describes the western holy places, centered on the Narmada river, the Vaidurya peak and the Viswamitra river. He recalls how Yayati's fall from heaven happened on the banks of the Viswamitra river and names the Pushkara lake. He closes with a verse stating that even imagining a pilgrimage to Pushkara cleanses sin.

Dhaumya finishes with the northern holy places, beginning with the Saraswati and Yamuna, where Sahadeva's sacrifice is recalled, and running on to Gangadwara and Badari. He describes Badari as the place where Narayana is worshipped by gods and sages, and he urges Yudhishthira to make the journey with the Brahmanas to ease his anxiety. The chapter then gives way to the next section.

The sage Lomasa arrives while Dhaumya is speaking and tells Yudhishthira that he saw Arjuna sitting beside Indra in heaven. Arjuna has won divine weapons from Rudra and other gods and has learned music and dance, and Indra promises that he will return soon. Indra also says Karna, though formidable, is far below Arjuna, and advises the brothers to practise asceticism while they wait.

Lomasa passes on Arjuna's request that he guard Yudhishthira through a tour of the tirthas, and Yudhishthira agrees at once. Lomasa advises him to travel light, and Yudhishthira sends away those who cannot bear hunger, cold, and the road. The citizens and Brahmanas return to Hastinapura, where Dhritarashtra provides for them, while Yudhishthira stays three nights at Kamyaka with a small company.

The Brahmanas who have been living with the Pandavas in the forest ask to join the pilgrimage, since the tirthas are dangerous and infested by beasts and Rakshasas. Yudhishthira agrees, and Vyasa, Parvata and Narada advise him to purify both body and heart before setting out. The party then departs on an auspicious day, dressed in bark and hides and armed, facing east.

Yudhishthira asks Lomasa why his wicked enemies prosper while he suffers. Lomasa answers that sinners may prosper for a time but are finally ruined, citing the Asuras who fell through pride while the gods gained prosperity by virtue and visits to the tirthas. He urges Yudhishthira to follow the gods' example, citing kings who won fame that way, and predicts the sons of Dhritarashtra will be destroyed.

The Pandavas bathe and give gifts at several rivers, then keep a vow near the Brahmasara lake at Gayasira, joined by many Brahmanas. There Shamatha tells how King Gaya once held sacrifices with mountains of food and rivers of butter and curds, so lavish that the gifts could not be counted. The account shows the pilgrimage as a path of both penance and generosity.

At Agastya's hermitage Yudhishthira asks why Agastya killed the demon Vatapi, and Lomasa explains. The demon Ilwala, angered at being refused a son like Indra, turned his brother Vatapi into a ram, fed him to Brahmanas, and then tore them open when Vatapi answered his call. Agastya, finding his ancestors hanging head-down in a pit and wanting a son to free them, creates a woman, Lopamudra, who is raised as a princess of Vidarbha.

Agastya asks the king of Vidarbha for Lopamudra, and the king, though reluctant, gives her when she urges him to. Lopamudra gives up her fine robes for ascetic clothing, and the couple take up penance at Gangadwara. Later, when she asks for a bed and ornaments of a princess before intimacy, Agastya says he lacks the wealth and sets out to find it.

Agastya goes to three wealthy kings in turn, Srutarvan, Vradhnaswa and Trasadasyu, asking for wealth without harming anyone. Each king says his spending matches his income, so Agastya, who will not take from anyone at another's cost, leaves empty-handed. The kings then propose asking the Danava Ilwala, the richest man on earth, and they all go to him.

Ilwala welcomes Agastya and the kings and serves them his brother Vatapi as cooked meat, but Agastya digests the demon, and Ilwala, learning this, gives the party a golden car and wealth. Lopamudra asks for one powerful son, who is born after seven years as Dridhasyu, later called Idhmavaha. Lomasa then tells the story of Rama of Bhrigu's line, who lost his energy to Rama, son of Dasaratha, and regained it at a sacred river.

Lomasa now recounts Agastya's deeds, beginning with the Kalakeya Danavas, who under Vritra harried the gods. Brahma advised the gods to ask the sage Dadhicha for his bones, and Dadhicha, giving up his life, let Twashtri forge them into the Vajra for Indra. The episode explains the origin of the weapon that will later be used against Vritra.

Armed with the Vajra and strengthened by Vishnu and the sages, Indra attacks Vritra, who is guarded by the Kalakeyas. Vritra is struck down, but Indra flees in doubt about whether the foe is really dead, and the leaderless Danavas retreat into the sea. There they plot to destroy the ascetics, on whom the worlds depend.

The Kalakeyas hide in the sea by day and come out by night to devour sages in their hermitages, including those of Vasishtha, Chyavana and Bharadwaja. Men find the mutilated bodies each morning, and sacrifices and sacred studies come to a halt. The gods, unable to stop the killings, turn to Narayana for protection.

The gods tell Vishnu that the killing of Brahmanas threatens earth and heaven alike. Vishnu explains that the Kalakeyas are hiding in the ocean and can be reached only if the sea is dried up, which only Agastya can do. The gods then go to Agastya and praise him as the one who has always protected them.

Yudhishthira asks why Vindhya suddenly swelled with wrath, and Lomasa explains. Vindhya, jealous of Meru around which the sun circles, demanded that the sun circle him too, and then grew tall enough to block the sun and moon. The gods asked Agastya to intervene, and he promised to go south and asked Vindhya to wait for his return; since he never came back, Vindhya has stayed low. The gods then request that Agastya drink the ocean so that the Kalakeyas can be destroyed, and he agrees.

Agastya drinks up the ocean while the gods praise him and slay the Kalakeyas, and some of the survivors flee into the netherworld. When the gods ask him to refill the sea, Agastya says the water has been digested and that they must find another way. The gods and the sages part in wonder and sorrow, and then gather with Vishnu and Brahma to consider how to refill it.

Brahma tells the gods that refilling the ocean must wait for the descendants of Bhagiratha's family. Yudhishthira asks Lomasa to tell how that family refilled the sea, and Lomasa begins with King Sagara. Sagara, childless, prayed to Shiva on Mount Kailasa and was promised many sons, and when his queen bore a gourd, a voice from the sky told him to keep its seeds in vessels.

The seeds in the gourd grow into sixty thousand violent sons who terrorize people and even the gods, and Brahma foretells their doom. When the horse of Sagara's sacrifice vanishes at the sea, the sons dig up the ocean in search of it and are burned to ashes by the sage Kapila. Sagara sends his grandson Ansuman, who recovers the horse and wins Kapila's favor, and the story points ahead to Bhagiratha, who will bring the Ganga down to earth.

Bhagiratha, grandson of Ansuman, grieves over his ancestors' fate and goes to the Himalayas to perform austerities for a thousand years. When Ganga appears, he asks her to descend to earth and wash the ashes of the sons of Sagara so they can enter heaven. Ganga agrees, but warns that only Shiva can bear the force of her fall, so Bhagiratha wins Shiva's favor.

Shiva agrees to bear Ganga's descent, and when the river comes down from the sky she divides into three streams and follows Bhagiratha to the sea, which she fills. Bhagiratha adopts Ganga as a daughter and offers water to his ancestors. Lomasa ends by summarizing how the sea was drunk, how Ganga was brought down, and how Vatapi was destroyed.

Yudhishthira and his brothers reach the Hemakuta hill, where strange things happen, and Lomasa explains that a wrathful sage named Rishava made the hill forbid speech. He tells how the gods hid the place from mortals and then sends the party on to the Kausiki river and Kasyapa's hermitage. He then tells the story of Rishyasringa, the horned sage born to a hind, and how Indra was made to send rain to the land of Lomapada.

Lomapada's courtesans prepare a floating hermitage near the hut of the young sage Rishyasringa, and send a clever courtesan to win his trust. She plies him with gifts, embraces and games until he is overcome with love and sits sighing. When his father Vibhandaka finds him in this state, he asks who has been to the hermitage.

Rishyasringa tells his father Vibhandaka about the visitor who came to his hermitage, describing her beauty, her ornaments, and the fruit and drink she offered him. He says her departure has left him longing for her and eager to follow her and take up the same austerities. The account shows how deeply the courtesan's visit has disturbed his mind.

Vibhandaka warns his son that the visitors were demons in lovely form, but while he is away searching for the courtesan, Rishyasringa is carried off on a floating hermitage to King Lomapada's land. The king gives Rishyasringa his daughter Santa, and rain returns to the land. To calm Vibhandaka's anger, the king arranges herds and ploughed fields along his route for his son, and the father is appeased and blesses the couple.

Yudhishthira bathes where the Ganga meets the sea and travels toward the land of the Kalinga tribes. Lomasa tells how Rudra seized a sacrificial beast and was appeased by the gods, and how the Earth, given away to Kasyapa, rose up as an altar into the sea so that mortals could cross it. He instructs Yudhishthira to recite a formula and mount the altar, and Yudhishthira does so, then spends the night on Mount Mahendra.

Yudhishthira spends a night among the sages, and Akritavrana, a follower of Parasurama, says Rama will appear on the fourteenth day of the lunar fortnight. Asked about Rama's wars against the warrior class, Akritavrana begins with the thousand-armed Arjuna of the Haihayas, whom Vishnu was asked to kill, and then tells how the sage Richika won Satyavati from King Gadhi with a thousand horses from Varuna. Bhrigu's blessing for the couple sets up the birth of Jamadagni and, later, of Rama.

Jamadagni marries Renuka, and their youngest son Rama is the most gifted of their five sons. When Renuka is stirred by desire at the sight of a king bathing, Jamadagni curses his elder sons for failing to act, and at his command Rama beheads his mother. Jamadagni grants Rama a boon that restores her, but later Arjuna's sons kill Jamadagni while Rama is away, and Rama returns to find his father dead.

Rama mourns his father, cremates him, and vows to wipe out the warrior caste, killing Kartavirya's sons and then exterminating the Kshatriyas seven times over. He makes five lakes of blood at Samantapanchaka, offers the earth to the priests, and gives an altar to Kasyapa before withdrawing to Mahendra. On the fourteenth day he appears to Yudhishthira and his brothers and honours the Brahmanas before the Pandavas head south.

Yudhishthira travels along the coast, bathing at many tirthas, including the Godavari and Agastya's holy spot in the Dravida country. He gives away cows, visits the altar of Richika's son and many shrines of the gods, and fasts for twelve days at Prabhasa. There the Vrishnis, led by Valarama and Krishna, come to see him and weep at the wretched state of the Pandavas.

Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas and the Vrishnis discussed at Prabhasa. Valarama, seeing Yudhishthira in misery, denounces the Kuru elders and the prosperity of Duryodhana, and wonders whether virtue brings any reward. He lists the brothers' heroic qualities and asks why they must suffer so in the forest.

Satyaki urges an immediate attack on Duryodhana with the Vrishni army, naming their warriors and vowing victory. Krishna replies that Yudhishthira will accept sovereignty only if it is won by his own arms, and that the allies should stand together in any case. Yudhishthira sends the Vrishnis home, and he goes on with Lomasa to the Payosini river.

Lomasa describes the lavish sacrifices that Nriga, Amurtarayasa and Gaya held on the Payosini, honouring Indra with Soma and paying priests immense gifts, and says a bath there brings Gaya's reward. Yudhishthira bathes there, then visits the sapphire hill and the Narmada, where Lomasa names the holy sites and Brahmanas receive gifts. Lomasa then speaks of Chyavana's feud with Indra, and Yudhishthira asks for the full story.

Chyavana, son of Bhrigu, sits in meditation until an anthill covers him. King Saryati's daughter Sukanya, playing in the woods, pokes the glowing eyes in the anthill with thorns, blinding the sage, who then blocks the army's calls of nature. Saryati asks for forgiveness, and Chyavana agrees to pardon the king on condition that he gives Sukanya to him as his wife.

The twin Ashvins see Sukanya bathing, mock her for marrying an aged man, and urge her to choose one of them instead. She refuses, and they offer to make Chyavana young again if she chooses one of them. After all three enter a pool and come out looking alike, Sukanya recognizes her own husband, and Chyavana promises that the Ashvins will drink Soma in Indra's presence.

Saryati hears that Chyavana has become young and visits the hermitage, and Chyavana agrees to officiate at his sacrifice. When Chyavana prepares Soma for the Ashvins, Indra forbids it, arguing that they are only physicians. Chyavana defies him, paralyses Indra's arm when he raises the thunderbolt, and creates a monstrous demon named Mada to devour Indra.

Frightened by the demon Mada, Indra agrees that the Ashvins shall have a right to Soma, and Chyavana disperses Mada among drink, women, dice and hunting. Chyavana then lives happily with Sukanya. Lomasa directs Yudhishthira to the lake, the Archika hill and other holy sites along the Yamuna, naming the sages and gods who worshipped there.

Yudhishthira asks how Mandhata was born and how he became so powerful. Lomasa tells how the childless king Yuvanaswa drank by mistake a jar of water consecrated for another king's wife, and how a son came out of his side; Indra gave his finger to the infant to suck, which gave him the name Mandhata. The boy grew into a mighty ruler who conquered the three worlds, performed great sacrifices and ended a long drought.

Somaka, a king with a hundred wives, finally has a single son, Jantu, and when an ant stings the boy, the commotion brings the king to the women's quarters. Somaka laments that one son is a burden and asks his priest for a rite that would give him a hundred sons. The priest says such a rite exists, but it requires a sacrifice of Jantu, which Somaka agrees to.

The priest sacrifices Jantu despite the mothers' cries, and after the smoke reaches them, they all conceive and bear a hundred sons. Later Somaka finds his priest tormented in hell for officiating, and insists on sharing his fate, which Dharmaraja allows for the same period. After both work off their sins they are freed and enjoy their rewards together.

Lomasa names sacred sites along the Yamuna and in the Kuru field, recalling how Ishtikrita, Amvarisha, Yayati, Bharata and Marutta performed great rites and gave lavish gifts there. He says that bathing at these places lets one see all the worlds. Yudhishthira bathes and says that from there he can even see Arjuna.

Lomasa points out a long series of sacred places, including the spot where the Saraswati vanishes underground, the Vipasa river where Vasistha was freed from his bonds, and the site where Lopamudra took Agastya as her lord. He notes that people who die at these sites are said to reach heaven, and that Shiva may be seen at the end of each age. He ends by telling how Usinara's sacrifice was tested by Indra and Agni in the form of a hawk and a pigeon.

Indra, in the form of a hawk, demands the pigeon that has sought King Usinara's protection, since hawks must eat pigeons. Usinara refuses to give up a suppliant and offers other food or any gift except the pigeon. When the hawk insists, Usinara cuts off his own flesh to match the pigeon's weight, and when the pigeon outweighs it, he climbs onto the scale himself; then Indra and Agni reveal themselves and promise him enduring glory.

Lomasa points out the hermitage of Swetaketu, who received speech from the goddess Saraswati, and mentions his nephew Ashtavakra, who defeated Vandin in debate. Yudhishthira asks why Ashtavakra was born crooked and how he won that victory. Lomasa tells of Kahoda, who was cursed by his unborn son for faulty recitation, lost a debate to Vandin, and was drowned, and of Ashtavakra's journey to King Janaka's sacrifice.

At the gate of King Janaka's sacrifice, the boy Ashtavakra argues with the gatekeeper, who says that only learned elders may enter. Ashtavakra insists that learning, not age or grey hair, makes a man, and he challenges Vandin, answering Janaka's riddles with unexpected cleverness. Janaka, impressed, admits him and sends him in to face Vandin.

In Janaka's assembly Ashtavakra challenges Vandin, and the two trade numbered verses counting from one to thirteen until Vandin falters and Ashtavakra completes the last one. Ashtavakra then orders Vandin drowned, as Vandin had drowned other Brahmanas, but Vandin reveals that he is a son of Varuna, and Kahoda, Ashtavakra's father, returns from the sea. Ashtavakra's crooked limbs are straightened when he bathes in the river Samanga.

Lomasa points out sacred sites along the Samanga, including the place where Indra was cleansed after slaying Vritra, and then tells how the sage Yavakri, son of Bharadwaja, sought Vedic learning through harsh penance. Indra first tries to dissuade him and then, disguised as an old Brahmana building a dam across the Ganga, makes him see the futility of his task, so Yavakri asks for boons instead. Bharadwaja warns his son that pride brings ruin, citing the tale of Medhavi, whose life depended on a mountain.

Lomasa tells how Yavakri makes advances to Raivya's daughter-in-law, who agrees out of fear and cleverness. Raivya, enraged, creates a woman and a demon from his own matted hair and sends them to kill Yavakri. The chapter shows the destructive power of a sage's anger and the cost of lust.

Bharadwaja comes home to find the sacred fires silent and learns from the blind Sudra warder that his son Yavakri has been killed. He mourns at length, blames Raivya, and curses his old friend. He then throws himself into a blazing fire.

King Vrihadyumna starts a sacrifice and takes Raivya's sons, Arvavasu and Paravasu, to help. Paravasu kills his father by mistake in the dark and asks his brother to take the penance for a Brahmana-killing, which Arvavasu does. Paravasu then falsely accuses Arvavasu, who wins the Sun's favour and the gods restore the dead, so the chapter explains how a wronged man was vindicated.

Lomasa guides the Pandavas past several mountains and points out the holy sites ahead, including Mandara and Kailasa, which are guarded by Yakshas and Rakshasas. He asks the gods, rivers and mountains to protect the king, and Yudhishthira tells his brothers to stay alert. The chapter ends with the group entering a dangerous region on their way toward Arjuna.

Yudhishthira asks Bhima to take the servants back, but Bhima refuses to leave anyone behind and offers to carry Draupadi and the twins over the rough mountains. Lomasa says the Gandhamadana mountain can only be reached through asceticism, and the party sets off after Suvahu, lord of the Pulindas, welcomes them and keeps their servants. Yudhishthira grieves over Arjuna's absence and resolves to go to Gandhamadana to find him.

Lomasa points out the holy river Alakananda and the bones of the demon Naraka, which Vishnu slew for Indra's sake. Yudhishthira asks how Vishnu raised the Earth, and Lomasa tells how an overcrowded world sank under its own weight until Vishnu lifted it as a one-tusked boar. The gods are sent to Brahma and then to Vishnu, and the Pandavas continue along Lomasa's route.

The Pandavas, with Draupadi and the Brahmins, travel toward Gandhamadana through forests, lakes and rugged country. As they enter the mountain, a violent wind, dust, hail and rain strike them, and each brother takes shelter alone. Once the storm passes, they regroup and continue toward the mountain.

Draupadi, unused to walking, collapses from exhaustion and the cold, and Nakula catches her. Yudhishthira laments that his addiction to dice has brought her to this suffering, and the Brahmins restore her with mantras and care. Bhima offers to carry the party himself or call his son Ghatotkacha, who comes at once and offers his service.

Yudhishthira asks Bhima to have his son Ghatotkacha carry Draupadi, and Ghatotkacha agrees and says other Rakshasas can help carry the rest. The company is flown over many lands to the jujube tree near Kailasa and the hermitage of Nara and Narayana. The sages welcome them, and the Pandavas settle there to make offerings and enjoy the forest and the river.

Draupadi asks Bhima to fetch more of the celestial lotuses, and he climbs Gandhamadana, scattering animals, fighting elephants and lions, and bathing in a lake. On a plantain slope he finds the ape Hanuman lying across the path to heaven, and Hanuman, woken, asks him to show kindness to living things and turn back. Most of the rest of the chapter is the translator's footnotes, which explain rites, yoga, cosmic terms, and a debate between Ashtavakra and Vandin.

Bhima demands that the monkey in his path move aside and asks who he is. Hanuman feigns weakness and asks Bhima to step over his tail, but Bhima cannot lift it, and he humbly asks the monkey's identity. Hanuman reveals himself as the son of the wind-god and begins to tell of Rama, Sita, and Ravana's abduction of her.

Hanuman continues his story: Rama befriends Sugriva, kills Vali, and sends search parties for Sita. Hanuman crosses the ocean, finds Sita in Lanka, and burns the city, and Rama then defeats Ravana and returns to Ayodhya. Hanuman says he has stayed on in this place by Rama's grace, and that this path is closed to mortals.

Bhima asks to see Hanuman's giant form from his leap over the ocean, but Hanuman says that form belonged to an earlier age and cannot be shown now. Bhima then asks about the yugas, and Hanuman describes how virtue, customs and human life decline from the perfect Krita age through the Treta and Dvapara ages to the Kali age. He ends by telling Bhima that a wise person does not chase unnecessary knowledge and that he should return home.

Bhima refuses to leave without seeing Hanuman's true form, so Hanuman grows to a huge size and says he can enlarge himself further. Bhima praises him, and Hanuman warns him not to take flowers from Kuvera's gardens by force and to keep to his duty as a Kshatriya. Hanuman then gives a long lesson on the duties of each class and on how a king should rule with counsel, spies and justice.

Hanuman shrinks back and embraces Bhima, whose weariness and strength are restored. He asks Bhima to keep his presence secret, and offers to punish the sons of Dhritarashtra if Bhima wishes. Bhima asks for his help in the coming battle, and Hanuman promises to roar from Arjuna's flagstaff to weaken the enemy, then vanishes.

Bhima continues along the path Hanuman described, passing woods, wild elephants, deer, and lakes. At midday he comes to a river filled with Saugandhika lotuses and feels that his errand is nearly accomplished. The chapter is a short transition toward Kuvera's lake.

Bhima reaches a beautiful lotus lake near Kailasa, which belongs to Kuvera and is guarded by Krodhavasa Rakshasas. He drinks the cool water and gathers the lotuses, which delights him. The armed guards see him in his deerskin and challenge him, asking his errand.

Bhima explains that he is Pandu's son and has come for lotuses for Draupadi. The Rakshasas say the lake is Kuvera's and that he must ask permission first, but Bhima refuses to beg, since a Kshatriya does not beseech. He plunges in, defeats the guards with his mace, and kills more than a hundred of them, and the survivors report to Kuvera, who smiles and lets him take the lotuses for Krishna.

Bhima gathers the rare flowers, and omens of battle appear, with wind, meteors, darkness and trembling earth. Yudhishthira, not finding Bhima, asks Draupadi where he is, and she explains that he went for the lotuses. The company follows him to the lake, where they find slain Yakshas on the shore, and Yudhishthira gently rebukes Bhima for his rashness; the garden warders are pacified, and the Pandavas wait on Gandhamadana for Arjuna.

Yudhishthira reviews the sacred places the company has visited and asks Bhima how to reach Kuvera's abode. An aerial voice says that place is not open to them and gives a route through several hermitages. Dhaumya advises accepting this, and the Pandavas return to the hermitage of Nara and Narayana.

While Bhima is away hunting, a Rakshasa named Jatasura, who has been posing as a learned Brahmana guest, seizes Yudhishthira, the twins and Draupadi, intending to take their weapons and Draupadi. Yudhishthira and Sahadeva confront him on grounds of virtue and Kshatriya duty, and Bhima returns and rebukes him for betraying his hosts. After a long fight with trees and rocks, Bhima kills Jatasura and is praised by the Brahmanas.

Yudhishthira recalls that Arjuna promised to meet them on Mount Sweta in the fifth year, so the company takes leave of the Brahmanas and sets out northward. They leave their sacred vessels with the sage Vrishaparva and pass through the Gandhamadana forest, which is described at length with its trees, birds, lakes and minerals. The chapter ends with the Pandavas reaching the hermitage of Arshtishena.

Yudhishthira and his brothers approach the ascetic Arshtishena, who greets them and asks whether they still keep to virtue, honour their parents and elders, and avoid sin. Yudhishthira says he tries to do so. Arshtishena warns that the region beyond the Kailasa peaks belongs to the gods and to Vaisravana, that trespassers are slain by Rakshasas, and asks them to stay until Arjuna returns.

Janamejaya asks how the Pandavas spent their time on Gandhamadana and whether Bhima fought the Yakshas and met Kuvera. Vaisampayana says they lived on ascetic food and heard Lomasa's stories for years, until Draupadi asked Bhima to drive the Rakshasas from the summit. Bhima climbs the peak, fights the Yakshas and Rakshasas, and kills Maniman, Kuvera's friend.

Yudhishthira finds Bhima on the summit amid the fallen Rakshasas and gently scolds him for rashness. The surviving Rakshasas report to Kuvera, who rides out with his Yakshas, but he is not angry and is grateful to Bhima, because the slaughter lifts a curse he had carried. Kuvera then explains that the sage Agastya cursed him after Maniman insulted the sage.

Kuvera advises Yudhishthira that patience, ability, timing, place and prowess bring success, and asks him to restrain the rash Bhima. He praises Arjuna, who is learning weapons in Indra's heaven, and promises the protection of his Gandharvas and Yakshas. Kuvera then leaves, the slain Rakshasas are removed, and the Pandavas stay on in the Rakshasa dwellings for several nights.

At dawn Dhaumya takes Yudhishthira's hand and points out the regions of the cosmos from the Himalayan heights. He names the realms of Indra, Vaisravana, Yama and Varuna, and then Mount Meru, home of Brahma and Narayana. He explains how the sun and moon circle Meru, how the seasons follow the sun's path, and how the sun governs time and life.

The Pandavas remain on Gandhamadana, practising rites and reciting the Vedas, but they grieve for Arjuna, and each day seems like a year. The narrator then tells how Arjuna spent five years in Indra's heaven and gained the celestial weapons before returning to the mountain.

Indra's chariot, driven by Matali, brings Arjuna down to Gandhamadana. He bows to his elders and brothers, and Matali is honoured and returns to heaven. Arjuna gives Draupadi jewels from Indra, tells how he learned weapons from Indra, Vayu and Shiva, and spends the night with the twins.

The next morning Arjuna greets Yudhishthira, and Indra descends with heavenly music and clamour. Yudhishthira honours him, and Indra says he will rule the earth and asks him to return to Kamyaka. The narrator adds that anyone who studies this meeting for a year will live a hundred years free of trouble.

Yudhishthira asks Arjuna how he gained the weapons and pleased the gods. Arjuna recounts his penance on the Himalaya, where a boar and a hunter appear, and his fight with them. The hunter is revealed as Shiva, who grants him the Pasupata weapon, with a warning that it must never be used lightly.

Arjuna recounts how, after his meeting with Shiva, the gods led by Indra and the world-guardians came to honour him and give him weapons. Matali takes him up to heaven, where Indra welcomes him, and he spends years there learning arms and music with Chitrasena. Indra asks him to pay his teacher's fee by destroying the Nivata-Kavacha Danavas who live under the ocean, and the gods equip him with a chariot, armour, a diadem and the conch Devadatta.

Arjuna reaches the ocean and sees the city of the Danavas beneath the waters. Matali drives the chariot down into the city, and the demons, taking Arjuna for Indra, shut their gates and then pour out in thousands. Arjuna sounds his conch, and the sages and gods gather to watch the battle.

The Nivata-Kavachas charge Arjuna's chariot in a mass, hurling darts, maces and clubs. Arjuna's arrows from the Gandiva and Matali's skilful driving trample and scatter many of them, and Arjuna uses Indra's weapon to cut their missiles to pieces. The demons then turn to illusion to fight on.

The Danavas send showers of rocks, a flood, fire, wind and darkness. Arjuna answers with Indra's weapons, including the Visoshana, to dry up the water and extinguish the flames. Matali falters under the illusions until Arjuna steadies him, and Arjuna dispels the illusions with his own, though he cannot yet see the hidden demons.

Arjuna tells how the Nivata-Kavachas hid behind illusions and buried his horses under rocks, until Matali urged him to use Indra's thunderbolt weapon, which destroyed them. He then enters their city, which Matali says was once Indra's, taken by the demons through a boon. Matali explains that the gods had been unable to defeat these demons and that Arjuna was destined to do so.
