On his way back, Arjuna sees the aerial city of Hiranyapura, home of the Kalakeya demons, whose mothers Pulama and Kalaka won a boon from Brahma that made their city almost invincible, with destruction only at mortal hands. Arjuna attacks it, calls on Rudra's weapon to destroy the Danavas, and watches their wives mourn. Indra praises him and tells him that Yudhishthira will rule the earth.

Indra tells Arjuna that no mortal can match him, and he gives him armour, a diadem, a garland and the conch Devadatta. After five years in heaven Arjuna returns to his brothers on Gandhamadana. Yudhishthira rejoices at his success and asks to see the weapons, and Arjuna promises to show them the next morning.

The next morning Arjuna displays his celestial weapons for Yudhishthira, and the earth and seas tremble while beings and gods gather round. The sage Narada warns Arjuna that celestial weapons must not be used without a worthy cause, as misuse would destroy the three worlds. When the gods leave, the Pandavas go on living in the forest with Krishna.

Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after Arjuna returned from heaven. Vaisampayana describes the years in Kuvera's gardens, and then Bhima, with Arjuna and the twins, urges Yudhishthira to leave the forest and reclaim the kingdom from Duryodhana. Yudhishthira bids farewell to Kuvera's realm and sets out with his brothers and the Brahmanas.

The brothers leave Kuvera's mountain and travel back through hermitages and the realm of Suvahu, then spend a year in the Visakhayupa forest. A passage there names Bhima as seized by a huge snake in a cave, with Yudhishthira as his protector, and the episode is developed in the following chapters. In the twelfth year of exile they move to the Saraswati and the Dvaitavana lake, where ascetics greet them.

Janamejaya asks how Bhima, who had defeated Kuvera's Yakshas, came to be struck with fear by the snake. Vaisampayana describes Bhima hunting and uprooting trees in the Himalayan forests, until he finds a huge snake in a cave. The snake coils around him, and a boon the snake holds drains his strength so he cannot break free.

The snake holds Bhima, who asks it to identify itself and to explain how it overpowered him. The snake reveals that it is King Nahusha, Yudhishthira's ancestor, turned into a snake by Agastya's curse for insulting Brahmanas, and that it will eat Bhima at a set hour. Bhima accepts fate and grieves for his brothers and mother. Meanwhile Yudhishthira sees ill omens, sets out to find Bhima, and discovers him caught in the snake's coils.

Yudhishthira finds Bhima caught and offers other food in exchange, but the snake insists on eating Bhima. It agrees to release him if Yudhishthira answers its questions about who a Brahmana is and what is worth knowing. Yudhishthira answers that conduct, not birth alone, marks a Brahmana, and that the highest thing to know is Brahma, beyond joy and sorrow. Persuaded by his answers, the snake says it cannot eat Bhima now.

Yudhishthira asks the snake, now revealed as Nahusha, how a person attains salvation, and Nahusha teaches about alms, kind speech, truth and non-violence, rebirth according to deeds, and how the senses and mind perceive. Asked how a learned man could fall into delusion, Nahusha admits that prosperity intoxicated him and recounts Agastya's curse. He says Yudhishthira's wisdom has freed him, and he returns to heaven, while the Brahmanas admonish Bhima for his rashness.

The rainy season comes to the forest with black clouds, swollen rivers and the calls of animals, and autumn follows with clear skies and bright nights. The Pandavas spend the holy full moon of Kartika by the Saraswati with holy men. In the dark fortnight they enter the Kamyaka forest with Arjuna, their charioteers and their cooks, and this chapter opens the Markandeya-Samasya section.

Krishna arrives at Kamyaka with Satyabhama and greets the Pandavas, praising Yudhishthira's virtue and offering to help them regain their kingdom once the agreed term ends. The ancient sage Markandeya arrives, and Yudhishthira asks him whether human action or God controls fate and whether deeds bear fruit in this life or the next. Markandeya answers that a person's deeds follow him into each rebirth, shaping his happiness and misery.

Markandeya tells the story of a Haihaya prince who mistook a sage in a black antelope skin for a deer and killed him. When the Haihayas went to the sage's father, Tarkshya, the dead sage was found alive again. Tarkshya explains that Brahmanas do not fear death, because of their virtue, hospitality, charity and devotion, and the Haihayas return home happy.

Markandeya tells how the sage Atri, wishing to give away wealth before retiring to the forest, goes to King Vainya's horse-sacrifice to ask for gifts. Gautama objects, and the dispute over whether the king or Indra is supreme is settled by Sanatkumara in the king's favour. Pleased with the verdict, Vainya gives Atri a huge gift, which Atri shares with his sons before going to the forest.

Markandeya says the goddess Saraswati once answered Tarkshya's questions about how a man can keep to virtue. She describes the rewards of Vedic study and of gifts, including cows, bullocks, clothes, gold and daughters in marriage, and of offerings to the sacred fire. Tarkshya then asks her for the rules for keeping the sacred fire.

Yudhishthira asks Markandeya for the story of Vaivasvata Manu. Manu, while doing penance, rescues a small fish, which grows until he takes it to the sea, and the fish warns him of a coming flood and tells him to build a boat and gather the seeds. The fish tows the boat to the Himalaya and reveals itself as Brahma, who will recreate the world through Manu. Markandeya says that hearing this story brings merit and heaven.

Yudhishthira asks Markandeya, who has lived through many ages, to explain the causes of things. Markandeya praises the Lord who creates the world, describes the lengths of the four yugas and the decline of the Kali age, and then tells how the world is destroyed by drought, seven suns, a fire, and floods. Alone on the waters, he finds the boy-god resting on a banyan leaf, enters his body, sees the whole universe within him, and asks him to explain it.

The boy-god reveals himself as Narayana, the source and destroyer of all things, who appears in many forms, takes human birth when virtue fails, and creates and withdraws the worlds. He explains that he showed Markandeya the universe within him to cure his melancholy, and that he will create again when Brahma wakes. Markandeya recognises him as Janardana, now Krishna of the Vrishnis, and the Pandavas bow to him and are consoled.

Yudhishthira asks Markandeya what will happen in the Kali age: how men will live and eat, and when the Krita age will return. Markandeya describes how virtue shrinks from age to age, and how in the Kali age people deceive one another, castes blur, rulers and Brahmanas fail in their duties, and portents and disorder spread. He ends by saying that after these terrible times creation begins anew, and a Brahmana named Kalki will be born to restore order.

Markandeya says that Kalki will destroy thieves and robbers, hold a great horse-sacrifice, and give the earth to the Brahmanas, and then virtue and sacrifice will return in the Krita age. He closes his teaching on the ages and advises Yudhishthira to be merciful, humble and devoted to his people, and never to humiliate a Brahmana. Yudhishthira promises to follow this counsel, and the listeners are filled with wonder.

Markandeya tells how King Parikshit of Ayodhya married a maiden on the condition that he never show her water, and how she vanished into a tank. His son Sala seized the sage Vamadeva's Vami horses and refused to return them, and Vamadeva's Rakshasas killed him. When Vamadeva again demanded the horses from Sala's successor, Dala, a dispute over a poisoned arrow ended with Dala's son killed, until the queen's plea freed Dala from sin and the horses were returned.

Markandeya explains that the royal sage Vaka lived long because of his great asceticism, and then recounts Vaka's meeting with Indra, who asks about the sorrows of the immortal life. Vaka answers that loss of loved ones, dependence on others, and the sight of the undeserving prospering are the chief pains of such a life. Indra then asks about its joys, and Vaka praises a simple meal eaten at home and shared with guests and Brahmanas.

Markandeya tells how King Suhotra of the Kurus and King Sivi, son of Usinara, meet on the road and each refuses to yield the way, both claiming equal worth. Narada quotes verses saying that the wicked should be overcome by goodness and the mean by charity. Suhotra then honours Sivi, walks round him, and gives him the way.

Markandeya tells how King Yayati, son of Nahusha, is approached by a Brahmana asking for wealth for his teacher. Yayati says he never boasts of gifts, never listens to requests for things he cannot give, and never regrets a gift. He gives the Brahmana a thousand cows.

Markandeya tells how King Seduka sends a Brahmana to King Vrishadarbha, who had vowed to give Brahmanas only gold and silver. When the Brahmana asks for a thousand steeds, Vrishadarbha strikes him with a whip, then makes amends by giving him the whole day's revenue, which is worth more than a thousand horses.

Markandeya tells how the gods test King Sivi: Agni takes the form of a pigeon and Indra that of a hawk. The pigeon seeks Sivi's protection and the hawk demands it as food, and Sivi offers flesh cut from his own body in its place. When the pigeon still outweighs his flesh, Sivi climbs onto the scale himself, and the gods reveal themselves and promise him a son, Kapataroman.

At King Ashtaka's horse-sacrifice, several kings ask Narada which of them will fall from heaven first. He says Ashtaka will fall for boasting of his gifts, Pratardana for giving his horses with a bitter remark, and Vasumanas for praising a flowery car the king never gave him. Narada says he himself will fall, since he is not Sivi's equal; Sivi, tested by the god Vidhatri, was willing to kill and cook his own son for a Brahmana.

Markandeya tells the Pandavas of the royal sage Indradyumna, who fell from heaven when his merit was spent and went looking for anyone who knew him. Markandeya sends him to the owl Pravarakarna, who points to the crane Nadijangha, and the crane points to the tortoise Akupara, who remembers Indradyumna's great sacrifices. A heavenly car then takes Indradyumna back, and an aerial voice says that only virtue lasts. Markandeya adds that Krishna once raised King Nriga from hell to heaven.

Yudhishthira asks when and how charity wins entry to Indra's heaven. Markandeya lists the kinds of life and gift that are futile, names the Brahmanas who deserve gifts, and calls food the greatest of gifts. He then describes the long, hard road to Yama's realm, where a traveller's past gifts decide his comfort, and closes with teachings on purity, the limits of outward austerity, and the greater merit of gifts made at sacred times.

Yudhishthira asks Markandeya why the king Kuvalaswa came to be called Dhundhumara. Markandeya begins with the sage Utanka, who performs long penances and praises Vishnu. Vishnu grants Utanka's wishes and foretells that a king named Kuvalaswa will slay the demon Dhundhu.

The chapter traces the line of Ayodhya's kings down to Kuvalaswa, whose father then hands him the throne and retires to the forest. The sage Utanka urges the new king to stay and protect his people instead. He explains that the demon Dhundhu lies hidden in a desert near his hermitage and must be killed.

Vrihadaswa agrees to let his son Kuvalaswa take on the task, and then he retires to the forest. Yudhishthira asks who the demon Dhundhu was and whose son he was. Markandeya answers with the story of how Vishnu killed the demons Madhu and Kaitabha, which is the background to Dhundhu.

Dhundhu, son of Madhu and Kaitabha, wins a boon from Brahma that no god or demon can kill him, and he harasses the hermitage of Utanka from beneath the sand. King Kuvalaswa and his sons, empowered by Vishnu, go out against him, and after his sons are burned, the king kills Dhundhu with the water from his own body and the Brahma weapon. From this victory the king takes the name Dhundhumara, and his three surviving sons carry on the Ikshvaku line. The chapter closes by saying that hearing the story brings virtue, children, long life and freedom from disease.

Yudhishthira asks Markandeya to explain the high virtue of women, the duties of sons toward their parents, and the duties of Kshatriyas. Markandeya answers that a mother's labour is the harder of the two, and that parents hope their sons will bring fame and virtue. He adds that a woman wins heaven by serving her husband, not through sacrifice, offerings or fasts.

The learned Brahmana Kausika, in anger, glares at a crane that fouls him from a tree, and she falls dead, which he then laments. Later, while waiting for alms, he is kept waiting by a housewife who first serves her husband. She explains her duty and sends him to a truthful fowler in Mithila to learn what true virtue is, and he calms down and returns home.

Kausika travels to Mithila and finds the fowler, a meat seller by hereditary trade, who already knows why he has come. The fowler explains his family duty, praises the just rule of King Janaka, and urges honesty and repentance as the marks of a good life. He then answers Kausika's question by listing the signs of truly virtuous conduct.

The fowler defends his cruel trade as the result of past actions, arguing that Destiny directs it and that meat offered to the gods and ancestors is lawful. He cites the kings Sivi, Rantideva and Saudasa, and points out that farming, eating plants and the natural world all destroy living creatures. He concludes that no one is free from harming life, and that keeping to one's own duty brings reputation.

The fowler teaches that a person's successes, failures and illnesses follow from past karma, and that lying can sometimes serve a greater good. He explains that the soul is eternal and passes from body to body according to its deeds, and that liberation comes through spiritual wisdom and self-restraint. Kausika then asks what the senses are and how they can be subdued.

The fowler describes how a man's mind slides from learning into desire, envy and greed, and then into sin, while the wise man sees this and turns to virtue. Kausika praises him as a sage, and the fowler begins to teach the Brahmanic doctrine of the elements, qualities and principles that make up the universe.

The fowler lists the qualities of earth, water, fire, air and sky, and explains that some qualities are perceived by the senses while others are known only by inference. He says the senses are the root of both spiritual progress and downfall, and he compares the self-controlled man to a charioteer who reins in wild horses. Mastering the senses, he concludes, is the path to spiritual light.

Kausika asks about the three qualities of nature, and the fowler defines tamas by dullness and anger, rajas by restless action, and sattwa by steadiness and patience. He adds that a man of good qualities can rise in status regardless of his birth, even from the Sudra caste to a Brahmana. The fowler then asks whether Kausika wants to learn more.

Kausika asks how fire and breath combine to form the living body, and the fowler describes the vital airs and the inner heat that digest food and sustain the frame. He identifies the soul with the Supreme Spirit, which yogins reach by turning inward. The fowler closes by urging the overcoming of anger and greed, along with peace, renunciation and non-violence, as the path to liberation.

The fowler leads the Brahmana into his fine house to meet his aged parents, who bless their son. The fowler says he serves them as his highest gods, bathing and feeding them and speaking only pleasant words, as a householder's duty. The Brahmana is impressed by this devotion.

The fowler tells the Brahmana that the lady in Mithila sent him, then rebukes him for leaving his parents, who have grown blind with grief, to study the Vedas without their permission. The Brahmana thanks him and asks why such a virtuous man is a fowler. The fowler reveals that he was once a Brahmana who accidentally shot a sage while hunting with a king, and was cursed to be born a fowler in the Sudra class.

The sage softens his curse, promising the fowler will stay pious, recall his past life and regain Brahmana status once the curse ends. The Brahmana tells him that character, not birth, makes a Brahmana, and the fowler teaches that wisdom and contentment overcome grief. The Brahmana then leaves to serve his own parents, and Yudhishthira says he is still eager for more of the teaching.

Yudhishthira asks why the fire-god hid in water, why Angiras acted as fire, and how Kumara came to be called Agni's son. Markandeya tells how Agni grew depressed at Angiras's brilliance, and how Angiras persuaded him to resume his place, which led to the birth of Vrihaspati. The gods learned the mystery from Angiras, and Markandeya prepares to describe the sacred fires.
Markandeya lists the children that Angiras had with his wife Subha. The son Vrihaspati is named first, followed by several daughters, each named for a quality such as beauty, light or sacrifice.

Markandeya lists the children of Vrihaspati and his wife Tara, who are themselves sacred fires. Each son has a name and a role, such as Sanju, Bharadwaja, Viswabhuk and Vadava, tied to particular sacrifices or functions. Swaha bears three sons linked to sattwa, rajas and tamas, which shows how the many fires arise from a single source.

A being born from a long penance, marked with five colours from five sages, goes on to create the fire of the manes, day and night, and many other beings. Among his creations are fifteen gods who obstruct sacrifices and must be appeased with hymns. The chapter closes with the father of this line, who is pleased with his sons.

Markandeya names many fires descended from Tapa and Bhanu, each with its own name and role in sacrifice, and the list shows how the fires multiply. He then gives the rites needed to correct the sacred fire when it is disturbed by death, contact with a menstruating woman, or other defilement.

Markandeya tells how the fire Swaha hid in the sea to avoid defilement, and how the sage Atharvan, who carried the oblations for a time, gave up his body. From that body came metals and woods, and Atharvan later restored the fire. He then names the rivers that are said to be the mothers of the fires, and explains that all the fires are one.

Markandeya begins the story of Kartikeya, who is to lead the gods. Indra, looking for a leader, hears a woman's cries in the Manasa mountains and finds the Asura Kesin trying to seize her. Indra drives Kesin off with his thunderbolt, and then asks the woman who she is.

The woman, Devasena, daughter of Prajapati, says her sister was carried off by Kesin and asks Indra to find her a champion husband. Indra reads omens in the union of Sun, Moon and Agni, hoping a son of Soma or Agni could be her husband, and Brahma approves his plan. Meanwhile the fire Adbhuta, overcome by desire for the Rishis' wives, resolves to look at them only as his household fire, and Swaha schemes to win him in disguise.

Swaha, disguised as Siva the wife of Angiras, woos Agni by claiming the other Rishis' wives sent her, and after their union she flies to the White Mountain and casts his seed into a golden lake. From it a six-faced child, Skanda, is born, who shows his might by tearing a mountain and roaring until the three worlds tremble. The gods and creatures then seek his protection.

The birth causes strange omens, and the seven Rishis divorce six of their wives, keeping only Arundhati, after Swaha reveals to Skanda that she is his mother. Viswamitra clears the wives of blame and performs the child's rites, though the Rishis still abandon their spouses. The gods urge Indra to kill Skanda, but he hesitates, and the Mothers take the child as their own and nurse him.

Indra marches out with the gods and their armies to destroy Skanda. Skanda's fiery breath burns the forces, and when the gods desert Indra he hurls his thunderbolt, which pierces Skanda and gives birth to a new being, Visakha. Indra then begs Skanda's protection, and peace returns.

The wound from the thunderbolt gives rise to a host of followers, male and female, who adopt Visakha as their father. The seven Mothers and their son Sisu are named, and Skanda is called the father of the Kumaras because of these followers. The battle is said to have been fought on the sixth day of the lunar fortnight.

Skanda, handsome and blessed with fortune, is urged by the Rishis to become Indra, but he declines the sovereignty and serves Indra instead. Indra asks Skanda to lead the celestial forces, and Skanda is anointed commander, honoured as the son of Rudra. He is then married to Devasena, whom Indra brings to him, and the day of his anointing is remembered as a sacred day.

The six wives of the Rishis, cast out on a rumour that they bore Skanda, ask him to adopt them as his mothers, and he agrees. The mother goddesses then ask him to take their place and give them back their offspring, and Skanda grants them other offspring in exchange, so they may protect children. He sets them and a host of spirits to trouble children until they reach sixteen, and Markandeya lists the spirits that afflict men after that age.

Swaha asks Skanda to grant her union with Agni, and he decrees that offerings made through Agni will carry her name. Brahma then sends Skanda to visit his father Mahadeva, and the chapter describes the spirits, bells and banners of Skanda and the grand procession of Mahadeva's army. An Asura attack follows, in which Mahisha seizes Rudra's chariot until Skanda slays him, and Skanda then routs the Danavas. Markandeya closes with a long list of Skanda's names and a prayer, promising fame, wealth and salvation to those who recite them.

Satyabhama asks Draupadi what secret keeps the five Pandavas so obedient to her, suggesting charms, drugs or vows. Draupadi rejects such charms as wicked and describes her humble, devoted service to her husbands, to Kunti, and in running the household, servants and treasury. Satyabhama apologises for her jest, saying such talk arises naturally between friends.

Draupadi advises Satyabhama on how to win Krishna's heart through honest, humble service rather than deceit. She urges her to greet him promptly, keep his secrets, avoid his enemies and wicked women, and adorn herself for him. The advice presents devotion to the husband as the source of reputation, prosperity and heaven.

Krishna takes leave of the Pandavas and the Brahmanas and calls for Satyabhama. Satyabhama comforts Draupadi, foreseeing the Pandavas' return to power and the ruin of the Kuru sons, and reports that the Pandava sons are well and cared for in Dwaraka. She then circles Draupadi, mounts Krishna's car, and they leave for his city.

Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did in the Dwaita forest after they reached the lake. A talkative Brahmana who has been visiting them carries news of their misery to Dhritarashtra, who laments their plight at length, blaming fate and the deceit of his own sons. Sakuni then tells Duryodhana in private, and Duryodhana, though foolish, is grieved.

Sakuni, prompted by Karna, urges Duryodhana to rule the earth without rival and to visit the Pandavas in their Dwaita forest home, flaunting his wealth before them. He argues that the happiness of seeing a defeated enemy surpasses any gift or kingdom, and suggests Duryodhana's wives mock Draupadi in her poverty. When they finish, Karna and Sakuni fall silent.

Duryodhana is pleased by Karna's words but doubts that his father will let him go to the Pandavas' forest, since he longs to see them humbled and suffering. Karna proposes a pretext: inspecting the royal cattle stations at Dwaitavana, a plan Sakuni also endorses. The three agree to put the idea to King Dhritarashtra.

Karna and Sakuni ask Dhritarashtra to let Duryodhana go to the cattle stations at Dwaitavana for the hunt and the herd count. The king warns that the Pandavas are near, that their anger and Draupadi's power could harm the Kauravas, and that Duryodhana should not go himself. Sakuni reassures him, and the king grudgingly gives permission for a large party to set out.

Duryodhana inspects and marks his cattle, and he and his court enjoy hunting, music, dancing and generous gifts in the woods. When he tries to set up pleasure-houses by the lake at Dwaitavana, where Yudhishthira is performing a daily rite, he finds that the Gandharva king Chitrasena has come there for sport and barred the way. The Gandharvas mock the Kuru messengers and refuse to yield.

Duryodhana orders his soldiers to punish the Gandharvas, and the Kuru army attacks the forest. Chitrasena rallies his host, and the Kuru army flees, leaving only Karna standing and fighting hard. The Gandharvas use illusions to overwhelm the Kauravas, and Karna's chariot is broken until he escapes on Vikarna's car.

The Gandharvas rout the Kauravas and seize Duryodhana, Dussasana and the royal ladies, and the fleeing soldiers appeal to the Pandavas to rescue them. Bhima answers with sarcasm, saying the Kauravas are now paying for their deceit and that the Pandavas are not wicked. Yudhishthira reproves him, telling him this is no time for cruel words.

Yudhishthira rebukes Bhima and urges his brothers to rescue Duryodhana, arguing that family honour must be defended even against kinsmen and that an insult from a stranger must be avenged. He tells them to try conciliation first and to use force only if the Gandharva king refuses. Arjuna pledges to free the Kauravas or drink the Gandharva king's blood, and the Kauravas regain their spirit.

The Pandavas arm themselves in gold-trimmed mail and march toward the Gandharvas, and the Kuru army cheers them on. Arjuna asks the Gandharvas to release Duryodhana, but they reply that they obey only Indra. When Arjuna threatens to free the Kauravas by force, the two sides begin a fierce battle.

The Gandharvas, far more numerous than the four Pandavas, press them hard. Arjuna's celestial weapons slaughter thousands and trap the Gandharvas who were carrying off the Kauravas. Chitrasena then vanishes by illusion, but Arjuna reveals him with a special weapon, and Chitrasena declares himself Arjuna's friend, after which the fighting stops.

Arjuna asks Chitrasena why he has punished the Kauravas, and Chitrasena explains that Duryodhana and Karna came to mock the exiles and that Indra ordered him to bring Duryodhana in chains. When Arjuna asks for Duryodhana's release, Chitrasena refuses, so the Gandharvas and Pandavas take the prisoners to Yudhishthira, who frees them and praises the Gandharvas. Yudhishthira then warns Duryodhana never to act rashly again and sends him home in shame.

Janamejaya asks how the humbled and shamed Duryodhana entered Hastinapura. Vaisampayana describes his slow departure and camp, and at night Karna comes to him, congratulating him on his survival and on the brothers' victory. Karna admits that he himself fled the battle, and Duryodhana answers in tears.

Duryodhana tells Karna that the Gandharvas overpowered them with illusions and took them captive through the sky. He says that when his soldiers appealed to the Pandavas, Yudhishthira ordered them to free the captives, and that Chitrasena then made peace with Arjuna.

Duryodhana recounts how Arjuna asked Chitrasena to free the Kaurava brothers, and how Chitrasena revealed their plan to mock the Pandavas. Overcome with shame, Duryodhana resolves to fast to death rather than return to the city, and offers the kingship to Dussasana, who weeps and refuses. Karna then urges the brothers to stop weeping, since the Pandavas were only doing their duty, and to return home.

Karna argues that it is no shame that the Pandavas rescued Duryodhana, since subjects should serve their king and the Pandavas were bound to help him. He warns that a king who starves himself would be mocked by other kings, but Duryodhana is firm in his resolve and will not rise.

Sakuni tries to rouse Duryodhana from his resolve to starve himself, urging him to return the kingdom to the Pandavas and make peace. Duryodhana refuses every counsel, and his friends say they cannot enter the city without him. The Danavas, who fear the loss of their ally, use a fire rite to summon him, and a goddess carries him off to the nether world, where he is flattered.

The Danavas urge Duryodhana to give up his fast, telling him he is of celestial origin and will be aided by demon-possessed warriors. They promise that Karna, possessed by the soul of Naraka, and the Samsaptakas will slay Arjuna. Duryodhana, believing it was a dream, returns to his army, and Karna encourages him to rise and vow to subdue the Pandavas.

Janamejaya asks what the Kauravas did while the Pandavas lived in the forest. Bhishma rebukes Duryodhana for going to the forest, and advises peace with the Pandavas. Duryodhana laughs at his advice, and Karna boasts he will conquer the earth alone and humble Bhishma.

Karna sets out on a campaign of conquest, subduing Drupada, the northern and Himalayan kings, the eastern and southern lands, and the Yavana kings in the west. He returns to Hastinapura with great tribute, and Duryodhana honours him with praise. The city is divided in its response, and Karna then bows to Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, who embrace him, and the Kuru princes begin to believe the Pandavas already defeated.

Karna tells Duryodhana that the earth is now free of enemies, and Duryodhana proposes to hold the Rajasuya sacrifice that the Pandavas performed. The priest refuses, since Yudhishthira and Dhritarashtra are still alive, and suggests the Vaishnava sacrifice instead, to be ploughed with gold tribute. Duryodhana agrees, and craftsmen begin to make the sacrificial plough.

Duryodhana's sacrifice begins with its rites, with Dhritarashtra, Vidura, Bhishma and Karna delighted. Dussasana sends a messenger to the Pandavas in the Dwaita forest to invite them. Yudhishthira declines to attend until his vow ends, and Bhima answers with a threat against Duryodhana, while Vidura entertains the guests.

After the sacrifice, the citizens praise Duryodhana, and Karna vows that he will not wash his feet or eat meat until he has slain Arjuna. Spies bring word of this vow to the Pandavas, who grow anxious and resolve to leave the Dwaita woods. Meanwhile Duryodhana rules the earth with his brothers and his elders, giving gifts to Brahmanas.

Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did in the forest after rescuing Duryodhana. Yudhishthira dreams that the surviving deer, the last of their herd, plead with him to leave the forest. Moved by pity, he resolves to take his brothers to the Kamyaka forest.

The Pandavas spend eleven years in misery, and Yudhishthira blames himself for their suffering. The sage Vyasa visits and teaches that happiness and sorrow alternate and that asceticism, truth and self-control bring merit. Yudhishthira asks whether charity or asceticism is greater, and Vyasa answers that charity is the harder discipline, then tells the story of Mudgala.

Yudhishthira asks why and to whom Mudgala gave a drona of corn, and Vyasa describes Mudgala as a sage who lives by gleaning and feeds his guests generously. The fierce sage Durvasa comes repeatedly to test him, and Mudgala stays calm and generous each time. A celestial chariot then arrives to take Mudgala to heaven, and he asks the messenger about its pleasures and drawbacks before going.

The celestial messenger describes the splendours of heaven, but also its drawbacks: one must exhaust one's merit and fall back, with regret and fear. Mudgala rejects heaven and asks for a region free from such faults, and the messenger describes the supreme seat of Vishnu, which Mudgala attains in liberation. Vyasa then consoles Yudhishthira, telling him that the kingdom will return after the thirteenth year, and goes back to his hermitage.

Janamejaya asks how Duryodhana treated the Pandavas in the forest. Duryodhana, hearing they live happily there, plots harm with Karna and Dussasana, and Durvasa arrives with ten thousand disciples to test the prince, who serves him patiently. Duryodhana asks the sage to visit Yudhishthira after Draupadi has eaten, and the conspirators celebrate the plan.

Durvasa arrives at the Pandavas' hermitage after Draupadi has already eaten, and Yudhishthira asks him to return after his bath. Draupadi, anxious about the missing food, prays to Krishna, who appears, eats the last grain left in the sun-given vessel, and sends Bhima to invite the sages. The sages, filled up and fearing the Pandavas' wrath, flee, and Krishna reassures the Pandavas before departing.

The Pandavas hunt in the Kamyaka forest, leaving Draupadi alone at the hermitage. Jayadratha, king of Sindhu, on his way to seek a bride in Salwa, sees her and is seized with desire, and he sends his companion Kotika to find out who she is.

Kotika approaches Draupadi, asks who she is and where her family comes from, and introduces himself as Suratha's son. He names his companions, including Kshemankara of Trigarta and Jayadratha, king of Sauvira, who is nearby with a large army, and asks Draupadi to say whose wife and daughter she is.

Draupadi answers Kotika, saying that although it is not proper for a woman to speak to a stranger alone, she will introduce herself. She is Drupada's daughter and the wife of the five Pandavas, who have gone hunting in the four directions, and she invites the visitors to dismount and await a welcome from her husbands. She then enters her cottage.

Kotika reports the encounter to Jayadratha, who is captivated by Draupadi and resolves to make her his own. Kotika tells him she is Drupada's daughter and the Pandavas' wife, but Jayadratha is undeterred. Jayadratha then goes to the hermitage himself and presses his suit.

Draupadi denounces Jayadratha in fury and warns that the Pandavas will destroy him. When he seizes her and drags her toward his chariot, she struggles and calls upon Dhaumya, who warns Jayadratha that he will pay for the deed. Dhaumya then follows the ravisher's army as Draupadi is carried away.

The Pandavas return from hunting, and Yudhishthira reads omens of trouble in the forest, including a jackal's cry that suggests the Kurus have turned to violence. At the hermitage they find Draupadi's maid weeping, and she tells them that Jayadratha has carried Draupadi off and urges them to pursue at once. Yudhishthira bids her be silent, and the brothers follow the tracks, rushing to rescue her.

Jayadratha, seeing the Pandava banners, asks Draupadi to name her husbands. She describes each brother, from Yudhishthira's virtue to Bhima's vengeance, Arjuna's steadiness and the twins' gifts, and warns that Jayadratha will be destroyed. The five brothers then fall on the enemy charioteers, darkening the air with arrows.

The Pandavas attack Jayadratha's army and slaughter many of its warriors, though Yudhishthira is wounded, and Jayadratha flees, leaving Draupadi behind. Bhima wants to pursue and kill him, but Yudhishthira asks him to spare the king for the sake of their sister Dussala. Draupadi urges her husbands to slay the wretch, and the brothers set off after him.

Bhima seizes Jayadratha, humiliates him, and forces him to declare himself a slave of the Pandavas, and Yudhishthira then frees him with a rebuke. Jayadratha, seeking revenge, obtains a boon from Shiva that he may check the Pandavas for a single day, except Arjuna. Shiva explains Arjuna's divine powers and recounts Vishnu's incarnations, and then vanishes with Uma while Jayadratha returns home.

Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after Draupadi's abduction. Yudhishthira, having rescued her, asks the sage Markandeya whether anyone has suffered as much as he and his brothers have, given the innocence of Draupadi and the trials of their exile.

Markandeya tells Yudhishthira that Rama also suffered when Ravana carried off his wife Sita, and that Rama recovered her with Sugriva's help. Yudhishthira asks about Rama's birth, his might, and Ravana's ancestry and quarrel with him. Markandeya begins the tale with Rama's royal family and the origins of Sita and Ravana.

Markandeya tells how the Rishi Visrava's three Rakshasa wives bear him sons, including Ravana, Kumbhakarna and Vibhishana. The brothers perform severe penances, and Brahma grants Ravana protection from all beings except men and grants Vibhishana immortality for his righteousness. Ravana then defeats his half-brother Kubera, takes Lanka and the Pushpaka chariot, and earns the name Ravana for terrorising the world.

The sages, gods and Siddhas, led by Agni, beg Brahma to protect them from Ravana, who cannot be killed because of his boon. Brahma replies that Ravana's death is near and that Vishnu will incarnate to achieve it. He then orders the gods to beget monkey and bear sons as Vishnu's allies, and sends a Gandharva woman to be reborn as the hunchback Manthara to stir up trouble.

Yudhishthira asks why Rama, Lakshmana and Sita were sent into exile. Markandeya describes Rama's virtues and Dasaratha's plan to make him regent, which Kaikeyi's maid Manthara turns into a plot against Rama. Kaikeyi claims two boons, making her son Bharata king and sending Rama away for fourteen years, and Dasaratha dies of grief while Rama is in the forest.

Ravana asks Maricha to help him by taking the form of a golden deer to lure Rama away from Sita. Maricha agrees, and Ravana disguises himself as an ascetic, while Rama and Lakshmana are drawn off in pursuit of the deer. Ravana seizes Sita, who refuses him, and flies off with her as the vulture Jatayu watches in distress.

The vulture Jatayu, a friend of Dasaratha, tries to free Sita from Ravana and is mortally wounded after his wings are cut off, while Sita drops her ornaments and cloth for her husband to find. Rama and Lakshmana return to find her gone, and the dying Jatayu points them south toward Ravana. They then kill a headless Rakshasa, who is revealed to be a Gandharva under a Brahmana's curse, and he directs them to seek Sugriva's friendship at Pampa.

Rama, grieving for Sita, is roused by Lakshmana and goes to Rishyamuka, where he allies with Sugriva. Rama kills Vali from hiding and Sugriva takes back the monkey kingdom. In Lanka, Sita is held in an Asoka grove under guard, and Trijata comforts her with a message of hope and a dream of Ravana's fall. The section matters because it sets up the alliance that will carry the war against Ravana.

Ravana comes to Sita in the Asoka grove, filled with desire, and boasts of his power, wealth and lineage to win her as his queen. Sita firmly refuses, saying she belongs to her husband and reproaching him for shaming his brother, the lord of treasures. Ravana vanishes, and Sita remains in grief under Trijata's care. The episode shows Sita's unbending loyalty to Rama and sets Ravana's pride against it.

Rama, still longing for Sita, sends Lakshmana to remind Sugriva of his pledge, and Sugriva says his monkeys are searching the whole earth. The searchers in the north, east and west find nothing, but the southern party returns with news. Hanuman reports that he found Sita in Lanka and carried back a token from her. The section matters because it turns the search into a known location for Sita and sets up the march on Lanka.

The monkey and bear armies gather around Rama and march to the southern sea. Since the sea is too wide to cross by boat, Rama prays to the Ocean, which agrees to let Nala's bridge carry the army across. Vibhishana, Ravana's brother, comes over to Rama and is made king of the Rakshasas. The army crosses to Lanka, and spies are caught and sent back, and Angada is sent as envoy to Ravana.

Ravana strengthens Lanka with trenches, stakes, catapults and armed guards. Angada delivers Rama's challenge in the king's court, and Ravana's men try to seize him, but he escapes and returns to Rama. The armies then clash at the walls: Rama's forces break down the ramparts and fight fiercely with the Rakshasas, and the monkeys withdraw after damaging the defenses. The section marks the outbreak of open war at Lanka.

Ravana's lesser demons slip into the monkey camp invisibly, but Vibhishana sees through the spell and they are killed. Ravana then marches out in formation and the armies meet, with Rama, Lakshmana and others each matched against a chosen foe. The section marks the start of the full battle of Lanka.

Prahasta attacks Vibhishana with a mace, but Vibhishana kills him with an enchanted javelin. Dhumraksha then drives back the monkeys until Hanuman turns the fight and kills him. Ravana, grieving, wakes his sleeping brother Kumbhakarna and sends him into battle, with the younger brothers Vajravega and Promathin joining. The section shows Ravana's army losing its leaders and Ravana turning to his last strong warrior.

Kumbhakarna devours several monkey leaders and seizes Sugriva, but Lakshmana wounds him with an arrow and cuts off his arms as they grow back. A Brahma weapon from Lakshmana finally kills him. Hanuman and Nala then kill Vajravega and Promathin, but the fighting goes on with heavy losses to the Rakshasas. The section records the fall of Ravana's strongest warrior.

Ravana, hearing of the deaths, sends his son Indrajit to end the war by killing Rama, Sugriva and Lakshmana. Indrajit challenges Lakshmana, and their duel goes back and forth until Angada wrecks Indrajit's chariot with a tree. Indrajit vanishes by illusion and shoots down Rama and Lakshmana. The section shows Indrajit's power of illusion as the main threat to the brothers.

Indrajit binds Rama and Lakshmana in a net of arrows, but Vibhishana revives them, and Sugriva's healing and a sacred water sent by Kuvera let them see the invisible. Indrajit returns to battle and Lakshmana kills him with three fiery arrows. Ravana, grieving, rushes to kill Sita, but Avindhya talks him out of it by urging him to kill Rama instead. The section shows Rama's side recovering and Ravana's rage turning toward Sita.

Ravana, enraged by his son's death, attacks with illusory warriors that Rama's arrows overcome. Matali brings Indra's chariot, and Vibhishana assures Rama that it is real, so Rama rides out to face Ravana. After a long duel, Rama fires a Brahma weapon that burns Ravana and his chariot to nothing. The section marks the death of Ravana and the end of the war's central conflict.

With Ravana dead, the gods honor Rama, who gives Lanka to Vibhishana. Rama then coldly doubts Sita's purity, and she is crushed; the gods, Brahma and Dasaratha among them, declare her innocent, so Rama takes her back. Rama returns to Ayodhya on the Pushpaka chariot, is reunited with Bharata, is crowned, and performs ten horse-sacrifices. The section closes the Ramayana episode with the restoration of Rama's family and kingdom.

Markandeya consoles Yudhishthira by pointing out that Rama and other heroes also endured hardship and that Yudhishthira has powerful brothers and allies. He urges the king to stop grieving and act as a warrior should. Yudhishthira is comforted and speaks again to Markandeya. The passage links Rama's trials to the Pandavas' own exile.

Yudhishthira says he grieves most for Draupadi, who once saved the brothers at the dice game and was carried off by Jayadratha, and asks whether Markandeya knows a more faithful lady. Markandeya begins the tale of Savitri, daughter of the Madra king Aswapati, who was born through a boon from the goddess Savitri after years of devotion. The girl grows beautiful, and when no suitor comes forward, her father tells her to choose a husband herself. The section introduces the theme of a wife's devotion.

Narada visits King Aswapati, who asks where his daughter has been. Savitri names Satyavan, son of the blind, exiled king Dyumatsena, and Narada praises his virtues. Narada then warns that Satyavan is fated to die within a year, but Savitri refuses to choose another man, and Narada approves the match. Aswapati accepts and prepares the wedding, setting up Satyavan's early death and Savitri's devotion.

King Aswapati brings Savitri to the hermitage of the blind, exiled Dyumatsena and asks that she be married to Satyavan. Dyumatsena hesitates because of their poverty, but Aswapati insists and the wedding is held with due rites. Savitri lives in the hermitage as a devoted wife, pleasing everyone, but Narada's warning never leaves her mind. The section sets up the fated death that will test her.

The fated day arrives. Savitri, who has counted the days, observes a three-night fast and receives the hermitage's blessing that she will never be widowed. When Satyavan goes into the forest with his axe, she insists on going with him despite her fast, and her in-laws give permission. She walks beside him through the woods, grieving and expecting his death at that hour. The scene builds the suspense that drives the next part of the story.

In the forest Satyavan falls ill from head pain and dies in Savitri's lap when Yama comes to take him. Savitri follows Yama and, through a series of replies on duty and righteousness, wins boons: sight and a restored kingdom for Dyumatsena, sons for her father, and a hundred sons for herself and Satyavan. Yama then restores Satyavan's life, and the couple sets out for the hermitage at night. The section is the turning point of Savitri's tale, showing her wisdom and devotion.

Dyumatsena regains his sight and searches the hermitages for his lost son, while the sages assure him that Satyavan must be alive. Satyavan and Savitri return at night, and Savitri explains how she won Yama's boons, including Satyavan's life. The sages praise her for rescuing the family's fortunes. The story ends Savitri's test and shows the reward of her devotion.

Messengers from Salwa report that the usurper has been killed by his own minister and invite Dyumatsena back to his throne. He is restored, with Satyavan as prince-regent, and Savitri later bears a hundred sons. Markandeya says Draupadi can likewise rescue the Pandavas. Yudhishthira, encouraged by the tale, continues to live in the Kamyaka forest.

Janamejaya asks why Yudhishthira feared Karna and why he kept that fear to himself. Vaisampayana explains that in the thirteenth year of exile Indra planned to beg Karna's earrings for the Pandavas, and that Surya warned Karna in a dream. Karna refuses to break his vow of giving, saying fame is worth more than his life. The passage sets up the loss of Karna's protection.

Surya urges Karna not to give up his earrings and armor. He argues that fame is of no use to the dead, that Karna should refuse Indra's request, and that with the earrings Karna could not be defeated by Arjuna. The advice shows Surya's protective concern and the stakes of the coming bargain.

Karna tells Surya that he cannot lie, would rather die than be untruthful, and will give his earrings and armor to any Brahmana who asks. Surya then advises him to demand an infallible dart from Indra in return, since such a dart never misses. Surya vanishes, and Karna tells him of the dream the next morning and waits for Indra's visit. The chapter ends with Karna set on his course.

Janamejaya asks what secret Surya kept from Karna and where Karna's earrings and armor came from. Vaisampayana explains that a fierce Brahmana once came to King Kuntibhoja asking to stay as his guest. The king entrusts the Brahmana's care to his adopted daughter Pritha, and the girl is told to serve him with great care. The section opens the story of how Karna was born and why his armor and earrings matter.

Pritha, now called Kunti, promises the king she will serve the Brahmana faithfully, saying that Brahmanas bring blessings when pleased and ruin when angered. Kuntibhoja gives the Brahmana fine quarters and asks Kunti to forgive any lapses. Kunti then takes up her duty with complete devotion, treating the guest as a god.

Kunti serves the Brahmana for a full year, providing food, bed and seat at all hours, though he often returns late or scolds her. Pleased, the Brahmana offers her a boon, but she says she already has everything she needs. He then teaches her a mantra that can summon any god who will serve her. The episode establishes the mantra that drives the next events.

Kunti, curious about the mantra, tests it while she is still unmarried, summoning the rising sun. Surya appears and insists that she yield to him, threatening her and her father with his anger and a curse. Kunti, bewildered by the celestial gods watching, begs him to go away. Surya argues that a maiden has her own freedom and refuses to leave without his purpose.

Kunti cannot dissuade Surya, fears for her father and the Brahmana, and finally agrees on condition that her son be born with armor and earrings. Surya promises a son with invulnerable armor and earrings made of Amrita, which he says came from Aditi. He enters her by yoga and leaves her a mother who remains a virgin, and when he departs she regains consciousness. The passage is the birth of Karna, the central tragedy of the Mahabharata.

Pritha, hiding her pregnancy, gives birth to a son who is born with armor and earrings. Fearing disgrace, she sets the child adrift in a box on the river Aswa, praying for his protection. The box drifts down the rivers to the Ganga and reaches the city of Champa, where the child survives because of his armor, earrings and destiny. The episode explains how the future Karna was abandoned at birth.

The charioteer Adhiratha and his childless wife Radha find the box in the Ganga, see the golden-armored infant, and adopt him as their son, naming him Vasusena and Vrisha. The boy grows up in the Anga kingdom, is trained by Drona, befriends Duryodhana and becomes a rival of Arjuna. Pritha learns of his life through spies. The section establishes Karna's upbringing and his enmity toward the Pandavas.

Indra comes disguised as a Brahmana while Karna is worshipping at noon and asks for his armor and earrings. Karna offers many other gifts, but refuses to give up the armor and earrings that make him unslayable. Indra admits that Surya warned Karna, and in exchange gives an infallible dart. Karna cuts his armor and earrings from his body, earns the name Karna, and Indra departs. The Kauravas are dismayed and the Pandavas rejoice, and the scene turns to the Pandavas returning to Dwaitavana.

The Pandavas settle in the forest of Dwaitavana. A deer runs off with a Brahmana's fire-sticks and churning staff, and the brothers chase it in vain, growing tired and thirsty. They rest under a banyan tree, and Nakula asks why disaster has come to them, since their house has never abandoned virtue. The section starts a new book on the forest and sets up the trouble ahead.

Weary and thirsty in the forest, the Pandavas reflect on the causes of their misfortunes, each brother blaming a past failure. Yudhishthira sends his brothers one by one to fetch water, and each drinks from a lake without answering an invisible being's questions and falls dead. Bhima too dies after drinking, and Yudhishthira, worried, goes to search and comes upon a beautiful lake. The episode sets up his meeting with the Yaksha at the lake.

Yudhishthira mourns his four dead brothers, recalls the prophecies that promised their success, and wonders who could have killed them. Before drinking, he goes to bathe in the lake, where a Yaksha, disguised as a crane, warns him and claims to have killed the brothers. Yudhishthira answers the Yaksha's long run of questions on duty, learning, wealth and conduct, and when offered one brother's life, he chooses Nakula out of fairness to both of his father's wives. The Yaksha is pleased and restores all the brothers. The episode is the Pandavas' great test of wisdom and of fair dealing.

The Yaksha reveals himself as Dharma, the Lord of justice and Yudhishthira's father, who had taken the fire-sticks in the form of a deer to test his son. He grants the Brahmana's fire-sticks back, promises that the Pandavas will spend their thirteenth year unrecognized in Virata's kingdom, and praises Yudhishthira's steadiness of virtue. The brothers wake refreshed and return the fire-sticks to the Brahmana, and the text closes with a promise of rewards for hearing this story. The passage ends the forest-exile test and sends the brothers into their year in disguise.

Yudhishthira asks the ascetics for leave to spend the thirteenth year of exile in disguise and, overcome with grief, nearly faints. Dhaumya and Bhima encourage him with examples of gods and heroes who hid successfully and went on to win. The Brahmanas bless the Pandavas and leave, and the brothers set out with Krishna to plan their year of concealment. The rest of this chunk is the translator's footnotes and the Project Gutenberg license, which are not part of the epic's narrative.

Janamejaya asks how his ancestors and Draupadi stayed hidden in Virata's city. Vaisampayana explains that after the asylum period Yudhishthira called his brothers together to choose a place for the thirteenth year of exile. Arjuna lists the neighboring kingdoms, and Yudhishthira settles on Matsya under King Virata, planning a disguise for each brother. The chapter sets up the whole plan of concealment that the rest of the Virata Parva follows.

Bhima chooses to pass as the cook Vallava and plans to show his strength through wrestling and fights with wild animals, while sparing the lives of his opponents. Yudhishthira then names Arjuna's famous feats at length and asks what role the great archer will take. Arjuna answers that he will appear as a eunuch named Vrihannala who teaches dance and song to the palace women, hiding his bowstring scars under bangles.

Yudhishthira asks Nakula and Sahadeva what roles they will take, and both choose work with animals. Nakula will look after horses under the name Granthika, and Sahadeva will tend cattle as Tantripala. Yudhishthira then worries about Draupadi, who has never done ordinary work, and Draupadi proposes to serve Queen Sudeshna as a hairdresser. Yudhishthira agrees but warns her to guard her conduct so that wicked men are not drawn to her.

Yudhishthira sends his priest, cooks and charioteers to Drupada's realm, and Draupadi's maids to the Panchalas, while Indrasena and others head to Dwaravati. Dhaumya then gives a long set of rules for living in a king's household, covering how to speak, sit, and act around the ruler. Yudhishthira thanks him, and Dhaumya performs the departure rites and takes the sacred fires away. The brothers set out with Draupadi, and the household servants go their own separate ways.

The Pandavas, disguised as hunters, cross the Yamuna and enter Matsya, and Arjuna carries the weary Draupadi near the city. Yudhishthira worries that bearing their famous weapons into the city would reveal them, so Arjuna suggests hiding them in a Sami tree near a cemetery. The brothers hide the bows and weapons, hang up a corpse to keep people away, and take new names for the year. The chapter ends with them entering the city as planned.

On the way to Virata's city, Yudhishthira prays to the goddess Durga, naming her many forms and asking for protection. The goddess appears and promises that the Pandavas will win the war and regain the earth. She also says that the Kurus' spies and the people of Matsya will fail to recognize them while they stay in Virata's city. The prayer gives the brothers divine cover for the disguised year.

Yudhishthira arrives at Virata's court looking like a king in hiding, carrying golden dice. Virata cannot place him, and Yudhishthira presents himself as the Brahmana Kanka, a skilled dice player and former friend of Yudhishthira. Virata makes him a close companion with wide powers, and Yudhishthira asks for protection from quarrels over dice, which Virata grants. Kanka then lives in the court without being recognized.

Bhima enters Virata's court disguised as a cook, carrying a ladle, a spoon and a dark sword, and shining like the sun. Virata cannot tell who he is, but Bhima presents himself as the cook Vallava and offers to work in the kitchen. He adds that he is also a wrestler who fights lions and elephants, and Virata gives him charge of the royal kitchen. Bhima rises in the king's favour without being recognized.

Draupadi, dressed as a hairdresser in a single soiled cloth, wanders the city offering her services. Queen Sudeshna sees her from a terrace, is struck by her beauty, and asks who she really is. Draupadi says she serves as a hairdresser and claims that her five Gandharva husbands guard her, so no one can take her. Sudeshna takes her into the household on condition that she never touches another's leftovers or washes their feet.

Sahadeva, dressed as a cowherd, comes to the royal cattle pens, and Virata is struck by his bearing. He calls himself Arishtanemi, a Vaisya who once tended the Pandavas' herds and would serve no master but the king. When Virata doubts he is only a herdsman, Sahadeva describes his old work and his knowledge of cattle, and the king puts a hundred thousand cows under his care. Sahadeva lives there, and no one but his brothers recognize him.

Arjuna appears at the court in women's ornaments and a braid, tall and commanding, so the king takes him for a noble and offers him a place. Arjuna calls himself Vrihannala, a singer and dancer, and asks to teach the princess Uttara. Virata agrees, but first has him tested in arts and examined by women, who confirm his condition. Arjuna then teaches music and dance in the women's quarters and goes unrecognized.

A fourth brother, Nakula, arrives at Virata's court and catches the king's eye by studying his horses. He offers his services as a horse trainer under the name Granthika, and Virata puts him in charge of all the royal horses and their keepers. Virata says he admires Nakula's bearing and wishes Yudhishthira were there. The chapter closes with the brothers living in Matsya, respected and still unrecognized.

Janamejaya asks what the Kuru princes did while living in disguise in Matsya. Vaisampayana describes how each brother earns a place: Yudhishthira wins at dice for the king, Bhima cooks and fights, Arjuna teaches the women, and the twins serve with horses and cattle. At a festival in the fourth month, Bhima defeats the champion wrestler Jimuta in a famous bout, and each brother is rewarded by Virata.

After ten months, Kichaka, the commander of Virata's army and Sudeshna's brother, becomes obsessed with Draupadi when he sees her serving in the queen's rooms. He makes a long and lustful proposal, offering wealth and status, and Draupadi refuses. She reminds him that she is married and that her Gandharva husbands would kill him if he persisted. Kichaka does not give up and claims power over the realm, and Draupadi warns him again of the danger he is courting.

Kichaka begs Sudeshna to help him win Draupadi, and Sudeshna arranges a plan: he is to prepare a feast of food and wine, and she will send the maid to fetch wine at his house. Draupadi objects, pointing out Kichaka's shamelessness and her vow to her husbands, but Sudeshna promises she will be safe. Draupadi prays to the Sun god, who sends a Rakshasa to guard her, while Kichaka rises in delight at her arrival.

Kichaka seizes Draupadi in the court and kicks her in front of the assembled men, and a Rakshasa sent by Surya knocks him senseless. Bhima's anger rises, but Yudhishthira holds him back to protect their disguise, and Draupadi denounces Virata and his court for allowing the insult. The courtiers condemn Kichaka and praise her, and Yudhishthira sends her to Sudeshna's apartments, where she vows to see Kichaka dragged down.

Still stung by the insult, Draupadi bathes and thinks about how to get her revenge, deciding that only Bhima can do it. At night she goes to his quarters and finds him in the kitchen. She wakes him and asks how he can sleep while Kichaka lives, and Bhima asks her what she needs.

Draupadi answers Bhima by listing the humiliations she and the brothers have suffered. She blames Yudhishthira's loss at dice for their fall, and she contrasts his former splendour at Indraprastha with his present life as the courtier Kanka. Her speech is a sustained lament over the brothers' loss of status and her own grief.

Draupadi continues her plea to Bhima by describing how painfully each brother has been reduced to a humbling role. Bhima works as a cook and fights beasts for the women's amusement, Arjuna teaches dance and song as Vrihannala, Sahadeva tends cows, and Nakula handles the king's horses. She also reports that Sudeshna and her women mock her, suspecting her of favouring Bhima, and the chapter ends with her grief at how the brothers must live.

Draupadi tells Bhima how far the brothers have fallen: she serves Sudeshna, grinds sandal for others, and fears Virata, and her hands are now marked with calluses. She clings to hope that fortune will turn when the year ends, since fate rises and falls like a wheel. Bhima, moved by her grief, covers his face with her hands and weeps with her.

Bhima answers Draupadi by cursing his own strength and Arjuna's bow for her hardship, and he admits he would have killed Kichaka if Yudhishthira had not restrained him with a look. Draupadi, though she does not blame Yudhishthira, repeats the story of Kichaka's pursuit, Sudeshna's jealousy, and the kick in the court, and she demands that Bhima kill him or she will take poison. Bhima consoles her, and then turns to his anger against Kichaka.

Bhima and Draupadi plot to lure Kichaka to the empty dance hall, where Bhima waits for him at night. Kichaka arrives expecting Draupadi, boasts of his wealth and beauty, and Bhima overpowers and kills him after a long wrestling struggle. The Kichakas then try to burn Draupadi on Kichaka's pyre, but Bhima uproots a tree and kills their kin, and the total slain reaches 106 with Kichaka. The episode ends Draupadi's persecution and makes the court marvel at the feat.

Citizens report the deaths of the Sutas to Virata, who orders the Kichakas cremated and sends a message to Draupadi through Sudeshna, saying she may go wherever she likes. Draupadi returns to the city, where people flee in fear, and she greets Bhima as a Gandharva who saved her. In the dance hall she meets Arjuna and the princesses, and when Sudeshna brings the king's message she asks for thirteen more days before she leaves.

News of Kichaka's killing spreads through the provinces, and people praise both Vallava and the dead commander as warriors. Duryodhana's spies return from their search having found no trace of the Pandavas, and they report that the charioteers reached Dwaravati without them. They tell Duryodhana that Kichaka's death by Gandharvas gives the Kauravas a fresh opportunity against Virata.

Duryodhana reflects that most of the hidden year is over and orders his courtiers to find the Pandavas before they return. Karna urges more spies, sent in disguise to every likely place. Duhsasana doubts the search will succeed and suggests the brothers may have perished or fled abroad, but he advises Duryodhana to act with energy.

Drona argues that the Pandavas cannot be destroyed, since they are brave, disciplined and loyal to Yudhishthira's virtue and wisdom. He advises a renewed search using Brahmanas, Charanas and ascetics who know the brothers.

Bhishma agrees with Drona about the Pandavas' virtue but advises against using spies to hunt them now. He describes at length how the land where Yudhishthira dwells would prosper, with good rain, harvests, cattle and honest people. He ends by urging Duryodhana to act wisely and honestly.

Kripa agrees with Bhishma but says Duryodhana should not ignore the Pandavas, since even a minor foe must be watched. He urges Duryodhana to track them by spies, learn his own strength and that of his allies, and build up his army and treasury before the brothers return. He then advises him to choose between fighting and making a treaty.

Susarman, the Trigarta king whom Kichaka had repeatedly defeated, urges Duryodhana to invade Virata's kingdom now that Kichaka is dead. Karna supports the plan and says the Pandavas are either gone or dead. Duryodhana orders the Trigartas to strike first at Virata's cattle, with the Kauravas following a day later, and both armies move out.

The Pandavas complete their year in disguise, and Virata, relying on them after Kichaka's death, learns that Susarman has seized thousands of his cattle. A herdsman brings the news to court, and Virata arms his brothers and sons, and orders chariots and armour for the disguised Pandavas. The brothers ride out with the king's army, which marches after the cattle tracks.

The Matsyas and the Trigartas clash at sunset in a huge battle that leaves the field strewn with dead and wounded men. Satanika and Visalaksha break deep into the Trigarta ranks, and Virata duels with Susarman, wounding him and being wounded in turn. Dust and arrows hide the field, and the fighting stops at nightfall with neither side the clear winner.

After a pause in the night fighting, the moon rises and the battle resumes, and Susarman and his brother seize Virata and carry him off. Yudhishthira urges Bhima to rescue the king, and Bhima, who wants to uproot a tree as a weapon, is told to use ordinary arms so that he is not recognized. Bhima routs the Trigartas, binds Susarman, and Yudhishthira then frees him on the condition that he declare himself a slave in every assembly.

Shamed by his defeat, Susarman goes home, and Virata thanks the Pandavas with gems, wealth and an offer of rule over the Matsyas. Yudhishthira answers graciously, and Virata sends messengers to proclaim his victory in the city, and the proclamation is made at sunrise.

While Virata is away chasing the Trigartas, Duryodhana's army invades Matsya, drives off the cowherds, and seizes sixty thousand cows. A chief cowherd rushes to the city and urges Virata's son Bhuminjaya to ride out and win back the herds, comparing his bow to a lute. The prince then begins to boast among the women of the palace.

Uttara, Virata's son, laments that his charioteer died in the earlier battle and says he could recover the cattle if he had a skilled driver. Arjuna, speaking privately to Draupadi, suggests that Vrihannala, once Arjuna's charioteer, be asked. Draupadi reluctantly vouches for Vrihannala's skill, but Uttara doubts a eunuch can drive, so Draupadi says Vrihannala will obey Uttara's younger sister, and the sister is sent to fetch him from the dance hall.

Virata's daughter, Uttara's sister, hurries to the dance hall and begs Arjuna, disguised as Vrihannala, to drive her brother's chariot against the Kurus. Arjuna first protests that he knows only singing, dancing and music, then pretends to be clumsy with the armour, and the maidens laugh until Uttara arms him himself. The women bless the chariot as it sets out, and Arjuna promises them cloth for their dolls if the battle goes well.

Uttara drives toward the Kuru army, but when he sees its size and its great warriors he is terrified and begs Vrihannala to turn back. Vrihannala rebukes him, Uttara jumps down and runs, and Arjuna chases him, his braid and red garments flying, which amuses some Kuru soldiers. The Kurus wonder whether the runner could be Arjuna, Arjuna catches Uttara and calms him, and forces the frightened prince back into the chariot.

The Kuru leaders see the figure in women's dress driving toward a Sami tree and fear that it is Arjuna. Drona reads a series of bad omens and identifies the driver by his many names and epithets, urging his men to stay on guard. Karna scoffs at Arjuna's worth, and Duryodhana says that if this is Arjuna the Pandavas will have to return to the forest, while a eunuch in disguise can be struck down; the Kuru elders applaud his courage.

At the Sami tree, Arjuna tells Uttara, who is still inexperienced, to climb it and bring down the Pandavas' bows. He explains that the bows hidden there, including the Gandiva, are the only ones strong enough for his own use.

Uttara objects to climbing the tree, since he has heard a corpse is tied in it and touching one would defile a prince. Arjuna assures him that there are only bows in the tree and no corpse, and Uttara climbs reluctantly. As he cuts the bindings and uncovers the weapons, they shine like the sun and frighten him, and he turns to Arjuna with a question.

Holding the weapons, Uttara asks Vrihannala whose they are, one by one, naming the bows, arrows, quivers and swords with their golden and animal decorations. He is struck by their beauty and wonders aloud who could own such a collection.

Arjuna, still disguised as Vrihannala, names the owners of each weapon. He identifies the Gandiva as his own, recounts how it passed through Shiva, Prajapati, Sakra, Soma and Varuna before he obtained it, and then assigns the other bows, arrows, quivers and swords to Yudhishthira, Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva.

Uttara admires the weapons and asks where the Pandavas are now. Arjuna reveals that he is Arjuna and names his brothers' court disguises, along with the Draupadi who is serving as the Sairindhri. Uttara asks for proof, so Arjuna recites his ten names and explains the origin of several of them. Convinced, Uttara apologizes for his earlier doubts and welcomes him.

Uttara offers to drive Arjuna into the enemy ranks, and Arjuna promises to rout the Kurus, describing his chariot as a fortress with its own walls and gates. Arjuna explains that his eunuch disguise was a year-long vow kept at his elder brother's command. Uttara praises him and names the horses, and Arjuna prepares for battle, summons his weapons and sounds the Gandiva, which frightens Uttara, who fears the size of the Kuru army. Arjuna answers by recalling his past battles against gods and demons.

Arjuna circles the Sami tree, takes down the lion banner and raises his own ape banner, a celestial gift. When he sounds his conch the horses kneel and Uttara sinks down in fear, and Arjuna comforts him and sounds the conch again. Drona, watching from the Kuru side, reads the omens as signs of disaster and says the driver must be Savyasachin.

Duryodhana argues that if the approaching warrior is Arjuna, the Pandavas have broken their pledge and must go back to the forest for twelve more years. He urges an immediate fight regardless of who the warrior is. Karna dismisses Drona's warnings as partiality to Arjuna and urges the army to stand firm.

Karna declares that he alone will stand against the approaching warrior, whether Arjuna or the Matsya king. He boasts at length that his arrows will cover and defeat Arjuna, that he has gained weapons from Jamadagni's son, and that he will hurl Arjuna from his chariot. He ends by saying the Kauravas may take the cattle or stay and watch.

Kripa warns Karna against fighting Arjuna alone, reminding him that Arjuna has rescued the Kurus from the Gandharvas, defeated many enemies single-handed and mastered the weapons under Indra. Kripa says Karna is like a fool who tries to take the fangs of a snake or swim the ocean with a stone around his neck. He urges the six great warriors to stand together with their troops in ranks, rather than facing Arjuna alone.

Ashvatthaman rebukes Karna's boasting, reminding him that the cattle are not yet won and that true heroes keep quiet about their deeds. He condemns Duryodhana's gains from dice as dishonest and recalls the insult to Draupadi, and he warns that Arjuna will destroy the Kurus. He tells Karna to use the same dice-tricks that won Indraprastha, and says he himself will fight the Matsya king rather than Arjuna.

Bhishma calls for unity, saying that Karna's boast was meant only to rally the army and that disunity among leaders is the worst calamity an army can suffer. Ashvatthaman replies that his father had praised Arjuna in anger, which is why he spoke. Duryodhana, with Karna, Kripa and Bhishma, urges Drona to forgive, and Drona agrees, asking that the army be arranged so that Arjuna cannot reach Duryodhana.

Bhishma works out the calendar and concludes that the Pandavas kept their promise, so Arjuna's appearance is lawful and battle cannot be avoided. Duryodhana refuses to return the kingdom and orders the preparations to go ahead. Bhishma advises the king to withdraw to the capital with a quarter of the army, send another quarter with the cattle, and fight with the rest, and then he arrays the troops around Drona, Ashvatthaman, Kripa and Karna.

Arjuna's chariot advances with a roar of its ape banner and the twang of the Gandiva, and Drona identifies Partha by his banner and bearing. Arjuna, suspecting that Duryodhana is retreating with the cattle by the southern road, asks Uttara to drive straight at the king. Kripa urges the Kuru warriors to counterattack, but Arjuna scatters their troops with arrows and conch-blasts, and the cattle turn back south.

Having recovered the cattle, Arjuna turns back to face the Kuru army, driving Uttara straight into the thick of it. He routs several warriors, kills Satruntapa, and drives Vikarna off the field. Karna then challenges him, and after a long archery duel Arjuna wounds Karna in many places until Karna quits the battle.

After Karna flees, the other Kuru warriors attack Arjuna, but his arrows fill the sky and scatter their ranks, and the field is littered with dead elephants and men. Arjuna holds back from killing the defenceless and instead strikes from behind, and the battlefield turns red as evening comes on. Uttara asks where to drive, and Arjuna names each Kuru leader by his banner, from Kripa and Drona through Duryodhana and Karna to Bhishma, who should be approached last.

Gods and heavenly beings come to watch the battle in their celestial chariots, led by Indra with his Vishvas and Maruts. The sky fills with divine light and fragrance, and the dust clears as Indra gazes at his son Arjuna and cannot look away.

Arjuna sends Uttara against Kripa, and the two sound their conches in challenge. Kripa and Arjuna shoot at each other, but Arjuna cuts Kripa's bows as fast as Kripa can string them, slays his horses and driver, and wounds him in the breast. When Kripa hurls a mace it is turned back, and Kripa's men try to rescue him, but Uttara wheels the chariot in circles to hold them off until Kripa is carried away.

Arjuna has Uttara drive toward Drona, praising the teacher's virtues and saying he will not strike unless he is struck first. Drona and Arjuna duel with celestial weapons, drawing admiration from the spectators on both sides. When Ashvatthaman charges at Arjuna, Arjuna turns to meet him, and Drona, wounded, withdraws from the field.

Ashvatthaman charges at Arjuna and the two fight fiercely while the sky is darkened by arrows. Ashvatthaman cuts the string of the Gandiva, and Arjuna restrings it and presses on, since Ashvatthaman's arrows soon run out. The Kurus cheer, and when Karna twangs his bow Arjuna turns to meet him.

Arjuna confronts Karna and reproaches him for his boasting and for watching Draupadi be humiliated in the court. Karna answers that Arjuna's words exceed his deeds and that he had been held back by morality, and Arjuna answers that Karna fled when his brother was slain. The two begin a duel, in which Arjuna cuts Karna's bow and steeds and wounds him in the breast, and Karna flees northward while Arjuna and Uttara taunt him.

Uttara, overwhelmed by the sights, sounds and stench of battle, says he can no longer hold the reins. Arjuna reassures him and tells him to stay steady as a prince of Matsya's line, then boasts of his divine weapons and vows to break the Kuru host. He drives toward Bhishma, cuts down Bhishma's banner, and when four Kuru princes attack him he wounds Duhsasana and Vikarna and kills the horses of Dussaha and Vivingsati, driving them off.

The Kuru warriors attack Arjuna together from every side, but he covers them in arrows, and elephants, horses and men fall in heaps. Their courage broken, the Kuru troops flee in terror, and Arjuna's arrows create a river of blood across the battlefield.

Bhishma, the grandsire, comes at Arjuna with his own bow and a shower of arrows, and the two fight with celestial weapons while the Kauravas and the gods watch. Arjuna cuts Bhishma's bow, umbrella and banner, and Bhishma repeatedly takes up a new bow and fights on. Indra and the Gandharva Chitrasena praise both warriors, but Arjuna finally wounds Bhishma in the breast, and Bhishma's charioteer carries him off the field.

Duryodhana attacks Arjuna and wounds him on the forehead, but Arjuna answers, slays Vikarna's elephant with a single iron arrow, and wounds Duryodhana in the breast. The Kuru army breaks and flees, and Duryodhana turns to run as well. Arjuna shames him for running away, reminds him of his royal duty, and urges him to turn back and fight.

Stung by Arjuna's taunts, Duryodhana turns his chariot back, and Karna, Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and the others close in to protect him. Arjuna stuns the whole Kuru army with a celestial weapon and his conch, then has Uttara strip the fallen warriors of their garments. Bhishma alone recovers and advises Duryodhana to go home, and Arjuna breaks Duryodhana's jewelled crown, salutes the elders, and sounds his conch as the Kurus depart.

Arjuna drives the recovered cattle back toward Virata's city, and a band of Kuru soldiers who had fled into the forest comes out and begs for mercy. Arjuna spares them and tells Uttara to claim the victory himself rather than praise the Pandavas, which might frighten Virata into hiding. Arjuna returns the weapons and the banner to the Sami tree, enters the city as Vrihannala, and sends word ahead, and the prince and his companions retrieve their garments from the tree before entering.

Virata returns in triumph with the Pandavas and learns that Uttara has gone out alone with only Vrihannala as driver. He sends a force after him, but Yudhishthira predicts victory, and news of the win arrives. Virata rejoices and turns to a game of dice with Kanka, but when Yudhishthira again praises Vrihannala the king strikes him with a die, drawing blood that Draupadi catches, and Yudhishthira warns that Uttara must come in without Vrihannala.

Uttara enters and finds Kanka bleeding and tended by Draupadi, and asks his father who struck him. Virata admits the blow, and Uttara begs him to make amends before a Brahmana's curse destroys him. Kanka forgives the king, and once the bleeding stops Vrihannala enters the court. Virata praises his son for defeating the greatest Kuru warriors.

Uttara tells his father that he did not win the battle himself, but that a celestial youth took the reins, drove him against the Kurus, and routed the great warriors, then challenged Duryodhana to fight. Virata asks to honour the youth who saved his cattle, but Uttara says the youth vanished and may return. Virata remains ignorant of Arjuna's identity, and Arjuna presents the new garments he has brought to Virata's daughter, delighting her and Uttara.

On the third day after the vow was completed, the five Pandavas enter Virata's council hall, bathed and finely dressed, and take their places on royal thrones. Virata, angry to see the dice-player Kanka seated like a king, demands to know how he dares.
