Arjuna answers with a long, teasing speech praising Yudhishthira's virtue, learning, power and wealth, and argues that he deserves the royal seat.

Virata asks which of the men is which, and Arjuna names each brother and Draupadi, recalling their deeds in the hidden year. Uttara describes the brothers' appearance and tells of Arjuna's great feats in the battle. Virata, feeling guilty for having wronged Yudhishthira, offers his daughter, also named Uttara, to Arjuna, and then begs forgiveness and makes an alliance with the Pandavas, offering Yudhishthira his kingdom, which Arjuna accepts on her behalf.

Virata offers his daughter to Arjuna, and Arjuna accepts her as a daughter-in-law for his son Abhimanyu, insisting that he lived with her in the palace without impropriety. The allies gather at Upaplavya, the wedding is celebrated with gifts and dowry, and Virata offers the Pandavas his kingdom and treasure. The allied kings gather in Virata's court the morning after Abhimanyu's wedding. Krishna reviews how the Pandavas were cheated at dice, served their exile, and endured the hidden thirteenth year, then argues they ask only for their rightful share. He proposes that a fair envoy be sent to Duryodhana before any war is considered. The chapter sets up the peace effort that drives the rest of the Udyoga Parva.

Balarama answers Krishna by urging peace: the Pandavas will give up half the kingdom, and an envoy should go to Duryodhana and to the elders with humble words. He recalls that Yudhishthira lost at dice through his own unskilled play and that Shakuni was not to blame. Satyaki then rises in anger to attack Balarama's position. The split between the peace party and the war party begins here.

Satyaki scolds Balarama for speaking softly and says the dice match was a trick, so Yudhishthira has no reason to beg. He vows to force Duryodhana to bow down through battle and lists the Pandava warriors and allies who would fight. He insists that Yudhishthira must get his kingdom back, or the enemy will fall in war. The chapter sharpens the case for war.

Drupada agrees with Satyaki that Duryodhana will not give up the kingdom peacefully. He still thinks the Pandavas should first send a message, but he advises against a mild approach and wants them to gather allies at once. He lists many kings to be called and names a priest to be sent to Dhritarashtra. The chapter shows the war camp beginning to prepare.

Krishna responds that the Pandavas' cause is just, but he asks Virata to send a message to the Kauravas before any fighting begins. He says that if the Kuru side refuses peace, the Pandavas will be called and Arjuna will act. Virata honors Krishna and sends him back to Dwaraka. The two camps then gather armies, and the chapter shows the war effort growing.

Drupada gives the priest detailed advice on how to approach Dhritarashtra. He says that the old king has knowingly followed his son, and that the envoy should stir up the elders and the soldiers so that the Kauravas lose heart. He tells the priest to leave at an auspicious time, while the Pandavas quietly prepare. The chapter ends with the priest setting out for Hastinapura with his followers.

Both Duryodhana and Arjuna travel to Dwaraka to ask Krishna for help in the coming war. Krishna is asleep when they arrive, and Arjuna is the first he sees. He offers his ten crore Narayana troops to one side and himself, unarmed, to the other, and Arjuna picks Krishna as his charioteer. Duryodhana takes the army and gains an extra force from Kritavarman, while Balarama refuses to fight for either side.

The king of the Madras, Salya, marches to join the Pandavas with a large army. Duryodhana secretly arranges lavish hospitality along the way, and Salya is so impressed that he offers a boon. Duryodhana asks him to lead the Kaurava army, and Salya agrees, then goes to visit Yudhishthira. There Yudhishthira asks him to weaken Karna in their future duel, and Salya agrees, though reluctantly, after consoling the Pandavas for their hardships.

Yudhishthira asks how Indra and his wife came to suffer great misery, and Salya tells the old myth in reply. Twashtri creates a three-headed son to rival Indra, and Indra has him tempted and then killed, first with a thunderbolt and then by a carpenter who cuts off his heads. Twashtri creates Vritra to destroy Indra, who is swallowed but escapes, and the gods finally turn to Vishnu for help. The story is told to console Yudhishthira that even gods suffer, and it ends before the Vritra battle is resolved.

Indra admits that Vritra has grown too strong for him, so the gods and sages go to Vishnu for help. Vishnu advises peace and says he will hide inside Indra's thunderbolt. The sages persuade Vritra to accept friendship, and he sets terms meant to keep him from being killed by any ordinary means. Indra kills him at dusk with a froth-covered thunderbolt that Vishnu animates, but Indra then falls into guilt for killing the holy man's son and hides, leaving the world without a king.

With Indra gone, the gods and sages make Nahusha king of heaven, and at first he is reluctant and then accepts. Once he holds power, he gives himself over to pleasure and lust. He then demands that Indra's queen Sachi come to his palace, and she takes refuge with the priest Vrihaspati, who promises to reunite her with Indra. Nahusha grows enraged at this refusal.

The gods try to calm Nahusha, who refuses to give up his demand for Sachi and argues that Indra himself was guilty of similar wrongs. They ask Vrihaspati to hand Sachi over, but he refuses to betray someone who has sought his protection and warns of the ruin that follows such betrayal. The gods then persuade Sachi to ask Nahusha for time, and she agrees to visit him.

Sachi asks Nahusha for time to look for Indra, and he agrees on condition that she come back. The gods turn to Vishnu, who tells Indra to perform a horse sacrifice to cleanse himself of the guilt for killing the holy man's son. Indra performs the rite and passes his guilt on to trees, rivers, mountains, earth and women. Still afraid of Nahusha, Indra vanishes again, and Sachi, grieving, calls on the goddesses Night and Divination to find him.

The goddess of Divination guides Sachi north of the Himalayas to a lake, where she finds Indra hidden inside a lotus stalk. Sachi shrinks to his size and praises his past deeds, then tells him about Nahusha's threats. She asks Indra to destroy Nahusha and take back the heavens. The chapter brings Indra and his queen back together, ready to act against the usurper.

Indra's plan is to have Sachi flatter Nahusha into being carried by sages in a palanquin, which Nahusha accepts. Sachi begs Vrihaspati to find Indra quickly, and Vrihaspati sends Agni, the fire god, to search for him. Agni searches the land and sky but refuses to enter the waters, saying water would extinguish him. The chapter shows the search for Indra stalled before its turning point.

Vrihaspati praises Agni at length, and Agni agrees to enter the waters and find Indra. Agni finds Indra hidden in a lotus stalk, and Vrihaspati praises Indra's past victories and urges him to act. Indra asks how Nahusha rose, and Vrihaspati explains that the gods had made him king and that he now terrorizes the worlds. Other guardian gods then offer their help against Nahusha in return for shares of sacrifice, and Indra allots them domains.

The sage Agastya visits Indra while the gods are planning how to defeat Nahusha. Indra asks how Nahusha fell, and Agastya explains that the proud king mocked the sacred hymns, insulted the sages carrying him, and kicked Agastya on the head. Agastya cursed him to roam the earth as a huge snake for ten thousand years. The gods and all the other beings rejoice at Nahusha's fall.

Indra returns to the three worlds, riding his elephant, reunited with Sachi and honored by the gods and sages, and he rules well. Salya then tells Yudhishthira that Indra's story shows a fallen rival can be overthrown and that the Pandavas will regain their kingdom in the same way. He predicts that Karna and Duryodhana will also be destroyed and says that hearing the tale brings victory. Yudhishthira asks Salya to undermine Karna by praising Arjuna, and Salya agrees and departs to join Duryodhana.

The chapter lists the armies that gather for the two sides. The Pandavas gather seven akshauhinis, which are large army divisions, from many allied kings. Duryodhana gathers eleven akshauhinis from his own allies, which fill the land around Hastinapura so that the city cannot hold them. The Pandava priest sent to the Kauravas sees how huge the Kaurava force has become.

Drupada's priest, now at Hastinapura, addresses the Kaurava leaders. He argues that the Pandavas have a rightful claim to half of their shared inheritance, that they were robbed and humiliated, and that they now want only a peaceful settlement. He points to the strength of the Pandava army and their allies, and urges the Kauravas to return what is due before it is too late.

Bhishma receives the priest courteously and agrees that the Pandavas have a legal claim, while praising Arjuna as unbeatable. Karna cuts in with a harsh reply, mocking the Pandavas and insisting that Duryodhana will not give up any land out of fear. Bhishma rebukes Karna, and Dhritarashtra settles the matter by sending Sanjaya to the Pandavas as his envoy.

Dhritarashtra instructs Sanjaya to go to the Pandavas at Upaplavya and greet them warmly. He praises the Pandavas' conduct and blames only Duryodhana and Karna for the hostility. Then he lists the Pandava allies and their formidable warriors, admits that he fears Arjuna and Krishna, and especially fears Yudhishthira's anger. He tells Sanjaya to say that he desires peace, but not in words that will provoke war.

Sanjaya arrives at Upaplavya and greets Yudhishthira warmly, asking after the Pandavas and Draupadi. Yudhishthira responds by asking after the Kaurava elders, the Brahmins, and the women of the household. He then recalls the Pandava feats of arms and asks whether the Kauravas still remember them. He concludes that peace is hard to reach while Duryodhana stays hostile.

Sanjaya replies that the Kaurava leaders are well, though some of their advisers are wicked. He says that Dhritarashtra himself does not approve of the injustice done to the Pandavas and grieves over it, and that he knows internal strife is a great sin. He praises the Pandava heroes, says that the future cannot be known, and asks Yudhishthira to act with wisdom so that peace is restored. Then he prepares to deliver Dhritarashtra's own message.

Yudhishthira asks Sanjaya to report Dhritarashtra's message to the assembled allies. Sanjaya greets the Pandava leaders, says that Dhritarashtra eagerly welcomes peace, and urges the Pandavas to accept it. He argues that a war would destroy the family, that victory and defeat would be equally empty, and that the Kaurava side is too strong to beat. He ends by asking the Pandavas to keep their ties to the Kurus, which the king and Bhishma also desire.

Yudhishthira replies that he would much prefer peace to war, but he refuses to be humiliated. He blames Dhritarashtra for listening to his wicked son Duryodhana and sending away the wise Vidura, and he names Dussasana, Sakuni and Karna as Duryodhana's advisers. He says the Kauravas underestimate Arjuna and the Pandava brothers, and he is willing to forgive if the Kauravas return at least the land of Indraprastha. The speech shows his willingness to compromise, though he holds firm on his share.

Sanjaya urges Yudhishthira to give up the war, arguing that a good name is worth more than kingdoms and that begging among his kinsmen would be better than winning by slaughter. He warns that desire, greed and wrath lead to sin, that virtue is the only path to lasting reward, and that the Pandavas had many chances to strike earlier and did not. He says that Bhishma, Drona and the other elders would all fall in the fighting. He ends by urging Yudhishthira to yield, saying that giving everything up is better than the path of war.

Yudhishthira answers that righteous conduct is the highest good but that dharma depends on circumstances, and that duties can shift in times of distress. He says that the Pandavas will not seek wealth by unrighteous means, not even the realms of the gods. He calls on Krishna to judge whether his refusal to accept peace or his decision to fight is justified, and he points to the strength of his allies, who follow Krishna's counsel. He closes by saying he always respects Krishna's views.

Krishna answers Sanjaya's appeal for peace by defending Yudhishthira's readiness to act and arguing that action, not inaction, brings reward. He points to the gods and sages, who gained their places through disciplined work, and he sets out the duties of each class, saying a king must punish wrongdoers and that Dhritarashtra's seizure of the Pandava share is unlawful. He recalls the insults at the dice game and the humiliation of Draupadi in the council hall. He says he will go to the Kauravas himself to try for peace, but warns that the Kauravas will be destroyed if they refuse.

Sanjaya takes his leave of Yudhishthira, who praises him for his honest and loyal service as envoy. Yudhishthira then gives him a long list of people to greet in Hastinapura, from Brahmins and the elders to the women, servants, and allied kings. He asks Sanjaya to bring a final message to Duryodhana: return Indraprastha or fight. The chapter closes Sanjaya's mission and leaves the choice of peace or war with the Kauravas.

Yudhishthira gives Sanjaya his final message for Dhritarashtra. He reminds the old king that the kingdom was given to the Pandavas through his grace, asks him to keep the family together, and urges him not to be indifferent to them. He asks Duryodhana to forgive the injuries done to the Pandavas and to give them five villages, which would end the quarrel. He says he is capable of both war and peace, and the choice rests with the Kauravas.

Sanjaya returns to Hastinapura and is admitted to Dhritarashtra's chamber. He passes on Yudhishthira's greetings and the Pandava good wishes, and Dhritarashtra asks after Yudhishthira's family and counselors. Sanjaya then answers with a blunt rebuke, saying that Yudhishthira is virtuous while Dhritarashtra's unjust policy will bring ruin on the family. He asks leave to rest before reporting to the full council the next morning.

Dhritarashtra, anxious after Sanjaya's blunt report and unsure what Yudhishthira's message will be, sends for Vidura. Vidura notes that Yudhishthira was wronged, that the blind king had no claim to the throne, and that the kingdom has been placed in the hands of Duryodhana, Shakuni, Karna and Dussasana. He then gives a long discourse on the marks of wisdom and folly, the value of forgiveness, and the dangers of greed and pride, and he urges the king to return the Pandavas' share of the kingdom.

Dhritarashtra asks Vidura for counsel, since he cannot sleep and fears what Yudhishthira intends. Vidura says he must speak frankly even if the message is unwelcome, and he warns against unjust aims and unrestrained senses. He explains how anger, desire, and cruel speech bring a king to ruin, and that the king's sons have been blinded by their hostility to the Pandavas. He urges Dhritarashtra to let Yudhishthira, who has borne great suffering to protect the king's reputation, rule the kingdom.

Dhritarashtra asks for more of Vidura's teaching. Vidura tells the tale of Virochana and Sudhanwan, who wager their lives in a dispute over a seat and then take the question to Prahlada. Prahlada rules that Sudhanwan is the superior and that he, though his own son is at stake, will not lie. Vidura draws from this that a ruler should never lie for land, that false speech brings ruin, and that virtue and good conduct are the only lasting foundation of fortune. He ends by urging the king to trust the Pandavas and to see them as his own sons.

Vidura tells the tale of the sage son of Atri, who teaches the Sadhyas to bear insults patiently, avoid harsh speech, and keep good company. Dhritarashtra then asks what makes a family noble, and Vidura answers that good conduct and disciplined religious life matter more than wealth, and that quarrels and disrespect to Brahmins bring families down. Dhritarashtra admits he has deceived Yudhishthira and fears destruction, and Vidura urges him to restrain greed and anger, make peace with the Pandavas, and stop Duryodhana. The advice is the last part of Vidura's counsel before the king is pressed toward the council.

Vidura lists the kinds of foolish people whose efforts are wasted, then answers Dhritarashtra's question about why people do not live to a hundred by naming six vices that cut life short. He warns that the Kaurava policy is folly, since the king has favored his lesser sons over the Pandavas, and he gives long advice on how a king should treat servants, counselors, and his own household. He presses again for peace, arguing that a rupture with the Pandavas would shame the Kurus and bring ruin, and he closes by praising wisdom as the highest strength.

Vidura continues his counsel with rules for hospitality, household management, and the handling of secrets. He tells the king which kinds of people to honor and which to shun, how to guard wives and the household, and how a king should choose and test ministers. He stresses patience, careful planning, and restraint in anger and quarrels. He ends by warning that the king has placed power in Duryodhana's hands and cast away the Pandavas, so his fortune will fade like that of Bali.

Dhritarashtra says that people are moved by destiny like puppets, and Vidura replies with maxims on friendship, kinship and good conduct. Vidura again urges that Duryodhana should have been cast off at birth and that the king should protect his relatives, especially the Pandavas, and undo the wrongs done to them. Dhritarashtra admits the force of this advice but says he cannot abandon his son. The chapter sets the old king's weakness against Vidura's steady counsel.

Vidura continues with teaching on the virtues and vices of students and rulers, the value of forgiveness, and the lasting nature of righteousness compared with fleeting pleasure. He describes the duties of each class and says that Yudhishthira is in danger of falling from the duties of a Kshatriya, so Dhritarashtra should restore him to the throne. Dhritarashtra admits that his mind leans toward the Pandavas but that Duryodhana turns him away, and he concludes that destiny cannot be resisted.

Vidura says he has said all he can, since he was born a Sudra, and that the sage Sanatsujata, who teaches that there is no death, can settle Dhritarashtra's doubts. Dhritarashtra asks how he might meet the sage, and Vidura summons him. The sage is then asked to explain the doubts that trouble the king. The section marks a turn toward a more philosophical teaching.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanatsujata whether death can be avoided or whether there is no death at all. The sage answers that ignorance is death and knowledge is immortality, and that desire, lust and anger are the path to death, while those who conquer their desires are beyond its reach. Dhritarashtra then asks whether ritual action can free a person, and Sanatsujata says that knowledge and renunciation lead more surely to liberation than ritual, while those who show off their learning gain nothing. The teaching shifts the question of salvation from ritual to inner knowledge.

Dhritarashtra asks what silence (mauna) means and whether learning can bring liberation, and Sanatsujata explains that the Supreme Soul is silent because the Vedas and mind cannot grasp it. He says that the Vedas do not free a person whose senses are unrestrained or who lives by deceit, and he describes the faults that spoil asceticism along with the forms of renunciation and self-knowledge. He stresses truth as the foundation of all religious life. The chapter closes with Sanatsujata's teaching that the Brahman is one, that it is found within oneself, and that reading alone does not make a true Brahmin.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanatsujata to keep teaching about Brahman, which he calls rare because it is free of worldly desire. The sage says Brahman is reached only after the senses are restrained and the will is absorbed into pure intellect, through the discipline of brahmacharya under a teacher. He then describes the steps of a disciple's devotion and says that knowledge alone leads to liberation. Asked what Brahman looks like, he says it cannot be seen in any visible thing, and is the source and basis of all that exists.

Sanatsujata lists the faults that ruin human life, including greed, anger, pride, and jealousy, and the twelve virtues of a Brahmin, such as truth, restraint, and forgiveness. He describes the eighteen faults of arrogance and the signs of true friendship, including sharing a friend's sorrow and giving even what is dear when a friend truly needs it. He teaches that sacrifice performed without knowledge brings no lasting reward, and that the way to Brahman is restraint of the senses and the search within. The chapter ends with his statement that this teaching is the only true philosophy.

Sanatsujata gives a long hymn-like teaching on the primal Seed, the Supreme Brahman, which is beyond sight and is seen only by yogins with the inner eye. He describes the body as a chariot, the four states of the Self, and the unity of the Self in all beings, with the refrain that the Eternal One is seen by yogins with their mental eye. He says that the one who knows Brahman is not defiled by good or bad deeds, and ends with the words that the Universal Father dwells in the heart of every creature. The chapter presents the highest teaching of the Sanatsujata section.

Dhritarashtra and his court spend the night listening to Sanatsujata and Vidura. In the morning the kings, the princes and the Kaurava leaders gather in a splendid hall to hear the envoy's report. Sanjaya returns from the Pandavas and announces his arrival, and he begins to tell the assembly what the Pandavas have sent. The chapter sets the stage for the formal reading of Yudhishthira's message.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to repeat exactly what Arjuna said in reply to the Kaurava court. Sanjaya relays Arjuna's defiant message: if Duryodhana will not return the kingdom to Yudhishthira, the Kauravas will be destroyed in war. Arjuna names each Pandava hero, predicts that Duryodhana will repent in every battle, and says that Krishna is his ally by divine favor and by Krishna's own past deeds. The message closes with a warning that the Kauravas will perish if they fight, while also stating that the Pandavas wish the Kauravas to keep living.

Bhishma warns Duryodhana with an old story: Nara and Narayana, two ancient sages who aided Indra, are the same beings as Arjuna and Krishna, so the Kauravas will face unbeatable foes. Karna answers with boasts that he will kill the Pandavas and that he is loyal to Duryodhana. Bhishma mocks Karna's record, recalling that Karna did nothing when Arjuna defeated the Kauravas and the Gandharvas, and Drona urges peace before war breaks out. Dhritarashtra does not answer them, and the Kauravas begin to lose hope.

Dhritarashtra asks how Yudhishthira is bearing the coming war and what forces the Pandavas have gathered. Sanjaya describes the Pandavas and their allies rejoicing and gathering around Yudhishthira, and when asked for the details of the forces he falls senseless. Once he recovers, he names the Pandava warriors and their allies one by one, from Dhrishtadyumna and Bhima to Krishna, Drupada and many kings.

Dhritarashtra is terrified of Bhima, whose strength and mace he describes at length, and he recalls how Bhima overpowered his sons even as children. He mourns that his sons will be destroyed in battle and blames Duryodhana's dice match and the force of Time for the ruin of the Kurus. He ends in despair, saying he cannot see how to save his sons and that Bhima and Arjuna will destroy them.

Dhritarashtra despairs of victory, saying that Arjuna with Krishna as charioteer and the Gandiva bow is unbeatable, and that Drona and Karna would not stand against him for long. He recalls Arjuna's past triumphs, including his victory over the gods at Khandava, and says that his sons' follies have brought an unstoppable force against them. He sees omens of ruin all around and believes that the Bharatas will be destroyed.

Dhritarashtra reflects that the Pandava side, with Krishna, Satyaki, Dhrishtadyumna and Yudhishthira's own virtue, is too strong for the Kauravas, and that he himself has treated the Pandavas unjustly. He urges his sons and the Kaurava leaders to consider peace, because the whole Kuru line would be destroyed in a war. The king's fears have turned into a plea for a settlement.

Sanjaya answers Dhritarashtra with a sharp rebuke. He says the king has always taken his sons' side, laughed when the Pandavas lost at dice, and never restrained the cruelty shown to them. He reminds the king that Arjuna once rescued the Kauravas from the Gandharvas, and that Arjuna, his bow, and his charioteer are unmatched. He concludes that the king's grief now comes too late, and that Duryodhana's hostility should be checked.

Duryodhana answers his father's fears with boasts. He recalls that when the Pandavas were in exile, Krishna and the allied kings urged Yudhishthira to reclaim his kingdom, and that the Kaurava elders vowed to defend the Kuru throne. He claims that his skill with the mace makes him a match for Bhima, lists the Kaurava champions, and says that his eleven akshauhinis far outnumber the Pandava forces. He tells Sanjaya to continue with news of the Pandavas.

Duryodhana asks Sanjaya how the Pandavas are preparing, and Sanjaya reports that Yudhishthira and his brothers are cheerful and confident. Arjuna, seeing omens, declares that victory will be theirs. Duryodhana asks about Arjuna's car and banner, and Sanjaya describes the celestial chariot, its magical banner, and the heavenly steeds given to each of the Pandavas.

Sanjaya lists the Pandava allies who have arrived, including Krishna, Satyaki, Drupada and his sons, Virata, the kings of Magadha and Chedi, and the Kekaya princes, and reports how each Kaurava champion has been assigned to a Pandava warrior. Dhritarashtra despairs that his foolish sons will be crushed by the Pandavas, while Duryodhana insists that the Kauravas are strong enough to win. Sanjaya then reports Dhrishtadyumna's fierce vow to fight and Dhrishtadyumna's message urging the Kauravas to surrender the kingdom before Arjuna destroys them.

Dhritarashtra pleads with Duryodhana to make peace, arguing that war is never good, that half the earth is enough for him, and that Karna, Dussasana and Shakuni are leading him astray. Duryodhana refuses and declares that he and Karna alone will fight the Pandavas, describing the battle as a sacrifice and vowing not to yield even a needle's point of land. Dhritarashtra then disowns his son, foresees the Kuru army being crushed by Bhima and Satyaki, and asks Sanjaya for more news.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to report everything Krishna and Arjuna said. Sanjaya describes finding the two at ease in the inner chambers and relays Krishna's message to the Kuru elders, warning of danger and stating that no one can match Arjuna in battle. Arjuna backs him up. The chapter shows the Kuru king hearing from his envoy how formidable the Pandava side is.

Vaisampayana reports that Dhritarashtra weighs the strength of both sides after hearing Sanjaya and concludes the Pandavas are stronger. He admits his fear to Duryodhana, expecting the gods and Agni to aid the Pandavas, and names Arjuna's bow and chariot as especially dangerous. He says he prefers peace to war. The chapter records the king's private doubts before the war begins.

Duryodhana answers his father's fear with anger, arguing that the gods act without desire and so will not help the Pandavas. He boasts of his own power over nature, snakes and armies, and predicts the Pandavas will be destroyed by him. He then asks Sanjaya again about Yudhishthira's war plans. The chapter shows the prince's overconfidence set against his father's caution.

Karna, unasked, says Rama cursed him for winning the Brahma weapon by deceit, but he still has it and vows to defeat the Pandavas alone. Bhishma rebukes him, warning that Krishna protects Arjuna. Karna admits Krishna's greatness, lays down his weapons, and says he will fight only in the court. Bhishma then mocks him, and the chapter turns to Duryodhana.

Duryodhana claims the Pandavas are ordinary men no stronger than the Kurus, and vows that he, Karna and Dussasana will kill them. Vidura replies with a long teaching on self-restraint, listing its virtues and the marks of a self-restrained person. The chapter sets the prince's boasting against the counsel of restraint.

Vidura tells Dhritarashtra a parable: a fowler's net catches two birds, which quarrel and fall into his hands, showing that kinsmen who fight over wealth become easy prey. He then recounts hunters who died trying to reach a jar of honey guarded by snakes, and warns that Duryodhana is blind to his own ruin in the same way. He urges the king to make peace with Yudhishthira.

Dhritarashtra pleads with his son Duryodhana to give up his course. He names the Pandava champions, Yudhishthira, Bhimasena, Arjuna, Dhrishtadyumna, Satyaki and Krishna, and says none can be easily beaten. He urges Duryodhana to accept the counsel of Bhishma, Drona and the other elders, and to share the kingdom with his cousins.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to repeat Arjuna's reply after Krishna's speech. Sanjaya relays Arjuna's warning that the Kaurava kings are doomed unless they return Yudhishthira's share, and otherwise Arjuna will send them to death. Sanjaya then says he has delivered the message and taken leave of Arjuna and Krishna.

After Duryodhana ignores Sanjaya's message and the kings withdraw, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya privately which side will fall. Sanjaya asks that Vyasa and Gandhari be present so he can speak without the king's ill will. Vyasa, now in the court, tells Sanjaya to tell the king all he knows about Vasudeva and Arjuna.

Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that Arjuna and Krishna are godlike equals, and he describes Krishna's discus and his past victories over demons and kings. He argues that Krishna is the supreme Lord who will use the Pandavas to destroy Duryodhana's sinful sons. Those who know him are not deceived by his illusion.

Dhritarashtra asks how Sanjaya can know Krishna as the Supreme Lord when he himself cannot. Sanjaya explains that faith and wisdom give him that knowledge, and that the king must subdue his senses to reach it. Duryodhana refuses to submit to Krishna even if he were to destroy mankind, and Gandhari and Vyasa rebuke the king and urge him to listen.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to explain the names of Krishna, hoping that knowing their meaning will help him reach the Supreme Being. Sanjaya lists many of Krishna's names and gives their meanings, such as Vasudeva, Hrishikesa and Janardana. He ends by saying the slayer of Madhu will come to prevent the slaughter of the Kurus.

Dhritarashtra says he envies those who will see Krishna in person. He praises Krishna at length as eternal, supreme and the creator of the three worlds. He places himself in Krishna's hands and calls on him by many names. The chapter reflects the king's reverence and longing even as he remains committed to the war.

Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after Sanjaya returned to the Kurus. Yudhishthira turns to Krishna for help, listing the Kauravas' broken faith and the miseries of poverty, and says he would rather have peace than war. Krishna agrees to go to the Kuru court to try to make peace, and Yudhishthira reluctantly consents.

Krishna tells Yudhishthira that a Kshatriya should not live by begging and that Duryodhana cannot be trusted to keep peace. He recalls the Kauravas' crimes, including the crooked dice game and the humiliation of Draupadi, and calls Duryodhana deserving of death. He agrees to make one attempt at peace, but he expects war, citing omens, and tells the Pandavas to prepare.

Bhima urges Krishna to address Duryodhana gently, describing him as proud, wicked and hard to teach. He warns that war will destroy the Bharatas, recalls earlier kings who destroyed their own kin, and would accept humiliation to avoid that ruin. He asks the elders to mediate, and the chapter closes with the start of the next section.

Krishna laughs at Bhima's sudden plea for peace and reminds him of his nightly rage and his oath to kill Duryodhana with his mace. He calls the change of heart a sign of fear, and urges Bhima to stand firm, since a Kshatriya should only enjoy what he wins by his own prowess. The exchange shows Krishna deliberately provoking Bhima's courage.

Bhima, stung by Krishna's rebuke, replies that Krishna does not know his real strength and boasts that he could hold earth and sky apart. He says he could trample the Kshatriyas who oppose the Pandavas. He claims he restrains himself only out of compassion for the Bharata race.

Krishna explains that his harsh words were meant to draw out Bhima's real mind, not to reproach him. He argues that human action has uncertain results, so one must act while accepting both fate and effort, without being broken by failure. He promises to seek peace at court, and says that if war comes he will drive Arjuna's chariot.

Arjuna agrees that Yudhishthira has spoken well, but asks Krishna to try for peace anyway, since Krishna is the friend of both sides. He recalls Duryodhana's crooked dice game and the insult to Draupadi, and says Duryodhana deserves death. He doubts that Duryodhana will ever deal justly with the Pandavas.

Krishna says he will strive for peace, but notes that fate can defeat human effort, so success is not certain. He calls Duryodhana wicked and expects him to refuse to give back the kingdom, supported by Sakuni, Karna and Dussasana. He reminds Arjuna of the earlier cattle raid of Virata and rebukes him for doubting his commitment.

Nakula says the Pandavas' circumstances have changed since their exile, and they now have a great army. He advises Krishna to speak mildly to Duryodhana first and then turn to threats, so that the prince grows afraid. He names the great warriors on the Pandava side and expects Krishna's persuasion, with the help of Vidura and the elders, to carry weight.

Sahadeva insists that war must come, and urges Krishna to provoke it even if the Kauravas offer peace, since only Duryodhana's death can answer the insult to Draupadi. Satyaki agrees and reminds Krishna of the Pandavas' suffering in the forest. The assembled warriors roar their approval and show their eagerness to fight.

Draupadi, weeping, reminds Krishna of the dice game, the Pandavas' modest request for five villages, and her own humiliation in the assembly. She argues that peace with such enemies is hopeless and asks Krishna to direct his wrath at Dhritarashtra's sons. Krishna comforts her with a vow that the Kauravas will fall and her husbands will prosper.

Arjuna urges Krishna to act as the friend of both sides and to warn Duryodhana of the consequences of refusing good counsel. Krishna agrees, and at dawn sets out in his chariot with Satyaki, amid omens, blessings from sages and the escort of the Pandavas and many kings. Yudhishthira asks Krishna to greet their mother and the elders, and Arjuna repeats his threat of war if the kingdom is not returned.

Vaisampayana describes Krishna's escort of car-warriors, foot-soldiers and horsemen as he heads to Hastinapura. Janamejaya asks about the omens, and Vaisampayana describes frightening natural signs at the start of the journey, followed by a warm welcome along the road. Krishna spends the night at Vrikasthala, feasting Brahmanas who host him.

Dhritarashtra learns from spies that Krishna is coming and urges his elders and sons to give him a grand welcome. Duryodhana builds lavish pavilions and sends gifts, women and garlands along the road. Krishna ignores all of it and goes straight to the Kuru capital.

Dhritarashtra tells Vidura that Krishna will arrive the next day, praising him as the leader of the Vrishnis. He lists the lavish honours he plans, including gold cars, elephants, servants, blankets, a precious gem and a procession of his sons, all but Duryodhana. He also orders Dussasana's mansion made ready as Krishna's lodging.

Vidura rebukes Dhritarashtra, saying the lavish gifts are a deception meant to win Krishna away from the Pandavas. He points out that the king refuses even five villages to his nephews, and says Krishna cannot be bought because of his bond with Arjuna. He urges the king to make peace and treat the Pandavas as his own sons.

Duryodhana dismisses Vidura's advice, saying Krishna should not be honoured because war is already decided. Bhishma reminds him that Krishna cannot be treated with disrespect and urges peace through Krishna. Duryodhana then proposes to imprison Krishna, Dhritarashtra rejects the plan, and Bhishma, furious, leaves the court.

Krishna leaves Vrikasthala at dawn and is welcomed into Hastinapura by the Kauravas, except Duryodhana, and by crowds of citizens. He is honoured in Dhritarashtra's palace and then visits Vidura's house. There Vidura asks after the Pandavas, and Krishna begins to tell him all they have done.

Krishna visits his aunt Pritha (Kunti), who weeps over her sons' hardships and asks after each of them. She blames her own father for giving her away and sends messages urging her sons to act with Kshatriya courage rather than live on others' charity. Krishna comforts her, and she accepts his words as true. He then leaves for Duryodhana's mansion.

Krishna goes to Duryodhana's palace, where he is honoured but declines the feast Duryodhana offers, saying envoys eat only once their mission succeeds. He rebukes Duryodhana for his unreasoning hatred of the Pandavas and says he will eat only Vidura's food. He leaves for Vidura's house, where the Kauravas offer him their homes, and he dines there on food Kunti prepares, after feeding Brahmanas first.

After Krishna has dined, Vidura warns him during the night that his mission is ill-judged. He describes Duryodhana as wicked, proud and convinced of victory, backed by Bhishma, Drona and Karna and by kings who fear Krishna. He argues that Krishna's words will be wasted on such men and asks him not to walk into a hostile assembly.

Krishna answers Vidura that he knows Duryodhana's wickedness but goes anyway, since a sincere attempt at peace earns merit even if it fails. He argues that a friend should be pulled back from ruin and that his conscience will be clear if the Kauravas refuse. He then lies down to sleep.

At dawn Krishna performs his rites, gives gifts to Brahmanas, and rides in procession through the decorated streets to the Kuru court. The kings rise to honour him, and he greets Dhritarashtra and Bhishma, and asks that the Rishis who have come down from the sky be given seats. Once Krishna is seated, the whole assembly falls silent.

Krishna addresses Dhritarashtra before the whole assembly and urges peace to avoid the slaughter of heroes. He asks the king to restrain Duryodhana and give the Pandavas their share of the kingdom, recalling their loyal exile and the Kauravas' dice fraud. He warns of the ruin war would bring, and the assembled kings silently approve, though none dares speak against Duryodhana.

Rama, son of Jamadagni, tells the Kuru court the parable of King Dambhodbhava, who boasted of his strength until he sought battle with the ascetics Nara and Narayana. Nara defeated him with blades of grass, and the humbled king learned restraint. Rama then reveals that Nara and Narayana are now Arjuna and Krishna, and urges Duryodhana to make peace.

The sage Kanwa adds his counsel to Duryodhana: only Vishnu is eternal, while all else, kings included, is perishable and reborn. He urges Duryodhana not to trust in mere strength and to make peace with Yudhishthira. He then tells the tale of Matali's search for a husband for his daughter Gunakesi, which ends with Matali entering the world of the Nagas.

Kanwa continues the tale of Matali's search. Narada meets Matali on the road, learns his errand, and takes him down to Varuna's realm to look for a groom. There Narada describes the marvels of the Naga world, including Varuna's son Pushkara, the weapons of defeated Daityas, and a bow that gave Arjuna's Gandiva its name.

Narada shows Matali the city of Patala and its marvels, including a fire fed by water, the moon's healing rays, Airavata's rain, and a mysterious egg that has no known origin. Matali finds no suitable groom there and asks to leave. The chapter then turns to a new section.

Narada shows Matali Hiranyapura, the Danava city built with illusions and guarded by mighty demons who could not be defeated by the gods. He describes their mansions and treasures, and asks Matali to look for a groom there. Matali refuses to seek a match among the enemies of the gods and asks to move on.

Narada takes Matali to the realm of the birds, the sons of Garuda, who feed on snakes but revere Vishnu. He names their many chiefs and offers to move on to another region if none of them suits. The chapter continues the catalogue of possible grooms.

Narada describes Rasatala, the home of Surabhi, mother of cows, whose milk formed the Milky Ocean. He explains that her offspring cows support the four quarters of the world, and that her milk becomes food suited to each kind of being. He quotes an old verse praising Rasatala above all other realms.

Narada describes Bhogavati, the Naga city ruled by Vasuki, where Shesha holds up the earth and countless Nagas dwell. Matali notices a young Naga standing by Aryaka and asks about him, saying he would make a fine husband for Gunakesi. Narada reveals the youth is Sumukha, grandson of Aryaka, whose father Chikura was killed by Garuda, and Matali is pleased to choose him.

Narada praises Matali and asks Aryaka to accept Sumukha as a groom for Gunakesi. Aryaka hesitates, because Garuda killed his son and has threatened to devour Sumukha within a month. Matali takes the matter to Indra's court, where Vishnu suggests a gift of Amrita, but Indra grants Sumukha only long life, and the marriage goes ahead.

Garuda, furious that Indra has spared the Naga Sumukha and so cheated him of his food, boasts that he is as strong as the gods' king. Vishnu presses one arm on him, humbling him, and then restores Sumukha to his breast so that the two become friends. Kanwa applies the lesson to Duryodhana, warning him to avoid battle with the Pandavas and to trust in Krishna, but Duryodhana scoffs and says fate rules him.

Janamejaya asks why Duryodhana's friends and elders did not restrain him. Vaisampayana replies that Krishna, Bhishma and Narada all counselled him, and Narada tells the tale of Galava, an obstinate disciple of the sage Viswamitra. The story shows how refusing good counsel brings disgrace and trouble.

Galava is stricken with grief and remorse at being unable to repay his teacher, and resolves to end his life. He resolves instead to seek Vishnu's protection, when his friend Garuda appears and offers to carry him across the sea to find the horses.

Garuda offers to show Galava the world, beginning with the eastern quarter. He describes it as the gate of day and time, where the sun rises, the gods were first anointed, and the Vedas were first sung. He asks whether Galava would prefer to go there or to hear about another quarter.

Garuda describes the southern quarter, given as a gift by Vivaswat to his teacher and home to the ancestors and to Yama's realm. He recounts many tales of kings, sages and sinners associated with it, including the river of the dead and the city of Bhogavati. He asks whether Galava wants to go there or hear about the west.

Garuda describes the western quarter, the realm of Varuna, where the sun sets and the sea is said to begin. He recounts its wonders, including the defeat of the Daityas, the Maruts' birth and the home of Vishnu and Kasyapa. He then asks Galava which way they should go.

Garuda describes the northern quarter as the most sacred direction, where Krishna and Arjuna dwell at the Vadari hermitage and Shiva rests on the Himalayas. He lists its wonders, including the Ganges falling from heaven, Kuvera's realm, the sages who guard the river's source, and Vishnu's footprint. He then offers to show Galava any quarter he likes.

Galava asks Garuda to carry him east, where the gods and virtue are said to dwell. The flight is so fast that Galava is terrified by the storm and the sparks, and he despairs of ever finding the steeds, saying death seems the only way out. Garuda laughs at him and proposes they rest on Mount Rishabha.

On Mount Rishabha they honour the ascetic lady Sandili and eat her food, after which Garuda wakes to find his wings gone. He admits he had wished to carry her off, and she forgives him on condition he never looks down on women, then restores his wings. The steeds still cannot be found, and Viswamitra meets Galava and demands his fee.

Garuda tells Galava that wealth must be begged from a king, and proposes King Yayati of Pratisthana, a descendant of Nahusha. When they reach the court, Yayati welcomes them, and Garuda explains how Galava has been sent by Viswamitra to fulfil his fee.

Yayati, though poorer than Garuda supposes, refuses to send Galava away empty-handed and offers his daughter Madhavi as a gift to pay the debt. Garuda departs, and Galava takes Madhavi to King Haryyaswa of Ayodhya, seeking a dower for her.

Haryyaswa admires Madhavi, but when Galava asks for eight hundred steeds he has only two hundred. Madhavi suggests four kings could each give steeds for one son, and Haryyaswa takes her for a single son, Vasumanas. When Galava returns for the balance, Haryyaswa cannot pay, so he gives Madhavi back, and Galava moves on to King Divodasa.

Galava takes Madhavi to Divodasa, king of Kasi, and asks him to father a son by her. Divodasa agrees to one son but says his wealth cannot cover the steeds. Narada lists many divine and royal couples, and Madhavi bears Pratardana; when Galava returns, Divodasa gives her back as agreed.

Madhavi, again a maiden, goes with Galava to King Usinara of the Bhojas. Galava asks for four hundred steeds for two sons, and Usinara, who has only two hundred of the right kind, agrees to father one son, Sivi. Galava then takes Madhavi back and goes to see Garuda.

Garuda tells Galava that the missing steeds cannot be found, since the kings bought them from Brahmanas and some were lost in a river. He advises Galava to offer Madhavi to Viswamitra as the remaining price, and Viswamitra accepts her, fathers a son, Ashtaka, and receives the six hundred steeds. Galava then returns Madhavi to her father and goes into the woods.

King Yayati brings Madhavi to a swayamvara at a sacred hermitage, but she passes over all suitors and chooses the forest as her lord, living as an ascetic like a deer. Years later Yayati grows proud in heaven and disregards the gods and sages. None there recognise him, and he loses his splendour.

Yayati, stripped of his heavenly glory, is hurled from heaven, and he asks to fall among the righteous. He lands among four kings holding a sacrifice in Naimisha, who ask who he is. Madhavi arrives and tells her father her sons will save him, and Galava offers an eighth of his austerities to help him back to heaven.

Yayati is recognised by the virtuous kings and rises back to heaven. Each of his four grandsons gives him the merit of his good deeds: Vasumanas his liberality, Pratardana his valour, Sivi his truthfulness, and Ashtaka his sacrifices. Yayati ascends on their gifts, and the kings declare themselves his daughter's sons.

Yayati returns to heaven with honours and asks why his merit was exhausted. Brahma replies that vanity alone caused his fall, and that pride and contempt for others are the greatest sins. Narada then turns the lesson to Duryodhana, urging him to give up pride and wrath and make peace with the Pandavas.

Dhritarashtra tells Narada he agrees with his counsel but has no power to make Duryodhana follow it. He asks Krishna to persuade his son, and Krishna gives a long plea for peace, urging Duryodhana to obey his father, make peace with the Pandavas, and stop relying on weak allies. Krishna warns that no one can defeat Arjuna, and that the Kauravas will be destroyed if they go to war.

Bhishma and Drona urge Duryodhana to heed Krishna and make peace, warning that the Pandavas cannot be beaten and that war will destroy the Bharata race. Vidura grieves for the aged Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, who would be left to wander as beggars. Dhritarashtra begs his son to accept Krishna's offer of reconciliation.

Bhishma and Drona plead once more with Duryodhana. They list the terrible scenes of war that have not yet begun, such as Krishna and Arjuna arming for battle and Bhima raising his mace, and urge him to make peace before those scenes come true. They ask him to embrace Yudhishthira and his brothers, who will embrace him in return.

Duryodhana angrily answers Krishna that he alone is blamed, that the Pandavas accepted the dice game, and that he has already returned the stolen wealth. He refuses to bow to the Pandavas, or even to Indra, and says he will not give them back even a needle's point of land while his father lives. He declares that a Kshatriya should die on the battlefield rather than yield.

Krishna rebukes Duryodhana for his crimes against the Pandavas, from the dice game and the insult to Draupadi to the attempts to burn and poison them. Dussasana threatens that the Kauravas will bind Duryodhana and hand him over to the Pandavas. Duryodhana storms out, and Krishna urges the elders to bind him, citing old examples of wicked men who were restrained for the good of all.

Dhritarashtra asks Vidura to fetch Gandhari, hoping she can persuade their son. Gandhari blames her husband for indulging Duryodhana, then pleads with her son to restrain his greed and wrath, make peace with the Pandavas, and accept Krishna's counsel. Vidura brings Duryodhana back, and the chapter closes with the next section heading.

Duryodhana, with Karna, Sakuni and Dussasana, plots to seize Krishna first. Satyaki overhears the plot and warns Krishna and the elders, and Krishna says he will not stoop to violence even if the plotters try. Dhritarashtra then orders Duryodhana back into the court, rebukes him, and Vidura recalls Krishna's feats to show that no one can seize him.

Krishna mocks Duryodhana's plan to seize him and reveals a dazzling universal form, from which gods, heroes and his own allies appear. Most of the kings are terrified, though Drona, Bhishma and Vidura hold firm. Dhritarashtra then protests his good faith, and Krishna takes leave of the elders and rides to Kunti's house in full view of the Kurus.

Krishna reports the failure of his mission to Kunti and asks what message she wants him to take to the Pandavas. Kunti urges Yudhishthira to act as a Kshatriya and fight rather than live on alms. She cites the example of Muchukunda and the power of kings to bring about a good or bad age, and warns that shirking battle brings shame.

Kunti tells an old tale of the warrior mother Vidula, who scolds her defeated son for lying down in despair. Vidula calls him a coward and urges him to rise and fight, saying that a man who avoids battle is no true man. The son replies that he has no use for the earth without his mother's favour, and she answers that a brave man should support others by his own strength.

Vidula continues her rebuke, telling her son that a Kshatriya who avoids battle is like a thief and that his fame depends on fighting. She recalls a Brahmana's prophecy that the son would one day regain greatness, and urges him to win back the kingdom. She argues that sovereignty is the door to heaven, and says a Kshatriya must bow only to Brahmanas.

In Kunti's tale, Vidula scolds her son for his despair and tells him a Kshatriya is made for battle, and that shirking action brings shame. The son replies that he lacks wealth and allies and asks what he can do. Vidula urges him to act with energy, win over the wronged and the angry, and treat his followers generously.

Vidula tells her son that a king in distress must not betray his cause, since his friends and loyal followers will stand by him. She offers him hidden treasure and faithful allies. The son's despair lifts, and he vows to win back his kingdom or perish in the attempt. Kunti then says this tale of Jaya should be read to any king who is down.

Kunti gives Krishna a message for each of her sons. She recalls a celestial voice that foretold Arjuna's victory and the recovery of the kingdom, urges Bhima and the twins to act as warriors, and reminds all of Draupadi's insult. She asks Krishna to protect her sons. Krishna takes leave of Kunti, speaks with Karna, and drives swiftly back to Upaplavya, while the Kurus lament Duryodhana's folly.

Bhishma and Drona warn Duryodhana that Kunti's words will be heeded, since the Pandavas now have Arjuna, Bhima, Gandiva and Krishna on their side. They recall Arjuna's past feats at Virata and in the cattle raid, and list the evil omens of coming slaughter. They beg Duryodhana to make peace and embrace Yudhishthira and his brothers.

Duryodhana says nothing, cheerless and with his face cast down. Bhishma laments that he must fight Yudhishthira, a man devoted to his elders and free of envy. Drona confesses his deep love for Arjuna but says his duty as a warrior forces him to fight him, and he urges Duryodhana to make peace.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what Krishna said to Karna during their ride out of the city. Sanjaya reports that Krishna revealed Karna to be Kunti's firstborn son, and so the eldest of the Pandavas by birth. Krishna urges Karna to join his brothers and be crowned king, with Yudhishthira serving as his heir.

Karna declines Krishna's offer. He says he was raised by the charioteer Adhiratha and cannot abandon Duryodhana, who made him king, and he asks Krishna to keep their talk secret. He then describes the coming war as a great sacrifice, with Arjuna as the Hotri, Gandiva as the ladle and the dead as the offerings. He prays that the Kshatriyas die at Kurukshetra and asks Krishna to bring Arjuna before him in single combat.

Krishna answers Karna with a smile, telling him that the Pandavas' victory is already certain. He points to Arjuna's banner and the signs that the Krita, Treta and Dwapara ages will vanish in battle. He sends word to Drona, Bhishma and Kripa that the season is good and the battle should begin on the new moon, a day ruled by Indra.

Karna answers Krishna that the destruction of the earth is at hand, and lists omens of defeat for the Kauravas, drawn from planets, animals, birds and the state of the camp. He then describes a vision in which the Pandavas triumph and the Kauravas go to Yama. Krishna replies that when a man cannot accept good counsel, his doom is near. Karna embraces Krishna, saying they will meet again in battle or in heaven, and Sanjaya reports that Karna went back in gloom.

After Krishna leaves, Vidura tells Kunti that Duryodhana will not hear reason and that war is near. Kunti laments the coming slaughter of kin, and recalls the mantra Durvasa gave her in girlhood, which she used to summon the sun god Surya and conceive Karna. She goes to the Ganga, where Karna is at prayer, and resolves to reveal the truth to him.

Karna meets Kunti at the Ganga and asks what she wants of him. Kunti reveals that he is her firstborn son by Surya, not Radha's or Adhiratha's, and urges him to join the Pandavas and take his place among them.

Kunti makes a final plea for Karna to join the Pandavas, and a voice from the sun god Surya backs her. Karna refuses, citing his loyalty to Duryodhana, his honor, and the wrong Kunti did him by abandoning him at birth. He promises that Kunti will keep five sons either way, since he will spare the other Pandavas and fight only Arjuna, and then mother and son part.

Krishna returns from Hastinapura and reports to the Pandavas, who ask him to repeat exactly what was said in the Kuru assembly. He repeats Bhishma's speech, in which Bhishma explains how the throne passed through Santanu's line and how his own vow shaped that line. Bhishma concludes that Pandu's sons are the rightful heirs and that Duryodhana should give them half the kingdom.

Drona backs Bhishma and tells Duryodhana to give the Pandavas half the kingdom, since righteousness brings victory. Vidura blames Bhishma for allowing Duryodhana's wrongdoing and warns of a great slaughter. Suvala's daughter then argues in the assembly that the kingdom lawfully belongs to the Pandavas.

Dhritarashtra speaks to Duryodhana and recounts a long family history of rulers who passed over eldest sons for the throne, including Yayati, who chose Puru over Yadu, and Pratipa, who passed over Devapi because of a skin disease. He applies the same logic to himself, since he was passed over for a bodily defect, and says Yudhishthira is the rightful heir. He ends by urging Duryodhana to give the Pandavas half the kingdom.

Krishna reports to the Pandavas on his failed mission. He describes Duryodhana storming out of the assembly and sending the allied kings to Kurukshetra under Bhishma's command. He recounts each stage of his peace effort, from conciliation to stirring division to offering five villages, and concludes that war is now the only path.

Yudhishthira asks his brothers to name a commander for his seven akshauhinis, and each brother proposes a candidate. Yudhishthira then leaves the final choice to Krishna, who approves the names and picks Dhrishtadyumna as overall leader. The army is set to march at dawn.

The Pandava army sets out for Kurukshetra with a tremendous din, its divisions moving in order. The narrator describes the commanders, the supply train, and Draupadi remaining at Upaplavya under guard. On reaching the field, the warriors blow their conches, and the noise fills the earth and sky.

Yudhishthira's army makes camp on level, grassy ground by the Hiranwati river, avoiding sacred sites. Krishna has a moat dug and sets up guarded tents and well-stocked camps for the allied kings. Skilled workers and healers join the camp, and many kings arrive to support the Pandavas.

Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana what Duryodhana did once the Pandavas camped at Kurukshetra with their powerful allies. Duryodhana tells Karna, Dussasana, and Sakuni to prepare the camps and the road, and the kings arm themselves. The narrator describes the capital filled with war preparations, comparing it to the sea stirred by the rising moon.

Yudhishthira asks Krishna what they should do, given the views of Duryodhana, Karna, Sakuni, Vidura, Bhishma, and Kunti. Krishna replies that Duryodhana rejects every counsel, so war is the only way forward. Yudhishthira reluctantly orders the army arrayed, and Arjuna insists they must fight, so the brothers resolve on war and spend the night in good spirits.

Duryodhana arranges his eleven akshauhinis, equipping each division with cars, elephants, horses, foot soldiers, and an enormous range of weapons and supplies. The narrator defines the military units from a sena up to a vahini, and gives the totals: seven akshauhinis for the Pandavas and eleven for the Kauravas. Duryodhana places a senior warrior over each division, and they all become eager to please him.

Duryodhana asks Bhishma to lead the army, arguing from an old story that an army needs one commander to win. Bhishma accepts but says he loves the Pandavas and will kill ten thousand men each day, and he asks that either Karna or he fight first. Karna vows not to fight while Bhishma lives. Bhishma is installed with gifts, omens appear, and Duryodhana marches his army to Kurukshetra.

Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas said on hearing that Bhishma led the Kaurava army. Yudhishthira calls his brothers and Krishna and asks them to choose seven leaders for his seven divisions. Dhrishtadyumna is placed over all the troops, and Arjuna over the leaders, with Krishna as his charioteer. Balarama arrives, speaks sadly of the coming slaughter, and leaves on a pilgrimage to the Saraswati rather than watch the battle.

Rukmi, a southern king and master of the celestial bow Vijaya, arrives at the Pandava camp with a large army. He recalls his old feud with Krishna over Rukmini and offers to kill the Kuru champions for Arjuna. Arjuna refuses his help, and Duryodhana also turns him away, so Rukmi withdraws and the Pandavas gather to consult again.

Janamejaya asks what the Kauravas did once the armies stood ready on Kurukshetra. Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to report what is happening in both camps, lamenting that he cannot restrain Duryodhana. Sanjaya says the blame lies with Duryodhana rather than fate or the gods, and then sets out three views on whether human acts are fated, freely chosen, or shaped by past lives.

Duryodhana sends his envoy Uluka to the Pandavas with a defiant message. Uluka first tells Yudhishthira the story of a cat who won the mice's trust and then devoured them, calling Yudhishthira a hypocrite, and then taunts each brother and Krishna over their past humiliations and dares them to fight. Duryodhana lists the Kaurava army and its leaders as unbeatable and rules out any compromise, so the war will go ahead.

Uluka delivers Duryodhana's message to Yudhishthira before the assembled Pandavas and their allies. He repeats the old taunts about the dice loss, the exile, and the humiliation of Krishna, and dares Bhima to fulfil his vow. He then turns to Arjuna, telling him to stop boasting and calling the Kaurava army, led by Drona and Bhishma, too strong to beat.

The Pandavas are enraged by Uluka's repeated taunts. Bhima vows to drink Dussasana's blood and kill Duryodhana's brothers, Sahadeva threatens Sakuni, and Arjuna says his answer will come through his bow. Yudhishthira rebukes Duryodhana as a crooked coward who relies on others, and Krishna promises to act only as Arjuna's charioteer.

Arjuna replies to Duryodhana with a vow to kill Bhishma before the eyes of the Kurus, and calls him a coward who hides behind others. The other Pandavas, Virata and Drupada, Sikhandin, and Dhrishtadyumna each send a reply, several swearing to kill Bhishma or Drona. Yudhishthira says he does not want the slaughter of kinsmen but accepts the war, and Uluka returns and reports to Duryodhana, who orders his army arrayed before dawn.

Sanjaya describes how Dhrishtadyumna arranges the Pandava army. He pairs each of his warriors against a Kaurava champion, with Arjuna against Karna, Bhima against Duryodhana, and Sikhandin against Bhishma, and keeps Drona for himself. The Pandava force then waits, steady as the ocean, for the battle to begin.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what his sons and Bhishma did after Arjuna vowed to kill Bhishma. Bhishma accepts command and reassures Duryodhana that he knows the military arts. Duryodhana asks Bhishma to rank the warriors on both sides, and Bhishma begins by ranking Duryodhana's brothers, Kritavarman, Salya, Bhurisravas, and Jayadratha.

Bhishma continues ranking Duryodhana's warriors, naming Sudakshina of the Kamvojas, Nila of Mahishmati, the Avanti princes Vinda and Anuvinda, and the five Trigarta brothers. He also names Lakshmana, Dussasana's son, Dandadhara, Vrihadvala of Kosala, and Kripa, each as a strong fighter who will fight hard for Duryodhana.

Bhishma continues the ranking with Sakuni, Ashvatthama, and Drona, whom he praises as a great teacher but says will not kill Arjuna out of affection. He names a further group of Kaurava fighters, including Vrishasena, Jalasandha, Vahlika, Satyavan, the rakshasa Alambhusha, and Bhagadatta. The chapter ends with Bhagadatta, a king who fights from an elephant and was once a friend to Arjuna.

Bhishma calls Karna only half a ratha, and Drona agrees, saying Karna boasts before every battle but retreats from each one. Karna angrily answers that he tolerates the insults only for Duryodhana's sake and vows not to fight while Bhishma lives. Bhishma says he will take on the battle himself, and Duryodhana asks his commanders to report on the strengths and weaknesses of the enemy before dawn.

Bhishma now ranks the Pandava warriors, with Yudhishthira and the twins as rathas, Bhima equal to eight rathas, and Arjuna, with Krishna as his driver, unmatched on the field. He says that he and Drona are old while Arjuna is young and fierce. The Kaurava kings grow fearful as they listen.

Bhishma names the Pandava allies, rating Draupadi's five sons as maharathas and Virata's son Uttara as a foremost ratha. He praises Abhimanyu as nearly the equal of Arjuna, and Satyaki, Uttamaujas, and Yudhamanyu as strong car-warriors. He also says the aged kings Virata and Drupada will fight hard for the Pandavas.

Bhishma continues the ranking with Sikhandin and Dhrishtadyumna, whom he calls an atiratha and the leader of the Pandava army. He gives lower ratings to Dhrishtadyumna's young son Kshattradharman, who is only half a ratha, and rates many Panchala, Chedi, and other allied kings as rathas or maharathas. The list ends with Srenimat and Vasudeva, both named atirathas.

Bhishma names Kuntibhoja, Bhima's maternal uncle, and Ghatotkacha, Bhima's rakshasa son, as strong Pandava fighters. He says he will oppose Arjuna and Krishna, but he declares he will never strike Sikhandin, because Sikhandin was born a daughter and Bhishma has sworn never to slay a woman or a former woman.

Duryodhana asks why Bhishma will not kill Sikhandin, given his earlier boast. Bhishma tells the story of his father Santanu and his vows, and of how he carried off the three princesses of Kasi, Amba, Ambika, and Ambalika, for his brother Vichitravirya. He brought them to Satyavati, after defeating the assembled kings.

Bhishma tells his mother Satyavati that he has abducted the princesses of Kasi, and she is delighted by his victory. When the wedding nears, the eldest princess, Amba, reveals that she had already chosen the king of Salwa and asks Bhishma, as a moral man, to let her go to him.

Bhishma lets Amba go to Salwa's city, but Salwa rejects her, mocking that Bhishma had carried her off. Amba protests her innocence and swears she never chose another husband, but Salwa refuses. Amba leaves in grief and anger, vowing that the righteous will protect her.

Rejected by Salwa, Amba laments that she has no one, blames Bhishma, her father, Salwa, and herself, and vows to take vengeance on Bhishma. She goes to a hermitage and tells the sages her story. The learned sage Saikhavatya comforts her and promises to help.

The ascetics in the forest argue over what to do with Amba, some urging her to go home and others urging her to plead again with Salwa. Amba refuses to return to Kasi and asks to live as an ascetic. Her maternal grandfather, King Hotravahana, arrives, hears her story, and sends her to the sage Rama, son of Jamadagni, who he believes can end her grief and even kill Bhishma.

Akritavrana asks Amba whether she wants Salwa to marry her or Bhishma to be defeated, and she says her heart was given to Salwa before Bhishma seized her. Rama arrives, and Amba begs for his protection. Rama promises to send word to Bhishma and fight him if Bhishma refuses, but Amba insists that Bhishma must be slain.

Rama tells Amba he takes up arms only at the command of Brahmanas, but says he will act for her, since both Bhishma and Salwa obey him. Amba repeatedly asks him to slay Bhishma. Akritavrana reminds Rama of his old vow to protect those who seek shelter and to slay the foes of Brahmanas, and Rama agrees to go to Bhishma with Amba, and to slay him if he refuses. The party reaches Kurukshetra and camps by the Saraswati.

Rama, son of Jamadagni, orders Bhishma to take Amba as his wife, since Salwa rejected her after Bhishma carried her off. Bhishma refuses, citing his vow, and Rama challenges him to a duel at Kurukshetra. Bhishma's mother Ganga pleads with him to back down, but he accepts the challenge and sets out for the field.

Bhishma and Rama fight on Kurukshetra, with Rama in a celestial car and Bhishma first dismounting to honor his teacher. Rama wounds Bhishma first, but Bhishma breaks Rama's bow and wounds him in return, sparing his brahminical status. At sunset Bhishma stops, grieved that he has fought his teacher.

The duel resumes at dawn with celestial weapons. Rama wounds Bhishma until he falls into a swoon, but Bhishma revives and wounds Rama in turn, and the ascetics comfort their teacher. The two warriors fill the sky with arrows until dusk, when the fight stops with neither side winning.

The duel with Rama resumes the next day and escalates, as both use celestial weapons. Bhishma cuts down Rama's lance and darts, but Rama's arrows break his chariot and wound him. Bhishma in turn wounds his teacher heavily, and the fight ends at sunset.

The fight resumes the next morning, and Rama kills Bhishma's charioteer and then knocks Bhishma down. Eight Brahmanas raise him up, and his mother Ganga guides his chariot, letting him wound Rama into unconsciousness. Omens of disaster follow, and the battle goes on for twenty-three days.

Bhishma, unable to defeat Rama, goes to bed and prays for the gods to show him a sign. In a dream eight Brahmanas promise that he will overcome Rama, and they reveal two weapons: Praswapa, which puts a foe to sleep, and Samvodhana, which wakes him.

Bhishma resumes the battle, remembering his dream. Rama hurls a dart that wounds Bhishma's shoulder, and Bhishma's arrow wounds Rama, who falls and recovers. Both invoke the Brahma weapon, and the world burns, so Bhishma resolves to use the Praswapa.

As Bhishma aims the Praswapa, the sage Narada and the gods warn him not to use it, since Rama is a Brahmana and his teacher. Bhishma withdraws the weapon, and Rama admits defeat, but his ancestors urge him to give up the fight, and Bhishma gives way too. The two part with mutual respect, and Rama summons Amba.

Rama admits defeat and tells Amba to seek Bhishma's protection, but Amba vows to kill Bhishma and leaves for severe penance. Bhishma has his spies follow her and consults Narada and Vyasa, who tell him not to grieve. After years of penance across many sacred sites, Ganga foretells that Amba will become a river, and half of her body stays a maiden.

Amba tells the ascetics of Vatsabhumi that she will not stop her penance until Bhishma is slain, even if it means taking on a man's form. The god with the trident, lord of Uma, appears and promises that she will kill Bhishma and be reborn as a man in Drupada's line. She then builds a funeral pyre by the Yamuna and burns herself, crying out that it is for Bhishma's destruction.

Duryodhana asks how Sikhandin, born a daughter, became a man. Bhishma explains that King Drupada prayed to Shiva for a son to avenge himself on Bhishma, and the god promised a child who would first be a daughter and later a male. The queen had a daughter, whom the king had raised as a son and named Sikhandin, with only a few people knowing the secret.

Drupada has Sikhandin trained in the arts and in arms under Drona, and when Sikhandin reaches maturity, the royal couple arrange a marriage with the daughter of the Dasarnaka king Hiranyavarman. The bride soon discovers that her husband is a woman, and her nurses tell the king. Hiranyavarman is enraged and sends a threatening messenger to Drupada.

Drupada is caught out and frightened, and tries to calm his brother-in-law with conciliatory messages, but Hiranyavarman prepares an army to march. His allies plan to bind Drupada, install a new king, and kill Drupada and Sikhandin. Drupada, afraid, turns to his queen for the truth about their child.

Sikhandin's mother admits that she had the daughter's birth concealed out of fear of her co-wives and because of the god's words, and Drupada confirms the deception. The king prepares his city's defences and prays, while Sikhandini, shamed by the trouble she has caused, goes to a haunted forest and fasts until the Yaksha Sthunakarna appears. She asks him to make her a true man so that her parents can be spared.

Sikhandini and the Yaksha Sthuna swap sexes for a time, so that Sikhandin becomes a man and can save the city. Sikhandin tells Drupada, and the Dasarnaka king's envoys are satisfied after women he sends confirm that Sikhandin is male. Kubera, lord of the Yakshas, learns of the swap and curses Sthuna to stay a woman until Sikhandin dies. Bhishma tells the Kauravas why he will not fight Sikhandin, and Duryodhana accepts his reasoning.

Duryodhana asks Bhishma how many days he needs to destroy the Pandava army, and Bhishma answers that he can slay ten thousand foot soldiers and a thousand chariot warriors each day, finishing in a month with his great weapons. The other commanders offer their own timelines, with Drona saying a month, Kripa two months, Ashvatthama ten nights, and Karna five days. Bhishma laughs at Karna's boast.

Yudhishthira, informed by his spies of the Kaurava commanders' boasts, asks Arjuna how long he needs to destroy the enemy. Arjuna answers that with Krishna's help he could destroy the three worlds in an instant, that he holds Shiva's weapon, and that it is not right to kill ordinary men with celestial weapons. He names the Pandava allies whose strength will win the day.

On the next morning, the Kaurava kings march out under Duryodhana, purified and armed, and take position at the far end of Kurukshetra in three divisions. Drona leads the first, Ashvatthama and Bhishma the second, and Kritavarman, Bhurisravas, and Salya lead the rear with Duryodhana. Duryodhana sets up a camp that looks like a second Hastinapura, with ample provisions for kings, followers, traders, and spectators.

Yudhishthira sends out his army in ordered divisions, with Dhrishtadyumna, Abhimanyu, and Draupadi's sons in front, Bhima and the twins in a leading division, and Krishna and Arjuna in the centre with Virata and the Panchala princes. Kshatrahan and Kshatradeva guard the rear, and Yudhishthira himself marches slowly behind the main divisions, with the baggage, the sick, and the weak. The chapter closes the Udyoga Parva, and the rest of the section is editorial footnotes explaining Sanskrit terms, the weapons, and the philosophy of the earlier sage's answers.

The Kurus, Pandavas and Somakas gather their armies on the plain of Kurukshetra, and Yudhishthira camps on the western side with troops drawn from all of Jamvudwipa. Both sides blow their conches, and then they agree on rules of fair single combat, such as matching opponents by vehicle and never striking those who are unready, fleeing, or unarmed. The chapter sets the stage for the battle and shows the code of conduct the fighters are meant to keep.

Vyasa, seeing the two armies ready to fight, takes the distressed Dhritarashtra aside and offers to let him watch the battle. Dhritarashtra says he does not want to see his kinsmen slaughtered and asks only to hear about it, so Vyasa grants the bard Sanjaya, son of Gavalgani, the power to see and narrate the whole war. Vyasa then lists frightening omens in the sky and on earth that foreshadow terrible losses.

Vyasa lists more portents, including monstrous births, unseasonal crops, planetary disturbances, eclipses on unusual days and bloody rivers, all forecasting a massacre. Dhritarashtra accepts that the slaughter is fated, but Vyasa urges him to restrain his sons and let the Pandavas have their kingdom, and Dhritarashtra admits his sons will not obey him. Dhritarashtra then asks what signs will show that a side is destined to win, and Vyasa lists omens of success and says that victory depends on chance.

After Vyasa leaves, Dhritarashtra sighs over the many kings gathered to kill one another and asks Sanjaya to describe the lands they came from. Sanjaya sorts living things into mobile and immobile, lists the fourteen kinds of animals and the plants, and says all creatures live by consuming one another. He concludes that the earth sustains everything, which is why kings kill each other to possess it.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya for the names and measures of the rivers, mountains, provinces and forests on the earth. Sanjaya first explains that all things are made from five elements, each with its own quality, and that the earth holds the qualities of the others as well. He then describes the wheel-shaped island Sudarsana, which he says resembles a peepul tree and a hare when seen in the moon.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya for more detail on the hare-shaped and peepul-shaped parts of the island. Sanjaya describes the six mountains that cross the land, the Varshas between them, and the golden mountain Meru at the centre with its surrounding islands, including Jamvudwipa where the listeners live. He covers the sacred places, the course of the Ganga and the lives of gods, sages and peoples around these mountains, which sets out the world in which the Kurus fight.

Dhritarashtra asks about the regions north and east of Meru and the Malyavat mountain. Sanjaya describes the Northern Kurus, a land of sweet fruit, milk-giving trees, golden sands and long-lived people, then the eastern land of Bhadraswa with its great Kalamra and Jamvu trees, which gave Jamvudwipa its name. He ends with Malyavat, where the fire Samvataka burns at the end of an age and ascetics enter the sun and then the moon.

Dhritarashtra asks for the names of all the Varshas, mountains and their inhabitants. Sanjaya lists Romanaka, Hiranmaya and the Airavata Varsha beyond the Sringavat mountains, with their long-lived peoples, and describes Hari (Vishnu) riding a golden car in the northern ocean as the source and end of all creatures. Dhritarashtra, lost in thought about his sons, answers that Time both destroys and creates everything and names Narayana and Vishnu as the power that destroys all creatures.

Dhritarashtra asks about Bharatavarsha, the land his son Duryodhana covets, and Sanjaya replies that the Pandavas do not covet it, while Duryodhana, Sakuni and other rulers do. He then names the mountains, rivers and many peoples and provinces of the land and of the south and north. He ends by saying kings have become greedy for earth like dogs fighting over meat, which is why the Kurus and Pandavas strive for it.

Dhritarashtra asks about the lifespan, strength and condition of the people of Bharatavarsha, Himavat and Harivarsha. Sanjaya explains the four ages, Krita, Treta, Dwapara and Kali, and how lifespans shrink from four thousand years to an uncertain span, while human character declines in the Kali age. He concludes that Haimavat and Harivarsha are superior to Bharatavarsha in every quality.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya for the size of Jamvudwipa and the oceans and islands beyond it, including Sakadwipa, Kusadwipa, Salmalidwipa and Kraunchadwipa, along with the sun, moon and Rahu. Sanjaya describes Sakadwipa, an island twice the size of Jamvudwipa where people are righteous and do not die, and then names its seven mountains, the Varshas between them, and the sacred Saka tree. The account gives the king a cosmic map of the world beyond his own land.
