Sanjaya describes the northern islands, each surrounded by an ocean of clarified butter, curds, wine or water, with their mountains, Varshas and long-lived, peaceful peoples. He covers the outer islands and Pushkara where Prajapati dwells, and the four great elephants whose breath gives life to creatures. He ends with the sizes of the planet Swarbhanu, the moon and the sun, urges Dhritarashtra to pacify Duryodhana, and closes by saying that hearing this Bhumi Parva brings merit.

Sanjaya rushes back from the battlefield and tells the grieving Dhritarashtra that Bhishma, the grandsire of the Bharatas, has been slain by Sikhandin and lies on a bed of arrows. He recalls Bhishma's great feats and his long resistance against the Pandavas, and blames the king's evil counsel for the disaster. The news marks a turning point, since Bhishma had been the mainstay of the Kaurava army.

Dhritarashtra, stunned, asks how Bhishma could have been killed by Sikhandin, who protected him, and how the Pandavas overcame him. He calls his own heart as hard as adamant for not breaking, and fears for the outcome now that the army has lost its foremost warrior. He demands every detail of the battle, saying he cannot regain his composure without it.

Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra not to blame Duryodhana, since men bring evil upon themselves by their own misdeeds, and recalls that the Pandavas long bore their injuries in the woods. He then says that the events were predestined and that he now has divine sight and hearing, granted through Vyasa, to report them. He recounts Duryodhana's orders to protect Bhishma at all costs, as Bhishma had vowed not to strike Sikhandin, and the guards Duryodhana names on the Pandava side.

After the night passes, the kings shout Array! and the armies rise and take their positions at dawn. Sanjaya describes the great show of banners, chariots and warriors, the Kaurava commanders such as Sakuni, Salya and Jayadratha who each lead an Akshauhini, and Bhishma in white at the head of the Kaurava vanguard. He ends by comparing the two armies to oceans at the end of an age.

Sanjaya describes the first day of the great battle, with ominous signs in the sky and the kings assembling as Vyasa had foretold. Bhishma urges the kings to fight bravely, since death in battle is a Kshatriya's duty and leads to heaven, and Karna alone lays down his weapons out of respect for him. The Kaurava divisions then advance under their named leaders, and their great formation is described in detail.

The field fills with uproar, banners and glittering armour as the two armies face each other. Sanjaya lists the Kaurava warriors who guard Bhishma from behind, the peoples pledged to fight to the death, and the huge forces of foot soldiers and chariots. He sums up the Kaurava army of eleven Akshauhinis as a great river divided.

Dhritarashtra asks how Yudhishthira could form a counter-array against Bhishma's great army with fewer troops. Sanjaya reports that Yudhishthira cites a precept of Vrihaspati for few against many, and Arjuna proposes the Vajra array, with Bhima at the front and the other Pandava warriors and allies placed around him, Sikhandin facing Bhishma, and Yudhishthira in the centre. Dawn then brings wind, dust, thunder and falling meteors, which the sons of Pandu face calmly.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya which side was eager to fight first and which side the omens favoured. Sanjaya says both armies were equally joyful and grand, with the Kauravas facing west and the Pandavas facing east, and the wind blowing against the Kauravas. He describes the Kaurava positions, with Duryodhana in the centre, Bhishma at the front in white, Drona at the rear and other leaders in their places, and says the Pandava army seemed invincible because Krishna and Arjuna led it.

Seeing Bhishma's impenetrable array, Yudhishthira grows pale and asks Arjuna how the few can hope to beat the many. Arjuna replies that victory comes through truth, compassion, righteousness and energy rather than sheer might, and that victory is wherever Krishna is. He backs this with the old story of the gods' victory through Hari's grace.

Yudhishthira sets the Pandava forces in counter-array and urges them to fight fairly and seek the highest heaven. Sanjaya describes the commanders in their places, Arjuna's car drawn by white horses and driven by Krishna, and Bhima leading the van. Krishna then points out Bhishma standing in the midst of his army and urges Arjuna to attack him.

As the Kaurava army approaches, Krishna tells Arjuna to purify himself and recite a hymn to Durga for victory. Arjuna dismounts and recites a long hymn praising the goddess by many names, and she appears in the sky and promises that he will soon defeat his foes with Narayana's help. The chapter ends with Krishna and Arjuna blowing their conches and with a list of the protections that reciting the hymn brings.

Dhritarashtra asks who advanced cheerfully, who struck the first blow, and whose troops were in higher spirits. Sanjaya replies that both armies were equally cheerful and fragrant, and that the collision was fierce, with music, conches, drums and roars.

The Bhagavad Gita opens as Dhritarashtra asks what his sons and the Pandavas did on the plain of Kurukshetra. Sanjaya reports that Duryodhana names the Pandava warriors and his own leaders to Drona, the conches sound, and Arjuna asks Krishna to drive his car between the armies. Krishna does so, Arjuna sees his kinsmen on both sides, and he sinks into grief, lays down his bow and sits down in his car.

Arjuna, overcome with pity, lays down his weapons and refuses to fight his teachers and kin, and Krishna rebukes his weakness. Krishna then teaches that the soul is eternal and cannot be killed, that a warrior should fight a just battle as his duty, and that one should act without attachment to the results. He ends by describing the steady-minded sage who is content within and free from desire, fear and anger.

Arjuna asks why Krishna praises devotion through knowledge yet urges him to dreadful action, and Krishna answers that no one escapes action by refraining from it. He teaches that one should act without attachment, as an offering, and gives the examples of the Lord of creation and of himself, who acts to keep the world in order. Krishna then names desire, born of passion, as the great enemy that drives people to sin and must be conquered.

Krishna says he first taught this imperishable path to Vivaswat, who passed it to Manu and Ikshaku, and that it was lost over time until he gave it again to Arjuna. Arjuna asks how this can be, since Vivaswat was born before Krishna, and Krishna answers that he is unborn yet appears in every age to protect righteousness. He then explains action without craving, the many kinds of sacrifice, and says that the sacrifice of knowledge burns away all action, urging Arjuna to cut his doubt with it.

Arjuna asks whether giving up action or acting with devotion is the better path, and Krishna answers that both lead to freedom but that acting with devotion is superior. He says the wise see the two paths as one, and that a person who acts without attachment, offering the fruit to Brahman, is untouched by sin. The chapter closes with the portrait of the sage who is at peace, equal toward all beings, and who knows Krishna as the enjoyer of sacrifice.

Krishna explains that a true renouncer does what is required without seeking the fruit, and he describes the practice of meditation, including posture, moderation in food and sleep, and steady attention on him. Arjuna protests that the restless mind is as hard to control as the wind, and Krishna replies that practice and detachment can tame it. Krishna then assures Arjuna that a devotee who falls short is not lost, and that the one who worships him with faith is the most devout.

Krishna explains that his nature has a lower eightfold form of earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, understanding and self-awareness, and a higher living form that sustains the universe. He is the source of all things, present in their qualities, but people are deluded by the three qualities and his illusion, so few know him truly. Those who turn to him reach him, while those who worship other gods receive only fleeting rewards.

Arjuna asks Krishna to define Brahman, the self, action and the other terms, and asks how the self-restrained can be known at the hour of death. Krishna answers that Brahman is supreme and indestructible, and that whoever remembers him at death goes to him. He describes meditation at the moment of death, with the breath held between the brows and the sacred syllable Om uttered, and explains the cycles of Brahman's day and night and the two paths, the bright path with no return and the dark path that leads back to rebirth.

Krishna calls his teaching the royal knowledge and royal mystery, and says he pervades all things while not being bound by them. He describes how he creates and dissolves creatures in cycles, and how those who worship him with devotion are cared for, even when they worship other gods without knowing it. He declares that devotion is open to all, including women, Vaisyas and Sudras, and urges Arjuna to fix his mind on him.

Krishna reveals that he is the source of the gods and great sages, so that they do not know his origin, and that whoever knows him as the unborn Lord is freed from sin. Arjuna asks him to describe his divine powers, and Krishna lists many of his manifestations, from Vishnu and Ganga to the Himalaya and the sacred syllable Om. He concludes that every glorious thing is only a fragment of his power, and that he upholds the whole universe with a part of himself.

Arjuna says that Krishna's teaching has dispelled his delusion and asks to see his true, sovereign form. Krishna grants him divine sight, and Arjuna sees a vast cosmic form with countless faces and weapons, in which warriors rush into Krishna's flaming mouths. Krishna reveals himself as Time, the destroyer, tells Arjuna to fight as his instrument, and then returns to his gentle human form, saying that only devotion can truly reach him.

Arjuna asks whether those who worship Krishna in personal form or those who meditate on the unmanifest are the best devotees. Krishna answers that those who fix their minds on him with faith are the most devoted, though the unmanifest path is harder. He offers to rescue such devotees and lays out a graded path for those who cannot manage fully, and he ends by describing the qualities of the devotees he loves most, who are free from hatred, content, steady and detached.

Krishna explains that the body is the field and the embodied self is its knower, and he lists the elements, qualities and virtues that make up the field and true knowledge. He describes the supreme Brahman as present everywhere, beyond the senses, and the light of all luminaries. He ends by saying that nature and spirit are both without beginning, that nature produces all the qualities while spirit only witnesses them, and that one who sees this is freed.

Krishna says he will teach again the supreme knowledge by which sages have reached perfection, and that the three qualities of nature, goodness, passion and darkness, bind the embodied soul. Each quality shapes a person's death, rebirth and reward, and a soul that sees the qualities as the only agents and rises above them attains immortality. Arjuna asks how such a person behaves, and Krishna describes his even-mindedness and his exclusive devotion.

Krishna describes the eternal fig tree, with roots above and branches below and leaves that are the Vedas, which must be cut down with detachment so that one can seek the supreme seat that no one returns from. He says that the individual soul is an eternal part of himself, carried from body to body like scent on the wind, and that he is the light in the sun, moon and fire. He identifies himself as the Supreme Person, beyond both the perishable and the imperishable, and says that whoever knows him worships him fully.

Krishna lists the divine qualities, such as fearlessness, purity, self-control, compassion and humility, which lead to liberation, and contrasts them with the demonic qualities of hypocrisy, pride, anger and ignorance, which lead to bondage. He describes demonic people who deny moral order, pursue endless desires, and are cast down into hell. He names lust, anger and greed as the three gates to hell and tells Arjuna that scripture should guide what he does.

Arjuna asks whether the worship of those who act outside the scriptures, but with faith, is of goodness, passion or darkness. Krishna explains that faith and everything else, including food, sacrifice, penance and gifts, come in these three forms according to a person's nature. He ends by naming Brahma as OM, TAT and SAT, and says that any act done without faith counts for nothing here or hereafter.

Arjuna asks Krishna to explain the true nature of renunciation and abandonment. Krishna distinguishes three kinds of each by quality, teaches the causes of action, the three qualities of knowledge, action, agent and understanding, and the natural duties of each social class, saying one's own duty is better even when imperfect. He then urges Arjuna to surrender everything to him and promises deliverance, and Arjuna says his delusion is gone and he will act as Krishna bids. Sanjaya closes by saying that he heard this dialogue through Vyasa's favour, and that where Krishna and Partha are, there is victory and justice.

Yudhishthira puts down his armour and weapons and walks on foot toward the Kaurava elders, followed by his brothers and Krishna, while the Kaurava side mocks him as frightened. He asks Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Salya for leave and blessings to fight, and each grants it while confessing that he is bound to the Kauravas by their wealth and must fight for them. Krishna then tries to win Karna to the Pandava side, Karna refuses out of loyalty to Duryodhana, and Yuyutsu, a son of Dhritarashtra, joins the Pandavas amid general praise.

Dhritarashtra asks who struck the first blow when the two armies were drawn up. Sanjaya describes the rush of Dussasana and Bhishma against the Pandavas, led by Bhima, and the awful roar that frightens Dhritarashtra's sons. The fierce first encounter is then described, with the Kaurava princes surrounding Bhima, the Pandava warriors striking back, and Bhishma shining above all the rest.

The battle begins in earnest on the forenoon of the terrible day, and Sanjaya describes a long series of single combats across the field. Bhishma and Arjuna, Satyaki and Kritavarman, Abhimanyu and Vrihadbala, Bhima and Duryodhana, the twins Nakula and Sahadeva, Yudhishthira and the king of Madra, and many others fight fiercely, until the whole field becomes a confused melee that the onlookers compare to a war of gods and demons.

Sanjaya describes the fighting among the foot soldiers, where men lose all regard for one another, and sires, sons, brothers and friends kill each other. Elephants, horses, chariots and foot soldiers are shattered in the chaos, and the wounded cry out for kin and water while some brave men endure in silence. Under this assault the Pandava divisions begin to waver before Bhishma, who shines on his silver-standard chariot.

Sanjaya describes how Bhishma, protected by Durmukha, Kritavarman, Kripa, Salya and Vivinsati, cuts through the Pandava ranks. Abhimanyu duels with Bhishma and his guards, knocks down Bhishma's palmyra standard, and is cheered by the Pandavas. Sweta, son of Virata, then charges Salya until seven Kaurava champions hold him back, and Duryodhana and Bhishma rescue Salya.

Dhritarashtra asks what the two armies did when Sweta charged Salya, and Sanjaya describes a great slaughter in which Bhishma stands alone among the Kauravas. Bhishma and Sweta duel, breaking each other's bows and standards, and a celestial voice tells Bhishma that his hour of victory has come. Bhishma kills Sweta with a shaft, the Pandavas grieve and the Kauravas rejoice, and at nightfall both armies withdraw.

Dhritarashtra, having heard of Sweta's death, asks what the Pandavas did next, reproaches Duryodhana for provoking the war, and fears what Arjuna will do in his anger. Sanjaya tells him to own his own part, then describes Sankha's attack on Salya, Arjuna's stand against Bhishma in his defence, and Bhishma's rout of the Panchala and Matsya troops until the Pandavas withdraw at sunset.

After the first day's fighting, Yudhishthira goes to Krishna in despair at Bhishma's power and says he would rather retire to the forest than see his kings destroyed, while complaining that Arjuna seems indifferent. Krishna comforts him and Yudhishthira makes Dhrishtadyumna commander of the army, who vows to slay Bhishma and Drona. Dhrishtadyumna then forms the Krauncharuma array, with Arjuna in the van and Drupada at its head, ready for the next morning's battle.

Duryodhana, seeing the Pandava Krauncha array, urges Bhishma, Drona and the other commanders to protect the front, and arranges his own army with Bhishma at its head, Drona and Ashvatthama in support, and Duryodhana's brothers and allied kings on the flanks and rear. Both sides then blow their conches, and the two armies advance to battle once more.

Duryodhana orders his army to attack, and Bhishma's arrows drive back the Pandava divisions. Arjuna asks Krishna to drive him straight at Bhishma, vowing to slay him, and Bhishma wounds many warriors, including Krishna. Duryodhana then urges Bhishma to kill Arjuna because Karna refuses to fight, and Bhishma goes after him in a duel that the gods watch with wonder, since neither man gains the advantage.

Dhritarashtra asks how Drona and Dhrishtadyumna fought, and says that fate seems stronger than effort, since even Bhishma could not escape Arjuna. Sanjaya describes the duel in which Drona breaks Dhrishtadyumna's bow, chariot and steeds, and in which Dhrishtadyumna's mace and dart are also broken. When Dhrishtadyumna charges on foot with shield and sword, Bhima comes to his rescue, and Duryodhana sends the Kalingas against Bhima.

Urged on by Duryodhana, the Kalinga king and his allies attack Bhima, but Bhima slays the king's son Sakradeva with a mace and cuts down the king's elephant and many of his men in a rampage. Dhrishtadyumna and Satyaki come to his aid, and Satyaki kills Bhishma's charioteer, forcing Bhishma to be carried from the field. The Kalinga army is broken and Bhima stands triumphant in the middle of the troops.

In the afternoon Dhrishtadyumna fights Drona's son, Salya and Kripa, while Abhimanyu duels with Duryodhana's son Lakshmana, breaking his bow before Duryodhana comes to his son's aid. Arjuna then rushes to rescue Abhimanyu, and the Kaurava kings charge him, but his arrows scatter them and fill the field with broken weapons. Bhishma sees the army routed and orders its withdrawal as the sun sets.

At dawn Bhishma forms the Kaurava army in the shape of a Garuda, the eagle, with himself at its beak, Drona and Kritavarman at its eyes, and Duryodhana on its back. Arjuna answers with a half-moon formation, with Bhima on one horn, Dhrishtadyumna and Sikhandin in the middle, Yudhishthira with his elephants, and Krishna guarding the other horn. The two armies then clash in a roar that reaches the heavens.

Once the armies are drawn up, Arjuna cuts down the leaders of the Kaurava car divisions, and the fighting becomes a general melee of cars, elephants, cavalry and infantry, with the field strewn with broken weapons and bodies. Bhishma, Drona, Jayadratha, Sakuni and others break the Pandava ranks in turn, while Bhima, Ghatotkacha and the sons of Draupadi grind down the Kaurava host. The chapter ends with Duryodhana, Abhimanyu and Satyaki joining the fight in a new, fierce round of combat.

Kings surround Arjuna with a storm of weapons, while Satyaki and Abhimanyu fight Sakuni's forces. Bhima wounds Duryodhana in the chest, and when Duryodhana swoons and is carried away, the Kaurava army flees, leaving Bhishma and Drona unable to stop it. Duryodhana rallies his men and rebukes Bhishma for sparing the Pandavas, and Bhishma vows to check them alone, so both sides sound their conches for the next round.

Stung by Duryodhana's taunts, Bhishma charges into the Pandava army, slaughtering their warriors so swiftly that he seems to be everywhere at once, and the Pandava host breaks. Krishna urges Arjuna to strike Bhishma, and their duel leaves Krishna and Arjuna pierced by arrows. Krishna leaps down with his discus to kill Bhishma, who invites the blow, but Arjuna holds Krishna back, and then Arjuna unleashes the Indra weapon, making a river of blood, until the Kauravas withdraw at nightfall lamenting their losses.

On the next morning Bhishma leads the Kaurava army forward, surrounded by Drona, Duryodhana, Jayadratha and other princes, against Arjuna's array. The two sides clash amid a storm of dust, conches and falling warriors. Bhishma then turns on Arjuna, and their arrowy single combat is watched by both armies as Abhimanyu charges deep into the Kaurava host.

Abhimanyu fights alone against Drona's son, Bhurisravas, Chitrasena and other warriors, and the Kaurava princes surround him. Dhrishtadyumna comes to his rescue, and in a duel Dhrishtadyumna kills Samyamani's son with a mace, provoking Samyamani to attack Dhrishtadyumna in turn. Salya joins the attack on Dhrishtadyumna, and a new round of fighting begins.

Dhritarashtra, doubting that his sons can win, presses Sanjaya for news, and Sanjaya blames the war on Duryodhana's policy. He reports the fighting in which Bhima, after the Kaurava elephant division is massed against him, leaps down and smashes the elephants with his mace. The chapter shows the Pandava side pressing hard and the Kaurava line breaking.

Duryodhana orders his whole army to surround and kill Bhima, and Bhima holds the line like a shore against the sea. Bhima's mace destroys ranks of men, horses and chariots, and Bhishma advances against him. Satyaki pushes forward toward Bhishma, and Bhurisravas moves to block him.

Satyaki and Bhurisravas duel while the two armies gather around them, and Bhima fights Duryodhana and his brothers. Bhima is wounded and swoons, then recovers and kills many of Dhritarashtra's sons, and Bhagadatta blinds him with arrows. Ghatotkacha attacks Bhagadatta's elephant, and Bhishma calls off the fight at nightfall, so both sides return to camp, Duryodhana grieving for his brothers.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya why the Pandavas cannot be beaten, and Sanjaya answers that their righteousness protects them while his sons' cruelty weakens them. Duryodhana then asks Bhishma what makes the Pandavas invincible, and Bhishma says it is Krishna who guards them. To prove the point he recounts how Brahma praised Vishnu and asked him to take birth among men.

Vishnu agrees to Brahma's request and then vanishes, and Brahma tells the gods that Vasudeva must not be treated as a mere man. Bhishma says the sages taught him the same truth and that Krishna's presence brings righteousness and victory. He also says Dhritarashtra's sons are wrong to hate Krishna and Arjuna.

Duryodhana asks Bhishma about Vasudeva's origin and greatness. Bhishma describes Vasudeva as the supreme being who created the elements, the gods, and the four social classes, and lists his deeds and titles. He ends by saying Yudhishthira has sought Krishna's protection.

Bhishma recites a hymn that sages say Brahman himself composed, in which many seers name Vasudeva as the highest lord. Sanjaya reports that Duryodhana begins to respect Krishna and the Pandavas, and Bhishma again urges peace. Duryodhana then withdraws to his tent and lies down to sleep.

At dawn the two armies line up, with Bhishma's Makara formation facing the Pandava Syena formation. Bhima and Arjuna both attack Bhishma, and Duryodhana urges Drona to break the Pandava line. Drona fights Satyaki, and Sikhandin's attack on Bhishma and Drona is held back, so the battle grows fierce on both sides.

Bhishma fights fiercely to shield Duryodhana's sons from Bhima, and the general battle turns into a massive slaughter. Sanjaya describes the uproar, the piles of heads and limbs, and the rivers of blood. Duryodhana then advances with Bhishma at the front, and the Pandavas rush against Bhishma in response.

Arjuna charges toward Bhishma, and his conch and bow strike fear into the Kaurava ranks, who seek Bhishma's protection. Many Kaurava allies move in to support Bhishma, and the battle spreads across the whole field, with heavy losses of elephants, chariots and men. Sanjaya describes omens, dust, and the way the fighting breaks apart into pairs of opponents.

The battle now spreads into many duels, with Sikhandin, Arjuna, Bhima, Yudhishthira, Satyaki and Ghatotkacha each facing an enemy leader. Bhishma holds back Bhima and cuts his bow, then kills Satyaki's charioteer so that Satyaki's horses bolt. Bhishma then wins the field against the Pandavas, while the Panchalas press on, and another round of combat begins.

Several duels reach their peak in this chapter. Arjuna and Aswatthaman trade shots until Arjuna spares him out of respect, Bhima and Duryodhana wound each other, and Abhimanyu breaks through the Kaurava princes until Kripa carries Lakshmana away. The chapter ends with Bhishma slaughtering the Pandava troops and the field littered with bodies.

Satyaki's duel with Bhurisravas grows into a fight between the two heroes, with Satyaki's sons attacking Bhurisravas and being killed one after another. Satyaki and Bhurisravas then continue on foot until Bhima and Duryodhana carry them off in their chariots. Meanwhile Arjuna destroys many Kaurava chariots, and at twilight Bhishma withdraws the army for the night.

On the next morning both sides form their battle arrays, with Yudhishthira's Makara formation opposing Bhishma's crane formation. The armies clash across the whole field, and Drona wounds Bhima and kills his charioteer. Drona and Bhishma then drive back the Pandava troops, and the battle turns into a confused fight in which both sides suffer heavily.

Dhritarashtra praises his army for its discipline, skill, loyalty and the many great warriors who lead it, comparing it to a vast ocean. He still attributes its slaughter to fate, says that Vidura had warned against this war, and admits that Duryodhana would not listen. The chapter shows him looking back in regret and blaming destiny.

Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that the disaster is his own doing for allowing the dice match and the war, and then reports the battle. Bhima breaks into the Kaurava host and fights off Duryodhana's brothers, and Dhrishtadyumna rescues him after his charioteer Visoka leads him to the spot. Drona then routs the Pandavas, and the chapter ends with the Kaurava warriors cheering his success.

Duryodhana recovers and returns to fight Bhima, but Bhima wounds him and his brothers. Yudhishthira then sends Abhimanyu and eleven other warriors after Bhima, and Dhritarashtra's sons retreat. The chapter shows the Pandavas taking control of this part of the battle.

Abhimanyu and Bhima press into the Kaurava ranks in the afternoon, and Abhimanyu strikes down Vikarna's horses. Other Kaurava and Pandava warriors fight in close combat, while Bhishma and Arjuna make the field a sea of blood and corpses. The chapter ends with Sanjaya describing the fearlessness of both armies.

At sunset Bhima confronts Duryodhana, vows to kill him to avenge the Pandavas' past humiliations, and shoots down his bow, horses, umbrella and standard. Kripa and Jayadratha rescue Duryodhana, and Abhimanyu and the Kaurava princes fight in a long series of duels. Bhishma then routs the Panchalas, and Yudhishthira embraces Bhima and Dhrishtadyumna at the end of the day.

The warriors on both sides rest, bandage their wounds and praise each other's feats. Duryodhana asks Bhishma for help, and Bhishma promises to fight to the end, admitting the Pandava allies are very strong. Duryodhana's army then marches out again, bright with banners and dust, looking like clouds at the end of an age.

Bhishma lists the great kings and forces on the Kaurava side and says they could defeat the gods, while admitting the Pandavas have Krishna. He heals Duryodhana's wounds with an herb and arranges the army in a Mandala formation, while Yudhishthira answers with a Vajra array. Arjuna and Krishna charge the enemy kings, and Arjuna uses the Aindra weapon to beat back their volleys until Bhishma steps in to rescue the fleeing kings.

Duryodhana gathers the kings to protect Bhishma, who charges toward Arjuna, and a series of duels follows. Drona kills Virata's son and steeds, Aswatthaman fights Sikhandin, Satyaki turns back Alamvusha with the Aindra weapon, and Kritavarman is beaten by Bhima. The chapter shows the Kaurava side holding its ground while many of its warriors are wounded.

Dhritarashtra complains that Sanjaya always describes the Pandavas as cheerful and unbeaten, and Sanjaya answers that his side's valour is undone by the Pandavas and that the disaster is the king's own doing. The chapter then reports a series of clashes: the Avanti brothers against Iravat, Ghatotkacha against Bhagadatta, and Sahadeva and Nakula against their uncle Salya.

At midday Yudhishthira fights Srutayush and defeats him, and Kripa and Gautama fight Chekitana in a duel that leaves several warriors unconscious. Dhrishtaketu, Bhurisravas and Abhimanyu clash, and Arjuna charges Susarman and his allies, turning the field into a bloody confusion. The chapter ends with Arjuna taking on the kings who guard Bhishma.

Arjuna cuts down the bows and warriors of the Trigarta kings and others who try to block his path to Bhishma. Yudhishthira scolds Sikhandin for not keeping his vow to kill Bhishma, and Sikhandin takes up the fight again. Bhishma then defeats Yudhishthira, and the battle ends with Bhima and Chitrasena in a fierce struggle.

Bhishma overwhelms Yudhishthira and then fights his way through the Pandava allies, but Bhishma passes Sikhandin by. The battle spreads across the field and then stops with the coming of dusk. Each army retires to its tents, where the fighters are tended and rest in the quiet of night.

At dawn both armies move out, and the Kaurava line is formed with Bhishma in front and Drona, Bhagadatta and Duryodhana behind. Yudhishthira answers with the Sringataka array, and then the armies clash in a fierce general battle. Bhishma charges into the Pandava ranks, and the Pandava warriors rush at him.

Bhima kills Bhishma's charioteer and then a group of Duryodhana's brothers, and Duryodhana, in grief, goes to Bhishma and accuses him of standing aside. Bhishma replies that he and Drona will not survive this battle, and that Bhima will kill whomever he targets, and urges Duryodhana to fight on. The chapter shows the Kaurava side losing heavily and the words of Vidura being recalled too late.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how his sons can keep being killed by one man, and Sanjaya answers that the king's refusal to listen to Vidura has brought this ruin. He then describes the midday battle, in which the Pandavas divide into three groups and attack Bhishma, Drona and the Kaurava ranks, and Bhima wrecks the Kaurava elephants. The field is left strewn with dead elephants, horses and men.

Sakuni and Kritavarma lead Kaurava forces against the Pandavas, and Arjuna's son Iravat, born of a Naga princess, arrives with a large body of horses. Iravat fights off the six sons of Suvala and kills them, but Duryodhana sends the Rakshasa Alamvusha against him, and Alamvusha kills Iravat through illusion and deceit. Both armies then suffer heavy losses, and Drona and Bhishma are feared on the field.

After Iravat's death, Ghatotkacha roars in fury and attacks the Kaurava army with a band of Rakshasas. Duryodhana fights back, and Ghatotkacha tells him his wrongs against the Pandavas and Draupadi and vows to take revenge. The chapter opens the next phase of the battle between the two heroes.

Ghatotkacha hurls a huge dart that kills Bhagadatta's elephant, and Bhagadatta falls to the ground. Bhishma sends many Kaurava warriors to rescue Duryodhana, and Ghatotkacha defeats them one by one, wounding many of them, including Salya and Bhurisravas, while the Kaurava line is left in danger.

Ghatotkacha rises into the sky after many Kaurava warriors surround him, and his roars echo across the field. Yudhishthira sends Bhima and a large body of warriors to rescue him, and the two sides clash in a bloody melee where even fathers and sons do not recognize one another. The chapter ends with the Kaurava army being driven back in confusion.

Duryodhana wounds Bhima, who then fights on foot against Duryodhana and Aswatthaman until Drona's warriors rush in. Drona faints from his wounds, and Nila, Ghatotkacha and Aswatthaman clash in turn. Ghatotkacha finally uses an illusion that convinces the Kaurava army it is being destroyed, and the Kauravas flee to their camp at sunset while the Pandavas celebrate.

Duryodhana complains to Bhishma that Ghatotkacha has beaten his army and asks to be allowed to kill the Rakshasa himself. Bhishma tells him to fight the Pandava leaders instead and sends Bhagadatta against Ghatotkacha, whose elephant fights a fierce battle with the Pandava warriors. Bhagadatta wounds Bhima and breaks his chariot, Arjuna arrives to fight, and Bhima later tells Krishna and Arjuna how Iravat was killed.

Arjuna grieves over Iravat's death and says the war for wealth is a shameful slaughter of kinsmen, but he fights on out of duty. In the afternoon Bhima cuts down many of Dhritarashtra's sons, Drona fights him, and the Pandava and Kaurava warriors clash across the field in brutal close combat. The chapter ends with a long description of the field strewn with corpses and both armies withdrawing for the night.

Duryodhana, Sakuni, Dussasana and Karna plan how to defeat the Pandavas, and Karna advises that Bhishma should lay down his weapons so that Karna can fight. Duryodhana then goes to Bhishma's tent with a grand retinue and urges the old commander either to kill the Pandavas or to let Karna take over. Bhishma says nothing in reply, and the chapter sets up the quarrel that follows.

Bhishma is hurt by Duryodhana's taunts but answers calmly, listing the Pandava feats that show their invincibility and saying Krishna protects them. He vows to kill the Somakas and Panchalas but will spare Sikhandin, who was born a woman. Duryodhana then orders his army to surround Bhishma and places him in the front of the battle, while Arjuna arranges for Sikhandin to stand before Bhishma.

Bhishma forms the Sarvatobhadra array, with Duryodhana in the middle and key commanders on each wing and in the rear. Yudhishthira answers with a Pandava array led by Bhima and the twins, with Sikhandin, Arjuna and Ghatotkacha in the middle. The two sides advance with trumpets and drums, and ominous signs such as falling meteors, jackals and dust heighten the sense of doom.

Abhimanyu charges into Duryodhana's army and routs many warriors, so that Duryodhana asks Alamvusha to stop him. Alamvusha first attacks Draupadi's five sons, kills their steeds and charioteers, and then fights Abhimanyu in a battle that is compared to a clash between Vritra and Vasava.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya for a full account of Abhimanyu's duel with Alamvusha and of the other Pandava warriors. Sanjaya describes the duel in which Abhimanyu defeats Alamvusha's illusions with a solar weapon, and then Bhishma and the Kaurava army try to stop Abhimanyu, Arjuna comes to his son's aid, and Drona fights Arjuna.

Dhritarashtra asks how Drona and Arjuna, who respect each other, came to fight, and Sanjaya explains that they fight without regard for kinship because a Kshatriya's duty requires it. The chapter follows Arjuna's battle with the Trigartas and Drona, including the clash of the Vayavya and Saila weapons, and then Bhima's rampage among the Kaurava elephants.

At midday Bhishma fights a fierce battle against Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, Drupada and Sikhandin, and he will not strike Sikhandin, who he regards as a woman. The general battle turns into a grim scene of chariots dragged across the field and a river of blood, and Duryodhana urges his commanders to fight without boasting. Sanjaya blames the war on Duryodhana's refusal to heed his advisers.

Arjuna routs Susarman's forces and the Kaurava army falls back, but Duryodhana and Bhishma attack Arjuna. The Pandavas surround Bhishma to protect him, and many duels follow, with Satyaki and Bhishma exchanging darts. The battle resumes with both sides fighting fiercely as the chapter closes.

Duryodhana orders Dussasana to protect Bhishma, who is surrounded by the Pandavas, and sends Sakuni and his horsemen against Yudhishthira and the twins. The Pandavas cut down the Kaurava cavalry, and Duryodhana then sends Salya against Yudhishthira. Bhima rushes to his brother's side as the sun sinks.

Bhishma destroys the Pandava army in a relentless attack, and his followers and foes are cut down until the Pandavas break into flight. Arjuna, urged by Krishna to fight, charges Bhishma, and the two exchange shots until Krishna leaps from the chariot and rushes at Bhishma with a whip. Arjuna clings to Krishna and begs him to stop, Krishna returns to the chariot, and Bhishma's attacks drive the Pandavas back until nightfall.

At nightfall Yudhishthira, despairing of defeating Bhishma, proposes to give up the fight, and Krishna offers to fight in his place. The Pandavas decide instead to go to Bhishma and ask how he can be beaten, and Bhishma explains that he will not fight someone who lays down weapons or a woman, so Arjuna must fight with Sikhandin before him. Arjuna is torn about killing his grandfather, but Krishna insists that the duty of a warrior requires it.

Dhritarashtra asks how Sikhandin and Bhishma met in battle, and Sanjaya describes the battle array on each side and the Pandava assault on Bhishma. On the tenth day Bhishma routs the Pandava warriors and breaks Sikhandin's division, then refuses to strike Sikhandin, who taunts him and wounds him. Arjuna urges Sikhandin to fight on and promises to hold back the Kaurava warriors.

Dhritarashtra asks how Sikhandin attacked Bhishma on the tenth day, and Sanjaya describes Bhishma destroying the Pandava forces. Arjuna then sweeps in, and Duryodhana, terrified, begs Bhishma for protection. Bhishma, reminding Duryodhana of his vow, vows to slay the Pandavas or die, and he wipes out vast numbers of their troops that day.

Arjuna urges Sikhandin to attack Bhishma, and the Pandava commanders rush to Bhishma's car while the Kaurava warriors go out to meet them. Dussasana blocks Arjuna, and the two fight a fierce duel in which Arjuna wounds Dussasana and then Duryodhana, who withdraws to Bhishma's car.

The fighting around Bhishma spreads into many pairs of duels, including Satyaki against Alamvusha and Bhagadatta, and Kripa against Sahadeva. Kaurava warriors gather to kill Satyaki, while the Pandava and Kaurava princes all fight for control of Bhishma's position. The chapter describes the widespread clash of heroes that ends in Bhurisravas facing Bhima.

Drona, watching omens of disaster in the sky and among the animals, tells his son Aswatthaman that Arjuna will attack Bhishma that day. He says Sikhandin is an ill omen, but Bhishma will not strike him, and he sends his son against Sikhandin and Bhima while he himself goes to meet Yudhishthira's forces. The chapter ends with Drona's orders for the day.

Ten Kaurava warriors, led by Salya, Kripa, Bhagadatta and Jayadratha, attack Bhima together on Drona's orders. Bhima holds them off, wounds each of them, and cuts down their weapons, but he is wounded in turn. Arjuna then comes to help his brother, and Duryodhana sends Susarman with a large force to kill both Arjuna and Bhima.

Arjuna and Bhima fight Susarman's forces and the Kaurava kings in a fierce battle that leaves many chariots, horses and elephants destroyed. Drona and the Magadha king join the fight against the brothers, and the battle turns general. Bhishma and Duryodhana advance on the Pandavas, Sikhandin rushes at Bhishma, and Dhrishtadyumna orders the Pandavas to attack him as the battle for Bhishma's fate begins.

Dhritarashtra asks how Bhishma fought on the tenth day, and Sanjaya describes Bhishma's grief at the slaughter he has caused. Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that he no longer wishes to live and asks to be slain with Arjuna and Sikhandin leading the attack. The Pandavas take up the challenge, and both armies clash in a general battle that Sanjaya compares to a fight between hawks over meat.

The duels around Bhishma continue. Abhimanyu fights Duryodhana, Aswatthaman fights Satyaki, and Paurava and Dhrishtaketu fight to the point of falling together, while Bhima crushes the elephant division and Drona and Dhrishtadyumna trade heavy blows. Arjuna then pushes through the Kaurava warriors toward Bhishma, and Bhishma's arrows drive back the Pandava forces.

Sikhandin attacks Bhishma with many arrows, but Bhishma will not strike him out of respect for his former sex. Arjuna urges Sikhandin on, and Dussasana holds back the Pandava warriors so that Bhishma is protected. The Kaurava army rallies and Arjuna scatters the Kaurava allies, defeats several leaders, and turns to Bhishma again until the armies are thrown into confusion.

The battle breaks into a chaotic melee in which the fighters no longer keep to their own kinds. Bhishma cuts down thousands of Pandava warriors, and Dhrishtadyumna urges the Somakas to attack him. Krishna then tells Arjuna to block Bhishma, and Arjuna and Sikhandin press their attack on the grandsire, who refuses to strike Sikhandin.

The Pandavas and Srinjayas gang up on Bhishma, and Arjuna and Sikhandin cut down his bows, but Bhishma keeps fighting. Bhishma concludes that he will die, and when he falls from his chariot at sunset he decides to wait on his bed of arrows until the sun turns north. The Kauravas despair, the Pandavas rejoice, and Bhishma waits in meditation.

Dhritarashtra laments that Bhishma has fallen, especially to Sikhandin, and asks what followed. Sanjaya describes the grief of the Kauravas, the news that reaches Drona, and the halt in the fighting as both armies come to Bhishma's bedside. Bhishma greets them and asks for a pillow, then rejects the soft cushions the kings bring and asks Arjuna for a proper one.

Arjuna supports Bhishma's head with three arrows, and Bhishma praises him and says he will wait on his bed of arrows until the sun turns north before dying. He refuses the physicians, and the kings from both sides gather around him before returning to their tents for the night. Krishna then praises Yudhishthira for the victory, and Yudhishthira credits Krishna's protection.

The next morning the kings of both sides gather around Bhishma and bring him water, but he refuses ordinary drink. Arjuna makes a spring of cool water rise from the earth with a special arrow, and Bhishma praises him and urges Duryodhana to make peace before the bloodshed continues. Duryodhana refuses, and Bhishma turns to yoga while still in pain.

Karna hears of Bhishma's fall and visits him on his bed of arrows. Bhishma embraces him, reveals that he is Kunti's son, and urges peace with the Pandavas, but Karna refuses to abandon Duryodhana and asks forgiveness for his past harsh words. Bhishma gives him leave to fight, Karna rides off, and the chapter closes the Bhishma Parva. The rest of the chapter is the translator's footnotes, mainly on variant readings and the sense of Gita verses.

Janamejaya asks what Dhritarashtra did after Bhishma fell, and Sanjaya begins his account. The Kaurava army is left without a leader and falls into despair, so the kings call for Karna to take charge. Dhritarashtra doubts that Karna can fill the gap Bhishma leaves and bring his sons victory.

Karna hears that Bhishma has fallen and hurries to the field to rescue the Kaurava army. He mourns Bhishma, declares that he will fight the Pandavas himself, and orders his armour, chariot and weapons made ready. The chapter ends with him riding out to battle in splendour.

Sanjaya describes Bhishma lying on his bed of arrows, the hope of the Kauravas gone. Karna dismounts in grief and approaches him on foot. He mourns the old warrior and vows to fight the Pandavas, Arjuna above all.

Bhishma, still lying on his bed of arrows, blesses Karna and tells him to lead the Kaurava army against the Pandavas. Karna takes his leave and returns to the Kaurava warriors. The Kauravas greet him with loud shouts, and Karna takes his place at the head of the army.

Duryodhana, pleased to see Karna ready on his chariot, says the army now seems to have a proper leader. He asks Karna whom to name as commander after Bhishma, since an army cannot hold together without one. Karna answers that Drona, their teacher in arms, should lead, because the other warriors would follow him.

Duryodhana turns to Drona, who is standing among the troops, and asks him to lead the army. He praises Drona's birth, learning, prowess and self-control, and compares him to the greatest gods and figures. The Kaurava kings cheer the choice, and Drona prepares to reply.

Drona agrees to lead, though he says he cannot kill Dhrishtadyumna, who was born to slay him. He is installed as commander with rites, and the army takes its formation, with Karna at the head of the bowmen. Both armies array for battle, omens of disaster appear, and the fighting begins with Drona driving into the Pandava ranks.

Yudhishthira orders his men to surround Drona, but Drona keeps cutting down warriors across the field. Sanjaya then reports that Dhrishtadyumna has at last slain Drona, a death that brings an uproar from creatures and the gods. The Pandavas celebrate their victory with loud shouts.

Dhritarashtra cannot accept that Drona, the greatest master of arms, has been killed. He asks how it happened: whether his chariot or bow broke, whether he was unarmed, and who failed to guard him. He calls the news unbearable and breaks off his questions for a while to recover himself.

Dhritarashtra faints on hearing of Drona's death, and his attendants and the royal ladies revive him. Once he regains his senses, he asks Sanjaya to describe the battle again. He then asks, hero by hero, which Kaurava warriors stood against each Pandava ally rushing at Drona, and he ends by calling on Krishna to restore his firmness.

Dhritarashtra recounts Krishna's feats from boyhood onward, including his victories over demons and kings, and concludes that the Kurus cannot win if Krishna and Arjuna fight together. He blames himself for the ruin of his family, now that Bhishma and Drona are dead. He asks Sanjaya to tell him everything about the battle.

Sanjaya begins the account of Drona's fall. Once made commander, Drona offers Duryodhana a boon, and Duryodhana asks him to take Yudhishthira alive. Drona is puzzled, but agrees on the condition that Arjuna is drawn away from the field, and Duryodhana then proclaims the promise to the whole army.

Yudhishthira learns through spies of Drona's pledge to take him, and he asks Arjuna to stay close and protect him. Arjuna vows that Yudhishthira will not be taken, though he will not harm his teacher, and says he has never broken a promise. The two armies join battle, and Drona breaks through the Pandava ranks toward Dhrishtadyumna's division.

Drona tears through the Pandava ranks with such fury that Sanjaya compares the carnage to a vast river of blood and corpses. The Pandava champions then rush at him, and many single combats break out across the field. Abhimanyu duels with Paurava, Jayadratha and Salya, and after he hurls back Salya's dart, the Kauravas surround him.

Dhritarashtra admits he envies those who can see such fights, but says he is not satisfied by the account and asks about Salya's combat with Abhimanyu. Sanjaya reports that Bhima, not Abhimanyu, takes up the fight with Salya, and the two strike each other with maces until both fall. Kritavarman carries Salya from the field, and the Kaurava army flees before the Pandavas.

Vrishasena, son of Karna, holds back the Pandava attack single-handed, until the Pandava princes and then Drona's son and others join the fight. Drona then charges Yudhishthira and kills his protectors, while the Pandava warriors cry out that the king is slain. Arjuna arrives with a devastating rush, and as darkness falls both sides withdraw from the field.

Drona tells Duryodhana that Arjuna must be lured away from Yudhishthira before Yudhishthira can be seized. The Trigarta brothers and their allies swear a fire-oath to draw Arjuna off and kill him or die trying, and Arjuna accepts their challenge. Yudhishthira blesses him and names Satyajit as his protector, and Arjuna rides out against the Trigartas, leaving both armies to clash.

The Samsaptakas, the band of warriors sworn to kill Arjuna, form up in a half-moon and meet him in the field. Arjuna blows his conch, and the enemy is stunned with fear, but they recover and pour arrows on him. After he kills Sudhanwan, his followers flee, until the Trigarta king rallies them and they return to face Arjuna.

Arjuna drives back into the Samsaptakas with Krishna at the reins. They bury him and Krishna in arrows, so he uses a weapon that creates thousands of images of himself and Krishna, and the troops in confusion kill each other. Krishna, worn out, calls to Arjuna, who then clears the sky with a wind weapon and slaughters the Samsaptakas. While this goes on, Drona attacks Yudhishthira.

After Arjuna has gone off after the Samsaptakas, Drona forms the Kaurava army in the shape of a Garuda and marches to seize Yudhishthira. Yudhishthira answers with a counter-formation and asks Dhrishtadyumna to keep Drona from him. Dhrishtadyumna vows to hold Drona back, but Durmukha engages him, and the battle becomes a chaotic slaughter of men and elephants as Drona presses on toward Yudhishthira.

Satyajit, the Panchala prince, fights Drona fiercely, but Drona destroys his bows, horses and charioteer and at last beheads him. Yudhishthira flees, and Satanika, a Matsya prince, is also beheaded by Drona. Drona then sweeps through the Pandava ranks, and many Pandava warriors close in on him in turn, all falling before him as Drona routs the Panchalas and Matsyas.

Dhritarashtra asks whether anyone dared to stand against Drona once the Pandavas were broken. Sanjaya reports that the Kauravas pressed their advantage, and Duryodhana gloated to Karna that the enemy was finished. Karna warns that the Pandavas will not give up, and that Bhima and the others are returning to surround Drona. Duryodhana then rides to Drona's car, and the Pandava warriors come back, all bent on killing him.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to name the warriors who rushed at Drona under Bhima, and by what marks they are known. Sanjaya gives a long roll-call of the Pandava allies, their horses, standards and bows, and describes the great host that advanced. He then reports the many single combats that broke out across the field, a battle that Sanjaya says had never been seen before.

Dhritarashtra asks how Arjuna fought the Samsaptakas and what the Kaurava warriors did in the meantime. Sanjaya describes Bhima routing Duryodhana's elephant division and killing the Anga king. Bhima then faces Bhagadatta's elephant Supratika, escapes it by getting under its belly, and the rumour spreads that he is dead. Bhagadatta's elephant then rampages through the Pandava ranks.

Sanjaya turns to Arjuna's deeds. Seeing Bhagadatta's rampage, Arjuna asks Krishna to drive toward him, but the Samsaptakas return to challenge Arjuna, and he is torn between the two. He decides to destroy the Samsaptakas first, which is what Duryodhana and Karna had hoped for, and he wipes them out with the Brahma weapon. Krishna praises him, and Arjuna then tells Krishna to go on to Bhagadatta.

Arjuna turns aside to fight Susharman, defeats him and his brothers, and then sweeps through the Kaurava host. He meets Bhagadatta on his elephant, and Krishna steers the car so that the elephant is on his left. Arjuna holds back from striking the rider from behind, keeping to the rules of fair fight, while the elephant kills many other warriors.

Dhritarashtra asks how Arjuna and Bhagadatta fought to the end. Sanjaya describes Arjuna cutting down Bhagadatta's weapons and armour and striking the elephant. When Bhagadatta's Vaishnava weapon lands on Krishna's chest and turns into a garland, Arjuna complains that Krishna had promised only to drive. Krishna explains the weapon's history and why he let it strike, and Arjuna then kills the elephant and Bhagadatta, whose death breaks the Kaurava warriors.

After killing Bhagadatta, Arjuna fights the Gandhara brothers Vrishaka and Achala, Sakuni's brothers, and kills them with a single arrow. Sakuni then conjures illusions against Arjuna, which Arjuna destroys one by one until Sakuni flees. Arjuna's arrows split the Kaurava host, and the field becomes a scene of carnage in which men abandon their own kin in panic.

Dhritarashtra asks how his men felt after the rout and how they rallied. Sanjaya says that the Kuru champions still followed Drona and seized an opening against Bhima's side, while the two armies fought furiously over Drona's life. Dhrishtadyumna finally checks Drona. Nila then attacks the Kaurava ranks, but Drona's son Ashvatthama kills him, and the Pandavas fear that Arjuna is too far away to help.

Bhima, unable to bear the slaughter of his army, attacks Valhika and Karna, and Drona wounds him in return. The Pandavas gather around Bhima and press in on Drona's car, while Arjuna, having destroyed the Samsaptakas, storms in and scorches the Kauravas. Karna meets Arjuna with the fire weapon, and when Satyaki and others attack him, Duryodhana and Drona rescue him. At sunset both armies withdraw, bloodied and worn.

The Kauravas retire humiliated, and Duryodhana rebukes Drona for letting Yudhishthira escape. Drona promises to form an impenetrable circular array and asks that Arjuna be drawn away, and the Samsaptakas lure him off. Abhimanyu breaks into the array, but he is overwhelmed by six warriors and finally killed by Duhsasana's son. Dhritarashtra grieves for the boy and asks how so many warriors could kill him.

Sanjaya lavishes praise on the Pandavas, Krishna and especially on Abhimanyu, who seemed to combine the best qualities of them all. Dhritarashtra asks for a detailed account of the boy's death, and Sanjaya asks him to bear his grief. He then describes the great circular array Drona formed, with Duryodhana in its midst, Lakshmana leading ten thousand warriors and Jayadratha, Sakuni and Salya on its flanks, and the battle begins.

The Pandava host, led by Bhima, attacks Drona's array, but Drona holds them back with a storm of arrows. Yudhishthira, unable to break the array, asks Abhimanyu to break in and open a passage, and Abhimanyu accepts, promising that the others will follow. Yudhishthira blesses him, and Abhimanyu orders his charioteer to drive into Drona's army.

Sumitra, Abhimanyu's charioteer, warns him that Drona is a master of arms and that Abhimanyu, pampered by luxury, is untested in battle. Abhimanyu laughs off the warning and drives on, breaking into the circular array while the Kauravas close in. He kills warrior after warrior, along with their elephants, steeds and cars, until the Kaurava army loses heart and flees, abandoning its wounded.

Duryodhana, enraged by the rout, turns on Abhimanyu, and Drona orders his warriors to rescue the king. Drona, Karna, Kripa, Salya and many others close in on Abhimanyu, who fights them all off. He kills the ruler of the Asmakas, wounds Karna, and drives Salya from his chariot in a faint, and then the Kaurava army runs. The gods and other beings praise him for his prowess.

Dhritarashtra asks which warriors tried to check Abhimanyu as he broke the Kaurava chariot ranks, and Sanjaya begins with Abhimanyu's exploits. Salya's younger brother rushes at him and is killed with his charioteer and car. His followers come next, and Abhimanyu fights them first gently and then with great ferocity, until the Kaurava chariots turn and flee.

Dhritarashtra, torn between shame and pride at his son's army being held off by one youth, asks Sanjaya for the full story again. Sanjaya tells how Abhimanyu strikes down many of the Kaurava chiefs. Drona praises Abhimanyu to Kripa, and Duryodhana sneers that Drona is shielding his pupil's son, then orders an attack. Duhsasana vows to kill Abhimanyu himself and goes in against him.

Abhimanyu taunts Duhsasana for his harsh speech, his part in the dice game, and his cruelty, and he swears to repay the wrongs done to his family. He wounds Duhsasana, who faints and is carried away, and the Pandavas cheer. Karna then comes forward and rains arrows on Abhimanyu, but Abhimanyu brings down his umbrella, standard, charioteer and steeds, and then breaks his bow.

Karna's younger brother rushes in and is slain by Abhimanyu with a single arrow. Karna, shaken, flees the field, and Abhimanyu sweeps through the Kaurava army, leaving only Jayadratha standing in the midst of it. The field becomes impassable with bodies, and Sanjaya says Abhimanyu blazed like the noonday sun among the enemy.

Dhritarashtra asks whether any great Pandava warriors followed Abhimanyu into the Kaurava host. Sanjaya says Yudhishthira, Bhima and the other leaders rushed in, but Jayadratha rallied the fleeing Kauravas and held the Pandavas back. Dhritarashtra asks what made Jayadratha so strong, and Sanjaya tells how, after Bhima humbled him for insulting Draupadi, he won a boon from Mahadeva (Shiva) that let him hold off the Pandavas.

Sanjaya describes Jayadratha's splendid chariot and his attacks on Satyaki, Bhima, Drupada, Yudhishthira and the other Pandava leaders. Yudhishthira cuts his bow, but Jayadratha quickly takes another and fells Bhima's bow and standard, forcing Bhima to leap onto Satyaki's car. No Pandava can get past him, and he closes the gap Abhimanyu had opened, thanks to Mahadeva's boon.

Abhimanyu cuts into the Kaurava ranks, disabling Vrishasena's chariot and killing the warrior Vasatiya. Many Kshatriyas then surround him, but he cuts down their bows, arms and heads until the field is strewn with bodies. He moves so fast that he seems almost invisible, blazing like the sun among the enemy.

Abhimanyu seizes Satyasravas, and a crowd of warriors rushes at him. Rukmaratha, the son of Salya, vows to take him alive, but he is slain, and Salya's princely kin come forward to fight. Abhimanyu uses the Gandharva weapon to create many illusory forms and kills a hundred princes. Duryodhana, alarmed by the slaughter, goes after him, and Abhimanyu's arrows force him to turn back.

Dhritarashtra asks what his army did next, after Duryodhana was beaten back and a hundred princes slain. Sanjaya says the Kaurava troops fled in despair until Drona, Kripa, Karna and others attacked Abhimanyu. Lakshmana, Duryodhana's son, rushed in alone, and Abhimanyu killed him with one arrow after taunting Duryodhana. Duryodhana's fury brings six great warriors against Abhimanyu, and he breaks through an elephant division and kills Kratha's son before the Kauravas retreat.

Dhritarashtra asks which of his warriors surrounded Abhimanyu as he rode through the army on his fleet steeds. Sanjaya says the kings fled before him, and Drona, Kripa, Karna, Ashvatthama and others attacked him, but he held them off and shot down their steeds, charioteers and bows. He killed Vrindaraka, wounded Ashvatthama and Karna, and then killed the ruler of the Kosalas, whose death sent ten thousand kings fleeing.

Karna and Abhimanyu trade arrows until both are drenched in blood, and Abhimanyu kills many more warriors, including Karna's counsellors and several princes. Drona then advises the Kauravas to disarm Abhimanyu rather than fight him head on, and Karna, Kritavarman and Kripa cut his bow, steeds and charioteers. Abhimanyu leaps into the air with sword and shield, but Drona and Karna cut those away too. He comes down and charges Drona with a car-wheel in his hands.

Abhimanyu, stripped of his bow, sword and wheel, takes up a mace and fights Ashvatthama, Kalikeya and Duhsasana's son, but Duhsasana's son strikes him on the head as he rises, and he falls dead. The Kauravas rejoice, though voices in the sky call the killing unrighteous. Yudhishthira rallies his routed troops, telling them the boy has gone to the regions of the righteous.

Sanjaya says the Kaurava army returns to camp in the evening, bloodied and shaken. At dusk the field is left to carrion eaters and Rakshasas, and a river of blood runs through the heaps of corpses. The warriors leave Abhimanyu lying among the dead, like a sacrificial fire no longer fed with butter.

The Pandava warriors lay down their arms and sit around Yudhishthira, who laments the death of his nephew Abhimanyu. He blames himself for sending the boy into Drona's array, and he fears Arjuna's wrath, which he expects will destroy the Kauravas. He says that even victory and sovereignty give him no joy without Abhimanyu.

Yudhishthira continues to grieve, saying a child was sent into an unequal battle and he cannot find peace of mind. Vyasa comforts him, saying the heroic youth has gone to heaven and that Death takes all beings. Yudhishthira asks what Death is, and Vyasa begins the story of King Akampana, whose son Hari was slain, which Narada told the king to ease his grief.

Shiva (Sthanu) begs Brahma to be gracious, since the fire of his wrath is consuming creation. Brahma explains that the earth had asked him to destroy her burdensome creatures, and that his anger rose when he could find no other means. Shiva pleads with him to quench the fire and spare the worlds, and Brahma holds in his wrath, from which a dark woman then emerges. Brahma names her Death and orders her to slay creatures, and she weeps, and Brahma catches her tears in his hands.

Narada continues the tale: Death, the woman Brahma has made, pleads not to be forced into killing creatures and turns to long austerities instead. Brahma tells her to take lives anyway, promising that no sin will fall on her, and she agrees out of fear of his curse. Narada consoles King Akampana by saying death is ordained for all and that his son's fate is not a cause for grief, and Vyasa then urges Yudhishthira to cast off his own grief and go back to battle.

Yudhishthira, still grieving, asks Vyasa for more examples of royal sages and their sacrifices. Vyasa tells the story of King Srinjaya, whose son's waste and sweat turned to gold and who was killed by robbers who wanted that wealth. Narada then consoles the grieving king with the example of Marutta, a royal sage of great sacrifice who also died.

Narada tells Srinjaya that King Suhotra, a mighty and generous ruler whose kingdom seemed to flow with gold, also met death after a life of sacrifices. Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who made no sacrifices, since such a great king has died too.
Narada tells Srinjaya that King Paurava, who gave away countless horses, elephants, cars and cattle at his sacrifices, also died. Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who gave nothing away.

Narada tells Srinjaya that King Sivi, son of Usinara, who gave away gold, cattle and even the earth to the Brahmins, also died. Rudra had granted him a boon of inexhaustible wealth and fame, and Narada again tells Srinjaya that he should not grieve for a son who made no sacrifices.

Narada continues his list of dead kings, which he gives to Srinjaya to ease his grief. He describes Rama, son of Dasaratha, who lived in exile, defeated the Rakshasa Ravana who had abducted his wife, and then ruled a golden age of long life and piety. Rama too died, so Narada tells Srinjaya again not to grieve for a son who made no sacrifices.

Narada recalls King Bhagiratha, who gave vast gifts at his sacrifices, with cars, cattle and maidens to the Brahmins. The river Ganga, in the story, chose him as her father by sitting on his lap, and he ascended to the realm of Brahma at the end of his life. Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who gave nothing, since such a great king has died too.

Narada says that King Dilipa, son of Havila, held hundreds of sacrifices, gave the whole earth to the Brahmins, and had golden roads laid for his guests. Dilipa too died, so Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who made no offering.

Narada tells of Mandhatri, son of Yuvanashva, who was brought out of his father's womb by the Ashvins and nourished from Indra's fingers, and who went on to conquer the whole earth. He performed a hundred Horse-sacrifices and a hundred Rajasuyas and gave away great treasures before dying. Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who gave nothing away.

Narada tells of Yayati, son of Nahusha, who performed many sacrifices and gave away the wealth of the earth. He later saw that desire is never satisfied, so he gave up his throne to his son and retired to the forest, but he too died. Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who made no sacrifice.

Narada tells of Amvarisha, son of Nabhaga, who fought a thousand kings alone and defeated them, and then held a hundred splendid sacrifices with lavish feasts and gifts of kingdoms to his priests. The great sages praised him, yet he too died. Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who made no sacrifice.

Narada says King Sasavindu had a hundred thousand wives, each of whom bore a thousand sons, all of whom performed sacrifices. At his Horse-sacrifice Sasavindu gave away his sons and enormous wealth to the Brahmins, and he too died after a long reign. Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who made no sacrifice.

Narada tells of Gaya, son of Amartaraya, who lived on the leftovers of the sacred butter offered to Agni for a hundred years, until Agni granted him learning, wealth and sons. He then held great sacrifices, including one with a golden altar, but he too died. Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who gave no sacrifice.

Narada tells of Rantideva, who kept a great host of cooks to feed Brahmins day and night, gave away gold by the crore, and sacrificed so many animals that a river was named after their hides. He too died, and Narada says Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who gave nothing away.

Narada continues with Bharata, son of Dushyanta, who as a boy in the forest mastered lions, tigers and elephants and so earned the name Sarvadamana, meaning the subduer of all. As an adult he performed many Horse-sacrifices and gave away enormous wealth, including gold to Kanva. He too died, so Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who made no sacrifice.

Narada tells of Prithu, son of Vena, crowned emperor at a Rajasuya, whose reign brought plenty: the earth yielded crops unbidden, the cows gave milk, and sea and mountains made way for him. When his subjects asked for food, he made the Earth yield her milk, with each class of beings milking her into its own vessel. He gave away golden images at his great Horse-sacrifice, and he too died, so Srinjaya should not grieve.

Narada tells of Rama, son of Jamadagni, who avenged his father by destroying Kartavirya and many thousands of Kshatriyas, filling lakes with their blood. After a hundred sacrifices he gave the earth to the sage Kasyapa, who told him to leave it, and he withdrew to Mount Mahendra. He too will die, Narada says, so Srinjaya should not grieve for a son who made no sacrifice.

Srinjaya, having heard the histories of the sixteen kings, says his grief has been dispelled and asks Narada what he should do. Narada offers him any boon, and Srinjaya asks only for Narada's favour, so Narada restores his slain son from hell. Vyasa then explains that Abhimanyu died bravely and has won heaven, and bids Yudhishthira rise and fight, before departing, leaving Yudhishthira consoled but troubled about facing Arjuna.

At sunset Arjuna, having destroyed many Samsaptakas, rides back to camp with Krishna, uneasy at omens and at the grim silence. He finds his brothers grieving and realizes Abhimanyu is missing, and he breaks into a long lament, asking how the boy died. He also learns that Yuyutsu rebuked the Kaurava heroes for rejoicing, and Krishna consoles him that warriors fall bravely in battle, before Yudhishthira begins to speak.

Yudhishthira tells Arjuna how Abhimanyu broke Drona's array, how Jayadratha's boon checked the Pandavas, and how six warriors surrounded the boy and cut him off from his car. Duhsasana's son finally killed him after he had slain thousands. Arjuna faints with grief, rises in fury, and swears to slay Jayadratha by the next sunset or enter the fire, invoking dire fates on himself if he fails. He stretches the Gandiva and blows his conch, and the Pandava camp answers with shouts.

On hearing the Pandava uproar, Jayadratha is terrified by Arjuna's oath and asks Duryodhana's leave to go home. Duryodhana reassures him by naming the great warriors who will surround and protect him. That night Jayadratha asks Drona how his skill compares with Arjuna's, and Drona answers that Arjuna is the better through discipline, but promises an array Arjuna cannot pierce.

Krishna rebukes Arjuna for swearing an oath without consulting him, and he reports the spies' news that the Kauravas are dismayed. Jayadratha, shaking with fear, pleads with Duryodhana for protection, and Duryodhana turns to Drona. Drona arranges a formation half cart and half lotus, with Jayadratha at its heart and six champions guarding him.

On the eve of the battle, Arjuna vows to kill Jayadratha before sunset the next day, even if the gods and all creatures guard him. He boasts that his bow and strength cannot be matched and that he will break through the line Drona commands to reach the Sindhu king. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna then asks Krishna to have his chariot ready by dawn. The vow sets the terms of the next day's fighting.

Through the night the Pandava and Kuru camps are restless, and omens of disaster appear in the sky and across the land. Krishna goes to comfort Subhadra and Uttara, who grieve for Abhimanyu. He tells Subhadra that her son died a hero's death and that Jayadratha will be killed the next day.

Subhadra mourns her son Abhimanyu at great length, praising his looks and courage and wishing him the rewards that virtuous people earn. Draupadi and Uttara come to her, and all three weep until they faint. Krishna revives and comforts them, saying Abhimanyu reached the highest goal and that the men of their family will follow his example.

Krishna and Arjuna settle in Arjuna's tent for the night, and Arjuna makes an offering to Shiva. The Pandava camp stays awake, fearing that Arjuna's vow may fail. At midnight Krishna tells his charioteer Daruka that Duryodhana and Drona will guard Jayadratha, and orders the chariot made ready, and Daruka agrees to carry out the orders.

Arjuna, unable to sleep and afraid he cannot keep his vow to kill Jayadratha by sunset, is visited in a dream by Krishna, who urges him to set grief aside. Krishna then points him to the Pasupata weapon, which belongs to Shiva. Arjuna and Krishna travel in spirit to Shiva's mountain and offer him a long hymn of praise, and Sanjaya notes that they then pray for the weapon.

On Shiva's mountain Arjuna asks for the celestial weapon, and Shiva agrees, sending the two heroes to a sacred lake. There two snakes turn into a bow and arrow, and a youth who comes out of Shiva's body shoots the arrow with it. Arjuna then learns the use of the weapon, receives the Pasupata, and he and Krishna return to camp in high spirits.

The morning of the battle opens with music, which wakes Yudhishthira. He bathes, honours the sacred fire, and gives gifts to many Brahmanas, then dresses in jewels and sits on a golden seat as bards sing his praises. The chapter closes with Krishna being brought in and welcomed by the king.

Yudhishthira greets Krishna and asks whether he slept well, and the other kings and warriors are introduced and take their seats. Yudhishthira pleads with Krishna to rescue the Pandavas from their sorrow and to make Arjuna's vow come true. Krishna replies that no bowman equals Arjuna and vows that Jayadratha will die that day, so that Arjuna returns in the evening.

Arjuna comes to Yudhishthira, who embraces him and hopes for his victory. Arjuna tells of his meeting with Shiva, and then he, Krishna and Satyaki ride out to battle with omens of victory. Arjuna asks Satyaki to guard Yudhishthira, and Satyaki agrees and goes to the king.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what the Kauravas did after Abhimanyu's death, and he laments that the usual sounds of celebration have fallen silent in his sons' camps. He recalls that he warned Duryodhana to make peace and that his son ignored him and followed bad advice on the dice game and the war. He asks Sanjaya to report exactly what Duryodhana and his allies decided.

Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that his grief now comes too late, like an embankment built after the water has run off. He lists the earlier chances the king had to stop the dice game, the war, and Duryodhana, and says the Kauravas bear the blame for fighting Krishna and Arjuna's side. Sanjaya then prepares to recount the battle.

The morning after the night passes, Drona arrays his troops, and warriors on both sides shout for Arjuna and Bhima. Drona sends Jayadratha to a guarded position behind him, promising that not even the gods can reach him there. Drona forms a large combined array, shaped like a cart, lotus, and needle, with Jayadratha at the tip, and the Kauravas are delighted by it.

The battle begins with ill omens for the Kauravas, and Durmarshana boasts that he alone will stand against Arjuna. Arjuna and Krishna blow their conches, which terrify the Kaurava army. Arjuna then drives into Durmarshana's elephant force and cuts down the Kaurava troops, who flee in confusion.

Dhritarashtra asks who fought Arjuna after the front of his army broke. Sanjaya reports that Duhsasana rushes in with a large elephant force, but Arjuna destroys it, and Duhsasana flees to Drona's Sakata array for protection. The chapter shows the Kauravas losing heavily and seeking shelter behind Drona.

Arjuna asks Drona for his blessing and says he wants to pass through Drona's array to reach Jayadratha. Drona replies that Arjuna cannot defeat Jayadratha without first defeating him. The two fight fiercely, Drona briefly overpowers Arjuna and hides him under arrows, and Krishna urges Arjuna to move past Drona. Arjuna then presses on into the army, followed by the Panchalas, and Jaya, Kritavarman and others rush to block him.

Drona pursues Arjuna, but Arjuna keeps moving through the Kaurava ranks, trading arrows with Drona and then with Kritavarman, Srutayudha and Sudakshina. Srutayudha dies when his magic mace, which Varuna had warned must not be thrown at an unengaged foe, turns back on him after he hurls it at Krishna. Sudakshina of the Kambojas also falls, and the Kaurava troops flee.

The Kaurava allies press in against Arjuna in great numbers, but he cuts them down. A spear thrust leaves him senseless for a while until Krishna comforts him, and then he destroys the brothers Srutayus and Achyutayus with a celestial weapon. He goes on slaughtering the Kaurava forces, including many foreign warriors, until the field is covered with blood. Finally he kills Srutayus of the Amvashthas and disappears under a mass of enemy chariots and elephants.

Duryodhana rushes to Drona in alarm, saying Arjuna has broken through the army and blaming Drona for failing to protect Jayadratha. Drona replies that Arjuna's chariot is too fast for him to catch, that he is too old, and that Duryodhana must fight Arjuna himself. Drona then ties a golden armour on Duryodhana with sacred words and explains that the armour once belonged to Shiva, passed to Indra for his battle against Vritra, and reached Drona through a chain of teachers.

The Pandavas and Somakas press into Drona's array at the gate, and Dhrishtadyumna forces the Kaurava host into three parts. Drona fights back fiercely and many single combats break out across the field, with Bhimasena, Yudhishthira, Satyaki, Sahadeva, Sikhandin, Ghatotkacha and others each facing a Kaurava champion. Jayadratha stays in the rear, guarded by Kripa, Drona's son, Karna and Salya.

Sanjaya describes a string of separate fights across the field, where Virata and Sikhandin, Satyaki and Duhsasana, the twins Nakula and Sahadeva and Sakuni, and Yudhishthira and Salya clash with fierce arrow fire. The Kaurava allies are forced back, and Sakuni flees toward Drona's division. Sanjaya warns that the anger of the Pandavas, set off by the king's own conduct, now threatens to consume the earth.

The battle grows more savage, with Bhimasena attacking Jalasandha and Yudhishthira attacking Kritavarman, while Drona and Dhrishtadyumna fight at the centre. Dhrishtadyumna leaps from his chariot with a sword and climbs onto Drona's car, but Drona cuts down his shield and horses. Satyaki rescues Dhrishtadyumna from Drona's grip, and the Panchalas pull Dhrishtadyumna out of the fight.

Dhritarashtra asks what Drona did after Dhrishtadyumna was rescued. Sanjaya describes a long, evenly matched single combat between Drona and Satyaki, in which Satyaki keeps cutting Drona's bows, and the two armies stop to watch. Drona grudgingly admires Satyaki's skill, and then both men use celestial weapons that cancel each other out. As the sun sets, the Pandavas and Kauravas rush to save their champions, and a dust-filled melee follows.

As the sun sinks toward the western hills, Arjuna and Krishna drive through the Kaurava ranks toward Jayadratha. Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti attack the tired horses, but Arjuna kills both brothers and their followers. Surrounded by the Kauravas, Arjuna dismounts to stand alone and holds them off, and Krishna then makes a well for the horses and Arjuna builds a hall of arrows.

Arjuna keeps the Kaurava kings at bay while fighting on foot, and Krishna unyokes the horses, tends them and gives them water. Once they are rested, the two heroes remount and race toward Jayadratha as the sun sinks. Duryodhana's side despairs, but Duryodhana himself rushes forward to block Arjuna.

Vasudeva and Arjuna break through Drona's division and the Bhoja division, leaving the Kauravas stunned and fearful for Jayadratha's life. The two heroes speak together about killing Jayadratha, and Arjuna vows he will not let him escape. Duryodhana then charges out to meet them to protect Jayadratha.

Krishna urges Arjuna to fight Duryodhana directly, calling him the root of the Pandavas' wrongs and recalling the dice game, the exile, and the insult to Draupadi. Arjuna agrees to take him on and the two heroes blow their conches, as the Kauravas fear the king is about to die. Duryodhana then taunts Arjuna to use all his weapons against him.

Duryodhana wounds both Arjuna and Krishna, but Arjuna's arrows cannot pierce his armour, which Krishna asks about. Arjuna explains that the armour was passed down from Indra through Angiras and Vrihaspati and that Drona put it on Duryodhana, but he still expects to defeat him. Aswatthaman cuts Arjuna's prepared arrows apart, and Arjuna then destroys Duryodhana's horses, chariot and bow. When Krishna blows his conch, the Kauravas scatter, and the protectors of Jayadratha surge forward to face Arjuna.
