The Kaurava warriors rush at Arjuna and Krishna, each eager to strike first. Eight champions, including Bhurishravas, Karna, Jayadratha, Kripa and Drona's son Aswatthaman, surround Arjuna. Arjuna answers with his own rapid arrows, breaking Salya's bow and wounding several of the champions, and the field echoes with the blasts of many conches.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe the battle standards of both sides, and Sanjaya lists them in detail. Arjuna's ape banner, Drona's son's lion tail, Karna's elephant rope and the other champions' emblems all stand out, and the Kaurava side has nine standards in its divisions. Sanjaya blames the king's policy for the many kings and armies lost in the fight, and the battle between Arjuna and the Kaurava champions goes on.

Sanjaya describes the afternoon fighting, when the Panchalas and Pandavas press hard against Drona's division. Many pairs of warriors clash across the field, including Dhrishtaketu and Viradhanwan, Sahadeva and Durmukha, and Bhima and Alamvusha. Drona fights Yudhishthira, cuts his bow and horses, and leaves him weaponless, and the Pandava troops fear their king has been killed before he escapes on Sahadeva's chariot.

Several duels end in one side's victory. Kshemadhurti is killed by Vrihatkshatra, Viradhanwan falls to Dhrishtaketu's iron dart, and Sahadeva defeats Durmukha, then Niramitra. Satyaki beats Vyaghradatta and then the Magadhas, and Drona charges at Satyaki in fury.

Somadatta's son attacks the five sons of Draupadi, but they surround him and each strikes a blow, and Sahadeva's son finally beheads him. Then the Rakshasa Alamvusha fights Bhima, conjures illusions, and rains down weapons that drive the Pandava forces back. Bhima answers with the Tvashtri weapon, which drives Alamvusha off the field.

Ghatotkacha, Hidimva's son, attacks Alamvusha, and the two Rakshasas fight a long duel of illusions. The Pandavas surround Alamvusha with chariots, but he breaks free and wounds many of them. Ghatotkacha then seizes him, hurls him to the ground and crushes him, and the Pandavas celebrate while the Kauravas mourn.

Drona fights Satyaki, and Yudhishthira sends his troops to rescue him. Drona then routs the Pandava and Panchala forces, killing many warriors, until Yudhishthira hears Krishna's conch and fears for Arjuna. Yudhishthira then begs Satyaki to go and help Arjuna, pointing out that the Kaurava army is closing in on him and that Satyaki is the only warrior who can do it.

Satyaki agrees to go to Arjuna's aid, and says he is ready to fight the whole Kaurava army for the king's sake. He repeats Arjuna's own request that Satyaki protect Yudhishthira, saying that Drona is eager to seize the king. Yudhishthira insists that Satyaki should go to Arjuna, and he lists the warriors who will guard him, with Dhrishtadyumna to hold back Drona.

Satyaki, afraid of being thought a coward, agrees to leave Yudhishthira and follow Arjuna. He names the Kaurava forces he expects to meet, including Karna's Rukmarathas, the Kiratas, the Kambojas and others, and asks for his chariot to be stocked for a fierce fight. Yudhishthira provides arms, Satyaki's horses are readied and he is blessed by the Brahmanas, and he sends Bhima to guard the king before charging into the Kaurava host.

Satyaki routs the Kaurava troops and fights Drona, who accuses him of abandoning Arjuna in cowardice and threatens him. Satyaki answers that he must follow his teacher Arjuna's path and will not waste time on Drona. He drives toward Karna's host, beheads Kritavarman's charioteer, and is then held up by the Kamboja division while Drona pursues him. Kritavarman fights him in a long duel, and the Pandavas and Panchalas strain to hold their ground.

Dhritarashtra laments that his army, though well paid and well led, is being broken by Arjuna and Satyaki, and asks Sanjaya what happened when the two heroes entered his host. Sanjaya tells him that the king's own greed and refusal to heed Vidura's counsel brought the ruin, and he describes Kritavarman's stand against the Pandavas. Kritavarman wounds Bhima and nearly defeats Sikhandin, and then holds off all the Pandava and Panchala forces on his own.

Satyaki, hearing the uproar, turns back to fight Kritavarman and defeats him, then drives on to face the Trigarta elephant force and scatters it. Jalasandha leads a fresh elephant attack, but Satyaki wounds him, cuts off his arms and beheads him. The Kaurava troops flee in despair, and Drona turns to face Satyaki.

Satyaki faces a volley from many Kaurava champions, then wounds Duryodhana, who is forced to flee and take refuge in another chariot. Kritavarman comes to fight Satyaki, but Satyaki wounds and drives him down, and then pushes on through the Kaurava ranks toward Arjuna.

Drona fights Satyaki in front of the army, and their duel is evenly matched. Satyaki's charioteer is knocked senseless, and Satyaki steers his own chariot while driving off Drona's attacks. He kills Drona's charioteer, sends the horses running, and the Kauravas flee, so Drona returns to guard his broken array.

Satyaki, who laughs at his enemies as already dead, drives on after defeating Drona and his allies. King Sudarsana tries to stop him, but Satyaki kills his horses and charioteer and then beheads Sudarsana. The Kaurava ranks are overwhelmed, and Satyaki presses on along the track Arjuna had taken.

Satyaki urges his charioteer forward, describing the path Arjuna has cleared and the sound of Gandiva that tells him Jayadratha will fall before sunset. He faces the Yavanas, Kambojas, Sakas and other foreign troops, and his charioteer assures him he has nothing to fear. Satyaki vows to slaughter these warriors and drives into their ranks, cutting down thousands and routing the survivors, while the Charanas and Gandharvas applaud him.

Satyaki drives through the Kaurava army toward Arjuna, shining like the sun and cutting down troops in great numbers. Duryodhana, Duhsasana, Sakuni and other princes gang up on him, but he wounds and routs them and cuts down Duryodhana's charioteer. The Kaurava army scatters, and Satyaki continues toward Arjuna's car while the Kaurava troops praise his skill.

Dhritarashtra despairs that his sons cannot stop Satyaki, and asks how one man can break through so many great warriors. Sanjaya blames the king's own counsel for the disaster, and describes how the Samsaptakas and other Kaurava forces rush at Satyaki, only to be slaughtered. When Duhsasana sends stone-throwing mountain tribesmen against him, Satyaki shatters their stones with arrows, and Drona, hearing the uproar, decides to go after him.

Drona upbraids Duhsasana for fleeing from one warrior, reminding him of the insults he hurled at Draupadi and urging him to make peace with the Pandavas if he has no stomach for battle. Duhsasana ignores him and goes off to fight Satyaki, while Drona charges the Pandava and Panchala ranks. Drona kills several princes, including Viraketu and the brothers Chitraketu and Chitravarman, then fights Dhrishtadyumna in a fierce duel, cuts off his charioteer's head, and routs the Panchalas before returning to his own line.

Duhsasana charges Satyaki, but Satyaki shrouds him in arrows and routs his escort. The Trigarta warriors, sent by Duryodhana, come against Satyaki and lose five hundred men, and Duhsasana is stripped of his bow, chariot and charioteers. Satyaki spares Duhsasana because he remembers Bhima's vow to kill all of Dhritarashtra's sons, and then he moves on along Arjuna's path.

Dhritarashtra asks how Satyaki alone could pass through his mighty army, and Sanjaya describes the fierce muster of both armies. Bhima and the Pandava princes urge their men to stop Satyaki and Arjuna, and Duryodhana drives deep into the Pandava host, wounding Bhima, Yudhishthira and others. Yudhishthira breaks Duryodhana's bow, but Drona comes to rescue the Kaurava king, and the battle grows more savage on every front.

In the afternoon Drona fights Vrihatkshatra, the Kekaya prince, and kills him after a long duel. Drona then slays Dhrishtaketu, the Chedi king, and his son, and the Panchalas begin to tremble. Drona also kills Jarasandha's son and Kshatradharman, and the Pandava host collapses until Drupada leads the Pandava princes against him.

The Pandava army is shaken, and Yudhishthira, unable to see Arjuna or Satyaki or hear Gandiva, grows anxious for both. He decides he must not seem to care only for his brother, and he resolves to send Bhima to aid Satyaki. He goes to Bhima and, overcome with grief, begs him to go to Arjuna and Satyaki and send word back.

Bhima sets out after Yudhishthira's orders, handing the king over to Dhrishtadyumna. Yudhishthira blesses him, and Bhima rides off to the sound of the conches, with the Panchalas behind him. Drona tries to stop him, and Bhima replies with scorn, then hurls a mace that crushes Drona's chariot and begins slaughtering the Kaurava princes.

Bhima's great mace routs the Kaurava warriors who try to surround him, and Drona attacks him again. Bhima seizes Drona's chariot and throws it down, then crushes the Bhojas, Kambojas and other troops in his path. Hearing Arjuna and Krishna answer his shout, Yudhishthira is relieved and praises Arjuna, but he then frets about whether Jayadratha will fall before sunset.

Dhritarashtra asks who dared to stand against Bhima, whom he fears more than Arjuna or Krishna. Sanjaya answers that Karna charges Bhima, and the two exchange a long archery duel that ends with Bhima cutting Karna's bow, killing his charioteer and horses. Karna has to take another chariot, and Bhima's victory shout brings cheers from the Pandava side.

With the army routed and Arjuna and Bhima gone after Jayadratha, Duryodhana rides to Drona and asks for a plan. Drona says the Kauravas must defend Jayadratha, who is the real stake in this battle, and sends Duryodhana to guard him. On the way, Duryodhana fights the Panchala princes Yudhamanyu and Uttamaujas, crushes their chariots and then takes refuge on the chariot of the Madra king, while the two princes push on toward Arjuna.

Karna turns to face Bhima, and Dhritarashtra asks in dismay how the two could fight, given Karna's past defeat and his bond with the Pandavas. Sanjaya describes how Bhima, despite wanting to reach Arjuna, is challenged by Karna and must fight him. The two trade a long, bitter series of arrows, Karna mocking Bhima and Bhima stung into fury, until Bhima cuts Karna's bow and kills his horses and charioteer, leaving Karna wounded and forced to seek another chariot.

Dhritarashtra asks what Duryodhana said when Karna retreated, and how Bhima fought on. Sanjaya reports that Karna returns on a new chariot, and Bhima, stirred by his memories of the Kaurava wrongs, charges Karna in full fury. Karna blows his conch and counterattacks, and the battle turns into a fierce, even clash that kills many men and animals, and Krishna and Arjuna fear the burden is too much for Bhima.

Dhritarashtra, shaken by news of Karna's repeated defeats at Bhima's hands, asks Sanjaya to describe their duel and worries that his son's arrogance has doomed the Kauravas. Sanjaya reports a fierce exchange of arrows, with Bhima cutting Karna's bow and killing his charioteer and horses, and Karna's dart shot down by Bhima. Durjaya, Duryodhana's brother, rushes in to help Karna, but Bhima kills him, and Karna, weeping, is left surrounded by Bhima's arrows.

Karna, beaten by Bhima once more, takes a fresh chariot and fights on, but Bhima smashes his steeds and charioteer and cuts down his banner, leaving him on foot. Duryodhana sends his brother Durmukha to help, and Bhima kills Durmukha with arrows. Karna is then badly wounded and flees, which shows how far Bhima has turned the battle against the Kaurava side.

Dhritarashtra, hearing that Karna has been beaten, says fate rules everything, recalls Duryodhana's boasts about Karna, and fears for his sons against Bhima's might. Sanjaya rebukes him as the real cause of the war and its ruin, since he followed his sons' bad counsel. Sanjaya then reports that five more of the king's sons charged Bhima and were killed by his arrows, while Karna and Bhima glared at each other.

Karna, grieving over his dead sons, fights Bhima fiercely, and each man wounds and disarms the other in turn. Bhima breaks Karna's bow and Karna's mace attack fails, so Karna retreats on foot. When Duryodhana sends six more brothers against Bhima, he kills each with one arrow, and Karna returns in another chariot, both men bloodied.

Karna charges Bhima again, but Bhima wounds him heavily and roars in triumph. Duryodhana sends seven more brothers, and Bhima kills them all with arrows, grieving only for Vikarna, who had sided with the Pandavas. Yudhishthira hears Bhima's roar as a sign of victory and goes after Drona. Sanjaya then tells Dhritarashtra that his own refusal to heed Vidura's advice is the reason for the disaster.

Dhritarashtra admits that his bad policy has brought this ruin and asks Sanjaya to describe the slaughter. Sanjaya reports that Karna and Bhima shower arrows on each other until the Kaurava troops, the Sindhus and the Sauviras among them, flee in terror. The field is strewn with bodies and broken weapons, and the chapter ends with Karna and Bhima compared to forest-burning fires.

Karna and Bhima fight a long, savage duel: Bhima wounds Karna in the ear and forehead, Karna breaks Bhima's bow and chariot, and Bhima hurls objects and a sword in return. Bhima, now carless, is pinned down, and Karna mocks him as weak and fit only for the forest, but spares his life out of respect for Kunti and Arjuna's vow. Arjuna then arrives with Krishna, drives Karna off with his arrows, and turns against the Kaurava army as Ashwatthaman retreats.

Dhritarashtra laments that his fame is fading and that Arjuna has broken into his army, fearing that the ruler of the Sindhus is already dead. He asks Sanjaya to describe how Satyaki fought in the thick of the battle. Sanjaya reports that Satyaki killed the Kaurava ally Alamvusha, then cut down the steeds of Duhsasana, and the chapter closes with Arjuna and Krishna rejoicing at his feats.

Satyaki, pushing deep into the Kaurava host to reach Arjuna, is surrounded by Trigarta warriors and beats them back, then drives through the Surasenas and Kalingas. Krishna announces his approach and praises him, but Arjuna frets over Yudhishthira, Jayadratha and the setting sun, and fears that the tired Satyaki will be overmatched by the fresh Bhurisravas. The chapter shows Arjuna torn between his duty to his friend and his larger battle plan.

Bhurisravas, a Kuru warrior, challenges Satyaki with boasts, and Satyaki mocks him in reply. Their arrow duel turns into a sword fight, then a wrestling bout, with both men bloodied and worn down. Bhurisravas seizes Satyaki by the hair and is about to behead him, and Krishna urges Arjuna to act; Arjuna's arrow cuts off the arm that holds the sword.

Arjuna cuts off Bhurisravas's arm just as he is about to kill Satyaki, and Bhurisravas angrily accuses him of unfairness. Arjuna answers that he was protecting his disciple, and reminds Bhurisravas of the wrong done to Abhimanyu. Bhurisravas then sits down to fast unto death, and Satyaki, despite the protests of the warriors, beheads him, which Satyaki defends, and the chapter closes with praise for Bhurisravas's end.

Dhritarashtra asks how Satyaki, so long unbeaten, could be thrown down by Bhurisravas. Sanjaya explains with the family history: Sini had carried off Devaki, Somadatta was thrown down by Sini in a wrestling bout, and Somadatta won a boon from Shiva for a son who would strike Sini's line. Sanjaya then praises the Vrishnis as unbeatable and blames Dhritarashtra's bad policy for all that has happened.

With Bhurisravas dead, Arjuna urges Krishna to drive him at once toward Jayadratha, since the sun is sinking and he must kill the Sindhu king before sunset to keep his vow. Duryodhana, fearing that failure, begs Karna and the other leaders to block Arjuna, and Karna, though badly wounded, agrees to fight on. The chapter is a long account of Arjuna cutting down Kaurava warriors, Karna's charioteer and steeds falling, and Ashwatthaman stepping in to protect Jayadratha, with the sun now red in the sky.

Arjuna sweeps through the Kaurava army with a celestial weapon, cutting down warriors and elephants until the field becomes a river of blood. As the sun nears setting, Krishna makes a false darkness so that Jayadratha thinks the day is over and looks up; Arjuna then beheads him with an arrow that carries the head to his father Vriddhakshatra's lap, and the old man's head shatters because of an old curse. The victory frees Yudhishthira to attack Drona in a night battle, and the chapter ends with the Pandavas triumphant.

After Jayadratha falls, Kripa and Ashwatthaman attack Arjuna, who hits them only mildly out of respect for his teacher. Kripa collapses, and Arjuna laments that he has struck his own preceptor. Karna charges at Satyaki, and Krishna tells Arjuna that Satyaki can handle him and that Arjuna should not face Karna yet. Satyaki and Karna then duel from chariots, and Satyaki leaves Karna carless, while Sanjaya recounts the losses among Dhritarashtra's sons.

Bhima, humiliated by Karna's taunts, reminds Arjuna of their vow and urges him to keep it. Arjuna answers Karna with contempt, vows to kill Karna's son Vrishasena, and the sun sets over the field. Krishna praises Arjuna for fulfilling his vow and then drives him across the battlefield, showing the heaps of dead kings and beasts, before he blows his conch and tells Yudhishthira that Jayadratha is dead.

Krishna goes to Yudhishthira with news of Jayadratha's death, and the king, weeping with joy, embraces Krishna and Arjuna and praises Krishna as the lord of all worlds. Krishna and Arjuna recount how the Kauravas will be destroyed by Yudhishthira's wrath, and recall Bhishma lying on his bed of arrows. Arjuna then embraces the wounded Bhima and Satyaki and congratulates them on surviving Drona and Karna, and the Pandava army rallies with fresh resolve.

After Jayadratha's death, Duryodhana is crushed with grief and doubts that any warrior can match Arjuna. He goes to Drona, lists the Kaurava allies who have fallen, and swears that he will either destroy the Panchalas and Pandavas or die in the field to join them. He asks Drona's leave to go where his fallen allies have gone, which shows his desperation.

Dhritarashtra asks how the Kauravas responded to the deaths of Jayadratha and Bhurisravas and what Drona said to Duryodhana. Drona answers with bitter reproach: he says Duryodhana ignored Vidura's warning, that the dice game and the insult to Draupadi brought this ruin, and that Arjuna could not be stopped. Still, he vows to fight on until the Panchalas are slain, and sends Duryodhana to tell Ashwatthaman to keep up the fight.

Duryodhana, stung by Drona's words, blames Drona for letting Arjuna pass through his formation and for allowing Jayadratha to be killed. Karna defends Drona, saying that Arjuna's youth, his weapons and Krishna's driving outmatched the old teacher, and that Fate has decided against the Kauravas. He urges Duryodhana to fight on regardless. The battle then resumes with fierce fighting between the two armies.

In the gathering dark, the Kaurava and Panchala forces clash everywhere, and Duryodhana drives into the Pandava host, scorching it with arrows until the Panchalas and Pandavas begin to flee. Yudhishthira cuts his bow and wounds him, and Duryodhana sits down on his car as a cry goes up that the king is slain. Duryodhana recovers, attacks again, and Drona steps in to guard him, so the battle grows fiercer. The chapter opens a new section, the Ghatotkacha-badha Parva, marked by a heading.

Dhritarashtra asks who protected Drona and how he died, and Sanjaya describes the Pandavas closing in on Drona at night with their divisions. The dark battle becomes a chaos of noise, blood and dust in which friend and foe cannot be told apart, and the sounds of animals and weapons fill the field. Drona, despite the odds, cuts down thousands of elephants, chariots and foot-soldiers that night.

Dhritarashtra asks how Drona fared in the night fight and who stood by him, and Sanjaya describes the chaotic clash. Drona kills many Panchala and Pandava warriors, including Sivi, and the Kalinga prince is killed by Bhima with his fists. Bhima crushes several Kaurava warriors, and Durmada and Dushkarna are destroyed when he sinks their chariot into the earth, so that kings flee in terror and the Pandavas honor Bhima.

Somadatta, enraged at Bhurisravas's death, swears to kill Satyaki, but Satyaki stands firm and wounds him until he falls senseless. Drona then breaks into the Pandava host, driving back Yudhishthira and the others, until Arjuna and Bhima turn toward him. Ghatotkacha attacks Drona's son Ashwatthaman on a fearsome iron chariot, and Ashwatthaman kills Ghatotkacha's son Anjanaparvan, and Ashwatthaman then fights through a huge Rakshasa army, killing many Pandava princes. Ghatotkacha is finally pierced by an arrow from Ashwatthaman and is carried off the field, apparently dead, while the Kauravas applaud Ashwatthaman.

Somadatta, still enraged, fights Satyaki until Bhima hits him with a mace and a shaft, knocking him senseless. Bhima then kills a string of Kaurava warriors, including Valhika and Somadatta's sons, while Yudhishthira destroys Kaurava divisions. Drona and Yudhishthira duel with celestial weapons until Drona's Brahma weapon is answered in kind, and Drona finally turns on the Panchalas, sending the Kaurava host into flight.

Duryodhana, facing the massed Pandava army, begs Karna to save his warriors, and Karna boasts that he will kill Arjuna with the dart given to him by Indra. Kripa mocks Karna's boasting, reminding him of past defeats and listing the Pandavas' many allies, including Ghatotkacha. Karna rejects the reproach, boasts again that he will kill Arjuna and Krishna and give Duryodhana the earth, and insists that victory rests with Fate.

Karna insults Kripa, and Ashwatthaman, enraged, charges at him until Duryodhana and Kripa hold him back, and Karna is then spared at Duryodhana's urging. Karna then fights the Pandava host with great skill, but Arjuna cuts down his bow, steeds and charioteer, and Karna flees in Kripa's chariot. Duryodhana tries to rally his troops and go against Arjuna himself, but Ashwatthaman promises to hold Arjuna back, and Duryodhana, doubting him, urges him instead to slay the Panchalas and Somakas.

Ashwatthaman, egged on by Duryodhana, vows to fight recklessly and to slay many enemies, and mocks the king for his suspicions. He charges into the Panchalas and Somakas, who attack him in force. Dhrishtadyumna meets him in a long duel, and when Ashwatthaman destroys his chariot and kills many Panchalas, the enemy troops scatter. The Kauravas applaud Ashwatthaman's triumph.

Yudhishthira and Bhima surround Ashwatthaman, and Duryodhana, aided by Drona, rushes to the fight. Yudhishthira destroys many kings' divisions, and Arjuna and Bhima attack Drona's army from both flanks, while Drona routs the Panchalas with the Vayavya weapon. In the gloom the Kaurava host breaks, and many kings flee in terror.

Satyaki, determined to kill Somadatta, duels with him at length, cutting down each other's bows, standards and steeds. Satyaki finally kills Somadatta with a fiery arrow, and the Kaurava warriors rush at Satyaki in grief. Meanwhile Yudhishthira fights Drona, who cuts his bow and standard, and Krishna urges Yudhishthira to leave the preceptor and go to Bhima and Arjuna, which he does.

In the dark night the fighters cannot see each other and recognize one another only by voice and name, and many warriors flee or are killed in confusion. Duryodhana orders the foot-soldiers to carry lamps, and the Kaurava host is lit up and reorganized under Drona, with Ashwatthaman and Sakuni on the flanks. The Pandavas answer by lighting their own lamps, and the whole field becomes a blazing scene as the fighting resumes.

With the lamps blazing, the two armies fight with fresh fury, and Arjuna pushes into the Kaurava ranks, weakening the kings. Dhritarashtra demands to know how Drona fared against Arjuna and who guarded him. Duryodhana then orders his brothers and the Trigartas to shield Drona, and the battle resumes in full force.

Yudhishthira orders the Pandava and Panchala forces to focus on Drona, and each Kaurava warrior is assigned a foe to block them, including Kritavarman against Yudhishthira. The duel between Yudhishthira and Kritavarman goes badly for Yudhishthira, who is stripped of his chariot, weapons and armour and must retreat. Kritavarman then returns to guard Drona's chariot wheel.

Satyaki kills the Kuru warrior Bhuri with a dart, and Ashwatthaman then charges him, drawing in Ghatotkacha, who wounds Ashwatthaman badly before Ashwatthaman finally pierces him and drives him from the field. Duryodhana then fights Bhima, cutting down bow after bow until Bhima hurls a mace that crushes Duryodhana's chariot, forcing him to flee. Believing Duryodhana dead, the Pandavas press on, and the night battle against Drona continues.

Karna faces Sahadeva, cutting down his bow, chariot, weapons and steeds until Sahadeva is left helpless. Karna mocks him and sends him off to fight his equals, telling him to go to Arjuna or home. Karna spares Sahadeva, out of respect for Kunti's wishes, and Sahadeva, beaten and mocked, climbs into another chariot.

Salya fights Virata, kills his horses and Satanika, and wounds him so that he falls senseless. The Pandava troops flee before Salya, so Krishna and Arjuna move toward him, and the Rakshasa Alamvusha challenges Arjuna. Arjuna cuts down Alamvusha's chariot, bow and steeds, and drives him off, then presses on toward Drona while the enemy flees.

Chitrasena's armour and bow are cut off by Satanika, and Chitrasena is left without chariot or weapons. Vrishasena fights Drupada, and Drupada is pierced in the chest and carried off, which leaves the Panchalas fleeing. Duhsasana then duels with Prativindhya, destroys his chariot and bow, and fights on until Prativindhya's brothers arrive and the battle turns into a general melee in the dark.

Sakuni and Nakula trade blows until Sakuni wounds Nakula, but Nakula recovers, cuts down Sakuni's bow, standard and chariot, and leaves him badly hurt. Kripa and Sikhandin also duel until Sikhandin is driven back by Kripa's arrows. The night fight spreads into a chaos in which men cannot tell friend from foe and even kin kill one another.

Dhrishtadyumna charges at Drona, but Drona cuts down his bow, and Karna and other Kaurava warriors gang up on him until he kills Drumasena and cuts off Karna's bow. Satyaki then comes to his aid and duels with Karna, wounding Vrishasena until he seems dead, and Karna, grief-stricken, presses Satyaki hard. Karna then hears Arjuna's bowstring and tells Duryodhana to kill Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna, and Duryodhana sends Sakuni out to fight Arjuna while Drona again battles Dhrishtadyumna.

The Kaurava kings surround Satyaki, but he cuts down many warriors with razor-headed arrows and routs Duryodhana, who loses his chariot and bow and flees on Kritavarman's chariot. Sakuni and his son Uluka then attack Arjuna with great force, but Arjuna drives them back and sends the Kaurava army fleeing, and Krishna and Arjuna blow their conches in triumph. Dhrishtadyumna then blocks Drona, leaving a river of blood, and the Pandavas sound their conches in victory.

Duryodhana rebukes Drona and Karna for abandoning him after the death of Jayadratha, and they return to the fight with fresh fury. Drona cuts down the Panchalas and Pandavas until the Pandava host flees in the dark, and Krishna and Arjuna march to face Drona and Karna with Bhima at their side. The night battle then grows into a fierce clash of two great oceans, in which the warriors fight by voice alone.

Karna defeats Dhrishtadyumna, killing his horses and driver, and routs the Panchalas with a rain of arrows. Yudhishthira, seeing his army broken, urges Arjuna to face Karna, and Krishna advises that Ghatotkacha, who possesses illusions and mighty weapons, should be sent against Karna. Ghatotkacha accepts the task, boasts of his strength, and rushes at Karna in a fierce duel that Sanjaya compares to Indra and Prahlada.

Duryodhana orders Duhsasana to defend Karna against Ghatotkacha, and the Rakshasa Alamvusha, son of Jatasura, asks for leave to avenge his father by destroying the Pandavas, which Duryodhana grants. Alamvusha and Ghatotkacha fight with illusions and weapons, and Ghatotkacha finally kills Alamvusha and throws his head onto Duryodhana's chariot. Ghatotkacha then taunts Duryodhana and turns to attack Karna, and the fight between the two heroes grows fierce.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe Ghatotkacha and his duel with Karna at midnight. Sanjaya gives a long portrait of the Rakshasa's form, car, steeds and weapons, then recounts the fight: Karna cuts down Ghatotkacha's illusions and weapons, while Ghatotkacha keeps shifting shape and vanishing, until Karna destroys his steeds and Ghatotkacha withdraws, promising to kill Karna. The duel shows how Karna's skill can match even the Rakshasa's trickery.

The Rakshasa Alayudha arrives with a large host to avenge his kinsmen, who were killed by Bhima, and asks Duryodhana to let him fight. Duryodhana accepts gladly and promises his own troops in support. Alayudha rides out on a chariot like Ghatotkacha's, and the Pandava kings take up arms with joy to meet him.

The Kauravas cheer Alayudha's arrival, and Duryodhana sends him to kill Ghatotkacha before Ghatotkacha can kill Karna by illusion. Alayudha fights Ghatotkacha, and Bhima, seeing his friend in trouble, joins the struggle against Alayudha and his Rakshasa followers. Krishna urges Arjuna to aid Bhima and tells others to face Karna and Drona, and Bhima and Alayudha finally fight with maces and then bare fists, both bloodied.

Krishna urges Ghatotkacha to abandon Karna and kill Alayudha, and Ghatotkacha does so in a duel with illusions, stone-showers and uprooted trees. Ghatotkacha is struck down by Alayudha's club but rises, mauls his foe, and cuts off Alayudha's head. He throws it before Duryodhana, who is dismayed and comes to believe that Bhima's vow against him and his brothers has already been fulfilled.

Ghatotkacha, exulting over Alayudha's death, returns to fight Karna, and the two heroes trade fierce volleys of arrows and illusions. Ghatotkacha kills Karna's steeds and driver, and his illusions spread terror through the Kaurava army, which begins to flee. Karna, with his chariot gone, finally hurls Indra's dart at Ghatotkacha, killing him, and Ghatotkacha's fall crushes a full akshauhini of Kaurava troops before Karna returns to the Kuru host in triumph.

The Pandavas grieve over Ghatotkacha's death, but Krishna rejoices and embraces Arjuna, which puzzles Arjuna. Krishna explains that Karna's celestial dart has been used up on Ghatotkacha, and that Karna, having given away his natural armour and earrings to Indra, is now weakened and can be slain when his chariot wheels sink into the earth. Krishna also recalls the other enemies he and Arjuna have overcome by stratagem.

Arjuna asks how Jarasandha and the others were slain, and Krishna explains that they would have sided with Duryodhana and been unbeatable without the proper means. He tells how Jarasandha was made whole from two halves by the Rakshasa woman Jara, and was later killed by Bhima after Valadeva's weapon destroyed his mace. Ekalavya was tricked out of his thumb by Drona and later killed by Krishna, the ruler of the Chedis was slain before Arjuna's eyes, and Hidimva, Vaka, Kirmira, Alayudha and Ghatotkacha have all fallen, leaving Karna's dart useless.

Dhritarashtra asks why Karna did not hurl his dart at Arjuna, and blames his son's poor judgment. Sanjaya tells how the Kaurava leaders had planned to kill Arjuna or, failing that, Krishna, and how Krishna's cleverness made the dart useless by sending Ghatotkacha. Satyaki asks Krishna why Karna did not use the dart at Arjuna, and Krishna explains that Karna's chief intent was Arjuna but that he himself had kept Karna distracted and sent Ghatotkacha to exhaust the weapon.

Dhritarashtra asks why Karna never used Indra's dart against Krishna or Arjuna when he had the chance. Sanjaya blames fate, saying the plan was made every night and forgotten every morning. After Ghatotkacha's death Yudhishthira is overcome with grief and rushes at Karna, until Vyasa stops him and urges him to keep to virtue and fight on.

Yudhishthira, still stung by Ghatotkacha's death, orders his whole army to attack Drona, and Duryodhana rushes to protect him. The fighting drags on until both armies are worn out and fall asleep at midnight. Arjuna calls a halt so both sides can rest, and the battle resumes only once the moon rises.

Duryodhana angrily tells Drona that he has spared the Pandavas and let them grow strong. Drona answers that he will fight to the end, swears to slay the Panchalas, and praises Arjuna's prowess. He then tells Duryodhana to face Arjuna himself and mocks Karna's boasting, and the battle begins again.

The battle resumes at dawn, with the Kaurava army split in two. Arjuna, urged on by Krishna and Bhima, forces his way into the Kaurava front, while Drona goes off to the north and wins a series of duels, killing Drupada, Virata and Drupada's three grandsons. Arjuna reports his battle with Ashvatthama, whom he drove off, and his destruction of five hundred warriors before he moved toward Karna's division. He says no other Srinjaya can resist Karna, and he asks Satyaki, Dhrishtadyumna, Yudhamanyu and Uttamauja to guard his chariot. He then vows to fight Karna and kill him that day, with all his kin, or else accept the shame of a broken vow. He asks Yudhishthira for his blessing.

Yudhishthira, furious that Arjuna has left Bhima behind and fled from Karna, accuses him of cowardice and breaking his earlier promise. He recalls the old prophecy of a heavenly voice that promised Arjuna great feats, and says it has come to nothing. He then mocks Arjuna's bow Gandiva, his car, and his banner, and says he would be better off not born. The chapter sets up the quarrel that follows between the two brothers.

Arjuna draws his sword to kill Yudhishthira for saying he should give up the Gandiva, and Krishna stops him. Krishna argues at length that Arjuna's vow is misguided and that truth and falsehood depend on circumstance, citing the stories of the hunter Valaka and the ascetic Kausika. Arjuna asks for a way to keep his vow without killing his brother, and Krishna proposes that Arjuna insult Yudhishthira by addressing him as 'thou' instead of with respect. The chapter shows Krishna's guidance on dharma, which steers the brothers toward a face-saving solution.

Arjuna, applauding Krishna's advice, turns on Yudhishthira with harsh words, saying he sits far from the fighting while Bhima does the real work. He blames the king for the gambling that brought the Kauravas' war on the family, and lists his own feats in battle. Realising his wrong, Arjuna is overcome with shame and draws his sword to kill himself, but Krishna stops him. Yudhishthira, in turn, offers his own head and prepares to leave for the forest, until Krishna and Arjuna beg his forgiveness and he accepts their apology.

Krishna tells Arjuna that his shame over the harsh words was misplaced, and urges him to make peace with Yudhishthira before going after Karna. The brothers embrace and make up, and Arjuna swears to kill Karna and his followers that day. Yudhishthira blesses him and urges him on to victory, as Indra once did against Vritra.

Arjuna prepares his chariot for the fight with Karna, and Krishna has his charioteer Daruka yoke the horses. Omens of success appear, with birds gathering and the directions growing calm, while all creatures expect Karna's death. Krishna then warns Arjuna not to underrate Karna, describing him as a warrior of great skill and power who is nearly Arjuna's equal. The chapter sets the stage for the final duel between the two.

Krishna gives Arjuna a long review of the war so far, naming the great warriors on both sides who have fallen. He credits Arjuna with slaying Jayadratha and recalls Karna's role in Abhimanyu's death and Karna's insults to Draupadi in the assembly. He urges Arjuna to kill Karna that day and not to spare his own kin or teachers on the other side. The chapter gives the moral and personal stakes behind the final duel.

Arjuna, reassured by Krishna, stretches his bow and vows to kill Karna that day, saying that his arrows will settle every score. He boasts of his own skill and of his past wrongs, and repeats the insults he suffered at Karna's hands. He says that Karna will fall and that Duryodhana, Dhritarashtra and the Kauravas will be destroyed. He then sets out for the battlefield to rescue Bhima and cut Karna down.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how the battle went when Arjuna went into it. Sanjaya describes the general melee, with the Pandava and Srinjaya forces hurling themselves at the Kaurava leaders in many pairings. Uttamauja kills Karna's son Sushena, and Karna's grief turns to rage as he cuts down Uttamauja's horses and chariot. Bhima then appears in the thick of the fighting, scorching Duryodhana's sons' forces.

Bhima, surrounded and anxious about Yudhishthira and Arjuna, asks his charioteer Visoka to drive him into the thick of the Kaurava host. Visoka reports how many weapons Bhima has left, and Bhima pledges to fight to the end. Visoka then tells him that Arjuna is coming, and Bhima rewards the news with villages, slaves and chariots. The chapter shows Bhima's ferocity and the relief of hearing that his brother is near.

Arjuna urges Krishna onward, and the Kaurava warriors surge forward to block him, but Arjuna cuts them down and pushes toward Karna's division. Bhima, hearing of his brother's coming, renews his assault and creates a river of blood across the field. Duryodhana then orders Shakuni to slay Bhima, and Shakuni is wounded and carried off from the battle. The Kaurava army, shaken by Bhima and Arjuna, rallies under Karna, their refuge, and goes back into battle.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what Duryodhana, Karna and the others did once Bhima had broken the Kaurava lines. Sanjaya reports that Karna, driven by Shalya, charges into the Pancala and Srinjaya ranks and wounds many Pandava warriors, including Satyaki, Bhima and the sons of Draupadi. The Pandava army falls back before him, and the Kaurava side rejoices. The chapter shows Karna's sudden recovery of the Kaurava fortunes.

Arjuna, having slain many of the enemy, sees Karna and orders Krishna to drive toward him, vowing not to return without killing him. Shalya warns Karna that Arjuna is coming alone and that Krishna is at his side, but Karna answers with confidence and boasts of his own strength. Karna then recounts Arjuna's feats and divine weapons and sends the Kaurava warriors to block Arjuna's path and tire him out. The chapter sets up the final clash between the two heroes, with Kaurava warriors pressing in on Arjuna from every side.

Arjuna leaves Karna's division to rescue Bhima and scatters the Kaurava host with a torrent of arrows, breaking their ranks and forcing them to flee. He then meets Bhima, who has been fighting alone, and tells him that Yudhishthira's wounds have been dressed and he is well. Ten of Duryodhana's brothers then try to block Arjuna, and he kills them all with his arrows. The chapter shows Arjuna's ferocious advance and his brothers' reunion.

Ninety Samsaptaka chariots charge Arjuna, and he destroys them all as Krishna drives toward Karna. A wider Kaurava force then rushes in to block his way, and Mlecchas on elephants attack his flank, but Arjuna routs them. Bhima, having cleared the rest of the Kaurava army, joins Arjuna and crushes the elephant divisions, and the Kaurava host breaks and flees. Karna then shelters the fleeing Kauravas and steps forward to face the Pancalas, who are overwhelmed by his shafts.

Karna destroys the Pancala warriors one by one, cutting down Janamejaya's driver, Satyaki's horses, and the sons of Karna, Prasena and others. Krishna urges Arjuna to go and kill Karna, and Arjuna and Bhima drive toward Karna's chariot, fighting along the way. Five Pancala commanders try to stop Karna, but he defeats them, and the sons of Draupadi rescue them. Duhshasana and Bhima then fight a fierce duel, in which Duhshasana wounds Bhima badly, and Bhima recovers and roars.

Duhshasana fights Bhima fiercely, but Bhima hurls his mace, knocks him from his chariot, and kills him. Bhima, recalling the insults to Draupadi, drinks Duhshasana's blood and boasts of it, and the Kaurava warriors flee in terror. Yudhamanyu kills Citrasena, and Bhima promises to kill Duryodhana next. The chapter is one of the most violent and vengeful in the book, and it marks the fulfilment of Bhima's oath.

Ten of Duryodhana's brothers attack Bhima to avenge Duhshasana, and Arjuna cuts them all down. Karna is shaken, and Shalya urges him to fight on, since the whole burden of the war rests on him. Karna's son Vrishasena fights Nakula, cuts down his chariot and horses, and then destroys his shield and sword. Nakula leaps onto Bhima's chariot, and Arjuna and Bhima counterattack, and Arjuna turns to face Vrishasena.

The Pandava warriors and the sons of Draupadi charge to aid Nakula, and the Kaurava leaders stand against them. Kripa, Ashvatthama, Kritavarma and others fight the Pancalas and Srinjayas while Kulinda elephants are cut down one by one. Vrishasena wounds Arjuna and Krishna, and Arjuna, enraged, vows to kill him before killing Karna and Duryodhana. Arjuna cuts Vrishasena down, and the sight of his son's death drives Karna into a rage as he rushes at Arjuna and Krishna.

Krishna sees Karna's chariot approaching, with Shalya at the reins, and urges Arjuna to stay calm and fight. He reminds Arjuna of Shiva's favour and of the boons Arjuna has won, and says only Arjuna can face Karna's arrows. Arjuna answers with confidence, vowing that Karna will be slain that day, and drives his chariot forward to meet him. The chapter sets up the final duel.

Karna and Arjuna close in on each other amid the cheers of their armies, and the gods and other beings take sides. Indra and Surya argue over which side should win, and Brahma and Shiva favour Arjuna while also urging that the outcome not destroy the world. Krishna tells Arjuna that Karna cannot harm him, and Arjuna answers by vowing to destroy Karna and Shalya that day. The chapter sets the stage for the climax of the duel.

Arjuna and Karna fight at the centre of a huge battle, with the gods and other beings watching from the sky. Arjuna drives back five Kaurava leaders, Duryodhana among them, and destroys their chariots, and the gods shower him with flowers. Drona's son then begs Duryodhana to make peace with the Pandavas, pointing out that Arjuna is invincible. Duryodhana refuses, citing Bhima's threats and Karna's confidence, and orders his troops to attack.

Arjuna and Karna, both furious, trade volleys of arrows, and Karna's shafts seem to hold their own against Arjuna's. Arjuna's weapons are repeatedly blocked by Karna's counter-weapons, including the Bhargava weapon, and the Pancalas and Somakas who come to Arjuna's aid are slaughtered. Bhima, angry at the setback, urges Arjuna on, and Krishna reminds him of his strength and of Shiva's gifts. Arjuna then unleashes the brahmastra, the mightiest weapon, and the Kaurava army is driven back, until Karna, undaunted, presses his attack.

Karna and Arjuna trade ever fiercer weapons, until the serpent Aswasena, who once hated Arjuna for the death of his mother, slips into Karna's quiver as an arrow. Karna shoots it, and Krishna presses down the chariot to save Arjuna, but the arrow knocks off Arjuna's diadem. Later Karna's chariot wheel sinks into the earth under a Brahmana's curse, and Karna, forgetting the brahmastra he once learned, begs Arjuna to wait while he frees the wheel. Krishna urges Arjuna to press on, and the chapter ends with Karna pleading for mercy on the rules of war.

Krishna confronts Karna with a long list of his past wrongs: the dice match, the abuse of Draupadi in the assembly, the attempts on the Pandavas' lives, and the killing of Abhimanyu. Karna, shamed, fights on and wounds Arjuna, but Arjuna, stirred to rage, cuts off Karna's standard and then kills him with the Anjalika weapon, which takes off his head. The Kauravas, seeing their champion dead, begin to flee. The chapter marks Karna's death and the collapse of the Kaurava front.

Shalya comes to Duryodhana's side on his bare chariot and mourns the fall of Karna and the destruction of the Kaurava army. Some Kauravas flee in terror, while Bhima and the Pandava troops celebrate with shouts and dance. Shalya tells Duryodhana that Destiny has favoured the Pandavas and that such losses are part of fate. Duryodhana, with his heart broken, sighs in grief.

Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how the Kaurava and Srinjaya armies looked after Karna's fall. Sanjaya describes the complete rout of the Kauravas, who flee in disorder, while Bhima slaughters 25,000 foot soldiers and Arjuna drives into the remaining chariots. Duryodhana, still determined, tries to rally his army with a speech about the honour of dying in battle, but his men flee regardless. The chapter shows the Kaurava army collapsing once Karna is gone.

Shalya, seeing Duryodhana near despair, describes the field strewn with dead elephants, horses and men, and urges him to withdraw to camp. Duryodhana weeps for Karna, and the Kaurava leaders lead the army back as the sun sets. Sanjaya describes Karna's corpse, which still shines like gold, and the cosmic portents that follow his death. Arjuna and Krishna then blow their conches in victory, and the Kauravas, deserting Duryodhana, leave the field.

After Karna falls, the Kauravas break and flee, and Duryodhana, on Shalya's advice, withdraws the army. Their leaders retreat in turn, and the Kaurava warriors leave the field in shame and fear. Duryodhana, stunned by defeat, orders his men to rest for the night.

Krishna praises Arjuna's victory over Karna and tells him to report it to Yudhishthira, who had earlier been too wounded to stay on the field. The brothers go to Yudhishthira's tent, where he embraces them and learns of Karna's death from Krishna. Yudhishthira praises Krishna and Arjuna, and the Pandava army rejoices. Vaishampayana closes the Karna Parva with a note of its merit, and Dhritarashtra's grief at the news is described.

After Karna falls, Duryodhana appoints Shalya as commander, and Shalya is killed by Yudhishthira. Duryodhana hides in a lake and is found and killed by Bhima. Sanjaya returns to the Kuru capital and reports the ruin of the army to the blind king Dhritarashtra, who collapses. The chapter sets up the collapse of the Kaurava side and the grief that follows.

Dhritarashtra mourns his sons and laments that all the losses seem to be destiny. He recalls Duryodhana's boasts and the heroes who have now died. He turns to Sanjaya and asks for a full account of the battle, including who now leads the army and how the Pandavas and their allies fared.

Sanjaya describes how the Kaurava army breaks and flees after Karna's death. Bhima and Dhrishtadyumna cut down the remaining troops, Arjuna scatters the rest, and Duryodhana alone tries to rally his men. He calls on them to fight to the end rather than run.

Kripa, seeing the army broken and the Pandavas' strength, urges Duryodhana to make peace. He reminds the king of the fallen heroes, of Arjuna's power and of the Pandavas' divine allies, and says the Kauravas cannot win. Kripa speaks in tears and nearly faints.

Duryodhana rejects Kripa's advice to make peace. He lists the wrongs the Pandavas have suffered at his hands and explains that he prefers death in battle to humiliation. He resolves to fight on, and the Kauravas camp for the night, ready to keep going.

The Kaurava warriors camp at the foot of the Himalayas and need a new commander. Duryodhana asks Ashvatthama to choose one, and Ashvatthama names Shalya, who accepts. Duryodhana then formally asks Shalya to lead the army, and Shalya agrees to give his all.

Shalya boasts that he alone can match the Pandava army and promises victory. He is formally installed as commander, and the Kauravas rejoice. In the Pandava camp, Yudhishthira worries about the new commander, and Krishna advises that Arjuna must kill Shalya, and the Pandavas sleep in relief.

The two armies arm and form up for a final battle, with the Kauravas under Shalya and the Pandavas under Yudhishthira. Dhritarashtra asks how Shalya and Duryodhana fell and asks for the strength of each army. Sanjaya gives the numbers and the dispositions of both sides, and the fighting begins at dawn.

Sanjaya describes the battle at its most violent, with bodies, elephants and chariots heaped on the field and the blood running like a river. Arjuna and Bhima stun the Kaurava army, and Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandi attack Shalya. The Kaurava troops break and flee, leaving their leaders and kinsmen behind.

Shalya charges into the Pandava host and holds it back, and the Kauravas rally to him. Nakula kills Chitrasena and then Karna's sons Satyasena and Sushena in a long duel, with the help of Sutasoma. Shalya rallies the Kaurava troops, and the battle becomes a general slaughter on both sides.

The battle grows more terrible as Shalya attacks the Pandava army and Yudhishthira. Omens appear, and the Kaurava commanders rush to protect Shalya. Bhima kills Shalya's driver with a mace after Shalya's lance hits him, and Shalya steps down from his chariot to face Bhima.

Shalya and Bhima fight a long, even mace duel, and both fall after the force of their blows. Kripa carries Shalya off the field, but Bhima gets up and challenges him again. The battle then spreads across the field, with Duryodhana wounding Chekitana with a lance, and Shalya fighting Yudhishthira until Yudhishthira cuts down his standard and wounds him.

Satyaki, Bhima, Nakula, Sahadeva and Yudhishthira attack Shalya together, but he holds them off and destroys their weapons one by one. Yudhishthira worries that Shalya will destroy the Pandava army, and the Pandavas continue to press him. Shalya's arrows darken the sky, and even the gods are astonished by his skill.

Arjuna fights Drona's son Ashvatthama and the Trigarta warriors, and his arrows scatter the Kaurava troops across the field. Arjuna cuts down Ashvatthama's mallet and mace, and Ashvatthama then kills the Pancala warrior Suratha. Arjuna fights on alone against a large Kaurava force, and the fight is fierce.

Duryodhana fights Dhrishtadyumna, Shikhandi meets Kritavarma and Kripa, and Shalya takes on the Pandava leaders one after another. He breaks Nakula's bow, then Satyaki charges him, and Shalya holds the field against many heroes. The chapter shows Shalya's skill as the Pandavas' main opponent.

The Kaurava troops push the Pandavas back, and Shalya alone fights the whole Pandava army. Yudhishthira, enraged, vows to kill Shalya, arranges his chariot with his brothers and Krishna, and challenges him. Duryodhana is wounded, Shalya's chariot is cut down, and Shalya is carried off by Ashvatthama, leaving the Kauravas in disarray.

Shalya fights Yudhishthira in a long, even duel, and Yudhishthira's dart finally kills him. Shalya falls with his face toward Yudhishthira, and his young brother is then killed too. The Kaurava army breaks in terror, and the Pandavas celebrate. Satyaki and Kritavarma also fight a duel, and Kritavarma is carried off.

After Shalya dies, his 1,700 Madraka chariot warriors charge into the Pandava host despite Duryodhana's orders to hold back. Shakuni points out that the Kauravas must support them, and the whole Kaurava army moves to help. The Pandavas, however, destroy the Madrakas, and the Kaurava army flees.

With Shalya dead, most of the Kaurava army flees in panic, and the Pandavas and Panchalas pursue them. Duryodhana tries to rally his troops, telling them that running is pointless and that they should die fighting. Bhima crushes 21,000 Kaurava foot-soldiers with his mace, and the Kauravas turn to fight again.

Salwa, king of the Mlecchas, rides a huge elephant into the Pandava army and drives it back in panic. Dhrishtadyumna attacks the elephant, which kills his chariot driver and horses. Bhima, Shikhandi and Satyaki stop the elephant, Dhrishtadyumna kills it with a mace, and Satyaki beheads Salwa with an arrow.

After Salwa's death the Kaurava army breaks, but Kritavarma rallies it and battles Satyaki. Satyaki kills Kshemakirti, then disarms and strips Kritavarma of his chariot. Kripa carries Kritavarma away, and Duryodhana stands alone against the Pandavas, while the Kaurava army once again flees.

Duryodhana fights almost alone against the Pandavas, wounding each of them, and the Kaurava warriors rally round him. The fighting spreads into many single combats: Ashvatthama and Bhima, Shakuni and Yudhishthira, Uluka and Nakula, and Kripa against the sons of Draupadi. Dust covers the field until the blood settles it, and the battle goes on at noon.

The Kauravas rally, but the battle turns into a chaotic slaughter in which Shakuni, with the Gandhara horsemen, attacks the Pandava rear. Yudhishthira sends Sahadeva and Draupadi's sons against him, and a massive, bloody cavalry and infantry struggle follows. Both sides are left exhausted, and Shakuni retreats with a small remnant, though the Kauravas and Pandavas go on killing one another, with omens of ruin all around.

Shakuni rallies his last seven hundred horsemen and sends them against the Pandavas, claiming the Pandava chariots are already beaten. Arjuna answers Krishna with a bitter speech, blaming Duryodhana's obstinacy for a war that should have ended after Bhishma's fall, and vowing to kill the Kaurava warriors. He then drives into the enemy host and burns through its ranks with his arrows.

Arjuna's arrows scatter the Kaurava army, and many of its warriors flee or fall. Dhrishtadyumna kills Duryodhana's horses and driver, and Duryodhana rides off on horseback. Three thousand Kaurava elephants surround the Pandavas, but Arjuna and Bhima destroy them. Ashvatthama, Kripa and Kritavarma search for Duryodhana, and a Kuru warrior, captured by Satyaki, tells how the Kauravas were beaten.

After the elephant division is destroyed, Duryodhana's brothers charge Bhima together, and Bhima kills them one by one. Srutarvan, the last of them, attacks Bhima, is disarmed, and is beheaded. Bhima then cuts down hundreds of Kaurava chariots, elephants, foot-soldiers and horses, and the surviving Kaurava army is left very thin.

Only Duryodhana and his son Sudarsana are left of Dhritarashtra's sons, and Duryodhana stays among his cavalry. Krishna urges Arjuna to strike at him, and Arjuna boasts that he will kill the remaining Kaurava warriors. Arjuna, Bhima and Sahadeva attack, Duryodhana wounds Sahadeva, and Arjuna destroys the Trigartas, while Bhima kills Sudarsana. The Kauravas are left in a desperate fight.

Shakuni attacks Sahadeva, while Bhima fights Uluka, and the battle becomes a field of severed limbs. Duryodhana urges the fleeing Kauravas back into the fight. Sahadeva kills Uluka and then breaks Shakuni's weapons one by one. He finally cuts off Shakuni's head, and the Kaurava army flees in terror.

The last Kaurava troops are wiped out and Duryodhana, alone and wounded, flees to a lake and hides in it by magic. Sanjaya is spared by Vyasa's intervention, finds Duryodhana at the lake, and hears his lament. The surviving Kaurava warriors and women flee the camp, and Yuyutsu brings the news to Vidura in Hastinapura.

Kripa, Ashvatthama and Kritavarma go to the lake and urge Duryodhana to fight on. Duryodhana, weary and wounded, refuses until the next day. Ashvatthama swears to kill every Panchala that night, but a group of huntsmen overhears the conversation and tells the Pandavas where Duryodhana is hiding. The Pandavas come to the lake, and the three warriors leave to rest under a banyan tree.

The Pandavas reach the lake where Duryodhana is hidden by his magic. Krishna urges Yudhishthira to fight illusion with cunning, citing past victories won by stratagem. Yudhishthira taunts Duryodhana for hiding like a coward. Duryodhana replies that he only rested from exhaustion, then declares he no longer wants the earth, which is empty of heroes, and offers to give it up and retire to the forest. Yudhishthira refuses the gift and insists that the Kauravas must fight.

Duryodhana rises from the lake, armed with his mace, and taunts the Pandavas. He says he is alone and unfit to face so many, but he offers a one-on-one mace duel. Yudhishthira agrees and promises him the kingship if he kills one of them. Yudhishthira then rebukes him for the killing of Abhimanyu, and Duryodhana arms himself and challenges the brothers to fight him one by one.

Krishna criticises Yudhishthira for offering the kingship to whoever kills a Pandava, arguing that Duryodhana is too skilled with the mace. Bhima answers that he will fight Duryodhana and kill him, and he speaks of the Pandavas' many wrongs. Duryodhana replies with defiance, boasting that he has never been beaten in fair combat and that the Pandavas have suffered enough. The two heroes are set to fight with maces.

Balarama arrives at the field to watch the mace duel between his two pupils, Bhima and Duryodhana. The Pandavas and Krishna greet him warmly, and he takes his seat among the kings to witness the contest.

Janamejaya asks why Balarama left the war and where he went. Vaishampayana explains that Balarama, unwilling to take either side, toured the Sarasvati river and its sacred sites, giving gifts along the way until he reached Kurukshetra. He begins the list of sacred spots with Prabhasa, where the moon was cured of a wasting curse.

Balarama bathes at the sacred pool of Udapana, which Vaishampayana ties to the story of the ascetic Trita. Trita's two brothers left him to die in a well, but he performed a sacrifice in his mind, the Sarasvati rose to lift him out, and he cursed his brothers to become wolves. The chapter is part of Balarama's tour of the holy places along the Sarasvati.

Balarama tours a series of sacred places along the Sarasvati, including Vinasana, Subhumika, the Gandharva shrine, Gargasrota, Sankha and Nagadhanwana. The river turns east so that the sages of Naimisha can find room for their rites, and Balarama reaches Sapta-Saraswat, where the sage Mankanaka once performed penances.

Janamejaya asks why the place is called Sapta-Saraswat and who Mankanaka was. Vaishampayana explains that the Sarasvati appears in seven forms, which join at this place, and recounts several sacrifices where she manifested. He then tells how Mankanaka's seed, kept in a jar, became seven sages, and how Mankanaka danced in delight at a juice that flowed from his wound until Mahadeva showed him ash and taught him humility.

Balarama goes on to Usanas, also called Kapalamochana, where Sukra once performed penance. Janamejaya asks how the place got its name, and Vaishampayana tells how Rama's severed Rakshasa head stuck to the thigh of the sage Mahodara until he bathed at the tirtha and was freed. Balarama then visits the asylum of Rushangu and nearby holy places.

Janamejaya asks how Arshtishena, Sindhudwipa, Devapi and Vishvamitra gained the status of Brahmanas. Vaishampayana tells how Arshtishena, after failing to learn in his teacher's house, won mastery of the Vedas through penance and gave the place its boons. He then tells how the Kshatriya king Vishvamitra, defeated by Vasishtha's magic cow, did austerities at this tirtha and became a Brahmana.

Balarama reaches the asylum of the sage Dalvya Vaka, who once cursed King Dhritarashtra's kingdom through a sacrifice after the king mocked him over dead cattle. The king begged forgiveness and the kingdom was restored. Vaishampayana then tells of Brihaspati and Yayati's sacrifices at this river site, before Balarama moves on to Vasishthapavaha.

Janamejaya asks why the Vasishthapavaha current is so swift and what caused the feud between Vasishtha and Vishvamitra. Vaishampayana tells how the rival sages fought for superiority, how Vishvamitra ordered the Sarasvati to bring Vasishtha so that he could kill him, and how the river carried Vasishtha to Vishvamitra's bank and back. Angered by the trick, Vishvamitra cursed the river to flow with blood for a year.

The cursed Sarasvati flows with blood, and Rakshasas gather to drink it. Sages purify the river, and the Rakshasas are freed by rules about the foods they may eat, and the river is turned into the Aruna branch. Indra, guilty of killing his friend Namuchi, is cleansed by bathing at this confluence. Balarama then visits the Soma tirtha, where Skanda won his command after defeating Taraka.

Janamejaya asks how Skanda was invested as commander of the celestial army. Vaishampayana tells how Shiva's seed fell into fire, passed to the Ganga and then to Himalaya, and grew into the child Skanda, who was nursed by the six Krittikas and grew six faces. The gods gathered to see him, Shiva divided himself into four forms to meet the four who were expecting him, and Brahma appointed Skanda commander. The gods then gathered by the Sarasvati at Himalaya.

The gods and many other beings gather at Himalaya for Skanda's installation as commander. Brahma, Kasyapa and the others pour sacred water over him, and each god gives him companions and warriors. A long catalogue lists the many strange-looking followers who join him, and they dance in joy at his coronation.

Vaishampayana lists the mother goddesses who become Skanda's followers, describes their forms and powers, and lists the weapons and gifts the gods give him. Skanda sets out against the Daityas, kills Taraka and other demon chiefs, and pierces Mount Krauncha to destroy Vana. The chapter ends with Balarama bathing at Taijasa, the place where Varuna was installed.

Janamejaya asks how Varuna was installed as lord of the waters at this tirtha. Vaishampayana tells how the gods made Varuna lord of rivers and seas, and how Agni hid in a Sami tree after Bhrigu's curse until the gods found him. Balarama then visits Brahmayoni, the Kuvera tirtha and Vadarapachana.

At Vadarapachana, the maiden Sruvavati, daughter of Bharadwaja, does harsh penance to win Indra as her husband. Indra tests her by asking her to boil jujubes, and she burns her own feet to keep the fire going, and he grants her a boon. The place becomes a sacred tirtha, and Vaishampayana tells how Arundhati and Shiva first made it holy. Balarama then goes on to the tirtha of Sakta.

Balarama visits a string of sacred sites: Indra's tirtha, where Indra performed a hundred horse sacrifices; Rama's tirtha, where Parashurama gave the earth to his teacher; and the Yamuna, where Varuna performed a Rajasuya. He then reaches the Aditya tirtha, where Surya gained his power and where Vyasa and others live.

Vaishampayana tells the story of Asita-Devala, a householder of perfect equanimity, and his guest, the mendicant Jaigishavya. Devala finds Jaigishavya in two places at once, sees him travelling through the heavens, and is told he has gone to Brahman. Devala then renounces the householder's life for liberation under Jaigishavya's guidance. Narada criticises Jaigishavya, but the gods defend him, and Balarama bathes at this place before going on to the Soma tirtha.

Balarama visits the tirtha of the sage Sarasvata, who taught the Vedas during a twelve-year drought. Vaishampayana tells how Sarasvata was the son of the sage Dadhichi and the river Sarasvati, and how the gods later took Dadhichi's bones to make a thunderbolt for Indra. In the drought, Sarasvata fed the sages and then taught the Vedas to 60,000 of them. Balarama gives gifts and moves on.

Janamejaya asks about a maiden who devoted herself to penance. Vaishampayana tells the story of the daughter of Kuni-Garga, who did penance without marrying until Narada said that she had no place in heaven without marriage. She offered half her merit to any husband, and the sage Sringavat accepted her for one night. She gave a boon to the tirtha and went to heaven, and Sringavat followed her. Balarama hears that Shalya has been killed and asks the sages about the battle.

The sages explain to Balarama that Samantapanchaka is the northern altar of Brahman and that Kurukshetra is named after King Kuru, who ploughed the field. Indra promised heaven to those who die there in battle or by fasting. The sages describe the sanctity of the land, its boundaries, and the blessings it brings.

Balarama visits a sacred hermitage, then climbs the Himalayan foothills through a series of tirthas. Narada arrives and tells him of the deaths of the Kuru heroes, the flight of the last three warriors, and Duryodhana's rise from the lake to face Bhima. Balarama sets out in his chariot to watch the duel between his two pupils.

Dhritarashtra asks how his son fought Bhima once Balarama arrived. Sanjaya explains that Yudhishthira honoured Balarama, who praised Kurukshetra as a holy field where warriors who die go to heaven. Duryodhana and Bhima take their places on a sandless spot south of the Sarasvati, with their maces, and the kings and gods gather to watch them, as the two circle each other like great beasts.

Dhritarashtra laments that his son, once a lord of armies, must now fight on foot with a mace. Sanjaya describes frightful omens, and Bhima vows to avenge the Kauravas' wrongs and to kill Duryodhana. Duryodhana mocks Bhima's boasting and challenges him to act, and the crowd cheers them on as they advance.

The mace duel between Duryodhana and Bhima is long and even. The two strike and circle, and the gods and onlookers cannot tell who will win. Duryodhana strikes Bhima on the head and flank, and Bhima answers with a blow that drops Duryodhana to his knees. Duryodhana rises and knocks Bhima down, wrecking his chest armour. Bhima recovers and stands again, and the blows and circling continue until the end of the day.

Arjuna asks Krishna who is the better fighter, and Krishna explains that Duryodhana has more skill but Bhima more strength. Krishna argues that Bhima must use a trick to win, and Arjuna gives Bhima a signal. Bhima strikes Duryodhana's thighs with his mace as Duryodhana jumps, breaking them, and Duryodhana falls with the sky and earth shaking around him.

Bhima stands over the fallen Duryodhana, mocks him for the old insults about Draupadi, and sets his foot on the king's head. The Somakas disapprove, and Yudhishthira rebukes Bhima for the insult and then mourns Duryodhana, blaming his fate and his own acts.

Dhritarashtra asks what Balarama did when Duryodhana was struck down. Sanjaya reports that Balarama condemned the blow below the navel and rushed at Bhima with his plough. Krishna stopped him by reminding him of the Pandava vow and Maitreya's curse, and Balarama left for Dwaraka. Krishna then asks Yudhishthira why he tolerated Bhima's act, and Yudhishthira explains his grief and his indifference. Bhima exults, and Yudhishthira tells his brothers the war is over.

The Pandavas and Panchalas rejoice over Duryodhana's fall, and Krishna orders them to stop their taunts. Duryodhana, propped up and in agony, bitterly accuses Krishna of trickery and lists the Pandavas' tricks against the Kaurava warriors. Krishna answers with a list of Duryodhana's own crimes, and Duryodhana declares that he dies a fortunate king and will go to heaven while his enemies remain in misery.

The Pandavas go to Duryodhana's emptied tent, and Krishna has Arjuna get down first. Arjuna's chariot, already scorched by Drona and Karna, bursts into flames and is burnt to ashes after Krishna leaves it. Krishna then embraces Yudhishthira and praises the victory. The Pandavas take the Kaurava treasure, camp by the Oghavati, and send Krishna to Hastinapura to comfort Gandhari.

Janamejaya asks why Krishna went again to Hastinapura after the war. Vaishampayana explains that Yudhishthira feared Gandhari's wrath over her sons' deaths and sent Krishna to calm her. Krishna speaks to Dhritarashtra about the causes of the war and to Gandhari about her own earlier words, comforts them both, and leaves in haste when he learns of Drona's son's plan to attack the Pandavas at night.

Dhritarashtra asks what Duryodhana said as he lay broken on the field. Sanjaya reports Duryodhana's lament: he recalls his wealth, power and honour, accuses Bhima of an unfair blow, and sends messages to his parents and his allies. He calls on Ashvatthama to avenge him, and then sends the messengers away.

Ashvatthama, Kripa and Kritavarma, the last Kaurava warriors, find Duryodhana lying broken on the field. Ashvatthama laments his fate, and Duryodhana tells him that death is fated and that he dies in battle as a Kshatriya should. Ashvatthama swears to kill every Panchala that night, and Duryodhana has Kripa install him as commander. Ashvatthama embraces the king and leaves, and the king lies alone through the night. The chapter closes the Shalya Parva.

After the defeat, the three surviving Kaurava warriors, Ashvatthama, Kripa and Kritavarma, flee south and then east into a dense forest and rest under a huge banyan tree. Dhritarashtra, through Sanjaya, laments the death of Duryodhana and asks what the three did next. That night Ashvatthama watches an owl slaughter sleeping crows and decides to copy the tactic by attacking the sleeping enemy camp. This decision drives the rest of the Sauptika Parva.

Kripa answers Ashvatthama's plan with a long argument that success depends on both destiny and human effort. He says that action is never fruitless, that idleness brings misery, and that Duryodhana ruined himself by ignoring his well-wishers. He advises that the three should first seek counsel from Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Vidura before acting.

Ashvatthama rejects Kripa's advice and argues that every man trusts his own judgment, which shifts with age and fortune. He explains that, though born a Brahmana, he is bound by Kshatriya duty to avenge his father. He then lays out his plan to attack the sleeping Panchalas in their camp and kill them, Dhrishtadyumna included.

Kripa and Kritavarma urge Ashvatthama to rest for the night and promise to fight beside him in the morning. Ashvatthama refuses, citing his grief for his father, his rage at the Pandava victory, and his desire to kill Dhrishtadyumna. He vows to slay his enemies while they sleep before he takes any rest.

Kripa again warns Ashvatthama that killing sleeping, disarmed or surrendered men breaks the rules of dharma and would stain his name. Ashvatthama answers that the Pandavas have already broken those rules, listing the unfair deaths of his father, Karna, Bhishma, Bhurishrava and Duryodhana. He yokes his chariot, tells his companions his plan to kill Dhrishtadyumna, and rides with Kripa and Kritavarma to the Panchala camp.

At the camp gate Ashvatthama meets a huge, terrifying guardian. Every celestial weapon he hurls is swallowed by the being. Left with no weapons, Ashvatthama recalls Kripa's warning, concludes that fate has turned against him, and resolves to seek the protection of Shiva.

Ashvatthama gets down from his chariot and praises Shiva under many names and titles. A golden altar and a blazing fire appear, surrounded by a host of strange beings. Ashvatthama offers himself into the flames, and Shiva appears, grants him a sword and enters his body, so that he sets out for the enemy camp filled with divine power.

Ashvatthama slips into the sleeping Pandava camp at night, kills Dhrishtadyumna in his bed, and then cuts down one warrior after another, including Draupadi's sons, Shikhandi and the Prabhadrakas. Kripa and Kritavarma kill the fugitives at the gate and set the camp on fire, and the night ends in a huge slaughter that leaves the Pandava host destroyed. Dhritarashtra asks why this was not done earlier, and Sanjaya explains that only the absence of Arjuna, Krishna and Satyaki made it possible, since the men were asleep.

The three surviving Kaurava warriors find Duryodhana still alive but dying, with his thighs broken and beasts of prey circling him. They lament his fall and blame the Pandavas for an unfair blow, and Ashvatthama tells the king that he has killed Dhrishtadyumna and his sons. Duryodhana, pleased, dies, and Sanjaya reports the death to Dhritarashtra, who is plunged into anxiety.

The charioteer of Dhrishtadyumna brings Yudhishthira the news of the night slaughter. Yudhishthira collapses in grief, reflects that the Pandava victory has turned to defeat through heedlessness, and sends for Draupadi. He then goes to the battlefield and is overwhelmed by the sight of his slain sons and friends.

Nakula brings Draupadi to Yudhishthira, and she collapses in grief for her slain sons. Bhima comforts her, and she vows to fast to death unless Ashvatthama is punished and his jewel brought to her. Draupadi urges Bhima to avenge her, and he sets out in pursuit of Ashvatthama's chariot, with Nakula as his charioteer.

Krishna warns Yudhishthira that Ashvatthama, who holds the brahmashira weapon, is a danger to Bhima. He recounts how Ashvatthama once came to Dvaraka asking for Krishna's discus in exchange for the brahmashira, and how the discus could not be lifted and was refused. Krishna notes that no close relative ever asked for such a thing, so Ashvatthama's request shows a wrathful and dangerous mind.

Krishna mounts his chariot with Arjuna and Yudhishthira and drives after Bhima, who is charging toward Ashvatthama. They catch up with Bhima at the bank of the Ganga, where Vyasa and other sages are seated, and Ashvatthama is there in grass garments. Ashvatthama turns a blade of grass into the brahmashira and releases it against the Pandavas, and it blazes like the fire that ends the world.

Krishna sees Ashvatthama's intent and tells Arjuna to use the weapon that can neutralise all others. Arjuna releases his own brahmashira to counter it, and the two weapons blaze, bringing thunder, meteors and trembling to the world. Narada and Vyasa step between the weapons to calm the heroes and ask why they used such weapons against men.

Arjuna withdraws his weapon at the sages' urging, which only a celibate, truthful and obedient warrior can do. Ashvatthama admits he released his weapon out of fear of Bhima and cannot recall it. Vyasa persuades him to yield his gem, but Ashvatthama finally agrees to aim the weapon at the wombs of the Pandava women.

Krishna declares that Virata's daughter will bear a child, Parikshit, who will survive the weapon and rule the kingdom. Ashvatthama defies him, but Krishna curses him to wander for three thousand years, and Vyasa confirms the curse. Ashvatthama gives up his gem, the Pandavas bring it to Draupadi, and she gives it to Yudhishthira, ending her fast.

Yudhishthira asks Krishna how Ashvatthama, a warrior of little skill, could kill so many great fighters single-handed. The answer is that Ashvatthama had won the favour of Mahadeva, and the story of Rudra's withdrawal from the work of creation is told to explain the god's power. Rudra, angered that the creatures had multiplied without him, retreats to the mountains to practise harsher austerities.

The gods hold a sacrifice without giving Rudra a share, and Rudra, in anger, builds a bow and attacks it, injuring the gods and breaking the sacrifice. When the gods beg for mercy, Rudra restores their limbs and the sacrifice and is given offerings as his share. The narrative concludes that Ashvatthama's feats were done through Shiva's grace, so Yudhishthira should not dwell on them but act next.

After the Kaurava army is destroyed, the blind king Dhritarashtra sinks into despair over the loss of his sons and allies. Sanjaya tries to console him by reminding him that grief is pointless and that he himself brought the ruin on his house through his indulgence of Duryodhana. Vidura then steps in to continue the comfort, setting up the long moral discourse that follows.

Vidura tries to lift Dhritarashtra out of his grief by arguing that death comes to everyone and that the warriors who died in battle have won a noble fate. He says that mourning cannot bring the dead back and only deepens suffering. He ends by telling the king that one's own actions decide one's fate.

Dhritarashtra says Vidura's words have eased his grief and asks how the wise free themselves from sorrow. Vidura answers that all worldly things are impermanent and that the body is like a house that wears out, while the soul passes from one body to another like a man changing clothes. He compares the fate of creatures to pots that break at many stages of making and to swimmers who dive and surface, and he says the wise attain the highest end.

Dhritarashtra asks Vidura how the wilderness of this world can be understood, and Vidura describes the course of life from conception through birth, suffering, and death. He shows how desire, greed, and pride blind people to their own mortality. He concludes that those who practise virtue and hold to truth can cross safely over life's difficulties.

Dhritarashtra asks Vidura for a fuller account of how the wilderness of duties can be safely crossed, and Vidura tells a parable. A Brahmana is trapped in a dangerous forest, falls into a pit, hangs upside down from creepers, and is threatened from every side. He keeps sipping honey and clinging to hope even as rats gnaw at the roots of the tree he hangs from.

Dhritarashtra asks how the man in the parable can be freed from his dangers and why he clings so strongly to life. Vidura explains that the parable is an allegory for human existence: the forest is the world, the pit is the body, and the dangers are disease, old age, death, desire, and the passing years. He concludes that understanding this allows a person to cut free from life's bonds.

Dhritarashtra asks Vidura to continue, and Vidura gives a fuller teaching on escaping the cycle of rebirth. He compares the body to a chariot, the senses to horses, and the mind to the driver, and says self-control, contentment, truthfulness and harmlessness lead to liberation. He ends by saying that the wise escape the wheel of life while the foolish keep wandering in it.

Dhritarashtra collapses in grief and tries to end his life, but the attendants revive him. Vyasa then reminds him that all things are impermanent and that the war was fated, and he tells the story of Earth's plea to the gods, which led Vishnu to send Duryodhana to bring about the destruction of the Kauravas. Vyasa argues that the Pandavas were blameless, urges the king to live for their sake and for his own good name, and Dhritarashtra agrees to bear his grief and go on living before Vyasa leaves.

After Vyasa leaves, Janamejaya asks what the king and the others did next, and Vaishampayana explains that Sanjaya returns with grim news: the kings and Duryodhana are dead and the rites must be performed. Dhritarashtra falls to the ground in shock, and Vidura again tries to console him, repeating that death is the common end of all creatures and that the fallen warriors have gone to heaven.
