Dhritarashtra orders his chariot and asks for Gandhari and the royal ladies, including Kunti, to be brought to him. They gather in grief and Vidura leads them out of the city toward the battlefield. The whole city, including its children and craftsmen, is seized with mourning, and the scene is described as a second cosmic dissolution.

On the road, Dhritarashtra meets Kripa, Ashvatthama and Kritavarma, the only three of Duryodhana's great warriors still alive. They tell him that Duryodhana has died and that they themselves killed the Pandava sons and the Panchalas in their sleeping camp, then fled before the Pandavas can retaliate. Kripa urges Gandhari and the king to accept the deaths as a warrior's honour, and the three then separate, with Ashvatthama going to Vyasa's hermitage.

Yudhishthira goes out with his brothers, Krishna and the women to meet his uncle Dhritarashtra, who has left Hastinapura in grief. The grieving women confront Yudhishthira with accusations, and the blind king embraces him without warmth. Dhritarashtra then tries to crush Bhima in his arms, but Krishna has substituted an iron figure, and the king breaks it and collapses in grief and blood.

Krishna, after the king has been washed, rebukes Dhritarashtra for his wrath and reminds him that his own choices and his son's bad counsel brought the ruin on him. The king admits his parental affection led him from righteousness and says he is now free of anger. He then embraces Bhima and the twin sons of Madri, and blesses them.

Gandhari, grieving for her hundred sons, wants to curse Yudhishthira, but Vyasa steps in and urges her to forgive. He reminds her that she always told Duryodhana that victory lies where righteousness is. Gandhari replies that she bears the Pandavas no ill will, blames Duryodhana and Shakuni for the ruin, and says her real anger is at Bhima's blow to Duryodhana's navel in the mace fight.

Bhima defends his conduct in the battle as a response to Duryodhana's injustices and to his own vow, and Gandhari scolds him for drinking Duhshasana's blood. Gandhari then rages at the Pandavas for the death of her sons, and Yudhishthira offers himself to her curse. She withholds it, and her gaze injures his toe, after which she comforts the Pandavas. The chapter closes with the reunion of Kunti and Draupadi and the grief of the women, and the section is marked as ending.

Gandhari, though far from the battlefield, sees its carnage through her spiritual sight and begins to lament. Dhritarashtra, the Pandavas, Krishna and the Kuru women travel to Kurukshetra, where the women find their dead husbands, sons and brothers torn by beasts and birds. Gandhari, speaking to Krishna, describes the horror of the field, and her lament ends as her eyes fall on her son Duryodhana.

Gandhari falls senseless at the sight of Duryodhana's body and then mourns over him, recalling how she had told him that victory lies with righteousness. She says her grief is for the blind king and for the reversal of Duryodhana's fortunes, and she describes the ruin of the women and the once-glorious prince. She ends by saying he has at least won the regions of heroes.

Gandhari moves on to lament the other sons she has lost, and she grieves most for the young widows wandering on the battlefield. She describes the ruin of the royal household and the shame of women now exposed to common eyes. She singles out Duhshasana, whose insult to Draupadi and whose death at Bhima's hands she recounts, and she recalls her unheeded warnings to Duryodhana to make peace.

Gandhari continues her lament by naming her dead sons one after another, Vikarna, Durmukha, Citrasena, Vivingsati and Duhsaha. For each she describes the body, the wounds, the scavenging birds and beasts, and the grieving women around him. The chapter stresses the beauty and promise of the young men lost in the war.

Gandhari continues her lament by mourning Abhimanyu, Arjuna's son, and imagines the grief of his young wife Uttara, daughter of Virata, as she mourns him and speaks to him. The Matsya ladies then drag Uttara away from the body of her slain father Virata, and Gandhari lists other fallen young men. The chapter shows the war's cost falling on the young and on the women left behind.

Gandhari mourns Karna, who was slain by Arjuna after he had killed many great warriors. She describes his wives and the mother of his son Vrishasena weeping over him, and Karna's widow blames the curse of his teacher and Arjuna's arrow for his death. She notes that Yudhishthira could not sleep for thirteen years because of his fear of Karna.

Gandhari mourns several fallen men who had once been powerful: the lord of Avanti slain by Bhima, Bahlika, and Jayadratha, who was killed by Arjuna. She tells how Jayadratha's wives guard his body and how her widowed daughter Duhshala runs about searching for her husband's head. She recalls the old wrong done to Draupadi and the sparing of Jayadratha out of regard for Duhshala.

Gandhari lists the great warriors who have fallen. She mourns Shalya, slain by Yudhishthira, and Bhagadatta, and then speaks of Bhishma lying on a bed of arrows, whose death she sees as the fall of a sun among men. She laments Drona, whose body is burned on a pyre attended by his wife Kripi and his disciples, who then carry her toward the Ganga.

Gandhari describes the death of Bhurishrava, whose arm was cut off by Arjuna and who was then killed by Satyaki while sitting in a vow. His widows weep over his severed arm, and Gandhari's speech of rebuke to Krishna is given through the widows. She ends by mourning Shakuni, slain by Sahadeva, and fears that he will sow discord among her sons in the next world.

Gandhari continues her lament over the fallen kings and warriors, from the Kambojas and Magadhas to Drupada, Dhrishtaketu and Vinda and Anuvinda. She then blames Krishna for standing aside while the Kurus destroyed each other, and she curses him that within thirty-six years he will lose his own kin and die in the wilderness. Krishna accepts the curse with a faint smile, saying that the Yadavas will fall by each other's hands, and the Pandavas are left stunned.

A holy figure, identified only as the holy one, tells Gandhari that her son Duryodhana's wicked character brought the carnage and that grief only multiplies grief. Dhritarashtra asks Yudhishthira how many fell and where the warriors have gone, and Yudhishthira tells him the tally and the destinations of the dead, which depend on how they died. Dhritarashtra asks how Yudhishthira knows this, and he credits a boon of spiritual vision from the sage Lomasa; Dhritarashtra then asks how the bodies should be honoured, and Yudhishthira orders the funeral rites performed for all the dead. The burning of the dead is described in detail before the Pandavas lead Dhritarashtra toward the Ganga.

At the Ganga, the Kuru women give water offerings to their dead, and Kunti reveals that Karna was her eldest son by the sun god, born before her marriage. The Pandavas grieve, and Yudhishthira laments that the secret was kept and that the war could have been avoided. He makes water offerings to Karna and to his widows and kin, and the section ends with the colophon of the Stri Parva and the Mahabharata's author.

After the war the Pandavas spend a month mourning on the banks of the Bhagirathi, and sages come to console Yudhishthira. Narada praises his victory, but Yudhishthira says it feels like a defeat and reveals that Karna, whom Arjuna killed, was Kunti's secret firstborn and the Pandavas' elder brother. He asks Narada to explain Karna's past, which begins the story of Karna's curse.

Narada tells the story of Karna's training and curse. Envious of Arjuna, Karna asks Drona for the Brahma weapon and is refused, so he goes to Rama and claims to be a Brahmin of Bhrigu's race. After he accidentally kills a Brahmin's sacred cow, the Brahmin curses him that his chariot wheel will sink into the earth and his foe will take his head in battle. This curse explains how Karna's death was foretold.

While Karna is learning from Rama, a worm bites his thigh as Rama sleeps on his lap, and Karna endures the pain silently so as not to wake his teacher. When Rama finds out, he learns that Karna is a Suta and not a Brahmin, and he curses that the Brahma weapon will fail Karna in battle against an equal. The episode shows Karna's patience and also the deceit that brought his downfall.

Karna, now with Duryodhana, goes to a bride-choosing in the city of Rajapura, where many kings hope to win the princess. Duryodhana seizes the maiden and drives away, and Karna beats back the kings who chase them. The episode shows Karna's martial skill and his loyalty to Duryodhana.

Jarasandha, king of Magadha, challenges Karna after hearing of his fame, and Karna nearly overpowers him. Jarasandha concedes and gives Karna the town of Malini, so Karna comes to rule Champa as well as Anga. Narada then lists the curses, boons and schemes that led to Karna's death and tells Yudhishthira not to grieve for him.

Narada falls silent, and Yudhishthira sinks into sorrow. Kunti, herself distressed, tells him that she and Surya tried to persuade Karna to join his brothers, but he refused. Yudhishthira blames her for keeping the secret, curses all women never to keep a secret, and falls into despair over his lost kin.

Yudhishthira mourns Karna and the other dead, blaming the war on Duryodhana, Dhritarashtra and his own covetousness. He calls the battle a kind of self-slaughter and finds no pleasure in the kingdom he has won. He resolves to give up the throne, go to the forest, and asks Arjuna's leave, which sets up Arjuna's reply.

Arjuna rebukes Yudhishthira for wanting to give up the kingdom, calling it a weak and foolish choice and arguing that a king who lives by begging cannot win fame. He argues that wealth is the basis of all virtue, pointing to Nahusha and to the gods, who gained their place through strife. He urges Yudhishthira to rule and to perform a great sacrifice, making the case for kingly action over renunciation.

Yudhishthira replies that he will go to the forest whatever Arjuna advises. He describes in detail the austere life he intends to lead: begging for food, avoiding injury to any creature, and remaining detached from pleasure and pain. He calls worldly life a fleeting illusion bound by birth and death, and says he wants a permanent, eternal state.

Bhimasena rebukes Yudhishthira, saying his judgment has been clouded by too much scripture and that giving up the kingdom after such a war would make the slaughter pointless. He argues that Kshatriyas must act, that renunciation is not a fit path for a warrior king, and that forest life alone does not win heaven. The chapter sets out the opposing view from another of the Pandava brothers.

Arjuna tells an old story in which Sakra (Indra), in the form of a golden bird, rebukes young Brahmin ascetics who gave up home for the forest. The bird teaches that the Vedic rites, sacrifice and the householder's duties are the true path to heaven. The ascetics return to domestic life, and Arjuna urges Yudhishthira to follow their example and rule the earth.

Nakula, the twin, answers Arjuna with a long argument that action and the householder's life are the proper path. He says the gods, ancestors and learned Brahmins all depend on sacrifice and duty, that true renunciation is inner detachment, and that a king who keeps the wealth won in war without sacrificing shows a lack of faith. He also warns that a king who neglects his subjects becomes an embodiment of Kali, the age of decline, and urges Yudhishthira not to grieve.

Sahadeva argues that giving up outward things brings no success while inner desire remains. He says the soul is eternal, so killing a body is not real slaughter, and that a king who holds the earth but does not enjoy it wastes his life. He also says a hermit still attached to the world lives in Death's jaws, and asks Yudhishthira to forgive his blunt words.

Draupadi, silent until now, speaks to Yudhishthira while his brothers sit around him. She reminds him of his earlier vow to defeat Duryodhana and enjoy the earth, argues that a king must use the rod of punishment, and says his retreat is a kind of madness that will spread to his brothers. She lists his conquests and urges him to rule, sacrifice and give gifts to Brahmins.

Arjuna argues that the rod of chastisement, meaning force and punishment, is what upholds righteousness, wealth and order, and that without it the strong would devour the weak. He says all creatures live by harming one another, that the gods themselves are slayers, and that killing an armed enemy in a just fight brings no sin, since the soul cannot be slain. He urges Yudhishthira to take up the rod, rule the kingdom and perform sacrifices.

Bhima, holding back his anger, rebukes Yudhishthira for his inaction and his clouded judgment. He compares grief to a sickness of body and mind and says Yudhishthira is dwelling on past woes, recalling the family's humiliations and hardships such as Draupadi's disgrace and the exile. He argues that the real battle now is with his own mind, urges a horse-sacrifice, and says Duryodhana has been slain.

Yudhishthira answers Bhima that desire can never be fully satisfied, and that a king with one stomach gains nothing from endless craving for power. He praises renunciation and inner calm, citing King Janaka's verse about having nothing even when his city burns. He ends by saying that understanding, not outward forms, is the supreme good.

Arjuna retells the tale of King Janaka of Videha, who gave up his kingdom to live as a beggar. His queen rebukes him that he has abandoned his duties to gods, guests and ancestors, and that a giver who sustains others is more honoured than a beggar. Arjuna then concludes that householders who practise charity, truth and worship can reach the regions of bliss.

Yudhishthira answers Arjuna respectfully but firmly, saying Arjuna knows war but not the deeper scriptures. He ranks renunciation and knowledge of Brahma above penance, and denies that wealth is the highest good. He describes the northern path of renunciation and the southern path of action, and concludes that men reach Brahma through asceticism, intelligence and renunciation.

The ascetic Devasthana answers Yudhishthira by arguing that a king who has won the earth should not abandon it, and that wealth belongs to sacrifice. He says the Creator made wealth for sacrifice and man to tend it, and he cites Indra, Mahadeva, Marutta and Harischandra as examples of great sacrifices that won glory. He concludes that everything should be devoted to sacrifice.

Devasthana continues with a teaching that Vrihaspati gave to Indra, in which contentment is called the highest bliss. Vrihaspati says people follow many different paths, and that the best religion is non-injury, truthfulness and compassion. He describes a righteous king who hands his crown to his son and retires to the forest, and says such a king wins good fruit in this world and the next.

Arjuna again urges Yudhishthira to act, saying that death in battle is the proper end for a Kshatriya, while renunciation and penance belong to Brahmins. He tells Yudhishthira to perform sacrifices and charity, as Indra did while fighting as a warrior. He says the slain have gained the highest end and that destiny cannot be resisted.

Yudhishthira stays silent, and Vyasa backs Arjuna: the householder's life is the highest duty, and a king's duties include wielding the rod of punishment. Vyasa tells of the brothers Sankha and Likhita, in which Likhita takes fruit without asking and confesses to King Sudyumna, who cuts off his hands as punishment. Sankha says the punishment has purified Likhita, whose hands return through penance, and Vyasa concludes that ruling by punishment is a king's proper duty.

Vyasa urges Yudhishthira to enjoy the kingdom with his brothers, pay his debts to gods, ancestors and guests, and perform great sacrifices before he ever takes up the later stages of life. He lays out a king's duties: protect subjects impartially, punish robbers, and rely on learned counsel. He illustrates these duties with King Hayagriva, who died in battle after ruling righteously and is now in heaven, and whose battle is described as a sacrifice.

Yudhishthira says his kingdom brings him no joy, and the lamentations of the widowed women keep him from peace. Vyasa replies that Time governs all events, that no one truly slays or is slain, and that grief grows when indulged. He teaches that happiness and sorrow alternate and should be borne with an untroubled mind, and that a king's sacrifice is battle while his yoga is good government.

Yudhishthira replies to Arjuna that wealth is not the only path, since sages gain heaven through study, penance and contentment. He notes the southern path of action and the northern path of yoga, and warns that wealth brings injury to others, anxiety and sin. He argues that wealth belongs to sacrifice and should go to deserving people, not be squandered on desire or given to the unworthy.

Yudhishthira grieves for the fallen heroes, including Bhishma, Drona, Abhimanyu, Karna and his own sons, and blames himself for their deaths. He confesses his deceit toward Drona about Ashvatthama, and declares that he will fast to death. Vyasa stops him, saying that all is destiny and that work and skill, not idleness, bring success.

Vyasa tells Yudhishthira the story of Asma's discourse. King Janaka of Videha asks the Brahmin Asma how to act when kin and wealth are gained or lost, and Asma explains that joy and grief come through destiny, that prosperity breeds vanity, and that death and decay cannot be escaped. He describes family ties as the passing company of travellers at an inn and urges study, sacrifice and righteous rule, which frees Janaka from grief. Vyasa closes by urging Yudhishthira to cast off his grief and enjoy the earth he has won.

Arjuna asks Krishna to comfort the silent Yudhishthira. Krishna (Vasudeva) says the fallen heroes died bravely and are beyond recall, and then recounts Narada's counsel to King Srinjaya, who grieved for his dead son. Narada lists many great kings, such as Marutta, Bharata, Rama and Yayati, who all died despite their sacrifices and gifts, and so Srinjaya should not grieve; Narada then restores Srinjaya's son to life.

Yudhishthira asks how Srinjaya's son came to be called Suvarnashthivin and why he died in childhood. Krishna relates that the sages Narada and his nephew Parvata, guests of Srinjaya, cursed each other after Narada fell in love with the king's daughter Sukumari. Narada was cursed to appear as an ape, and the two later lifted their curses. Krishna says Narada himself is present and can explain the rest.

Narada tells Yudhishthira the rest of the story. Srinjaya asks Parvata for a long-lived, heroic son, and Parvata grants a son named Suvarnashthivin but warns that he will not live long. Indra, fearing the boy, sends a thunderbolt in the form of a tiger that kills the five-year-old prince by the Bhagirathi. Narada restores the boy to life with Indra's permission, and the prince later rules for a very long time.

Vyasa tells Yudhishthira that protecting subjects and punishing wrongdoers is a king's duty, and that the Kauravas were transgressors who had to be stopped. Yudhishthira confesses that the deaths he caused for the kingdom still burn in him. Vyasa asks whether man or the Supreme Being acts, argues with the example of an axe that the one who cuts is responsible, and urges Yudhishthira to live and perform expiations rather than give up his life.

Yudhishthira laments that he alone caused the deaths of kin, friends and kings, pictures the widows' suffering and his own fall into hell, and asks what life he should now take up. Vyasa answers that Time, through the workings of past acts, took the lives of the fallen, and that killing to save a family or kingdom is no transgression. He recommends the Horse-sacrifice as expiation and urges Yudhishthira to comfort his brothers, install the kin of the fallen on their thrones, and rule.

Yudhishthira asks which acts make a man liable to expiation and which acts free him from sin. Vyasa lists many lapses, such as waking after sunrise, marrying out of turn, killing a Brahmin and selling Vedic knowledge. He then names acts that carry no sin, such as striking down an armed Brahmin who attacks with intent to kill, or lying or stealing for a teacher in distress. The list sets up the rules of expiation that follow.

Vyasa describes the expiations for sin: years of mendicant austerity, gifts of cattle and wealth to Brahmins, fasts, and the great Horse-sacrifice. He prescribes penances for lesser faults, and says deliberate sins are graver than accidental ones. He notes that expiations are meant for believers and not the faithless, and urges Yudhishthira to atone through right conduct rather than take his own life.

Yudhishthira asks which food is clean, which gifts are praiseworthy, and who deserves a gift. Vyasa recounts Manu's discourse to a company of Rishis, which classes some foods as forbidden for Brahmins and some gifts as worthless or harmful. Manu holds that a gift to an unlearned Brahmin is wasted and that a bad gift harms both giver and receiver. The chapter gives rules on giving that match the expiation teaching before it.

Yudhishthira asks to hear the duties of kings and of all four orders, and how virtue can be reconciled with kingship. Vyasa directs him to Bhishma, the aged Kuru grandsire who knows the duties of kings. Yudhishthira objects that he cannot approach Bhishma after having had him slain by deceit, but Krishna urges him to accept his duty. Yudhishthira agrees and enters the city in a grand procession.

As the Pandavas enter the city, crowds and women praise them and Draupadi, and Yudhishthira blesses the Brahmins with gifts. A Rakshasa named Charvaka, disguised as a mendicant and a friend of Duryodhana, publicly accuses Yudhishthira of killing kin and urges him to give up his life. The Brahmins expose Charvaka as the Rakshasa, and their utterance kills him on the spot.

Krishna tells Yudhishthira to honour Brahmins, and explains that the Rakshasa Charvaka had won a boon that protected him from every creature except those he offended, the Brahmins. Brahma had arranged that Charvaka would befriend Duryodhana, insult the Brahmins, and be destroyed by their curse. Krishna urges Yudhishthira not to grieve for kin who died in their duties, and to protect his subjects and worship Brahmins.

Yudhishthira takes his seat on a golden throne, surrounded by Krishna, Satyaki, his brothers, Kunti and the elders. Priests perform the coronation rites, and Krishna and Dhritarashtra pour sanctified water over the new king's head. The people bring gifts and the Brahmins bless him, and he rewards them and is installed as king of the restored realm.

Yudhishthira tells his subjects that Dhritarashtra is his father and god, and asks them to serve the old king as before, since he lives for him alone. He dismisses the citizens and assigns offices: Bhima as heir apparent, Vidura as counsellor, Sanjaya over finance, Nakula over the army, Arjuna over the forces, Dhaumya as priest, and Sahadeva at his side. He also tells Vidura and Yuyutsu to carry out Dhritarashtra's wishes.

Yudhishthira performs funeral rites for each of his fallen kinsmen and allies, and Dhritarashtra gives gifts for his sons' sake. The king gives wealth to Brahmins in the names of Drona, Karna, Abhimanyu, Ghatotkacha, Virata, Drupada and others, and founds food-halls, water-places and tanks in their memory. He honours Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Vidura, and cares for the widows, the blind and the destitute, and then enjoys peace.

Yudhishthira thanks Krishna for restoring his ancestral kingdom and praises him in a long hymn. He calls Krishna Vishnu, Hari, the creator and dissolver of the universe, and names him by countless forms and titles. Pleased by the hymn, Krishna begins to speak warmly to the king.

Yudhishthira sends the people home and asks his brothers to rest after their wounds and exile. He gives each brother a palace that once belonged to a Kaurava prince: Bhima takes Duryodhana's, Arjuna Dussasana's, Nakula Durmarshana's, and Sahadeva Durmukha's. The counsellors return to their homes, and Krishna retires with Satyaki to Arjuna's palace, where all feast and sleep.

Janamejaya asks what Yudhishthira did after regaining his kingdom, and what Krishna did next. Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira gives gifts to Brahmins, servants and guests, and honours his elders, Kripa, Vidura, Yuyutsu and Dhritarashtra. He then goes to Krishna and finds him seated in deep meditation, and speaks to him gently, but Krishna does not answer.

Yudhishthira asks Krishna why he is so still in meditation. Krishna says Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, is thinking of him, and that he had been concentrating on Bhishma in return. He urges Yudhishthira to go and learn the duties of kings from Bhishma before he dies, and Yudhishthira agrees. Krishna's chariot is then readied for the journey.

Janamejaya asks how Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, gave up his body and what yoga he followed. Vaisampayana describes how, at the sun's northward turn, Bhishma drew his soul inward while many sages, including Vyasa and Narada, sat around him. Bhishma hymned Krishna at great length as the Supreme Being, the creator and dissolver of all things, and Krishna granted him heavenly knowledge before departing with the others.

Krishna, Yudhishthira and the others ride to Kurukshetra, where the battlefield is still strewn with bones and remains. Krishna points out the lakes of Rama, son of Jamadagni, where Rama is said to have offered Kshatriya blood to his ancestors after destroying the Kshatriyas. Yudhishthira doubts the story and asks how the Kshatriya order could have been wiped out and then revived, and Krishna sets out to explain it.

Krishna tells Yudhishthira how Rama, son of Jamadagni, came to destroy the Kshatriyas. A mix-up of sacred food shapes the family line, and Rama gets a great axe from Mahadeva. After the sons of Arjuna, the Haihaya king, kill his father Jamadagni, Rama wipes out the Kshatriyas many times over, until Kasyapa takes the earth and the surviving Kshatriyas, hidden among herders and others, are restored as kings.

Yudhishthira is amazed at Rama's deeds, and Krishna and Yudhishthira go to Bhishma lying on his bed of arrows on the banks of the Oghavati, surrounded by sages. Krishna asks whether Bhishma's mind is still clear, praises his mastery over death and his learning in all the duties, and urges him to dispel Yudhishthira's grief. Bhishma hymns Krishna, who reveals his divine form and tells Bhishma that fifty-six days remain before he will depart at the sun's northward turn, and that he should instruct Yudhishthira.

Bhishma replies that his pain and weakness leave him unable to speak in Krishna's presence, and asks Krishna to instruct Yudhishthira himself. Krishna grants Bhishma a boon that keeps his mind and memory clear and frees him from pain and confusion. The sages worship Krishna, heavenly flowers fall, and the company leaves at sunset for the city.

Krishna wakes before dawn, performs his rites, and gives a thousand cows to Brahmins. He sends Satyaki to ask Yudhishthira whether the king is ready to visit Bhishma. Yudhishthira asks that no soldiers accompany them, so that Bhishma's last teaching is not crowded out, and the party drives out to the bed of arrows.

Janamejaya asks what was said when Bhishma lay on his bed of arrows. Narada urges the Pandavas to question Bhishma before he dies, and Yudhishthira asks Krishna to speak first. Krishna asks after Bhishma's health, and Bhishma says his pain has gone and his memory is clear through Krishna's favour. Krishna answers that Bhishma's fame must be enhanced, and urges him to teach Yudhishthira as a father teaches his sons.

Bhishma agrees to teach, saying his mind is steady through Krishna's grace, and asks Yudhishthira to question him freely. Krishna notes that Yudhishthira is too ashamed to approach, given the slaughter he caused. Bhishma defends the Kshatriya duty of fighting, even against kin and teachers in an unjust battle, and says a righteous battle brings heaven and fame. Yudhishthira bows at his feet, and Bhishma invites him to ask without fear.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to teach the duties of kings, which he calls the highest science and the reins that hold the world together. Bhishma tells him to honour gods and Brahmins, to act with prompt exertion rather than rely on destiny, and to keep to truth. He teaches that a king must be neither too mild nor too fierce, that Brahmins should be banished rather than physically punished, and that a king should care for his subjects as a mother cares for her child. He warns that servants who grow too familiar with the king will disrespect him.

Bhishma insists that a king must be ready for action, making peace or war as the situation requires. He gives examples of severe discipline, such as Sagara exiling his son Asamanjas and Uddalaka casting off Swetaketu, and advises the king to keep his counsels secret and to employ honest servants. He governs with justice and generosity, and describes the best king as one whose subjects live without fear.

Bhishma says protecting subjects is the core of kingly duty, as Vrihaspati and other sages teach, and lists the means of protection: spies, fair taxation, honest officers, fortifications and care of allies. He says exertion is the root of kingly duty, and that a king must be candid yet sometimes shrewd in policy. He declares he has taught only part of the subject, and the listeners praise him, while Yudhishthira promises to ask more the next day.

Yudhishthira asks why one man should rule the whole world when all men are alike in body and mind. Bhishma explains that in the first age there was no king or punishment, but greed, anger and error spread until the Vedas and righteousness declined, and the gods turned to Brahma. Brahma composed a great treatise on the science of chastisement, later abridged by Shiva, Indra, Brihaspati and Kavi, and the chapter traces its transmission to Vena, a tyrant slain by the sages, and to Prithu, the first true king, from whose rule kingship and its honour are said to come.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to set out the general and special duties of each of the four orders. Bhishma lists nine duties shared by all, then the duties of Brahmins (self-restraint and Vedic study), Kshatriyas (giving without begging, protecting subjects and fighting robbers), Vaisyas (gifts, study, sacrifice and fair earnings from herding and trade), and Sudras (service to the higher orders, with minor sacrifices). He concludes that sacrifice and devotion belong to every order, with the Brahmin foremost.

Bhishma names the four modes of life, Brahmacharya, Garhasthya, Vanaprastha and Bhaikshya, and sets out the duties of each. The student serves his teacher and studies the Vedas, the householder begets children, keeps faith with his wife and is hospitable, the forest hermit withdraws with the sacred texts, and the mendicant has no fixed home and no attachments. He ends with a verse on the householder's virtues.

Yudhishthira asks for duties suited to men in their own position. Bhishma replies that the four modes of life belong to Brahmins, and that a Brahmin who takes up the callings of other orders is disgraced and bound for hell. He stresses that men act under the influence of Time and their own propensities, and that the study of the Vedas is as worthy as kingly power, farming or trade.

Bhishma says that drawing the bowstring, warfare, farming, trade, herding and service for wages are improper for a Brahmin. A Brahmin who falls from his duties becomes like a Sudra, and gifts to such men bring no merit. He describes the duties of the other orders, and concludes that the Kshatriya's duties underlie all the others, as the elephant's footprint covers the tracks of other animals.

Bhishma argues that all duties, including those of the four modes of life, fall under kingly duty, since disorder in royal duty brings evil on all creatures. He tells how King Mandhatri, seeking to see Narayana, met the god in the form of Indra and asked how to perform his duties. Indra explains that kingly duty came first from the Supreme, contains all other duties, and protected the others when Vishnu destroyed the Asuras, so that Kshatriya duty is the foremost of all.

Indra continues that kings must uphold their duties by reclaiming land, giving gifts, avoiding begging and ruling impartially, and that Brahmins who neglect their own duties should be punished like Sudras. When Mandhatri asks what duties foreign and robber tribes should keep, Indra says they should honour parents, teachers and kings, follow the Vedas, and make gifts. Indra warns that when kingly duty fails, men will fall into disorder and false sects, and honours the king who watches over men's duties. Bhishma closes by saying Narayana departed and that the path of the ancients should be followed.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the four modes of human life in more detail. Bhishma says a righteous king who rules well, gives gifts, honours the worthy and protects his people earns the merit of every mode of life. He closes by urging Yudhishthira to keep to the king's duty of protection, which he calls the most meritorious of all.

Yudhishthira asks what the chief duties of a kingdom are. Bhishma says the first duty is to choose and crown a king, since anarchy leaves a land open to robbers and mutual destruction. He tells how Manu was persuaded to accept kingship in return for a share of the people's wealth and merit, and how a king should carry himself once crowned.

Yudhishthira asks why Brahmanas call the king a god. Bhishma answers with a teaching that the sage Vrihaspati gave to King Vasumanas of Kosala, in which the king is the root of all duties and the guardian against chaos. Vrihaspati lists the forms a king takes and urges loyalty to him, and Vasumanas accepts the teaching and begins to protect his subjects.

Yudhishthira asks what further duties a king has in defending his realm, handling spies and winning his subjects' trust. Bhishma says a king must first master himself, then gives long practical advice on spies, peace and war, taxation, justice, fortifications and the seven limbs of a state. He ends by arguing that the king's conduct decides which age of the world comes, from the Krita age down to Kali.

Yudhishthira asks whether a king who follows such conduct can gain lasting happiness in this world and the next. Bhishma lists thirty-six virtues a king should practise, such as restraint, kindness, fair taxation, careful punishment and humility towards elders. Vaisampayana ends the chapter by saying Yudhishthira accepted the teaching and ruled by it from then on.

Yudhishthira asks how a king should protect his subjects so that he avoids grief and does not offend against righteousness. Bhishma gives a brief list of duties: honour learned Brahmanas, control lust and anger, collect a fair share of the produce as tax, and never fill the treasury by unrighteous means. He calls the protection of subjects the highest duty of a king, with rewards that only a king can earn.

Bhishma says a king should appoint as his priest someone who protects the good and punishes the wicked. He retells a dialogue between King Pururavas and the wind god Matariswan on the origin of the four orders and whom the earth belongs to. The wind god concludes that the Brahmana holds first place by birth, that the priest shares in the king's merit, and that sacrifice and order depend on a king.

Bhishma says a king should choose a learned priest, and that king and priest should be friends so the subjects stay content. Sage Kasyapa tells King Aila that quarrels between Brahmanas and Kshatriyas bring ruin, and that Rudra, the god of destruction, arises in the hearts of sinners and strikes the land. Kasyapa adds that the sinless must keep away from the sinful, and that the next world rewards the righteous and punishes the wicked differently.

Bhishma says a kingdom's safety rests on the king, and the king's safety rests on his priest. He retells how King Muchukunda, after conquering the earth, met the Lord of Alaka's Rakshasa army, which his priest Vasishtha stopped through penance. Muchukunda refuses to hold sovereignty as a gift and insists on ruling by his own might, and Bhishma concludes that a king who yields precedence to Brahmanas wins fame.

Yudhishthira asks how a king can raise his subjects and earn heavenly regions. Bhishma says a king should be generous, protect his people, honour the righteous and share in their merit and their sins. Yudhishthira then declares he would rather give up the kingdom for asceticism, and Bhishma replies that his gentleness does not fit a king, urging him to keep to his duty and rule. Bhishma ends by praising the man who gives relief from fear.

Yudhishthira asks how Brahmanas who keep to their duties differ from those who do not. Bhishma says learned, even-minded Brahmanas match Brahma and the gods, while the ill-born and those who abandon their duties are like Sudras. He adds that the king may tax or discipline the unworthy and should support a learned Brahmana who has turned to theft out of want before banishing him for continued theft.

Yudhishthira asks whose wealth a king may claim and how he should conduct himself. Bhishma says the king may take wealth from everyone except worthy Brahmanas, but must keep Brahmanas supported, since a Brahmana who turns thief reflects on the king. He illustrates this with the story of the Kaikeya king, who wins release from a Rakshasa by listing how righteously his kingdom is run.

Yudhishthira asks whether a Brahmana in distress may take up Vaisya work and what goods he may sell. Bhishma says he may farm or keep cattle, but must not sell items such as wine, salt, honey, meat or cooked food, while fair exchange by agreement is lawful. Asked what happens when the orders rise against a weakened king, Bhishma says that Brahmanas and others may take up arms to protect the Brahmanas and the people, and that whoever shields the helpless deserves to rule.

Yudhishthira asks what conduct and character the priests who serve at his sacrifices should have. Bhishma describes the learning, honesty and self-control a fit priest needs. Yudhishthira then questions the fixed gift of dakshina, and Bhishma says a sacrifice needs its dakshina and sound character, and that true penance lies in harmlessness, truth and compassion.

Yudhishthira asks how a king should choose and trust his ministers, since no task is done alone. Bhishma sorts friends into four kinds, adds a fifth who serves righteousness, and warns that a king must weigh trust and mistrust with care. He advises giving each task to one capable, honest minister and treating kinsmen with outward trust and inner watchfulness.

Yudhishthira asks how to win both friends and foes when kinsmen turn hostile. Bhishma tells of Vasudeva confiding to the sage Narada that his kinsmen wound him with cruel words and split the Vrishnis and Bhojas. Narada says the trouble is internal and self-made, that the wealth given away cannot be reclaimed, and that the remedy is gentle speech, generosity and forgiveness, not steel.

Bhishma gives a second means: a king must protect the person who reports ministers embezzling the treasury. He tells of the sage Kalakavrikshiya, who used a crow in a cage to expose the corrupt officers of King Kshemadarsin of Kosala, and was saved only after the officers killed the crow. The sage warns the king of the dangers of royal service and urges him to weaken the guilty men one by one, and the king makes him his priest and rules well with his counsel.

Yudhishthira asks what qualities a king's legislators, war ministers, courtiers, generals and counsellors should have. Bhishma answers at length: choose people of good birth, proven loyalty, learning and self-control, test their records, and avoid the greedy, cruel or self-serving. He also advises that counsel be kept secret, sought in quiet places, and given by at least three ministers.

Bhishma tells a short story in which Sakra (Indra) asks his priest Vrihaspati which single act wins the regard of all creatures. Vrihaspati answers that agreeable speech does so, since sweet, smiling words win love while frowns breed hatred. Even a king who must punish should speak sweetly, and Bhishma says Sakra followed this advice and urges Yudhishthira to do the same.

Yudhishthira asks by what method a king can earn lasting blessedness and fame. Bhishma says a pure king who protects his subjects gains merit and fame here and hereafter. He then sets out the make-up of a royal council drawn from all four orders, and rules for fair justice, punishments matched to offences, the protection of envoys, and the advice never to trust anyone fully.

Yudhishthira asks what kind of city a king should live in, and whether he should use an existing city or build one. Bhishma says the king should choose among six kinds of citadels: water, earth, hill, human, mud and forest. He describes a well-defended, well-stocked and righteous capital, and advises the king to keep spies, stores, craftsmen and learned ascetics close at hand.

Yudhishthira asks how a kingdom can be consolidated and protected. Bhishma describes a layered administration, with a headman for each village and superiors over ten, twenty, a hundred and a thousand villages, all reporting upward and watched by spies. He advises taxes that the people can bear, likening the king to a herdsman who must not drain the cow, and urges kindness toward the Vaisyas who sustain trade and farming.

Yudhishthira asks how a king should act if he still craves more wealth despite his riches. Bhishma says a king should draw revenue gently, like a bee gathering honey or a leech drawing blood, raising demands by degrees. He also says the king shares in his subjects' sins and merits, so he must check drinking, gambling and other vices and keep beggars off the streets. He closes with a charge to love all creatures and rule with truth and restraint.

Bhishma says fruit-bearing trees must not be felled, and that a Brahmana in want should be supported rather than driven away. He advises the king to use spies to watch his people and to examine his own conduct and reputation. When Yudhishthira asks how one man among equals comes to rule the rest, Bhishma answers that the strong prey on the weak and that the king must protect traders and farmers from heavy taxes.

Bhishma recounts the teaching that the sage Utathya gave to King Mandhatri, son of Yuvanaswa. Utathya says a king rules rightly only by upholding righteousness, that a king who does so is godlike, and that pride and unrighteousness bring ruin. He urges the king to honour Brahmanas and avoid vice, and warns that neglecting righteousness brings drought, floods, disorder and the collapse of property and worship.

The sage Utathya tells Mandhatri that rain, prosperity and the four ages all depend on the king's conduct. A righteous king who corrects the orders is like a washerman who cleans cloth without stripping its colour, while a heedless king brings ruin on all creatures. Utathya lists the king's duties, including protecting the weak, punishing wrongdoers, honouring priests and avoiding pride, and Bhishma says Mandhatri obeyed and became lord of the whole earth.

Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king should behave. Bhishma tells how King Vasumanas asked the sage Vamadeva for counsel on keeping to his duties. Vamadeva says righteousness is the highest guide and that kings who follow it conquer the earth, while kings who rely on force, wicked ministers or caprice bring their own downfall.

Vamadeva continues his counsel to Vasumanas. He warns that a king's conduct is copied by his people and kinsmen, so he must be honest, kind and fair, and must choose capable, loyal officers. He advises watching rival kings through secret agents, attacking only weaker neighbours, sharing the duties of state with trusted ministers, and never trusting those who wish him ill.

Vamadeva says a king should win victories without battle where he can, and should first make his own power secure before seeking new lands. A contented army, a loyal and compassionate people, and a king who controls his temper make his power sound. Bhishma says that King Vasumana followed this counsel and that Yudhishthira would likewise conquer both worlds.

Yudhishthira asks how a Kshatriya should act in seeking to conquer another Kshatriya. Bhishma says the invader should first call on the people to accept him and pay tribute, and fight only those who resist. He then sets out rules of fair combat between warriors, such as matching armour with armour and not striking the fallen, unarmed or wounded, and says a victory won by sinful means is no victory.

Bhishma says a king should never conquer by unrighteous means, since such victories bring no heaven and weaken both king and land. He sets out rules for dealing with the vanquished: spare the disarmed, keep a defeated king in one's palace for a year, return captured women after a year, give captured cattle to Brahmanas, and never harm a Brahmana who comes to make peace. He advises winning over conquered subjects with soothing words and gifts.

Yudhishthira asks how a warrior-king can win heaven when Kshatriya practice involves so much slaughter. Bhishma says kings are cleansed by punishing the wicked, supporting the good, and offering sacrifices and gifts, and that protecting people from robbers is itself a great gift. He concludes that a hero who fights bravely and dies in battle wins heaven, while a coward who flees or dies at home without honour does not.

Yudhishthira asks what regions unreturning heroes win by dying in battle. Bhishma tells how King Amvarisha, in heaven, sees his former general Sudeva ranked above himself, though Sudeva had made fewer sacrifices to the gods. Indra explains that battle is itself a sacrifice, with warriors as priests and blood as the final libation, and that brave heroes who die fighting win the highest regions. Bhishma says Amvarisha accepted this teaching.

Bhishma tells how King Janaka of Mithila rallied his warriors before a battle with Pratardana. Janaka showed them the heaven awaiting brave men and the hell reserved for deserters, and then set out the battle order. He advised against over-pursuing a routed enemy and ended by praising heroism as the support of the world.

Yudhishthira asks how kings should lead their troops into battle even if that means bending the rules of righteousness a little. Bhishma says a king may use crooked policy only to counter enemies, then gives a long set of military preparations: stocking arms, choosing the season and safe roads, picking camp sites, placing troops by wind and sun, sparing the helpless, and rewarding brave men. He ends by describing an oath of steadfastness and battle formations, including tricks to make a small force look larger.

Yudhishthira asks what temperament, appearance, dress and arms make combatants fit for battle. Bhishma says each people should fight with the weapons it knows, and notes the fighting styles of various regions. He then lists bodily and temperamental marks of brave fighters, and says the fiercest tribes of the outlying districts make the best vanguard, though they turn angry if treated gently.

Yudhishthira asks for the known signs that an army will succeed. Bhishma lists omens of success, such as cheerful troops, favourable winds, auspicious birds and animals, and bright sacrificial fires. He advises trying conciliation, division and gifts before fighting, and says victory in battle depends largely on fate. He ends by urging a mix of severity and mildness toward the defeated, with genuine grief for the slain.

Yudhishthira asks how a king should treat a mild foe, a fierce foe and a foe with many allies. Bhishma tells how Vrihaspati advised Indra to avoid open quarrel, hide his feelings, speak sweetly while planning, strike at the right moment, and corrupt the enemy's forces by division and gifts. Vrihaspati then lists the marks of a wicked person, and Bhishma says Indra followed this teaching and subdued his foes.

Yudhishthira asks how a righteous king who has lost his officers, treasury and army can still find happiness. Bhishma tells of Kshemadarsin, the prince of Kosala, who fell into distress and went to the sage Kalakavrikshiya. The sage teaches that all things are impermanent and that grief for lost wealth is useless, and advises him to let go of craving, enjoy what he has, and perhaps retire to the forest.

The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells King Kshemadarsin that, if he still has courage, he can recover his kingdom by a line of policy. He advises him to humble himself before Janaka, the ruler of Mithila, to earn that king's trust, and then to weaken his foes through division, luxury, a drained treasury and misdirected sacrifices. He ends by saying that poison and fraud can destroy a hostile kingdom.

Kshemadarsin refuses to win back his kingdom by fraud and says he will live only by honest means. The sage Kalakavrikshiya praises his righteousness and brings him to Janaka, the ruler of Videha, who recognises his worth. The two kings make peace and trust each other, and Janaka honours his guest with his own daughter and jewels, reasoning that peace is the high duty of kings.

Yudhishthira recaps the earlier teachings and asks how a king should treat the many brave men around him so that they stay loyal and undivided. Bhishma says enmity between the king and the nobility arises from greed on the king's side and wrath on theirs. Nobles who stay united, honour their leaders and settle quarrels early prosper, while disunion and oppression drive them to the king's enemies.

Yudhishthira asks which duties matter most for earning merit now and in the next world. Bhishma answers that honouring mother, father and teacher is the chief duty, and that they should be obeyed and served with humility. He says the teacher deserves the greatest reverence because he gives an immortal life, and that neglecting or injuring any of the three is a grave sin.

Yudhishthira asks how someone who wants to follow virtue should tell truth from falsehood, and what eternal virtue is. Bhishma says truth is generally right but must be withheld when it serves evil, and that a falsehood may be told to save a life or another's wealth or to escape sinful men. He concludes that righteousness is what upholds creatures and prevents their injury, so the honest should be met with honesty and the deceitful with deceit.

Yudhishthira asks how creatures can overcome the many afflictions that beset them. Bhishma answers with a long list of people who overcome difficulties: those who keep to their duties, speak the truth, give without taking, honour guests and parents, and avoid harm and greed. He ends by identifying Krishna as Narayana, the Lord who protects those who seek his refuge, and says reciting these verses helps one overcome difficulties.

Yudhishthira asks how to tell people who are truly tranquil from those who only appear so. Bhishma tells of a cruel king, Paurika, reborn as a jackal who lives purely and refuses meat. A tiger takes the jackal as his minister, but envious old servants frame him for stealing the tiger's meat, and the jackal, though cleared, leaves the court and ends his life by fasting, going to heaven.

Yudhishthira asks what a king should do to be happy. Bhishma warns against the example of a camel of the Krita age, who won from Brahman a boon of a very long neck after great austerities. The camel grew idle, and while sheltering from a storm in a cave, a jackal and his wife ate his neck and killed him. Bhishma uses the tale to urge a king to avoid idleness and to act with intelligence, aided by wise counsel and allies.

Yudhishthira asks how a king without the usual aids should behave toward a powerful foe. Bhishma tells of the Ocean asking the rivers why they never sweep away the canes on their banks, though they uproot great trees. Ganga explains that the cane bends with the current and survives, while rigid trees resist and are torn away, and Bhishma concludes that a wise man facing a stronger foe should yield like the cane.

Yudhishthira asks how a learned, modest man should respond when an ignorant, conceited person abuses him in public. Bhishma advises patience: the man who does not answer anger takes the abuser's merit, and the abuser takes the patient man's demerit. The boasts and slanders of fools are empty, like a crow's cawing, and slanderers who speak ill of others behind their backs should be avoided, while one who endures their reproaches suffers no pain from speech.

Yudhishthira asks how a king can keep his kingdom and royal line prosperous, and how he should choose servants, since a king who keeps company with wicked men loses his loyal servants. Bhishma answers that no king can rule alone and that he needs wise, honest and well-born ministers and officers. He adds that accounts and treasuries must be honestly supervised, justice fairly administered, and the subjects won over by kindness.

Bhishma tells an old tale heard at the hermitage of Rama, son of Jamadagni. A sage in a forest is served by its beasts, and a devoted dog stays by him, but a leopard threatens the dog. The sage transforms the dog into a leopard to save it, and then, when a tiger comes, into a tiger, so that the beasts of the forest leave it alone.

The transformed dog, now a tiger, is threatened by an elephant and then a lion, and the sage changes it into each in turn. It is changed into a Sarabha to meet a fierce beast, and then grows ungrateful, planning to kill the sage. The sage reproves it, reminds it of its origin as a dog, and turns it back into a dog.

The dog, returned to its own form, is driven out of the hermitage. Bhishma draws the lesson for kings: examine servants carefully for truth, purity, learning, conduct, birth and self-control before employing them, and do not keep men of low birth. He describes the qualities of a good minister, the virtues of a righteous king, and the value of a loyal army, and says a king who wins the loyalty of his men can conquer the earth.

Bhishma says that, taking the lesson of the dog story, a king should give each servant the office he is fit for and never raise a man above his station. He advises choosing honest, learned and well-born ministers, keeping the treasury and granaries in trustworthy hands, and caring for kinsmen and the city. He closes by asking Yudhishthira what further he would like to hear.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to restate the duties of kingship in a form that is easy to remember. Bhishma answers at length that protecting all creatures is the highest duty, and that a king should be like a peacock, varying his conduct to suit each purpose and keeping counsel secret. He should watch for danger, collect taxes gently as a bee gathers honey, appoint honest officers, avoid waste and greed, and act with intelligence and patience, so as to protect his people and earn the rewards of virtue.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain Chastisement itself: its nature, form, origin and the power that keeps it watchful, since so much seems to depend on it. Bhishma says Chastisement is the principle by which righteousness is upheld and is also called Vyavahara, a term that Manu first declared. He describes its fearsome form and many names, and explains that legal procedure rests on Vedic and royal authority. He ends by saying that no one, not even a mother, father, brother, wife or priest, is exempt from the justice of a king who rules by duty.

Bhishma tells how King Mandhatri visits the penitent king Vasuhoma and asks where Chastisement came from. Vasuhoma explains that Chastisement vanished during Brahman's sacrifice, causing disorder, until Vishnu created it anew and it was entrusted to the gods, sages and finally to Manu and his sons. Chastisement must be used with discrimination, and Bhishma says whoever heeds this teaching will gain the fulfilment of his wishes.

Yudhishthira asks how Virtue, Wealth and Pleasure relate, and what their roots and fruits are. Bhishma says Wealth rests on Virtue, Pleasure is the fruit of Wealth, and all three aim at liberation, with the flaws of greed for reward and hoarding to be purged. He then tells how King Angaristha asks the sage Kamandaka how a king can undo sins committed through lust or ignorance, and Kamandaka prescribes Vedic study, respect for Brahmanas, banishing wicked men and seeking the company of the good.

Yudhishthira asks how virtuous behaviour is acquired. Bhishma recounts how Duryodhana, grieved at Yudhishthira's splendour at Indraprastha, asked his father Dhritarashtra the same question, and Dhritarashtra answered that good conduct wins the earth. He then tells the tale of Prahlada, who lost his sovereignty to Indra when a Brahmana disciple drew away his conduct and with it righteousness, truth, good deeds, might and prosperity. Dhritarashtra concludes that abstaining from injury, compassion and charity build good conduct, and that wicked men who prosper do not keep their fortune long.

Yudhishthira asks what Hope is and where it comes from, lamenting that Duryodhana's obstinacy destroyed the hope he had cherished of peace. Bhishma introduces the discourse between Sumitra and Rishabha and tells how King Sumitra of the Haihayas chases a wounded deer far through forests and across rivers without giving up.

King Sumitra, worn out by the hunt, arrives at a hermitage, where the ascetics honour him and ask why he has come. He tells them he is of the Haihaya race, has lost his deer, and is left disappointed in his hope. He then asks which is vaster, hope or the firmament, and says he wishes to hear the answer only if it is proper for the sages to give it.

The sage Rishabha, asked by Sumitra, recalls meeting the emaciated sage Tanu near the hermitage of Nara and Narayana. There King Viradyumna came searching for his lost son Bhuridyumna and asked Tanu what is greater than hope. Tanu explains that Bhuridyumna had insulted a holy sage by refusing him a golden jar and vegetable bark, leaving the sage disappointed, and the sages gather around the king to ask what brought him there.

King Viradyumna asks Tanu what is exceedingly hard to obtain, and Tanu says that hope is the most slender thing of all. He lists the hopes that are slenderer still, such as hope placed in a giver who never gives, or in a father who longs to see his lost son again. The king is moved, Tanu produces the lost prince and reveals himself as the god of righteousness, and Sumitra then casts off his own hope. Bhishma urges Yudhishthira to be calm and collected like Himavat.

Yudhishthira says he is never satiated with Bhishma's teaching on morality. Bhishma tells of the sage Gotama, who spent sixty thousand years in austerity on the Paripatra hills and was visited by Yama, the regent of the dead. Gotama asks how one can clear the debt owed to one's parents and win pure regions of bliss, and Yama answers that devotion to truth, purity, penance and reverence for one's parents, together with generous horse-sacrifices, win many regions.

Yudhishthira asks what a weak king should do when he is surrounded by enemies and treacherous ministers, with an empty treasury and no army, and whether he should seek wealth by evil means or give up his life. Bhishma says the question is subtle and that a king in extreme distress may take wealth from anyone except ascetics and Brahmanas, since treasury, army and people depend on one another. He insists that the treasury should be filled by righteous means where possible, and warns that filling it by oppression leads to ruin.

Yudhishthira asks what a weak, besieged king should do when his land is lost, his treasury is empty and his councils have leaked. Bhishma advises peace with an honest invader, and giving up land or even the capital to a treacherous one to save his life. If peace fails, the king should fight bravely, because a warrior who dies in battle goes to heaven.

Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana can make a living when proper rule has collapsed, robbers control the means of life, and he cannot abandon his family. Bhishma says he should live by his learning, and that in hard times a king may take wealth from the wicked and give it to the good. Even then the king must not oppress priests or Brahmanas, and he should not believe slander.

Bhishma explains that a king must keep his treasury full, drawing on his own realm and his enemies' lands by a middle course. He argues that a weak king with an empty purse loses respect and power, so he must not bend before enemies. On robbers, he advises bringing them under control rather than destroying them outright, since those who exterminate them live in fear.

Bhishma says a Kshatriya's clear duties are religious merit and wealth, and that endless debate about the unseen future should not stop him from them. He argues that power is the foundation of righteousness and that the powerful can do much that the weak cannot. He then lists the penances by which a man who has fallen into sin can cleanse himself and win back respect.

Bhishma tells the story of Kayavya, a robber of mixed birth who was devout, protected Brahmanas and ascetics, and cared for his blind parents. When thousands of robbers choose him as their leader, he sets rules: spare women, children, ascetics and Brahmanas, and plunder only where it is due. Bhishma says that robbers who keep these rules win a good afterlife, and that hearing the tale brings safety from fear.

Bhishma quotes verses attributed to Brahman on how a king should fill his treasury. The wealth of sacrificers and of the gods must not be taken, but wealth of those who neglect sacrifice may be taken for the army and for worship, and the king should pass it on to good people rather than hoard it. He ends by comparing moral questions to dust that grows finer the more it is ground.

Bhishma tells a fable of three Sakula fish in a lake that fishermen are draining. One fish sees the danger and leaves early, another escapes by biting the string when caught, and the slow one is caught and dies. Bhishma's lesson is that foresight and quick thinking bring success, procrastination brings ruin, and well-timed action gets the best results.

Yudhishthira asks how a weak king surrounded by many foes should choose friends and enemies, and when to make war or peace. Bhishma answers with the fable of a mouse and a cat caught in the same hunter's net, in which the mouse makes a timely alliance with the cat, frees him, and then refuses his later offer of friendship. The moral is that alliances rest on self-interest, so a ruler should seem trusting while staying wary, and should act at the right time.

Yudhishthira asks how a king can rule if he trusts no one, and Bhishma answers with the tale of the bird Pujani and King Brahmadatta. After the prince kills her chick, Pujani blinds him in revenge, and the two then argue over whether an injury can ever be forgiven. Brahmadatta appeals to Time and to reconciliation, while Pujani holds that enmity between injurer and injured never truly ends, so she leaves; the tale closes with advice that a king should protect his subjects and never provoke a stronger foe.

Yudhishthira asks how a king should act when righteousness and people have declined and robbers plague the land. Bhishma tells how Satrunjaya, king of the Sauviras, asked the sage Bharadwaja how to gain, grow, guard and use wealth. Bharadwaja replies that a ruler must rely on firm punishment, cut the roots of his foes, and mix sternness, mildness and deceit as the moment requires, and the king prospers by following this advice.

Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana and a king should live when righteousness has collapsed and famine and robbery have overrun the land. Bhishma tells of the sage Viswamitra, who in a twelve-year drought steals a dog's haunch from a Chandala's hut to stay alive. The Chandala argues at length that the meat is unclean and the theft sinful, but Viswamitra answers with hunger, precedent and the claim that saving life comes first, then eats the meat after offering it to the gods. The story teaches that a wise man may act against normal rules to survive great distress, and can later regain his merit.

Yudhishthira is appalled that Bhishma's teaching seems to excuse cruelty and to make robbers respectable, and asks whether any kingly rule may never be broken. Bhishma replies that duty must come from wisdom gathered from many sources rather than a one-sided reading of scripture, and that a king must be severe when the occasion demands and mild otherwise. He closes by saying that Brahmanas must always be honoured, since they can bring either great blessing or great harm.

Yudhishthira asks what merit comes from protecting a suppliant, and Bhishma says it is great, citing King Sivi and a pigeon that fed a foe who sought refuge with its own flesh. He then tells the story as Rama, son of Bhrigu, told it to King Muchukunda. A cruel fowler who lives by killing birds is caught in a storm and sets out to find shelter for the night beneath a great tree.

A pigeon lives with his family in a tree, and when his wife does not return on the stormy night he laments her absence. He praises the faithful wife as a man's true home, companion and support, and says a man without one should go to the forest.

The she-pigeon, already caught in the fowler's cage, hears her husband's grief and urges him to welcome the fowler as a guest. She argues that refusing a suppliant is as sinful as killing a Brahmana or a cow, and tells him to take other wives if she dies.

The pigeon welcomes the fowler and gives him warmth, but when the hungry fowler asks for food he has none. Bound by his duty to a guest, he throws himself into a fire he has lit so that he may be offered as food, and the fowler is overcome with grief.
Moved by the pigeon's death, the fowler blames himself and vows to give up his cruel trade for a life of strict penance. He throws away his weapons and cages and frees the captive she-pigeon.

The she-pigeon mourns her husband and says life means nothing without him, then throws herself into the fire. She sees her husband in heaven on a celestial car, and the two ascend together as a reward for their merit.

Seeing the pigeon couple in heaven, the fowler resolves to win the same reward through austerity. He gives up food and deliberately runs into a forest fire, and is taken up to heaven for it. Bhishma ends by praising the protection of suppliants as a high merit and saying that hearing this tale cleanses sin.

Yudhishthira asks how a person who sins through ignorance can be cleansed. Bhishma tells how King Janamejaya, son of Parikshit, killed a Brahmana, was abandoned by his priests and subjects, and wandered in penance. The sage Indrota, son of Sunaka, harshly rebukes the king when he comes to him for help.

Janamejaya, tormented by remorse, begs the sage Saunaka for instruction and protection. Saunaka answers that folly is no cause for anger, but insists that the king repent, drop his pride, and honour Brahmanas, even if others mock him for it. The king swears never again to harm a Brahmana in thought, word or deed.

Saunaka tells the repentant king that a wise ruler must combine sternness with compassion, and recommends penance, gifts, sacred bathing places and graded remedies for each repeated sin. He cites the gods' question to Vrihaspati about how a righteous person cleanses sin, and Vrihaspati's answer that righteous acts done with understanding wash sin away. The sage then assists Janamejaya in the horse-sacrifice, and the purified king returns to his kingdom in splendour.

Yudhishthira asks whether anyone has ever been restored to life after death. Bhishma tells how a Brahmana's only son dies, and how his kin at the cremation ground are argued back and forth between a vulture, who says the dead cannot return, and a jackal, who keeps them hoping. When the sun sets and the kin plead for help, Sankara appears and restores the child to life for a hundred years, showing that prayer and grace can overturn what seems final.

Yudhishthira asks how a weak man who has foolishly provoked a powerful enemy should act when that enemy comes to destroy him. Bhishma introduces the story of the Salmali tree, a great tree on the Himalaya that shelters elephants, birds and travellers. The sage Narada praises it and asks whether the wind god Pavana is its friend, since its branches are never broken by storms.

The sage Narada tells the Salmali tree that the wind must protect it through some special friendship, since no other tree or mountain stands against the wind. The tree boasts that it is stronger than the wind and has defeated him before. Narada rebukes this arrogance and says he will report it to the wind-god.

Narada reports the tree's insults to the wind-god, who comes to the Salmali in anger and threatens to show his power. The tree laughs at the threat and says that true strength lies in wisdom, so the wind promises a test the next day. Seeing that it is weaker, the tree decides to rely on its intelligence and resolves to protect itself from the wind's attack.

The Salmali cuts off its own branches, leaving itself bare, and waits for the wind. The wind arrives, delighted to find the tree stripped, and says that the tree's own counsel has put it under his power. Ashamed and remorseful, the Salmali repents, and Bhishma concludes that a weak man should not provoke a powerful one and that the wise defeat the strong gradually, as the Pandava Arjuna defeated Duryodhana's army.

Yudhishthira asks what is the source and foundation of sin. Bhishma replies that covetousness is the root of sin, giving rise to anger, lust, pride, deceit and countless other vices, and that it can never be satisfied. He then describes the good people who are free of covetousness, fearless, content and devoted to the good of all, and says they should be honoured and learned from.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain ignorance in detail. Bhishma says ignorance leads to sin, infamy and hell, and that attachment, hatred, vanity and many other faults are all called ignorance. He treats ignorance and covetousness as two sides of the same fault that grow and fade together, and says that kings such as Janaka gained heaven by restraining covetousness.

Yudhishthira asks which duties bring the highest merit. Bhishma answers that self-restraint is the highest duty, made up of forgiveness, patience, truthfulness, mildness, liberality and compassion, and leads the restrained person to freedom and the highest state. He admits one drawback, that others may think a self-restrained man weak, but says its merits far outweigh this. Yudhishthira, delighted, asks him to go on.

Bhishma teaches that penance is the root of all achievement, from the creation of the world and the Vedas to the status of the gods. He says that many kinds of wrongdoing can be cleansed by penance, and that abstaining from food is the highest form of it.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain truth, its signs, how it is gained and what it brings. Bhishma calls truth the eternal duty and the foundation of all righteousness, and sets out its thirteen forms, such as impartiality, self-control and forgiveness. He ends by saying that truth outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices when the two were weighed against each other.

Yudhishthira asks about the origins of wrath, lust, envy, pride, malice and related vices. Bhishma calls these thirteen fierce foes that attack the heedless, and traces each to its source and cure, such as wrath springing from covetousness and dying away through forgiveness. He says tranquillity can subdue them all, and notes that Yudhishthira has already conquered them through respect for his elders.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe malevolent people, whom he says he has not known well. Bhishma portrays them as boastful, deceitful, covetous and quick to slander, who eat greedily alone and regret their gifts. He contrasts them with the generous man who first gives to Brahmanas and then shares with kin, and advises that the malevolent be avoided.

Bhishma sets rules for giving to Brahmanas: the learned and impoverished should be supported, the king may take wealth from those who refuse to fund sacrifices, and a hungry Brahmana may take a single meal in an emergency. He then lists the acts that make a Brahmana fallen and the expiation prescribed for each, from drinking liquor and killing a Brahmana to lesser faults, and says the gravest sins can be cleansed only by death. The chapter ends with a heading for the next section.

Nakula asks Bhishma whether the bow or the sword is the foremost weapon, and who first made the sword. Bhishma recounts the creation of the world, the rise of the Danavas, and how Rudra, born from a sacrificial fire, slew them with the sword called Asi, which was then handed down through a line of kings to the Pandavas. He ranks the sword highest among weapons and says the bow was first made by Prithu.

After Bhishma falls silent, Yudhishthira asks his brothers and Vidura which of Virtue, Wealth and Desire is greatest and which the mind should serve. Vidura ranks Virtue highest, Wealth middling and Desire lowest, while Arjuna argues that Wealth is needed for the other two, the twins argue that Virtue and Wealth should be pursued in order, and Bhima argues that Desire is the foremost. Yudhishthira judges their arguments mistaken and concludes that liberation is the highest good, since all acts follow the will of the Ordainer.

Yudhishthira asks what kinds of men make worthy friends, and Bhishma lists the men to avoid, such as the covetous, the cruel and the deceitful, and the men to befriend, such as the well-born, the grateful and the steady. Yudhishthira asks who the ungrateful injurers of friends are, and Bhishma begins a tale. It concerns a poor Brahmana named Gautama who, having taken up with a village of robbers and learned to kill cranes, is visited by an old friend who begs him to return to his proper duties.

Gautama leaves the robbers' village for the sea, is separated from a merchant caravan when an elephant attacks it, and wanders into a beautiful forest. He rests beneath a great banyan tree, where the crane prince Rajadharman, son of Kasyapa, arrives at evening. Gautama, hungry, first eyes the crane as prey, but the crane greets him warmly as a guest.

Rajadharman hosts Gautama with food, flowers and a soft bed, and reveals that he is a son of Kasyapa. Learning that Gautama is poor and seeks wealth at sea, the crane promises to help, citing four ways of gaining wealth. He sends Gautama to his friend, the Rakshasa king Virupaksha, who he says will give him wealth.

Virupaksha questions Gautama about his birth and practices, and Gautama gives only his name and race, adding that he lives among hunters with a Sudra widow as his wife. Out of loyalty to his friend the crane, the king honours Gautama at a great feast for a thousand Brahmanas and sends him away with gold. Gautama, laden with the gold, returns to the banyan, where the crane welcomes him, and he plots to kill the crane for its flesh.

Gautama kills his sleeping crane host, roasts its flesh and flees with the gold. When the Rakshasa king Virupaksha finds that his friend has not returned, he sends his son, who finds the mutilated body and captures Gautama. The Rakshasas refuse to eat such an ungrateful man, since ingratitude, unlike other sins, has no expiation.

Virupaksha has the crane burned on a pyre, and the goddess Surabhi's milk revives him. Indra explains that the crane was cursed for missing the Grandsire's assembly, and at the crane's plea Indra restores Gautama to life too, though Gautama is cursed to sink into hell for his ingratitude. Bhishma concludes that ingratitude is shameful and that friends should always be honoured.

Yudhishthira asks how a person should set aside grief after losing wealth or a loved one, and Bhishma says that reflection can dissolve sorrow. He tells how a Brahmana consoled King Senajit, who was mourning his dead son, by reminding him that all must pass away and that grief is folly. The rest of the teaching continues in the next scene.

Yudhishthira asks what good thing one should seek while time carries life away. Bhishma tells of a learned Brahmana's son, Medhavin, who asks his father how to act when death is always near. The father gives the usual stages of life, but the son warns that death and decay surround every creature, and urges pursuit of truth and renunciation over ritual.

Yudhishthira asks whence happiness and misery come to rich and poor who follow different practices. Bhishma gives verses sung by a Brahmana, miserable with a bad wife and hunger, who says that happiness and sorrow come from destiny and that poverty freed from desire brings true ease, while the wealthy grow anxious and proud. Bhishma concludes that renunciation is the highest good, as he heard from a Brahmana at Hastinapur.

Yudhishthira asks what a man who craves wealth and cannot find it should do to be happy. Bhishma says the happy man is even-minded toward joy and sorrow, honour and insult, speaks truth, and seeks no worldly gain. He tells the story of Manki, whose two new bulls are carried off by a camel, and who concludes that destiny rules wealth and that desire is the real enemy. Manki then renounces his desire and attains a state of immortal peace.

Bhishma cites King Janaka, who says he owns nothing even if his kingdom burns, and the sage Vodhya, who names six teachers of tranquillity. Vodhya's teachers are the courtesan Pingala, an osprey, a snake, the bee, a shaft-maker and a maiden with an anklet. Each one shows that hope agitates the heart and that living free of hope, possessions and strife brings peace.

Yudhishthira asks how a person can live free of grief and reach a good end. Bhishma tells how King Prahlada questions a serene wandering Brahmana, who lives by the Ajagara vow, taking whatever food and rest come to him without desire or grief. The sage explains that all creatures are subject to death and change, so one should accept what comes, and Bhishma concludes that such a man passes his days in great delight.

Yudhishthira asks whether kinsmen, action, wealth or wisdom should be a person's refuge, and Bhishma says wisdom is the highest refuge. He tells how Indra, disguised as a jackal, speaks to the despairing Brahmana Kasyapa, who has been knocked down by a careless Vaisya and wants to end his life. Indra persuades him that a human birth and a Brahmana's status are precious, and that his pride in argument had caused his fall, and Kasyapa worships Indra and goes home.

Yudhishthira asks whether gifts, sacrifices, penances and service to teachers bring wisdom and happiness. Bhishma answers that a mind swayed by desire and anger runs toward sin, and that deeds bear their fruit in later lives, following a person as his shadow does. Charity and faith bring prosperity and unbelief brings suffering, but a penitent person can cleanse the past through penance and knowledge.

Yudhishthira asks who created the universe, what creatures are, and where the dead go.
