Bhishma passes on the teaching that the sage Bhrigu gave to Bharadwaja: a primeval being called Manasa creates the elements, a lotus, and Brahman, and the universe is his body. Bhrigu then describes the boundless sky and its layers of water and fire, and explains that the earth is the lotus whose centre is Mount Sumeru.

Bharadwaja asks how the creator, dwelling in Meru, made the diverse objects of the world. Bhrigu says the creator first made water, which sustains life, and that earth and mountains are solidified water. He then tells how seers who fasted for a thousand years heard a celestial voice describe the sequence: space, then water, then wind from water's pressure, then fire from friction, and finally earth from solidified fire.

Bharadwaja asks why only the five primal elements are called creatures. Bhrigu answers that they are called great because they pervade all things, and that all bodies and senses are built from them. Bharadwaja objects that trees show none of the signs of the elements, but Bhrigu argues that trees feel, see, smell and taste, and so have life, and he then describes how the elements and their properties appear in living bodies.

Bharadwaja asks how bodily heat dwells in the body and how wind moves it. Bhrigu explains that heat lies in the head and works with the breaths to drive life, the senses, excretion, digestion and bodily movement. He adds that yogins who hold the soul within the brain can reach Brahma through the main channel of the body.

Bharadwaja objects to the account: if life were only wind or inner heat, it would merge back into outer air or fire at death, and nothing would remain of the person once the elements separate. He asks what knows, hears or speaks after such a separation, doubts that a gift of a cow helps the dead, and concludes that everything arises from seeds and perishes at death.

Bhrigu says the living creature is not destroyed with the body but passes into another form, as fire vanishes into space when its fuel is consumed. Bharadwaja objects that the analogy fails, and asks who feels pain, hears or sees once the body is only a union of the elements. Bhrigu replies that an inner Soul witnesses the senses, migrates from body to body, and survives the body's dissolution.

Bhrigu describes creation: Brahman first made the Prajapatis, then Truth, Duty, Penance and the Vedas, and then all beings, including the four classes, each assigned a colour. Bharadwaja objects that all men share the same passions and bodily functions, so colour cannot separate them into classes. Bhrigu replies that all men were once Brahmanas and that conduct made some Kshatriyas, Vaisyas or Sudras, while those who fell from knowledge became Pisachas, Rakshasas and other beings.

Bharadwaja asks by what acts one becomes a Brahmana, a Kshatriya, a Vaisya or a Sudra. Bhrigu describes the Brahmana by his purifying rites, Vedic study, daily duties, hospitality and truthfulness, the Kshatriya as a warrior who studies and gives gifts, the Vaisya as a cattle-keeper or farmer, and the Sudra as one unclean in conduct who ignores the Vedas. He ends by urging mastery over greed and anger, and renunciation of the self, as the path to Brahma.

Bhrigu teaches that truth is Brahma and the root of penance and creation, that untruth leads to darkness, and that happiness is the aim of all action. Bharadwaja doubts that happiness is the highest aim, since Brahma and Shiva, who conquered desire, do not seek it. Bhrigu replies that those ruled by anger and greed suffer disease, death and loss, while heaven knows no hunger, thirst or sin, so happiness is the highest goal.

Bharadwaja asks what gifts, righteousness, conduct, penance, Vedic study and fire offerings bring. Bhrigu says offerings burn sin, study brings peace, gifts bring pleasure, and gifts to the good follow the giver after death. He then describes the stages of life set down by Brahman: the student under a teacher, the householder who supports the others and enjoys family, wealth and pleasure, and the forest dweller, each with its own duties.

Bhrigu describes the austere life of forest hermits, who sleep on bare ground, live on roots and leaves, and endure heat and cold through penance. He then describes wandering renouncers who give up home, possessions and family and do no harm to any creature. Bharadwaja asks about the region beyond the known world, and Bhrigu describes a righteous northern land across the Himalaya, contrasting it with this world as the field where good and evil deeds bear fruit.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the rules of proper conduct. Bhishma lists daily habits and courtesies that mark a good person: where and when to relieve oneself, washing and worship, eating manners, honouring Brahmanas and elders, and never hiding a sin from good men. He ends by saying that righteousness is the source of lasting happiness after death.

Yudhishthira asks what the Adhyatma teaching is and how the universe is created and dissolved. Bhishma explains that the five great elements, the mind, the understanding and the soul make up a person, and that the three qualities of goodness, passion and darkness shape the understanding. He describes the soul as a silent witness, distinct from the understanding although they are found together, and he ends by recommending detachment and self-knowledge as the way to freedom.

Bhishma now describes four kinds of yoga meditation, which great sages practised to reach liberation. The yogin must withdraw his senses into the mind, sit still in a quiet place, and steady a mind that keeps wandering. Patience and repeated effort are needed, and the result is a happiness that cannot be won by action or fate alone, leading to Nirvana.

Yudhishthira asks what fruit silent reciters of the sacred mantras receive, and which path, Sankhya, yoga or work, they belong to. Bhishma answers with an old story of Yama, Time and a Brahmana, and explains that silent recitation fits both the Sankhya and yoga paths. He then describes how a reciter who takes up renunciation withdraws from worldly concerns, meditates on Brahma, and at last reaches the pure, immortal Soul.

Yudhishthira asks whether reciters have any end beyond the high one already named. Bhishma lists the kinds of recitation that lead to hell, such as doing it with pride, for desire, or without faith, and says even a half-finished discipline leads there. When Yudhishthira asks why reciters who reached Brahma are still reborn, Bhishma blames their lack of true knowledge.

Yudhishthira asks what kind of hell a reciter may be sent to. Bhishma says that even the heavenly regions of the gods count as hell when set against the supreme region of the Soul. That region is free from change, pain, time and the three qualities, and a reciter who unites with his Soul goes there.

Bhishma tells the story of the Brahmana, a reciter of the Gayatri, who is offered heaven by Dharma but refuses to leave his body. Time, Death and Yama come to take him, and king Ikshvaku arrives and asks for the fruit of his recitations. The Brahmana gives it away, the two argue over duty and truth, and Dharma and Heaven declare that both men have earned equal merit.

The king offers to share the Brahmana's reward and his own merit, and two strangers, Virupa and Vikrita, then arrive disputing a debt over a cow gift. After the king, who feels bound by both kingly and Brahmanical duty, accepts the Brahmana's gift, Virupa reveals that he and Vikrita are Desire and Wrath, sent to test them. Bhishma then explains where reciters go, and the Brahmana and king are absorbed into Brahma with the gods' approval.

Yudhishthira asks about the fruits of yoga and knowledge, and how the creature-soul can be known. Bhishma tells how the sage Vrihaspati asked his teacher Manu about the cause of the universe, the fruits of sacrifice and knowledge, and the path of the departing soul. Manu teaches that acts driven by desire lead to hell, that liberation comes by freeing oneself from acts, and that the supreme being is beyond the senses and beyond sex or form.

Manu teaches that all things return through the elements to space and that the Self, which is the true cause, is beyond the senses and their objects. He explains that knowledge sits in the body like a lamp that lights the senses, and that the Soul is never born or destroyed. Passing from body to body, the Soul carries the results of its acts with it.

Manu explains that the Soul is a silent witness that cannot be grasped by any single sense and is known only through scripture and wisdom. He gives images to show how something real can be unseen, such as the far side of the Himalayas, the moon at its dark phase, and Rahu passing over the sun or moon. He ends by saying the Soul keeps the fruits of its acts even after it leaves the body.

Manu compares sleep and death to a dream, in which the body lies still while the inner spirit goes on, and says the Soul can be seen only when the senses are calm, like a reflection in still water. Ignorance, delusion and desire cloud this view, so the senses must be restrained. Knowledge removes sin, and the Soul is freed when it is withdrawn in turn into mind, understanding and the Supreme.

Manu advises that sorrow should not be brooded over, since brooding makes it grow, and that mental sorrow should be met with wisdom while physical pain is treated with medicine. He explains that the mind must be quieted, the senses shut and the understanding drawn inward, so that the seeker can reach Brahma, which lies beyond all qualities and words. Creatures are born again according to righteousness or sin, and only freedom from attachment leads to Knowledge.

Manu explains that the soul lodges in many kinds of bodies according to its past acts, and that knowledge, desire, resolve and action form a chain. Breaking this chain through knowledge leads to Brahma, which is beyond all qualities and cannot be reached by study or effort. He identifies Vishnu, who is beyond Time, as the Supreme Brahma, and says renunciation and self-restraint lead to liberation.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe Vishnu, called Narayana, Govinda and Kesava. Bhishma tells how the Supreme Being created the elements, Consciousness and the lotus-born Brahman, slew the demon Madhu, and then brought forth the sages, the gods, the four orders of men and the lords of the regions. He ends by stating that Narada and others proclaim Krishna as the Supreme God, beyond any ordinary man.

Yudhishthira asks who the first Prajapatis were and which great Rishis dwell in each direction. Bhishma names the seven sons of the self-born Brahman, the later Prajapatis, and the gods such as the Adityas, Aswins, Vasus and Maruts, along with their social standing. He then places the great Rishis in the four quarters and says that reciting their names cleanses a person of sin.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma why Krishna took the form of an animal. Bhishma recounts a visit to Markandeya's hermitage where the sage Kasyapa told how the Danavas oppressed the gods and the earth. Brahman promises that Vishnu will take the form of a boar to destroy them, and when the boar fights the demons and roars, the universe trembles, until the gods are told that the sound comes from Krishna, the Supreme God.

Yudhishthira asks for the yoga that leads to emancipation, and Bhishma tells of a disciple who asks his preceptor about the origin of himself and his teacher and why beings with the same material cause have different ends. The preceptor identifies Vasudeva as the Supreme cause, traces creation and the revival of lost knowledge, and describes primordial matter with its modifications. He concludes that the Soul is the true doer, that it can be seen only through yoga, and that it passes from body to body according to its acts.

Bhishma explains that living beings come from the unmanifest and that the Soul is eternal and untouched by the qualities that bind it. He compares the universe to a wheel driven by passion, with the Soul as its unmoved witness. He concludes that true knowledge burns the seeds of rebirth, and that this resolves the disciple's doubt.

Bhishma says that the wise prefer abstention from acts, avoid impure acts, and recognise that the body is made of the elements and must be fed only as medicine. He describes how the qualities of goodness, passion and darkness produce different states of mind. Yudhishthira asks which faults should be abandoned, and Bhishma answers that goodness, the means of liberation, must cut away passion and darkness.

Bhishma traces how passion and darkness lead to delusion, wrath, desire and pride, and how these bring acts, bonds, birth and sorrow. He describes the womb and presents women, desire and children as part of the bondage that the wise should avoid. He concludes that the senses are formed by past acts, and that freedom comes when knowledge weakens the senses and thirst is ended.

Bhishma explains that the regenerate, especially those learned in the Vedas, are the best of men, and that Brahmacharya, a discipline of restraint, is the highest means to Brahma. He sets out the rules a practitioner should follow, such as avoiding women and performing expiations after desire arises, and describes how desire draws the vital fluid through the body's ducts. He concludes that one who acts only to sustain the body and balances the three qualities escapes rebirth.

Bhishma urges seekers to see the sorrows of the world, to avoid attachment and pride, and to practise truth, non-injury and forgiveness. He advises restraint of speech, thought and body, a simple life of alms, and the gradual control of the understanding, mind and senses. He ends by saying that ignorance is dispelled and that the seeker reaches Brahma, which is eternal and deathless.

Bhishma tells the yogin to give up sleep and dreams, which arise from passion, darkness and fatigue. He explains that the mind keeps working while the senses rest, and that dreams draw on impressions from past lives. In deep sleep the mind rests in the Soul, and crossing darkness reveals the Supreme Brahma, which is reached by withdrawing the senses and mind.

Bhishma says no one can know Brahma without understanding the body, the Soul, dreams and sleep, and the two paths of activity and renunciation. He contrasts Prakriti and Purusha, illustrates the Soul's distinction from the qualities with the image of a turban, and urges yoga and detachment. He then describes the many ways people worship Brahma and ends by saying that the universe is woven by desire, and that knowledge of Prakriti and Purusha frees one from it.

Yudhishthira asks how King Janaka of Mithila reached emancipation after giving up worldly pleasures. Bhishma answers with the story of King Janadeva of Janaka's line, who is unsatisfied by his hundred teachers until the sage Panchasikha comes to teach him the Sankhya doctrine. Panchasikha argues that the Soul is separate from the body and survives death, and he refutes sceptics and others who deny this, and the king is filled with wonder.

King Janadeva asks Panchasikha again about existence and non-existence after death, and objects that if nothing survives death then knowledge, rites and action seem pointless. Panchasikha calms him by describing the body as a union of elements, senses and mind, and by urging renunciation of all things as the highest path. He uses images such as the silkworm, the lotus leaf and Janaka's burning city to show that the Soul is untouched by the body, and Janadeva finds peace.

Yudhishthira asks what brings happiness, what brings woe, and what frees a person from fear. Bhishma says self-restraint is the foundation of all rites, penances and truth, and that the self-restrained person sleeps and wakes happily, is fearless and reaps great results. He ends by urging Brahmanas to master lust and wrath and to live calmly, with their passions under control.

Yudhishthira asks whether twice-born men who eat the leftover meat and wine of sacrifices, hoping for children and heaven, act rightly. Bhishma says that eating forbidden food is a fall, though those who do it in ritual observance rise to heaven and fall again when their merit ends. He then says that fasting alone is not true penance, and that renouncing acts and humbling oneself before all creatures are the highest penance.

Yudhishthira asks whether man is truly the doer of his good and bad acts. Bhishma tells how Indra visits the wise Daitya Prahlada, now fallen and bound, and asks how he stays so calm. Prahlada answers that beings arise by their own nature rather than personal effort, that the Soul does not act, and that the wise are free from grief, and he names simplicity, self-control and service to elders as the path to wisdom.

Yudhishthira asks how a king who has lost his fortune can still live with dignity. Bhishma tells how Indra asks Brahma where the once generous Vali has gone, and Brahma says he has been reborn as an ass and must not be killed. Indra finds Vali living as an ass and mocks his fall, and Vali replies that he does not grieve over lost wealth.

Indra mocks Vali again, asking whether he grieves over his fall from power and the loss of his kinsmen. Vali replies that all bodies, fortunes and lives are transitory and governed by Time, and that no one is truly the doer of acts. He says that Indra himself is subject to Time and will one day pass away, and he urges Indra to be calm and avoid boasting.

Indra sees the goddess of prosperity, Sree, come out of Vali. She says she is leaving him because he has turned against truth, gifts and the Brahmanas and has begun to boast, and that no being can bear her forever. Indra is told to divide her into four parts, which are given to the earth, the waters, fire and the good among men. Vali then predicts a future battle, and Indra, bound by Brahma's command not to kill him, lets him go.

Indra visits the Asura Namuchi, who has lost his fortune and is bound, and asks whether he grieves. Namuchi replies that grief only wastes the body and pleases foes, and that no one can take another's sorrow. He says that all events are ordained by the one Ordainer and that the wise accept pleasure and pain with calm.

Yudhishthira asks what helps a man who has lost his friends, sons and kingdom. Bhishma says fortitude is the highest support in distress, and tells how Indra finds the defeated Vali calm in a cave and asks why he does not grieve. Vali replies that Time, not personal merit, governs rise and fall, that many kings before him have fallen, and that grief only weakens a person. Indra, restraining his anger, accepts that all things are subject to Time, promises that Vali's bonds will loosen as the world declines, and returns to heaven.

Yudhishthira asks for the signs that show a person is heading for greatness or for ruin. Bhishma tells how Narada and Indra, bathing and talking by the Ganga, see the goddess Sree descend to them, and she explains that she dwells with the valiant, the virtuous and the devoted, and that she left the Danavas when they turned to vice. She recalls their former virtues and then the decay that drove her away, such as disrespect for elders, neglect of rites and disorder in homes. Indra welcomes her, and the gods and the world are renewed with prosperity.

Yudhishthira asks how a person reaches Brahma, which lies beyond primordial nature. Bhishma tells how the sage Devala asks Jaigishavya why he is neither pleased by praise nor angered by blame, and what supports his wisdom. Jaigishavya describes the wise as even-minded, free from envy and recrimination, untroubled by past or future, and indifferent to gain and loss, and says that only such people reach Brahma.

Yudhishthira asks which man is dear to all and possesses every merit. Bhishma recites what Kesava once told Ugrasena when Ugrasena asked about the sage Narada's merits. Kesava lists Narada's learning, purity, humility, self-control, freedom from envy, anger and greed, and his even regard for all beings, and explains that for these reasons Narada is worshipped everywhere.

Yudhishthira asks for the origin and end of creatures, the divisions of time, and the lengths of the ages. Bhishma recounts how Vyasa taught his son Suka that before creation only Brahma exists, then measured time from winks of the eye up to a day and night of Brahman. He describes the four yugas, whose length and virtue decline from the Krita to the Kali, and says that a thousand such yugas make one day of Brahman, after which Brahman wakes to create again.

Vyasa describes how Brahma, waking at the dawn of his day, creates the universe through Avidya and Mind, producing Space, Wind, Light, Water and Earth, each carrying the qualities of the one before. The Creator enters the combined body to make all beings, and creation repeats with the same attributes each time. He then weighs the views that effort, fate, nature or their union cause effects, names penance as the highest good, and explains that the Vedas are the source of names, forms and actions. He ends by saying that Time creates and swallows all beings, and that he has explained creation, time, sacrifice, the Vedas and action.

Vyasa describes how the universe is withdrawn at the end of Brahman's day. Fire burns everything, and the elements dissolve one into the next, each losing its quality to the element that follows, until Mind, Time and energy are absorbed into the supreme Iswara. Creation and dissolution repeat through Brahman's days and nights, each lasting a thousand yugas.

Vyasa turns from creation to the duties of a Brahmana. He says that the Brahmana should study under a preceptor, pass through the modes of life with householder life as their root, and pay his three debts by having children, studying the Vedas and performing sacrifices. He stresses gifts to the deserving, and closes with a long list of kings and sages who won heaven by giving.

Vyasa urges the Brahmana to study the Vedas, live with faith, restraint and moderation, and do his duties without harming any creature. He describes life as a river of Time that carries all beings toward Yama, and says only the wise, who cross it on the raft of knowledge, are saved, while fools sink. He concludes that acting without clear vision keeps a person in the cycle of rebirth.

Vyasa says that knowledge is the raft that carries a person across the stream of Time and life, and that the wise can help the ignorant across. He lists the requirements of yoga, compares the body to a chariot whose parts are virtues and knowledge, and describes the stages of concentration in which the yogin gains power over the elements. He concludes that the Sankhya and yoga paths both lead to the same emancipation.

Vyasa tells Suka that the meditative person should cling to knowledge alone as the raft to emancipation. Suka asks what this knowledge is, whether it is learning, action or abstention from action. Vyasa replies that those who think all things come from nature alone gain no truth, that wisdom in applying means leads to success, and that Brahmanas who know the Vedas and the Soul are the highest of beings and are like gods.

Vyasa says that the duties of a Brahmana are obligatory when they lead to knowledge, and he reviews the rival views on what causes action, such as effort, necessity, nature and time. He notes that people of the Krita age devoted themselves to penance, that the duties of each order differ, and that the Vedas decline in later ages. He ends by saying that Time creates, sustains and destroys all creatures, and that they rest upon it.

Suka asks by what means a learned and wise man can attain Brahma, which lies beyond perception, inference and the Vedas, and whether penance, celibacy, renunciation, Sankhya or yoga is the way. Vyasa answers that only knowledge, penance, mastery of the senses and renunciation lead there. He describes the elements, senses, mind and knowledge that make up the body and the Soul, which is beyond body and nature, present in all beings, and is reached by the inner light, so that one who sees all beings in the Soul reaches Brahma.

Vyasa gives the yoga method for attaining knowledge. He says that the five impediments of desire, wrath, greed, fear and sleep must be overcome, that the senses and mind must be restrained and fixed on the Soul, and that after six months of steady practice Brahma appears like a smokeless flame. Supernatural powers must be disregarded, and the yogin must treat praise and blame, gain and loss, and even a clod of earth and a lump of gold alike. Such practice lets even a woman or a person of low birth reach the highest end.

Suka points out that the Vedas both command action and enjoin its renunciation, and asks where each path leads. Vyasa describes two paths: action, which brings rebirth, and knowledge, which leads to eternal Brahma beyond pairs of opposites. He says the person of knowledge remains subtly existent like the moon at the end of the dark fortnight, while the doer of acts is like the new moon, and that the soul stands above mind and knowledge.

Suka asks which course of righteousness good people should follow under the rule of Time, since the Vedas seem to command both action and its abstention. Vyasa says that the path of Brahmacharya, forest austerity and detachment, shown by the great Rishis, leads to Brahma. He then explains that the four stages of life form a ladder to Brahma, and that the Brahmacharin's duty to his preceptor and his study lead on to householder life.

Vyasa describes the duties of the householder, who keeps a household fire and stores grain in one of four ways, each with fewer duties and greater merit than the last. He says the householder should never cook only for himself or kill animals except in sacrifice, should honour guests, feed everyone including the undeserving, and avoid quarrels with his relatives. Such a householder raises his ancestors and descendants and earns heaven, but the forest life is higher still.

Bhishma introduces the forest stage of life, and Vyasa describes how a householder who sees wrinkles, white hair and grandchildren retires to the forest, tends his fires, eats once a day, and lives simply. He then describes the forest practices and the fourth stage of full renunciation, in which the old man gives up all ties, performs a final sacrifice of the self, eats very little, and walks through the world causing no harm.

Suka asks how a seeker of the highest knowledge should practise yoga in the final stage of life. Vyasa says that after purifying himself in the earlier stages, the renouncer should practise yoga alone, beg for food, speak little, and treat abstention from injury as the highest duty. He describes the true Brahmana as free of attachment and fear, honoured by the gods, and the one who sees the Soul within the body, and he ends by saying that the renouncer is free of fear and wanders in equanimity.

Vyasa explains the order of reality, running from the senses through the mind, understanding and Mahat to Prakriti and finally Brahma, which has nothing above it. He says the Yogin who draws the senses and mind into the inner Soul, and purifies his heart, reaches immortality, and that this teaching is the essence of the Vedas, to be given only to the worthy. He ends by inviting Suka to ask whatever else he doubts.

Suka asks Vyasa to explain Adhyatma again, what it is and where it comes from. Vyasa says that the five great elements make up all beings, distributed unequally, and that creation and destruction are their transformations. He then explains which element gives rise to each sense and quality, the roles of understanding, mind and Soul, and the three qualities of goodness, passion and darkness.

Vyasa explains that the understanding, when it forms ideas, becomes the mind, and that its modifications are the senses. The three qualities bind it, while the Soul, above it, stays a witness that the qualities cannot grasp. The Soul becomes visible only when the darkness of passion is removed, and the Soul and understanding are different yet always united, like a fish and the water it lives in. He concludes that a person who acts without attachment is not soiled.

Vyasa says that the understanding creates the objects of the world, while the Soul presides over them and stays apart from them. Some hold that the qualities persist after knowledge while others hold they are destroyed, and Vyasa advises one to act without anger, joy or envy and to cut the knot of the heart through knowledge. The wise who know the Soul are free from distress and reach liberation, and acts done without desire for fruit leave no bondage.

Suka asks his father Vyasa for the highest of all duties. Vyasa says it is restraining the senses, turning the mind inward, and knowing the Supreme Soul within, and he compares worldly life to a dangerous river that must be crossed with understanding. He adds that the Soul is free of sex, pleasure and pain, and that whoever knows it is not reborn. The teaching is to be passed on by a teacher to a worthy and self-restrained disciple.

Vyasa lists the conduct of a true Brahmana: no craving for scents, tastes, honour or fame, and no harm to any creature. Freedom from desire is the only real bondage to escape, and the man who is free of it is said to reach Brahma. The chapter ends with a yogin who transcends Prakriti and so avoids returning to the world.

Vyasa says a teacher should first recount the earlier teaching on the inner Soul to a disciple who seeks liberation. He then links the five elements and time to the living body, and assigns each sense to an element. The mind, understanding and Soul are counted as the ninth, tenth and eleventh, and a person who sees all beings as unstained is free from errors of action.

Vyasa describes the subtle Soul that outlasts the gross body and can be seen only by yogins who have controlled their senses. He says that people ruled by rajas and tamas cannot see the Jiva within their bodies, even though it is a part of the Supreme. He then names the yoga duties taught by Sandilya, and ends by saying that one who understands the seven subtle entities and the Supreme cause can behold high Brahma.

Vyasa uses the image of a tree of desire that grows in the heart, from the seed of error, and says that yoga can uproot it. He then compares the body to a city ruled by understanding, with the mind as its minister and the senses as its citizens. Rajas and tamas corrupt the understanding, and the mind joins with rajas and seizes the Soul and hands it over to them.

Bhishma repeats the teaching that Vyasa gave his son on the entities, listing the properties of the five elements, the mind and the understanding. Yudhishthira asks how the understanding can have five properties, and Bhishma explains that it has sixty properties in all, counting the elements. He says these entities are created and not eternal like the Soul, and that the Brahma knowledge should be sought for peace of heart.

Yudhishthira looks at the fallen kings on the battlefield and asks what it is that dies, and why death takes living beings. Bhishma tells of King Anukampaka, whose son was killed, and of the sage Narada, who starts a story to console him. Narada begins by describing how the Grandsire's creatures multiplied until the worlds were overcrowded, and how the Grandsire's wrath set off a destroying fire.

Shiva pleads with the Grandsire to stop the fire that is burning all creatures. The Grandsire explains that he had wanted to lighten the burden on the earth, and that his wrath had risen when he could find no other way. Shiva asks him to spare the world and to let creatures be reborn again and again. The Grandsire calms his fire and brings forth a female figure, Death, whom he orders to slay all creatures.

Death refuses to kill creatures who have done her no harm and asks to be excused, but the Grandsire insists that she must carry out his order. She performs many long austerities at sacred places, and she keeps asking to be excused, while the Grandsire repeats his command. In the end he gives her Desire and Wrath as her agents and says that the tears she shed will become diseases, and that wind is the life of all beings. The chapter closes by telling the king not to grieve for his son, who has gone to heaven.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what righteousness is, where it comes from, and whether it serves this world, the next, or both. Bhishma says the sources of righteousness are the practice of the good, the Smritis, and the Vedas, with the purpose of an act as a fourth. He then gives examples of right conduct, such as truth, honesty, charity, and not doing to others what one would not want done to oneself. He ends by urging Yudhishthira never to set his mind on wrongdoing.

Yudhishthira says that duty cannot be learned from the scriptures alone, because it depends on circumstances, on the age, and on what good people actually do. He points out that the Vedas and Smritis may disagree and that the rule that the good define righteousness goes in a circle. He concludes that righteousness is only what the learned of old declared it to be.

Bhishma tells the story of the forest ascetic Jajali, who stood motionless for a long time while birds nested and reared their young in his matted hair. When the birds left, Jajali grew proud and claimed great merit, and a voice in the sky told him that the merchant Tuladhara of Varanasi was far more righteous. Jajali travels to Varanasi to meet him, and Tuladhara greets him and says that Jajali's pride came from his own mistaken view of his acts.

Jajali asks Tuladhara, a merchant who sells scents and herbs, how he gained such steady understanding. Tuladhara says true morality is universal friendliness and harmlessness, and describes how he trades honestly and treats all creatures with equal mind. He argues that harmlessness is the highest duty and gift, criticizes cruelty to animals and the sale of living creatures, and retells how the Rishis took on the sin of King Nahusha. He ends by saying he treats those who praise him and those who injure him alike.

Jajali objects that Tuladhara's doctrine of harmlessness would end farming, food, and sacrifice, and so end the world. Tuladhara replies that he does not reject sacrifice, only the greedy and violent kinds, and that offerings made with faith and without desire of fruit lead to Brahma. He says harmless offerings of plants, herbs and clarified butter are proper, and that the Soul is itself a sacred place. Bhishma says the wise applauded these duties.

Tuladhara asks Jajali to call back the birds that once nested on his head, to see who truly follows the duty of harmlessness. The birds answer that acts done without harm bring good results, while acts that injure others destroy faith. Bhishma says Tuladhara and Jajali both went on to heaven, and that Jajali became calm after hearing these teachings.

Bhishma tells of King Vichakhy, who pitied the animals at a cow-slaughter sacrifice and blessed the kine. Vichakhy condemns animal slaughter in sacrifice, saying harmlessness is the highest duty and that only the greedy or foolish praise it. Yudhishthira asks how a man who avoids all harm can keep his body alive, and Bhishma says one should acquire merit so the body does not suffer and death does not come early.

Yudhishthira asks whether a hard duty should be judged quickly or after delay. Bhishma tells of Chirakarin, son of Gautama, who was ordered in anger to kill his mother and who took a long time to decide, weighing the duty to his father against the duty to his mother. When Gautama returned and repented, he learned that Indra had tempted the wife, so she was innocent, and he praised his son for his delay. The chapter closes with the lesson that one should reflect long before acting, especially when violence is at stake.

Yudhishthira asks how a king can protect his subjects without harming anyone. Bhishma tells of the debate between King Dyumatsena and his son Satyavat, where Satyavat says killing can never be righteous and Dyumatsena argues that unpunished crime would destroy all distinctions. Satyavat proposes that Brahmanas guide the other orders, that offenders be punished gently, and that killing be avoided. Dyumatsena answers that punishment has grown harsher as righteousness has declined through the ages, and the chapter ends with Satyavat's advice on the ages and the role of Manu.

Yudhishthira asks which is better, the duties of the householder or the duties of yoga, since both lead to the same end. Bhishma tells the story of the sage Kapila, who protests when King Nahusha is about to kill a cow for a guest. A sage named Syumarasmi, speaking through the cow, argues that the Vedas authorise sacrifice with animals and that sacrifice upholds the world. The passage ends with the claim that those who do not sacrifice have neither this world nor the next.

Kapila argues that ascetics who renounce action reach Brahma and so have no need of household life. Syumarasmi answers that the householder supports every other stage of life, and that Vedic rites are needed for the dead and for sacrifice. Kapila then describes the self-control of the four doors of the body, and Syumarasmi asks how the Vedas can both urge and forbid acts. Syumarasmi finally asks to be taught about Emancipation, and Kapila says that knowledge of the one Soul is the way across the river of life.

Kapila says the Vedas are authoritative, and that rites purify the body so a twice-born man can receive knowledge of Brahma. He recalls men of old, such as King Janaka and the Brahmana Yajnavalkya, who lived by duty, were free from expiation, and attained Brahma. Syumarasmi asks who reaches the highest place in heaven, and Kapila replies that householders are blessed but cannot enjoy the joy of renunciation. Kapila ends by saying that acts only cleanse the body, while knowledge is the highest end.

Yudhishthira asks which of religion, profit and pleasure is the highest, and Bhishma tells of a poor Brahmana who prayed to the cloud Kundadhara for wealth. Kundadhara asks the gods to make the Brahmana virtuous instead, and they grant it. The Brahmana goes to the forest, gains spiritual power, and boasts that his word can bestow kingdoms, so Kundadhara shows him kings suffering in hell. Kundadhara rebukes his greed, the Brahmana repents and is forgiven, and the story teaches that virtue brings more lasting happiness than wealth.

Yudhishthira asks which sacrifice is performed for virtue alone, not for heaven or wealth. Bhishma passes on Narada's story of Satya, a Brahmana who lived on gleanings and worshipped Vishnu, and of his wife Pushkaradharini, who disapproved of his cruel rites. When a deer asks to be sacrificed, Satya is tempted to slay it, but Dharma, who had taken the form of a deer, stops him, saying that killing is no part of sacrifice. Narada concludes that abstaining from injury brings the fullest reward.

Yudhishthira asks how a man becomes sinful or virtuous, and how he reaches renunciation and liberation. Bhishma explains that desire follows the senses, that attachment and greed then lead to hypocrisy and sin, and that the righteous man, guided by the wise, turns to virtue and knowledge. Such a man eventually gives up even the rewards of virtue and reaches liberation.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for the means by which liberation is won. Bhishma says there is only one path to liberation, and lists the remedies that go with it: forgiveness against anger, patience against lust, study against error, and contentment against greed. He says the soul must finally be controlled by the soul, and that giving up desire in speech, body and mind is the path of liberation.

Narada asks the sage Asita-Devala how the universe was created and how it is destroyed. Asita names five primal essences, water, space, earth, wind and heat, with Time as the sixth, and says that these together with ignorance and past acts cause creation and destruction. He describes the senses, the mind and understanding, sleep and dreams, and the Jiva that passes from body to body until knowledge frees it to reach Brahma.

Yudhishthira laments that he and his people have killed kin and friends in pursuit of wealth, and asks how to end this thirst. Bhishma tells of the king of Videha, who has nothing yet is happy because he does not cling to possessions, and who advises that desire grows like a cow's horns and that giving it up brings the highest happiness. The sage Mandavya is pleased with this teaching and turns to the path of liberation.

Yudhishthira asks what good a man should seek while time runs swiftly. Bhishma tells of a learned son, Medhavin, who asks his Vedic father what to do, and the father advises study, household life, sacrifice, and then forest life. The son answers that Death and old age are always near, so one should practise truth, give up desire, and seek inner knowledge rather than offspring or ritual killing. The father follows the son's advice, and Bhishma urges Yudhishthira to do the same.

Yudhishthira asks what conduct, knowledge and practice lead to Brahma. Bhishma describes the renouncer who is frugal, calm, and free from attachment, who does no harm, who does not speak ill of others, and who begs only what he needs. He lives alone in quiet places, takes praise and blame alike, and wanders without a home. Bhishma says the sage Harita taught this path, which leads to bright and lasting regions.

Yudhishthira laments that even kings born of the gods suffer, and asks when he can renounce. Bhishma replies that nothing lasts, that rebirth has an end, and that the soul is darkened by ignorance until knowledge removes it. He then tells how the Daitya Vritra, deprived of his kingdom, showed no grief and spoke of the cycle of rebirth, and asked the preceptor Usanas how to reach high Brahma. The chapter ends by pointing to Usanas's answer, which Bhishma is about to recount.

The sage Sanatkumara comes to Usanas and Vritra and teaches them the greatness of Vishnu, saying that the universe rests in him and that he is reached by restraint of the senses and purification of the heart. He describes the cycles of creation, the colours of beings that follow from the three qualities, and the stages by which a soul moves through rebirths until it attains Brahma. Vritra is comforted and gives up his life-breath in yoga, and Yudhishthira then asks whether Krishna is that same Lord, which Bhishma affirms and ends by reassuring the Pandavas.

Yudhishthira asks how Vritra, a devoted and learned Asura, could be defeated by Indra. Bhishma describes the great battle, in which the huge Vritra overwhelms Indra with rocks and illusions, and Indra is stupefied until the sage Vasishtha revives him. Mahadeva sends a fever into Vritra, Vishnu enters Indra's thunderbolt, and Indra vows to slay the Asura. The Asuras lose their memory and their illusions vanish, and Indra's appearance is so awe-inspiring that no one can look at it.

Bhishma describes Vritra's fever and death at Indra's thunderbolt, and the sin of Brahmanicide, a fierce woman, which comes out of Vritra and seizes Indra. Brahma divides that sin among Agni, the trees and herbs, the Apsaras and the Waters, each with a condition on how it may pass to men. Indra is cleansed by a horse sacrifice, and Bhishma says the cocks born of Vritra's blood are unclean food for the twice-born, and that reciting this tale on Parva days removes sin.

Yudhishthira asks how the fever arose before Vritra was slain. Bhishma tells how Mahadeva sat on Mount Meru with a great court, and how the god Daksha held a horse sacrifice without giving Mahadeva a share. Uma is grieved, and Mahadeva sends his followers to wreck the sacrifice, and a fierce being born from his sweat burns it. Brahma makes peace, Mahadeva accepts a share, and Fever is spread among many creatures. Bhishma adds that Vritra was first struck by Fever, and that reading this tale brings freedom from disease.

Janamejaya asks how Daksha's horse sacrifice was destroyed and how its divided parts were made whole again. Vaisampayana tells how Daksha held the sacrifice on Himavat without inviting Shiva, how the sage Dadhichi warned that it would be ruined, and how Uma asked Shiva to win a share. Shiva creates the fierce Virabhadra, who with Mahakali and a host of spirits wrecks the sacrifice, and Daksha, who is then humbled, asks Shiva to make the wrecked offerings useful to him. Shiva agrees, and Daksha praises him with his thousand and eight names.

Yudhishthira asks for the names by which Daksha praised the great god. Bhishma gives Daksha's long hymn, which lists Shiva's many names and forms, ends by asking forgiveness for leaving him out of the sacrifice, and is answered with Shiva's grace and a share of the sacrificial fruit. Shiva then teaches Daksha the Pasupata religion, which is open to all, and disappears with Uma and his followers. Bhishma says that anyone who hears or recites the hymn is freed from fear, disease and sin, and gains success.

Yudhishthira asks what Adhyatma is and where it comes from. Bhishma explains that the five great essences, earth, wind, space, water and light, form all bodies, and that the understanding creates the senses and the three qualities, while the Soul is only a witness. He says the understanding and the Soul are joined eternally, and that knowledge carries one across the river of delusion.

Yudhishthira asks how sorrow and death can be kept away from living creatures. Bhishma tells of the sage Samanga, whom Narada finds always cheerful and free of anxiety. Samanga explains that he knows past, present and future, that all creatures live by the fruits of past acts, and that the wise are those whose senses are free of error. He has conquered desire through penance, so grief cannot trouble him.

Yudhishthira asks what is beneficial for a man who doubts the scriptures and lacks self-restraint. Bhishma recommends honouring teachers and hearing the scriptures, and tells how Galava asks Narada which course is beneficial when the scriptures disagree. Narada says the four stages of life each have their proper duties, that true excellence lies in friendship, truth, mildness, contentment and study, and that boasting and idleness should be avoided. He also advises where to live and under which kings, and says that the highest good is hard to describe.

Yudhishthira asks how a king should behave and what makes a man free of attachment. Bhishma recounts how the sage Arishtanemi taught King Sagara that the true happiness is liberation, and that attachment to children, wealth and a wife is the trap. Arishtanemi says each creature lives and suffers by its own acts, and lists the marks of a freed man, including contentment, equal regard for all, and awareness of death and disease. Sagara follows this teaching and rules his subjects well.

Yudhishthira asks why the sage Usanas, called Kavi and Sukra, sided with the Asuras, and how he gained his name and why he cannot reach the middle of the sky. Bhishma explains that Usanas used yoga to enter the god Kubera and rob him of his wealth. When Kubera complained to Shiva, Shiva raised his lance, Usanas sat on its tip, and Shiva bent the lance into his bow Pinaka and swallowed him. Usanas wandered inside Shiva until Shiva told him to leave by the urethra, and Uma then saved him from Shiva's anger and made him her son.

Yudhishthira asks what good acts lead to benefit in this world and the next. Bhishma tells how King Janaka asked the sage Parasara what is beneficial for all creatures. Parasara says that righteousness through right action is the highest good, that the four classes each have their duties, and that acts and their fruits belong to each person, refuting the sceptic who denies this. He ends by saying that a man should not do what he would condemn in others.

Parasara continues his teaching to Janaka. He compares the body to a chariot that the mind must steer with the reins of knowledge, and he says that wrongs done knowingly bring sorrow while wrongs done in ignorance can be expiated. Acts done with judgment increase merit, and kings should protect their subjects, while devotees should later retire to the forest and treat all creatures as their own selves.

Parasara says that people mostly act for themselves, so gifts and debts matter greatly. He says that wealth must be earned by fair means and never at others' expense, and that a man owes debts to the Rishis, the gods, the Pitris, his fellow men, his servants and himself, each of which can be paid in a set way. He cites examples of sages who won success through devotion and says that parents, the sacred fire and the teacher must be honoured.

Parasara explains the duties of the four classes. The Sudra should serve the higher classes and keep company with good people, the Vaishya should farm and tend cattle, the Kshatriya should protect, and the Brahmana should study and enjoy. Each class that keeps to its own duty helps keep righteousness whole, and gifts made with respect bring the greatest merit.

Parasara says that wealth earned by each class's proper means is praised, and that a Brahmana may take up another class's work in need but must not fall to the lowest order's tasks. He traces how pride, wrath and desire, the Asuras, spread among men, and how Shiva destroyed the Asura chiefs with his arrow and lance. The seven Rishis then set up Indra and the kings, and some kings took to Asura ways, so Parasara urges avoiding harm and seeking knowledge of the Soul.

Parasara moves on to penance. He says that householders grow attached to wealth, kin and pleasure, and that despair, awakening, study and penance follow from this, so penance is open to all classes. He warns that penance done for reward brings misery, that the pleasures of the senses are short-lived, and that householders should enjoy wealth honestly while doing their duties. He ends by saying that the householder is the refuge of all other orders.

Janaka asks why men of different classes differ in colour when all are said to have sprung from Brahmanas. Parasara explains that the classes arose when penance declined, that the four classes came from the Lord's mouth, arms, thighs and feet, and that mixed castes arose from their intermixture. He adds that sages born of mixed wombs became Rishis through penance, and he sets out the special and common duties of the classes, with the rule that a man is stained more by his acts than by his birth.

Parasara speaks at length on devotion to elders, the rules of battle for Kshatriyas, and the course of death and rebirth. He says that the body dissolves into its elements, that the soul roves for a time before taking a new body, and that the righteous die well while ignorance is the chief foe. He urges the four stages of life, rates human birth as the best, and recommends sacred places, cremation rites, and the Vedas for those without stain. Bhishma says the sage taught all this to the king of Videha.

King Janaka asks the sage Parasara what is good, what the best path is, what cannot be destroyed, and where one need not return from. Parasara answers that detachment and knowledge are the highest good, that harmlessness is the greatest gift, and that sin clings only to the attached. He adds that family and wealth cannot help after death, and that each creature bears the fruit of its past acts. Janaka hears the teaching and is greatly pleased.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what he thinks of truth, self-restraint, forgiveness and wisdom. Bhishma tells of Brahma appearing as a golden swan before the Sadhyas, who ask the swan about the highest good. The swan teaches restraint of speech and wrath, forgiveness, truth and self-control, and says that truth is the only way to heaven. The Sadhyas then ask what covers the world and what makes a Brahmana divine, and the swan answers that ignorance and attachment cover the world and that study, vows, and wisdom mark the true Brahmana.

Yudhishthira asks how the Sankhya and Yoga systems differ. Bhishma says that each school praises itself and gives its reasons, but that both are approved and both require purity, compassion and vows, differing mainly in the scriptures they follow. He describes how the strong Yogin breaks the bonds of the world and gains great powers while the weak are lost, and sets out meditation, diet, the difficult path of Yoga, and its highest fruit of union with Brahma. The chapter closes the second part of the Shanti Parva.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to set out the Sankhya philosophy. Bhishma presents its view of the world, the elements and qualities that make up the body and cosmos, the faults of the body, and the path by which the wise rise through the qualities to liberation. Yudhishthira then asks whether a liberated person keeps consciousness, a question he says bears on which way of life is superior.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the difference between the Deteriorating and the Undeteriorating, and Bhishma answers with an old teaching of Vasishtha to king Karala of Janaka's race. Vasishtha describes the cycles of creation and destruction, the sequence of elements and senses that make up every embodied being, and a twenty-fifth principle that lies beyond them. He explains that union with Prakriti makes the Indestructible seem destructible, and that knowledge reveals its true nature.

Vasishtha continues by explaining how the soul, forgetting its true nature, falls under ignorance and is reborn again and again among gods, men and lower beings. He lists the many bodily ailments, ascetic practices, rites and worldly roles the soul takes on while it believes itself bound by them. He says Prakriti drives the cycle of birth, death and acts, and that the soul, though free of all attributes, imagines it has them.

Vasishtha closes the teaching by comparing the soul to the moon, which waxes and wanes while one of its sixteen portions stays constant. Under ignorance the soul is repeatedly reborn, and its pure nature becomes tied to the three qualities of Prakriti. Emancipation is described as release from that union.

King Janaka asks Vasishtha how Emancipation can exist if Purusha and Prakriti are always joined, as male and female are in creation, and he asks for direct evidence of it. Vasishtha answers that memorized texts without understanding are of no use. He explains that Sankhya and Yoga teach the same truth, that the Supreme Soul is beyond all attributes, and that unity marks the Indestructible while multiplicity marks the destructible.

Janaka says he is still confused about unity and multiplicity, and asks Vasishtha to explain again the knower, Jiva, knowledge, ignorance, and both the Sankhya and Yoga systems. Vasishtha describes the Yoga practice of contemplation, breath control and stillness, and the vision of the Supreme Soul it brings. He then sets out the Sankhya chain of principles, how they dissolve back in reverse order, and how the Soul is the true knower freed from returning to the world.

Vasishtha defines knowledge (Vidya) and ignorance (Avidya) in terms of the Sankhya principles, with Prakriti as ignorance and the Purusha beyond the twenty-four as knowledge. He explains why both Prakriti and the Jiva can be called indestructible or destructible. He then gives the Jiva's lament at being caught in Prakriti like a fish in a net, and its resolve to turn to the Supreme Soul, before noting that Sankhya and Yoga teach the same knowledge.

Vasishtha contrasts the Supreme Soul with the Jiva, which takes on the qualities of Prakriti through ignorance and is freed only by recognizing itself as distinct from her. He says the teaching must be given only to worthy and humble disciples, never to deceitful or unworthy ones. Bhishma closes the whole discourse by tracing its line of transmission from Hiranyagarbha through Vasishtha and Narada to himself, and by assuring the king that knowledge frees him from ignorance.

A king of Janaka's race, Vasuman, meets a Rishi of Bhrigu's line while hunting and asks what brings lasting benefit to a man whose body is unstable and whose desires are strong. The Rishi advises restraint, righteous conduct, generous gifts from honestly earned wealth, firmness, and the company of virtuous people. The king accepts the counsel and turns his mind to righteousness.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for teaching on what is free from duty, doubt, birth and death. Bhishma offers an old dialogue in which king Daivarati of Janaka's race questions the Rishi Yajnavalkya about the senses, Prakriti, Brahma and the limits of life. Yajnavalkya begins his answer with the list of principles and the stages of creation.

Yajnavalkya measures the length of Brahma's day and night and describes how Brahman, born from a golden egg, creates the earth and sky. He then traces the creation of the five elements, their qualities, and the senses. He ends by saying the mind rules the senses, so the senses act only through it.

Yajnavalkya explains how creation is dissolved at the end of Brahman's day. Maharudra, urged by the Unmanifest, burns all living things, and then fire, water, wind, space, mind, consciousness and Mahat are each absorbed in turn into Sambhu. He then announces that he will turn to the three frames of teaching, Adhyatma, Adhibhuta and Adhidaivata.

Yajnavalkya pairs each sense and faculty with three aspects: its inner organ (Adhyatma), its outer object (Adhibhuta), and its presiding deity (Adhidaivata). He then explains that Prakriti multiplies the three qualities into countless forms, and he lists the qualities that belong to Sattwa, Rajas and Tamas. The passage sets up the teaching on the qualities that follows.

Yajnavalkya explains that the three qualities are present in all things and that their mixtures decide a being's destiny, from the realms of the gods down to the lowest forms of life. He says Purusha stays unchanged, and that Prakriti, though inanimate, creates only when Purusha presides over her. Janaka then asks how one can be called inanimate while the other is intelligent, and asks for teachings on Emancipation, Sankhya, Yoga and the signs of death.

Yajnavalkya explains that Purusha seems to take on attributes as a clear crystal takes on the colour of a nearby flower, while in truth he is beyond them. Prakriti, unintelligent by nature, seems alive only through her union with Purusha. He argues that Purusha and Prakriti are distinct, using images such as the worm in the fig, the fish in water and the fire in a pot, and he then turns to the teaching of Yoga.

Yajnavalkya says Sankhya and Yoga aim at the same liberation and that people who see them as different lack understanding. He describes the Yoga practices of breath and sense control, the eight powers they bring, and the two kinds of practice, with and without attributes. He ends with the stillness of one who is absorbed in Samadhi and beholds the Supreme Soul.

Yajnavalkya explains that the exit point of the soul at death decides which heavenly region it reaches, with each part of the body linked to a particular deity or realm. He then lists the bodily and sensory signs that foretell death within a year, six months, a week or a single day. He advises the wise to unite with the Supreme Soul and live in abstinence, so as to overcome death.

Yajnavalkya recounts how the sun god Surya gave him the Yajush texts, how the goddess Saraswati entered him, and how he compiled the Satapatha Brahmana and taught it to his disciples. He then answers the Gandharva Viswavasu's long list of questions about the universe, Prakriti, Purusha, knowledge and ignorance, and the Supreme Soul. He ends by saying that liberation comes through knowledge that is open to every order of people, and Bhishma adds how king Daivarati gave up his kingdom to live as a renunciant.

Yudhishthira asks whether great power, wealth and long life can be kept safe from death and decay by penance, ritual, knowledge or medicine. Bhishma offers the old dialogue in which Janaka of the Videhas asks the sage Panchasikha the same question. Panchasikha answers that time carries every creature along without a raft, and that only the eternal path of renunciation leads beyond birth and death.

Yudhishthira asks whether liberation can be won while living a householder's life. Bhishma tells how the mendicant Sulabha, having heard that king Dharmadhyaja of Janaka's line was devoted to renunciation, enters his mind by Yoga power to test him. The king claims his freedom is compatible with ruling and rebukes her, and Sulabha answers at length, defending her conduct and arguing that souls cannot be mixed by contact. Janaka, hearing her reasoning, has no reply.

Yudhishthira asks how Suka, son of Vyasa, came to renounce the world. Vyasa, seeing his son living carelessly, gives him a long exhortation to master the senses, practise truth and righteousness, honour the wise and prepare for death, which takes each person alone with only his deeds. Moved by these words, Suka leaves home to seek a teacher of the path to liberation.

Yudhishthira asks whether gifts, sacrifices, penance and service to teachers really bring benefit. Bhishma answers that evil conduct brings poverty and fear, while faith, restraint and generosity bring joy and heaven. Every deed, good or bad, ripens at its proper time and follows the doer, even into the next life.

Yudhishthira asks how Suka, the son of Vyasa, was born and why his mind turned to the subtle Brahma so early. Bhishma says that merit rests on restraining the senses, and tells how Vyasa, after long penance on Mount Meru, won from Mahadeva the boon of a son of great purity.

Vyasa's desire for the apsara Ghritachi causes his seed to fall while he is kindling a fire, and Suka is born from the fire-sticks. The gods and celestial beings celebrate, Mahadeva invests the boy with the sacred thread, and Suka masters the Vedas under the teacher Vrihaspati. Even as a youth his mind is set on the path of liberation rather than household life.

Vyasa sends his son Suka to king Janaka of Mithila to learn the path to liberation, and tells him to travel on foot like ordinary people and to show humility. Suka makes his way across many lands and is kept waiting at the palace gate. He is then tested by a troupe of palace women, but remains unmoved and spends the night in Yoga.

King Janaka receives Suka with full honour and asks the purpose of his visit. Suka asks what a Brahmana's duties are and whether a man of purified understanding must still pass through the four stages of life. Janaka explains that right knowledge, guided by a teacher, is the boat that carries one across the world's ocean, and tells Suka that he already has that knowledge.

Satisfied, Suka leaves Mithila for the Himalayas, passing stories of Skanda's dart and Mahadeva's penance, and reaches his father Vyasa, who is teaching disciples there. His disciples then ask Vyasa for a boon that the Vedas be shared only among them, and Vyasa sets out rules on who may receive Vedic teaching and how it should be given.

Vyasa's disciples leave the mountain to teach and perform sacrifices among the people, and Vyasa is left alone with Suka, troubled by the silence of Vedic recitation. Narada points out that the Vedas are lost when they are not recited, and urges Vyasa to resume with his son. A violent wind interrupts their recitation, and Vyasa explains the winds and the two paths after death before going to bathe in the Ganges.

Narada visits Suka, who honours him and asks what will help him most. Narada passes on the teaching of Sanatkumara, that attachment brings sorrow and that desire and wrath destroy one's good. He describes the river of life that must be crossed by the boat of the body, and says that even the understanding must be cast off through knowledge of the Supreme Soul.

Narada counsels Suka that wisdom is the cure for sorrow, since grieving over what is past only doubles one's pain. He says that wealth, youth, life and union all end in loss, so one should cultivate contentment, guard the senses and find peace in the self. The man who turns his mind inward and needs nothing from outside reaches happiness.

Narada explains that fortune, misfortune, the results of childbirth and disease, and the soul's passage from one body to the next are all beyond human control, and that only the self can be protected. Suka reflects on this teaching and resolves to reach an eternal and fearless state through Yoga, even by entering the sun. He takes leave of his father, who asks him to stay, and departs for Kailasa.

Suka sits in Yoga on a mountain peak, sees his own soul, and rises through the sky, where heavenly beings and Apsaras marvel at him. He tells Narada that he has found the path to liberation, and asks the points of the compass, forests, seas, rivers and mountains to answer his father's calls once he has gone beyond reach. They agree to do so.

Suka sheds all the attributes and dwells in Brahma, and the heavens react with omens as he breaks through the twin peaks of Himavat and Meru. His father Vyasa follows and grieves, calling his name, until Suka answers only as an echo that still sounds in mountains. Mahadeva consoles Vyasa, telling him that his son has reached the highest end and that a shadow of him will remain at Vyasa's side.

Yudhishthira asks who is the highest deity and the highest Pitri, and how emancipation and lasting heaven can be reached. Bhishma relates how Narada visited Narayana, who had taken fourfold form as the sons of Dharma, and praised him as the source of all. Narayana replies that the inner soul, called Kshetrajna, is the highest object of worship, that unmanifest Prakriti is its companion, and that those who know him are merged into him.

After Narayana's teaching, Narada visits the White Island, whose strange inhabitants Yudhishthira asks about. Bhishma then tells how King Uparichara, a devotee of Narayana, was tied to the treatise of duties composed by the seven seers under Narayana's command. He explains that this treatise was to be passed down through Vrihaspati, and that it would be lost with the king's death.

At king Uparichara's great Horse-sacrifice, where no animals are slain and Vrihaspati presides, Hari takes his share unseen, and Vrihaspati is angry. The Sadasyas calm him, and the sons of Brahman describe their penance, their journey to the White Island and the voice that told them only the favour of its devout people brings the sight of Narayana. Vasu later falls through a Brahmana's curse and rises again through Narayana's grace.

Yudhishthira asks why king Vasu fell from heaven and was sunk into the earth despite his devotion to Narayana. Bhishma tells how the gods and Rishis argued over whether sacrifices should use animals or grain, and how Vasu, judging for the gods, was cursed to fall. The gods secured him provisions, and Narayana sent Garuda to lift him back to heaven.

Narada reaches the White Island, where the white people honour him, and he settles there in silent recitation and Yoga. He then praises Narayana in a long hymn that lists his many forms, as the soul beyond attributes, the source of the Vedas, sacrifices, deities and the cosmos. He closes by saying he is a devoted disciple who longs to see the god.

Narada's hymn brings Narayana before him in a wondrous universal form, and the god explains his nature as the Purusha beyond the attributes, his fourfold manifestation, and his successive descents into the world. Narada then goes to Vadari and later repeats the teaching in Brahman's abode. Bhishma explains how the narrative has been handed down and that hearing it with devotion brings the highest end, and the frame closes with the recitation at Naimisha.

Saunaka asks why Narayana, who ordains renunciation, also grants the deities shares in sacrifice. Sauti relays Vaisampayana's answer to king Janamejaya, recalling how Vyasa taught his disciples that creation flows from the Supreme Soul through Aniruddha and the eight Prakritis, and how the gods came to Brahman for their roles. Narayana then grants the gods their shares in sacrifice, foretells the decline of righteousness through the four ages, and charges Brahman with the work of creation.

King Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana to explain the meanings of the names by which Vyasa and his disciples praised Hari. Vaisampayana recalls how Arjuna once asked Krishna the same thing. Krishna explains that his names arise from his nature and deeds, including Narayana, Vasudeva, Vishnu, Damodara and Kesava, and that he and Rudra are one.

Arjuna asks how Agni and Soma came to share one nature, and Krishna answers with a long account of creation from the primal darkness, the honour owed to Brahmanas, and many stories of gods who were cursed or saved. These include Indra's sins, Viswarupa's death, Nahusha's fall, Soma's waning and the marks on the moon, and the origins of many of Krishna's own names. Arjuna then asks who won the battle between Rudra and Narayana, and Krishna explains that Brahma stopped it and the two made peace, each marking the other.

Saunaka praises Sauti's recitation and asks why Narada went back to Vadari after seeing Narayana on White Island. Sauti explains that Janamejaya put the question to Vyasa during the snake sacrifice, and Vaisampayana then tells how Narada travels to Vadari and finds Nara and Narayana doing penance. Narada reports what he saw and decides to stay with the two sages. The chapter sets up the sages' teaching and frames the Narayana-centred devotion that the rest of the section develops.

Nara and Narayana praise Narada for having seen Narayana and explain how the Supreme Soul is the source of the elements. They describe the path by which the liberated pass through successive forms into Vasudeva, and why they themselves took birth in Dharma's house. Narada becomes wholly devoted to Narayana and stays at Vadari for a thousand celestial years. The chapter gives the teaching that the rest of the section builds on.

Nara asks Narada what rites he performs for the Pitris and why. Narada explains that he worships Vishnu through rites to the deities and Pitris, and recounts the old exchange of knowledge between sons and sires. Nara and Narayana then tell how Vishnu, as a boar, raised the Earth and made three mud balls as offerings, which became the Pitris, and why they are called Pindas. The chapter gives the origin story behind the Pinda offering, grounding it in Vishnu's act.

Narada, after a thousand years with Nara and Narayana, returns to his own hermitage while the two sages stay on at Vadari. Vaisampayana then tells Janamejaya that hating Narayana brings ruin, that Vyasa is Narayana on earth, and urges him to carry on the horse sacrifice. Sauti reports that the king did so and ends with a long praise of Narayana as lord of the sages, refuge of the worlds, and slayer of demons. The chapter closes the Narada frame and returns the story to the sacrifice.

Janamejaya asks why Hari took the horse-headed form that Brahma saw in the northern ocean, and what Brahma did afterwards. Vaisampayana tells how the world dissolves, how Brahma arises from Aniruddha, and how two demons seize the Vedas, leaving Brahma in grief. Narayana then takes the horse-headed form, recovers the Vedas, and slays the demons Madhu and Kaitabha, earning the name Madhusudana. The story closes by presenting Narayana as the source and soul of every quality and the refuge of both religions.

Janamejaya asks who first taught the path of wholehearted devotion to Narayana, why it is said to surpass knowledge, and why most Brahmins follow other vows. Vaisampayana traces this teaching from Narayana through Brahma's many births and a long line of teachers, down to Narada, Vyasa, and Yudhishthira. He explains the three dispositions of Sattwa, Rajas, and Tamas, says that the Sattwa type is closest to liberation through Narayana's grace, and concludes that the path is hard to practise. The chapter gives the doctrinal basis of devotion for the rest of the section.

Janamejaya asks whether the Sankhya, Pancharatra, and Aranyaka systems teach the same duties. Vaisampayana first honours Vyasa and then recounts Vyasa's own birth as he told it to his disciples: Narayana made Brahma, appointed a sage to arrange the Vedas, and foretold his own rebirth as Vyasa. Vaisampayana then surveys the main schools, all of which he says centre on Narayana, and begins Janamejaya's question of whether there are many Purushas or only one. The chapter sets up the dialogue between Brahma and Mahadeva that follows.

Brahma tells Mahadeva what the one Purusha is like: eternal, beyond the reach of anyone without self-control, present in every body, and called Kshetrajna. Brahma explains that this Purusha is Narayana, the Supreme Soul, and that the universe and its many souls come from him in the fourfold form of Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Sankarshana, and Vasudeva. He adds that Brahma himself arose from this Purusha, and that the Sankhya and Yoga teachings agree with this account. The chapter states the chapter's central doctrine of a single, all-pervading Purusha.

Vaisampayana turns to a new topic: Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which duties are foremost for each stage of life. Bhishma replies that duties can all lead to heaven if performed faithfully. He then says he will repeat a story that Narada once told Indra, which sets up the teaching that follows. The chapter is a short introduction to a new frame story about how to choose one's duty.

Bhishma tells of a Brahmin householder in the city of Mahapadma who has many children and wealth, but is troubled about which of three kinds of duty to follow. When a learned guest visits, the host confesses that he wants to hand his household to his son and seek liberation, yet cannot give up his attachments. The guest admits he is equally confused and lists the many routes to heaven that people follow. The chapter sets the puzzle that the rest of the story will try to resolve.

The guest offers to guide the host, though he says the question is hard. He points him to a wise Naga named Padmanabha who lives in a city in the Naimisha forest on the Gomati, and he describes the Naga's many virtues. The host is directed toward a teacher he can trust. The chapter moves the search to a new teacher.

The host is deeply relieved by the guest's words and says he now knows what to do. The two spend the night in talk about renunciation, and the night passes quickly. In the morning the host honours the guest, takes leave of his family, and sets out for the Naga's dwelling.

The Brahmin reaches the Naga's house and announces himself as a guest. The Naga's devoted wife welcomes him and explains that her husband is away for a month, pulling the Sun's chariot, and will return in fifteen days. The Brahmin says he will wait on the bank of the Gomati and asks her to tell the Naga he has come.

The Naga's kinsmen are alarmed to see the Brahmin fasting by the Gomati, and they plead with him to eat, arguing that his fast shames their hospitality. The Brahmin says he will only break his fast after the Naga returns, and he asks them to go home. The chapter shows the guest's vow standing firm and the household's concern.

The Naga returns home after fifteen days, washes his feet, and asks his wife whether she kept up worship and hospitality in his absence. She explains the duties of each class and of the householder, then reports that a Brahmin has been waiting by the Gomati for many days. She urges her husband to go and grant the guest's request.

The Naga asks whether the Brahmin is a human or a god, since few humans would seek him out. His wife argues that the guest is sincere and that a man of standing must not turn away a needy visitor. The Naga admits he has been moved by her teaching, cites the ruin that wrath brought to Ravana and to Kartavirya's sons, and agrees to go and meet the Brahmin.

The Naga goes out to the waiting Brahmin, wondering what has brought him, and greets him with courtesy. The Brahmin gives his name as Dharmaranya and explains that he has come to see Padmanabha on business, reciting the Vedas and practising yoga while he waits. The Naga identifies himself and offers to help in any way, and the Brahmin says he will reveal his request after first asking a question. The chapter opens the direct meeting between the two.

The Brahmin asks the Naga, who pulls the Sun's chariot in turns, to describe any wonder he has seen on his journeys. The Naga praises the Sun as the source of creatures and of the rains, and the dwelling place of the Supreme Soul. He then describes a radiant being who approached the Sun at noon and merged into it, so that the Nagas could no longer tell the two apart.

Surya himself explains who the radiant being was: a Brahmin who reached heaven through the Unccha vow, living on fruit, roots, fallen leaves, water, or air, and devoted to Mahadeva. The Naga reports this explanation, adding that the Brahmin now travels round the Earth from within the Sun's disc. The chapter closes the Naga's story of the wonder and answers the Brahmin's question.

Dharmaranya leaves the Naga, having learned from him that the Unccha vow, living by gleaning, is the right path to take. He goes to the sage Chyavana to be formally initiated into it. Bhishma traces the teaching back through Janaka, Narada, Indra, and the Vasus, and says it answers Yudhishthira's question about the highest duty. The main text ends with the close of the Santi Parva, and the rest of the chapter is a long run of translator's footnotes that explain Sanskrit words, variant readings, and difficult passages.

This last section of the chapter has no narrative of its own in this file. It is a run of Ganguli's translator notes, numbered from 594 on, that explain Sanskrit words, variant readings, and the doctrine of Bhishma's teaching on the mind, the soul, yoga, the three qualities, and the illusion of the world. The notes also compare the teaching with Sankhya, Vedanta, Buddhist, and sceptical views of rebirth. They matter as the translator's guide to how the difficult closing doctrine should be read.

Yudhishthira, stricken by the war's dead and by Bhishma's wounded body, asks how he can find peace of mind. Bhishma answers with the tale of Gautami, whose son dies of a snakebite, and the fowler Arjunaka, who wants the serpent killed. Mrityu (Death), the serpent and Kala (Time) each deny being the true cause, and Kala concludes that every creature's own karma decides its fate. Bhishma applies the lesson to Yudhishthira's grief, and Yudhishthira is calmed and asks again.

Yudhishthira asks whether any householder has ever conquered Death through virtue, and Bhishma tells of Sudarsana, son of Agni, and his wife Oghavati. When Mrityu sends a Brahmana to test Sudarsana's vow of hospitality, Oghavati accepts the guest out of duty, and Sudarsana affirms that honoring a guest is his highest duty. Dharma appears to praise the couple as having conquered Death, and Bhishma concludes that a guest's blessing is worth more than a hundred sacrifices.

Yudhishthira asks how Viswamitra, born a Kshatriya, came to be a Brahmana when that status is so hard for the other classes to reach. He lists Viswamitra's feats, including destroying Vasishtha's hundred sons, founding the Kusika line, and rescuing Sunasepha. He contrasts this with Matanga, a Chandala who could not win Brahmanhood, and asks how the change could happen without a new body.

Bhishma explains how Viswamitra became a Brahmana, beginning with King Gadhi, whose daughter Satyavati is sought in marriage by the sage Richika.
