Gadhi asks for a dowry of a thousand horses, which Varuna supplies, and Richika then arranges sacred food for mother and daughter that is meant to decide the sons' castes. Satyavati's mother swaps the portions and trees, Satyavati pleads to keep her own son from being a Kshatriya, and Gadhi's wife bears Viswamitra, who though a Kshatriya by birth becomes a Brahmana and founds many Brahmana lines.

Yudhishthira asks about the merit of compassion and the marks of devout men. Bhishma answers with the tale of a parrot named Suka, whose tree is withered by a fowler's poisoned arrow, and who refuses to leave it even as he dies with it. Indra, disguised as a Brahmana, is moved by the bird's constancy, and grants a boon that revives the tree, after which the parrot joins Indra in heaven. The lesson is that companionship with the good brings people the ends they desire.

Yudhishthira asks whether Exertion or Destiny is the stronger force in shaping a life. Bhishma tells how Vasishtha put this question to Brahma, and Brahma answers with the image of seed and soil: past deeds (destiny) bear fruit only when joined to present effort. Brahma gives examples of kings and others who fell or rose through their own deeds, and concludes that destiny and exertion together are what work.

Yudhishthira asks what the fruits of good deeds are, and Bhishma explains that deeds bear fruit in later lives in a similar bodily state. He lists the rewards for hospitality, austerity, fasting and vows, and for honoring father, mother and teacher, and says past deeds follow a person as a calf finds its mother. Vaisampayana closes by reporting that the princes were delighted, and that falsehood in speech brings evil just as improper rites do.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma whom he honors, whom he likes, and what helps in this world and the next. Bhishma says he most values learned Brahmanas and those who feed them generously, and that he holds Brahmanas dearer than his own kin. He explains why Brahmanas must be served with respect, since their energy and penance can destroy those who anger them, and that Kshatriyas must protect them and the Vedas.

Yudhishthira asks what becomes of people who promise a gift to Brahmanas and then fail to give it. Bhishma says such a person's good deeds turn fruitless, and tells of a jackal and an ape, once friends, now reborn as animals, who explain the sins that led to their state. Bhishma concludes that promised gifts to Brahmanas must be kept, because Brahmanas carry a fire-like energy and gifts to them bring the highest heaven.

Yudhishthira asks whether teaching a low-born person is blameworthy. Bhishma tells of a Sudra who joins a Himalayan asylum, is taught the rites for the ancestors by a Rishi, and is later reborn as a king who makes that same Rishi his priest. The king keeps laughing at the priest because he remembers their past, and reveals that the priest's teaching cost him his penances. Bhishma concludes that Brahmanas should not instruct the low-born, and that teaching for pay pollutes the teacher.

Yudhishthira asks where the goddess of prosperity, Sree, always dwells. Bhishma recounts how Rukmini asked Sree this question in Krishna's presence, and Sree answered that she stays with the diligent, self-controlled, grateful and devout, and avoids the idle, dishonest, ungrateful and quarrelsome. She also describes the women and places she favors and shuns, and finally says she dwells in Narayana, whose presence makes a person grow in righteousness, fame and wealth.

Yudhishthira asks whether man or woman takes greater pleasure in union, and Bhishma answers with the tale of king Bhangaswana. After a sacrifice that Indra dislikes, Bhangaswana is turned into a woman by a magic lake, bears a hundred sons, and later sees them killed in a quarrel that Indra stirs up. When Indra offers her a boon, she chooses to remain a woman, saying women take greater pleasure in union, and Bhishma presents this as the answer to the question.

Yudhishthira asks how a person should conduct himself to pass well in this world and the next. Bhishma answers that one should avoid ten kinds of wrong action, three of the body, four of speech and three of the mind. He names each of them, and says that good and evil deeds bring their own certain results.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to recount the names and power of Mahadeva, and Bhishma defers to Vasudeva (Krishna), who alone can speak of him fully. Vasudeva tells how he went to Himavat to win a son for Jambavati and met the sage Upamanyu, whose own childhood longing for milk led him to austerities and a vision of Shiva, who tested him in Indra's form and then granted him boons. Vasudeva then recounts his own vision of Mahadeva with Uma and hymns him, and the chapter presents Shiva as the supreme cause of all gods, creatures and weapons, ending with Shiva offering Vasudeva eight boons.

Vasudeva tells how, after his vision of Mahadeva, he asked for boons such as firmness in virtue, victory in battle, fame, Yoga and many children. Mahadeva agreed, and Uma added further blessings, including a son named Samva and a household of sixteen thousand wives. Vasudeva reported all this to Upamanyu, who then declared that there is no deity like Sarva.

Upamanyu tells how the sage Tandi, after ten thousand years of devotion, saw Mahadeva and praised him in a long hymn that calls him the source, end and highest truth of all things. Mahadeva, pleased, grants Tandi indestructibility, knowledge and a son who will write Sutras, and Tandi later passes on a thousand names of Mahadeva, first recited by Brahma. Upamanyu now offers these names to Krishna as an aid to his spiritual progress.

Upamanyu recites the thousand-and-eight names of Mahadeva as an essence of Brahma's ten thousand names and of Tandi's hymn, which is said to cleanse all sin and lead to the highest end. He traces the transmission of this hymn from Brahma through Sakra, Mrityu, the Rudras, Tandi, Sukra, Gautama, Manu, Narayana, Yama, Nachiketa and Markandeya, and then gives it to Krishna. Krishna closes by saying that daily recitation for a year brings the fruit of a horse-sacrifice and protection from demons and snakes.

The Island-born Krishna urges Yudhishthira to recite the thousand-and-eight names of Mahadeva, and a line of sages then describe how Mahadeva rewarded their devotion with knowledge, forgiveness, weapons, sovereignty or the return of lost merit. Galava recounts how Mahadeva brought him safely home to his father, and Krishna repeats Upamanyu's teaching that devotion to Mahadeva frees even sinners. Krishna closes by saying that reciting the hymn for a month earns the merit of a horse-sacrifice and benefits every class.

Yudhishthira asks what the saying about performing all duties jointly in marriage means, since spouses die at different times and women are called false by the ordinances. Bhishma answers with the story of the sage Ashtavakra, who asks the sage Vadanya for his daughter Suprabha and is sent on a long northern journey first. On the way he passes through Kuvera's realm, spends a year of dance and music without noticing, and reaches a golden mansion, where an aged woman urges him to lie with her and he wonders whether she was made ugly by a curse.

The old woman tends to Ashtavakra's bath with soft hands, and when midnight comes she goes to his bed. Ashtavakra refuses, saying he will not lie with another man's wife, but she insists she is her own mistress, claims to have kept a vow of celibacy as a maiden, and asks him to marry her. Ashtavakra questions why any woman would be independent and resolves to keep his restraint, although he is drawn to her.

Yudhishthira asks why the lady feared no curse from Ashtavakra and how he returned safely. Bhishma reports that she was the embodiment of the northern quarter, who devised the trial at Vadanya's request, and who promised Ashtavakra a safe return, a chosen bride and a son. Ashtavakra reports his journey to Vadanya, who gives him his daughter Suprabha in marriage, and he settles at his hermitage free from mental fever.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which Brahmanas are proper recipients of gifts, and Bhishma answers that any Brahmana who keeps the duties of his order is worthy, with or without outward marks. Bhishma then recounts what Earth, Kasyapa, Agni and Markandeya say about which givers are purified and which Brahmanas fail, and holds that Truth outweighs a thousand horse-sacrifices. He also covers the Sraddha rites, the marks of Righteousness, the offences equal to Brahmanicide, and which Brahmanas are worth honouring, since one worthy Brahmana can rescue a whole family.

Bhishma gives Yudhishthira the rules for Sraddha offerings: the proper timing, the foods that become the portion of Rakshasas when impure or improperly given, and which Brahmanas may and may not be invited, with the ritual words to be spoken and the sin of falsehood. He then sets out the deeds that send people to hell, such as lying, adultery, robbery and eating without sharing, and the deeds that lead to heaven, such as feeding the needy, charity and honouring parents. The chapter closes his teaching on rites and gifts.

Yudhishthira asks what makes a person guilty of Brahmanicide without actually killing a Brahmana. Bhishma reports that he once put the question to Vyasa, who answered with a list of such acts. These include refusing alms to an invited Brahmana, ruining a learned Brahmana's livelihood, blocking thirsty cattle, disparaging the Srutis, and robbing or harming the helpless.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about the merit of visiting, bathing in and hearing about the sacred waters on earth. Bhishma recounts the teaching that Angiras gave to Gautama, a long catalogue of named tirthas with the rewards each brings, such as heaven, the merit of a horse-sacrifice, cleansing from sin including Brahmanicide and foeticide, beauty and power. Angiras closes by saying that this teaching, recited or heard, leads to a good birth and memory of past lives.

Vaisampayana describes the many great Rishis who visit Bhishma on his bed of arrows and then vanish, and Yudhishthira asks which countries, rivers and mountains are most sacred. Bhishma tells of a poor Brahmana who keeps the Sila vow and asks a visiting Rishi the same question, and the Rishi answers that the places along the Bhagirathi Ganga are holiest. The Rishi then praises the Ganga at great length, saying her waters cleanse sin, rescue ancestors and lead to heaven, and Bhishma urges Yudhishthira to honour her too.

Yudhishthira asks how a Kshatriya, Vaisya or Sudra can attain the status of a Brahmana. Bhishma tells of Matanga, who was raised with Brahmana rites but was born of a mixed union, and who learns from a talking she-ass that he is in fact a Chandala by birth. Matanga resolves to win Brahmanahood by severe penance, and Indra appears and warns him that a person of impure birth cannot reach that status.

Matanga persists with his penance, standing on one foot for a hundred years, and Indra returns to explain that a person must pass through many lower births before reaching Brahmanahood. Indra describes a long path through the Pukkasa, Sudra, Vaisya and Kshatriya orders and through the lower kinds of Brahmana, each lasting thousands of years. He ends by urging Matanga to ask for some other boon, since the status of Brahmana is beyond his reach.

Matanga, born to a Chandala mother, spends a thousand years in penance trying to become a Brahmana. Sakra (Indra) tells him that someone of his birth can never reach that status, and Matanga, grieving, pushes his austerities until he collapses. Sakra then grants him other boons, and Matanga dies. The chapter is used to show that Brahmana status is very high and cannot be won by penance alone.

Yudhishthira asks how the king Vitahavya became a Brahmana, since Viswamitra did as well. Bhishma tells how Vitahavya's hundred sons overran the kingdom of Kasi, and how Divodasa's son Pratarddana defeated them in battle. Vitahavya fled to the sage Bhrigu, who protected him and made him a Brahmana by his word alone. The chapter ends with the family line from Gritsamada down to Saunaka, which shows the Brahmana descent of this house.

Yudhishthira asks which men in the three worlds deserve reverent worship. Bhishma tells an old story in which Narada worships a large group of Brahmanas, and Krishna asks him whom he honours. Narada names the Brahmanas he reveres by their virtues and says those who keep such virtues escape every calamity. Bhishma closes by urging Yudhishthira to honour the gods, the ancestors, the Brahmanas and guests.

Yudhishthira asks what merit comes from protecting living beings who seek shelter. Bhishma answers with the story of a pigeon chased by a hawk, which takes refuge in the lap of king Vrishadarbha. The hawk demands the pigeon as its food, and the king ends up offering flesh cut from his own body, which the text presents as the highest act of protection. The story ends with the king's reward in heaven and the claim that hearing it cleanses sin.

Yudhishthira asks which act a king should put first to win happiness in this world and the next. Bhishma answers that honouring learned Brahmanas is the foremost duty of a king. He describes the many kinds of Brahmanas, their great power, and the ruin that comes to those who speak against them. He ends by saying that no one can truly defeat the Brahmanas.

Bhishma tells Yudhishthira that Brahmanas must be honoured because the kingdom's peace and the gods' favour depend on them. He lists the benefits of feeding and supporting them and the defeats of Kshatriyas who fought them. He then gives a dialogue in which the Earth tells Vasudeva (Krishna) that serving Brahmanas cleanses sin and that harming them leads to ruin. Bhishma closes by urging Yudhishthira to honour the superior Brahmanas.

Bhishma says Brahmanas are worthy of worship by birth, because they are the mouths of the gods and guides of all creatures. He quotes verses attributed to Brahma that set out the Brahmanas' duties and the rewards of study, sacrifice and self-restraint. He ends by describing their great power and urging the king to honour them with gifts and service. The section closes with a note that the parva continues in another volume.

Bhishma tells of Sakra (Indra), who visits the Asura Samvara in disguise and asks how he rose above his kin. Samvara credits his respect for Brahmanas and his willingness to learn from them, and he repeats what his father heard from Soma about the power of Brahmanas. Sakra then takes up the same devotion to Brahmanas and gains the chiefdom of the gods. The story is offered as an example of honouring Brahmanas.

Yudhishthira asks whether a stranger, a long-known companion, or a traveller from afar is the best recipient of a gift. Bhishma says all three can be worthy and lists the qualities that make a recipient deserving, such as learning, truthfulness and self-restraint. He condemns quarrelsome and vain Brahmanas and sets out the householder's duties to the gods, sages, ancestors, Brahmanas and guests. The chapter teaches that the worth of the person matters more than how well one knows them.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe the nature of women, whom he calls the root of evil. Bhishma tells of Narada questioning the Apsara Panchachuda, who at first refuses to speak ill of her own sex and then does so at Narada's urging. She lists the faults she ascribes to women, including restlessness, a readiness to break restraints, and an inability to be satisfied. The chapter presents these as a view attributed to Panchachuda, and it sets up the next chapter's question about men and women.

Yudhishthira presses Bhishma with doubts raised by the previous account: why men still attach themselves to women despite their faults, whether women can deceive and sway men, and whether anyone has ever restrained them. He asks Bhishma to explain how men can protect women and whether women can truly be kept within the bounds set by the scriptures.

Bhishma says women were created by Brahma after the gods feared that humans would become too righteous, and that they were given desire and anger. He then tells how the sage Devasarman, about to leave for a sacrifice, asks his disciple Vipula to guard his wife Ruchi from Indra. Devasarman describes Indra's endless disguises, and Vipula enters Ruchi's body by yoga power so that Indra cannot approach her. The chapter sets up the test of Vipula's devotion.

Indra comes to the hermitage in a beautiful form, intending to seduce Ruchi, but finds that Vipula has bound her body and speech from inside. Indra speaks to her, and she is forced to say words Vipula controls, while Vipula watches Indra's approach from within her. When Vipula reveals himself and rebukes Indra, mentioning Gautama's curse, Indra flees in shame. Devasarman rewards Vipula with a boon that he will never fall from righteousness.

Vipula, after his success, grows proud of his penance. When Devasarman's sister-in-law asks for celestial flowers, Vipula is sent to fetch some and finds them where Ruchi had dropped them. On the road he hears two couples swear oaths naming his fate in the next world, and he searches his conscience and recalls that he never told his teacher about entering Ruchi's body. He then brings the flowers and honours his teacher. The chapter shows that even a just act can leave a hidden fault.

Devasarman greets his returning disciple Vipula and explains that the two couples and the dice players were Day and Night and the six Seasons, who see every hidden deed. Vipula had not told his teacher the whole truth, but Devasarman judges that his protection of Ruchi was proper and sends him to heaven. Bhishma then recounts a lesson he had from the sage Markandeya: women must be guarded, virtuous women are blessed, and men should not become overly attached to them. Only Vipula is said to have protected women successfully.

Yudhishthira asks how a father should choose a husband for his daughter, and Bhishma answers at length on marriage. He names the several forms of marriage, separates the righteous forms from the unrighteous, and sets rules on how many wives each caste may take, on suitable ages and on whom a girl may not marry. Yudhishthira then asks whether a dowry alone makes a bride a wife, and Bhishma answers that only the rites of marriage do, recalling his own seizure of maidens for Vichitravirya. The chapter's main point is that the taking of the hand with proper rites creates the marriage.

Yudhishthira asks what should happen when a dowry-giver walks away from a marriage, and Bhishma answers with a set of rules on the girl's maintenance and on the rights of daughters and their sons. He cites the case of Savitri and an opinion of a king of Videha's line, and says a woman is never free. He then argues that a daughter sold for a price, or a dower taken for a daughter, is a sinful sale, and recites Yama's warning of punishment in hell for those who sell their children. The chapter treats marriage by sale as wrong.

Bhishma says a maiden for whom no dowry has been taken is not sold, and that a wife should be respected and kindly treated, since a family's prosperity depends on how its women are treated. He recalls Manu's instruction that men must protect and honour women, and he quotes a verse of a princess of Videha's house on a woman's duty to serve her husband and her lifelong need for protection. The chapter closes by saying that honouring women is honouring prosperity itself.

Yudhishthira asks how a Brahmana's sons from different wives should divide his property, since a Brahmana may take wives from all four classes. Bhishma sets out the shares: out of ten parts, the son of the Brahmana wife takes four, the Kshatriya wife's son three, the Vaisya wife's son two, and the Sudra wife's son one part only if his father gives it. Yudhishthira objects that all the sons are Brahmanas by birth, and Bhishma answers that the Brahmana wife ranks first and that Kshatriyas, who protect society, are rightly given a larger share than Vaisyas. Yudhishthira then asks about the rules for other classes, and Bhishma gives the Kshatriya and Vaisya rules and the law for the eldest son, which Kasyapa is said to have declared.

Yudhishthira asks what duties fall to people born of mixed unions between the four classes. Bhishma explains that the four classes were set up for sacrifice, and then lists the offspring of each mixed pairing, such as the Suta, Magadha, Chandala and Nishada, with the work each is assigned. He warns that such unions multiply lower castes and bring grief to the father. Yudhishthira then asks how a man of mixed birth can be recognised, and the chapter ends with the warning that men of wisdom should not become overly attached to women.

Bhishma says a person's birth shows in his conduct, since a son takes after his parents and cannot hide his origin for long. Yudhishthira asks for the kinds of sons recognised by law, and Bhishma lists the sons born of wives, of outsiders, and of mixed unions. A debate follows over whether the seed or the soil makes a son, and Bhishma rules that the soil-owner's son belongs to him, and that a found and raised child becomes the rearer's son. The chapter ends with the purification rites for such children.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about compassion, the bonds formed by living together, and the blessedness of cows. Bhishma begins a story about the sage Chyavana, who takes a vow to stand still in the water at the Ganga and Yamuna confluence for a long time. A group of fishermen nets him along with a heap of fish, and he refuses to be parted from the fish. The fishermen, terrified, report to king Nahusha. The chapter sets up the story's test of compassion and devotion.

King Nahusha comes to the river and offers Chyavana ever larger sums to free him: a thousand coins, a hundred thousand, a crore, and finally half his kingdom. Chyavana rejects each offer and tells Nahusha to consult the Brahmanas. A sage born of a cow proposes a cow as the price, since Brahmanas are beyond price, and Chyavana praises cows as the source of sacrifice, prosperity and heaven. The fishermen, moved by Chyavana, return the cow, and Chyavana sends them and the fish to heaven. Both sages grant Nahusha boons before he returns to his city.

Yudhishthira asks why Rama, the son of Jamadagni, a Brahmana by birth, took up Kshatriya ways, and how a Kshatriya son of Kusika became a Brahmana. Bhishma tells how Chyavana, foreseeing that his own race would be stained by Kshatriya practice through a Kusika descendant, decides to bring ruin on the Kusika line. He asks king Kusika to let him stay, and the king and queen serve him for twenty-one days without food. When the sage finally leaves unseen, the king is left in grief, searching for him.

After Chyavana vanishes, king Kusika and his queen keep serving him. He returns repeatedly, burns the food they prepare, and then makes the royal couple yoke themselves to a battle-car and drag him about, goading them until they bleed. Through all of it they show no anger, and Chyavana finally heals their wounds, gives away treasure, and sends them home young and beautiful again. The chapter shows the sage testing the king's patience, which the king passes.

Kusika goes back to the wood and sees a golden palace, celestial trees and musicians, which vanish when he tries to approach. He realises that Chyavana has shown him these marvels by his yoga power and that penance is superior even to sovereignty. Chyavana, satisfied that the king has come through the ordeal without sin, offers him a boon. Kusika's reply sets the stage for his questions to the sage.

Chyavana offers Kusika a boon and asks him to state his doubts. Kusika asks why the sage put him through his long trials, the feast he burned, the car, the gifts, and the vanishing palace. Chyavana explains that he came to destroy Kusika's race because the gods foretold a clash of Brahmana and Kshatriya energy in it, but he found the king blameless. He then tested the king to show the rewards of penance and promised that a descendant of Kusika would become a Brahmana. Kusika asks for the details of how this will happen.

Chyavana explains the wider pattern. The Kshatriyas and the Bhargavas will fall out, and the Kshatriyas will destroy the Bhrigu line until a sage named Urva rises with fury that he cools in the sea. Urva's line leads to Jamadagni, who marries Kusika's granddaughter, and their son Viswamitra is born a Kshatriya. Richika then gives a Brahmana son to Kusika's line in exchange, so the two lines are joined by marriage. Kusika accepts the promise, and Bhishma says the events of Rama and Viswamitra came about as Chyavana foretold.

Yudhishthira is overwhelmed by the deaths of many kings and kinsmen in the war and says he wants to undertake severe penance. Vaisampayana then introduces Bhishma's reply, in which Bhishma lists the rewards that different acts of penance, austerity, vows, and gifts bring in the next life. He especially praises gifts of cows, land, houses and other goods to Brahmanas. Yudhishthira, moved by the account, sets aside his disgust at the householder's life, and the brothers agree to follow the grandsire's words.

Yudhishthira asks what rewards come from planting trees and digging tanks. Bhishma says a tank brings a man honour in the three worlds and that water in a tank in each season counts as a particular sacrifice, with water given to kine and other creatures counting most. He says gifts of water are the highest of gifts and that planting trees brings fame, honour among the Pitris, and rescue for one's ancestors. The chapter urges making tanks, planting trees, sacrificing and speaking the truth.

Yudhishthira asks which gift is best among those not found in the Vedas, and which follows the giver after death. Bhishma says the best gifts are kindness, relief for the distressed, and gifts given without pride; gifts of gold, cows and land cleanse sin. He urges giving to worthy, learned Brahmanas, especially those who do not ask, and calls such giving a sacrifice. He ends by insisting that kings must honour Brahmanas, since kingly power yields to them, and he says he loves them above all.

Yudhishthira asks whether a gift is more meritorious when given to a Brahmana who asks or to one who does not, if they are otherwise equal. Bhishma says a gift to one who does not ask earns more merit, since a Brahmana's firmness lies in not begging. He says begging brings shame and that the giver is said to grant life to the one who asks. Bhishma urges kings to seek out such contented Brahmanas, invite them, and feed and honour them, calling this a sacrifice that pleases the gods.

Yudhishthira asks where the rewards of gifts and sacrifices are earned, which is greater, and who should receive gifts. Bhishma says a king should give to righteous Brahmanas, support them with food, cattle and dwellings, and protect their means of living, and that such giving benefits a king more than grand sacrifices. He warns that a king who extorts wealth gains no merit from the sacrifices it pays for, and that a king who fails to protect his people, or lets learned Brahmanas go hungry, bears a share of their sins. The chapter ends by urging Yudhishthira to be a protector his subjects will trust.

Yudhishthira asks which gift is the foremost of all, and Bhishma answers that the gift of earth is the highest, since land lasts and brings wealth to its giver. He says a king should give land to learned Brahmanas, that taking land from the righteous is a grave sin, and that the gift of earth cleanses even great sinners. Bhishma then tells how Indra asked Vrihaspati which gift leads to heaven, and Vrihaspati gave the same answer, that the gift of earth is supreme. The chapter closes with Indra giving the whole earth to Vrihaspati and with advice to recite these verses at funeral rites.

Yudhishthira asks what gifts bring a king immediate gratification from the Brahmanas and lasting rewards. Bhishma says he once put the same question to the sage Narada, who answered that food is the foremost of gifts, since all life and every rite depends on it. Narada urges giving food to Brahmanas, guests and anyone in need, and describes the heavenly mansions earned by such giving. The chapter ends with a heading that marks the start of Section LXIV.

Yudhishthira asks about gifts tied to the planetary conjunctions and the lunar mansions. Bhishma recalls a discourse in which the sage Narada told Devaki, the mother of Krishna, which gifts to make under which lunar constellations. Each mansion is linked with a particular offering and its reward, such as Payasa under Krittika or a cow under Mrigasiras. Bhishma adds that Devaki later passed the teaching on to her daughters-in-law.

Bhishma lists the gifts praised by earlier authorities: Atri on gold, King Harischandra on gold's cleansing power, and Manu on the gift of drink. He explains that digging wells and tanks where cows, Brahmanas and people can drink wins large merit, and that gifts of ghee, firewood, umbrellas and cars bring prosperity, protection and success. The chapter ends with Sandilya's view that a car is the best gift.

Yudhishthira asks about the merit of giving sandals to Brahmanas and of giving sesame, land, cows and food. Bhishma says a sandal-gift protects the feet and brings the merit of a vehicle, and that sesame seeds, made by Brahma as food for the Pitris, purify the giver. He tells how the gods asked Brahma for a piece of earth to hold a sacrifice, and how they then granted a share of their merit to the gift of earth. He goes on to praise gifts of shelter, land, cows (which should not be given to butchers or atheists) and food as the highest acts.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to describe the merits of giving drink, after hearing that food is the highest gift. Bhishma says food and drink together are unmatched among gifts, since all life depends on food and food depends on water. He describes how nectar, plants and the very sources of life come from water, and says the gift of water brings fame, long life, victory over enemies, and a place in heaven. Manu is cited as the authority.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma again about the merit of gifts of sesame, lamps, food and robes. Bhishma tells the story of Yama, lord of the dead, who sends a messenger to fetch a learned Brahmana named Sarmin, but the messenger brings the wrong man, a Brahmana who wants to finish his life in peace. Yama sends him back and instructs him to give sesame, water and resting places, and to light lamps; Sarmin does so. The chapter goes on to praise lamps, gems, robes and a son as the greatest acquisition.

Yudhishthira asks again about gifts, especially the gift of earth, and which objects any class may give to earn merit. Bhishma names three gifts of equal worth, kine, earth and knowledge, and says that cows are the mothers of all creatures and must be treated with care. He then explains which cows and which recipients are fit, and warns that a cow should not go to the unrighteous, and that taking a Brahmana's property is as grave as the merit of a cow-gift is great.

Bhishma tells the story of king Nriga, who was cursed for taking a cow that had been given to a Brahmana by mistake. Yadava youths find a huge lizard stuck in a well and ask Krishna for help, and the lizard reveals itself as the soul of Nriga. Nriga explains that he gave away a cow that another Brahmana had lost, and that when he offered a hundred thousand cows in exchange, both Brahmanas refused. Yama then punishes him for breaking his oath and taking a Brahmana's property, and Krishna frees him to heaven. Vasudeva's verse on not taking a Brahmana's property closes the tale.

Yudhishthira asks for more on the merit of giving cows, and Bhishma tells the story of the sage Uddalaki and his son Nachiketa. When Nachiketa cannot find the firewood and ritual items that the current has carried off, his father curses him to meet Yama, and the boy dies; the father's grief brings him back to life. Nachiketa then tells how Yama showed him the heavenly regions of cow-givers, with rivers of milk and ghee, and taught the rules for giving cows, including substitute cows made of ghee, sesame or water when real cows are not available.

Yudhishthira asks about the regions reserved for those who give cows, having heard of Nriga and Nachiketa. Bhishma introduces a dialogue between Brahma and Indra. Indra is puzzled that the residents of the cow-givers' regions outshine the gods of heaven, and asks what those regions are like, how long their rewards last, and how gifts of many cows compare with gifts of a few. The chapter ends with Indra's questions still open.

Brahma answers Indra's questions about the regions reserved for cow-givers, describing a realm where time, decay and disease do not reach and where cows roam freely. He lists the virtues needed to reach it, such as forgiveness, obedience to teachers, truthfulness and compassion for kine, and the sins that bar the way. He then sets out the merit of giving cows according to the giver's class and the means of acquiring them, and the rules for choosing recipients and performing the gift.

Indra asks what becomes of a man who knowingly steals a cow or sells one for profit. Brahma answers that anyone who kills, eats or sells cows, or lets others slaughter them for gain, will rot in hell for as many years as the cow has hairs, and that a stolen cow given away still brings sin. He adds that gold is the best Dakshina for a cow-gift. Bhishma says this teaching came down from Brahma through Indra, Dasaratha, Rama, Lakshmana and the sages to his own teacher, and he urges Yudhishthira to recite it.

Yudhishthira asks what rewards come from vows, study, gifts, the refusal of gifts, teaching, valour in battle, purity, celibacy, service to parents and teachers, and compassion. Bhishma answers that self-restraint is worth more than giving, since a giver may act in anger but a restrained man does not. He describes the honours of teachers, the Vedic students, heroes of many kinds, and the truthful, and he says truth outweighs a thousand horse-sacrifices. He ends with the merits of lifelong celibacy and of serving parents and elders, which keep a man from hell.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for the exact ritual of giving cows. Bhishma says a lawfully acquired cow given away rescues the giver's whole family and recounts how king Mandhatri asked Vrihaspati for the rite: honour Brahmanas the day before, give cows of the Rohini class, spend the night in the cow-pen with mantras, and give the proper substitutes when a cow is not available. He lists kings who won heaven by following the rite and urges Yudhishthira to do the same. The chapter closes by noting that Yudhishthira obeyed, took up a cow-based diet and simple life, and stopped yoking cattle to his chariots.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma once more about giving cows, and Bhishma lays down rules on which cows to give: healthy, young, gentle and fragrant ones, with calves, and never sick, dry or unwilling animals. Yudhishthira asks why the tawny Kapila cow is so praised, and Bhishma tells how Daksha made the cow Surabhi from his breath and how her daughters were born from nectar. The story goes on to Mahadeva's angered glance, Daksha's blessing that the milk stays pure, and Mahadeva's becoming lord of cattle, which is why he bears a bull on his standard. Yudhishthira then gives many cows and bulls to Brahmanas.

Bhishma tells how king Saudasa of Ikshvaku's line asks his priest Vasishtha which sacred thing, if recited, brings great merit. Vasishtha answers by praising cows as the refuge of all creatures, the source of sacrifice, offerings and prosperity, and says that gifts of cows bring merit in proportion to the giver's devotion. He lists the everyday rules for honouring cows, such as not eating their flesh, never soiling their dung, and saying their names each morning and night, and he ends with the verse-like formula for a safe refuge in cows.

Vasishtha tells Saudasa how the cows, after a hundred thousand years of penance, asked Brahma for the boon that they would be the finest of gifts and that their dung would purify people; Brahma granted it, and cows became the refuge of the world. He then lists the heavenly regions won by giving cows of different colours, calves, and bulls to particular deities, from Brahma and Surya down to Prajapati. The giver of cows rises to heaven, is attended by celestial women, and returns to earth in a noble family.

Vasishtha gives a mantra that calls cows the source of ghee and milk and asks that they always stay near him, to be recited morning and evening to cleanse daily sins. He describes the heaven reached by those who give a thousand cows, with rivers of milk, curds and cheese. He calls cows the refuge of the universe and says a Kapila cow given with its calf and a brass milking vessel lets the giver pass safely into Yama's realm. Saudasa then gives many cows to Brahmanas and gains many heavens.

Yudhishthira asks which is the most sacred thing, and Bhishma says cows, which uphold all creatures and rescue their givers. Bhishma tells how the sage Suka asked his father Vyasa which sacrifice and act is greatest. Vyasa explains that cows were once hornless until they worshipped Brahma, who gave them horns and their desires; he describes the rich land of the cow-givers, and gives mantras, purification by cow products, and the rewards of cow worship. Suka is then said to have worshipped cows every day.

Yudhishthira asks why cow dung is said to hold Sree, the goddess of fortune. Bhishma tells how Sree came into a herd of cows, dazzled them with her beauty, and asked to dwell in them. The cows first refuse her because she is fickle, then, when she pleads, they grant her a place in their urine and dung. Sree agrees and vanishes, which explains why cow dung is sacred and holds prosperity. Bhishma says he will continue on the glory of cows.

Bhishma says that those who give cows and eat the remnants of the sacred offerings are always counted as sacrificers, since no sacrifice works without ghee. He tells how the gods and sages gathered before Brahma after the Daityas were defeated, and Indra asked why the realm of cows lies above the realm of the gods. Brahma explains that cows are the limbs of sacrifice, sustain creatures, and serve with patience, and that the goddess Surabhi won an eternal realm called Goloka through her austerities. Indra then worships cows every day, and Bhishma says anyone devoted to cows gains his wishes.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma why gold is the best of all sacrificial gifts and where it came from. Bhishma explains that after his father's rites a hand rose from the ground, which led him to a dream in which his ancestors urged him to give gold. He then retells how Parashurama, seeking a deeper purification, was taught by the sages and Vasishtha that gold, born from Agni, is the highest cleanser and carries all the gods. The chapter closes with a myth of Rudra's seed, which grew into a fiery power and set the stage for the Asura Taraka's attacks on the gods.

The gods cannot kill the Asura Taraka, who is protected by Brahma's boon, and Uma's curse keeps them from having children. Brahma sends them to find Agni, who must father a son; Agni hides in water and trees, cursing frogs, elephants and parrots on the way, and then impregnates the river Ganga. The golden seed becomes Kartikeya, who later slays Taraka, and gold is thereby established as Agni's offspring and the best gift. Vasishtha's long account of the cosmic sacrifice of Rudra, and the dispute over its offspring, ends with a lesson on the merit of giving gold at different times of day.

Yudhishthira asks how Taraka was finally destroyed, since the gods could not slay him. Bhishma tells how the six Krittikas bore Agni's divided seed, how the child was reared in a reed forest as Kartikeya, and how the gods gave him gifts and made him their commander. Once grown, the youth killed Taraka, and the chapter closes by urging gifts of gold again.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to set out the rules for the Sraddha, the rites for dead ancestors, as he did for the four orders. Bhishma says the Pitris must be honored first and sets out which lunar days bring which benefits. He adds that the dark fortnight and the afternoon are the better times for the rite.

Yudhishthira asks which offerings to the Pitris last forever. Bhishma lists the foods and how long each keeps the ancestors satisfied, from sesame and fish up to several kinds of meat, and names some offerings that never run out. He closes with verses on the Magha constellation and the merit of sending a son to Gaya, and of offering water on death anniversaries.

Bhishma describes the optional Sraddhas to be performed under each lunar constellation, a teaching first given by Yama to King Sasavindu. Each constellation brings its own benefit, such as children, cattle, wealth, knowledge or a kingdom. Sasavindu followed these rules and easily ruled the whole earth.

Yudhishthira asks which Brahmanas should receive the offerings made at Sraddhas. Bhishma says they must be examined before being invited, lists the kinds who pollute the family line and should be excluded, and then names the learned and disciplined who sanctify it. He warns that feeding unworthy people, or using the rite to entertain friends, brings no merit and can even harm the ancestors.

Yudhishthira asks who first established the Sraddha, what its essence is, and which foods and grains must be kept out of it. Bhishma traces the rite to the sage Nimi, who held an offering for his dead son, and tells how Atri confirmed that Brahma himself had ordained it. Atri then names the deities to be honored, lists foods and grains that must not be offered, and bars outcastes from the place of the rite.

After Nimi's rite, the sages began holding Sraddhas, but the offerings became so heavy that the Pitris and gods fell ill with indigestion. They went first to Soma and then to Brahma, who pointed them to Agni, and Agni agreed to share the offerings with them. That is why a share of each Sraddha is first given to fire, and Bhishma ends by setting out the order of offerings and the Pitris to be honored.

Yudhishthira asks whether vowed Brahmanas may eat Sraddha offerings and what separates a giver from a receiver of gifts. Bhishma answers with the tale of starving sages who refused King Vrishadarbhi's gold-filled figs, and the king's Rakshasi Yatudhani, who was sent to kill them. A stranger, Sunahsakha, destroyed her, tested the sages with a missing lotus-stalk, and then revealed himself as Indra, rewarding them for resisting greed.

Bhishma tells of a group of sages touring the holy waters, when Agastya finds that the lotus-stalks he gathered have been stolen. Agastya laments that righteousness is failing and says he would rather leave the world, and the sages swear their innocence with a long series of curses on the thief. Indra then confesses that he took the stalks only to hear the sages discuss duty, and he blesses the thief instead, so Agastya takes his stalks back. The chapter closes by promising merit to anyone who recites the tale.

Yudhishthira asks who began the custom of giving umbrellas and sandals at religious rites, and why. Bhishma tells how the sage Jamadagni, angry that the noon sun had delayed his wife Renuka, vowed to pierce the sun, and Surya came to him disguised as a Brahmana to argue that the sun sustains all life. The story is set up as the origin of the custom.

Jamadagni refuses Surya's plea and insists on shooting the sun at midday, but Surya begs for protection. Jamadagni agrees to shield him and asks for a remedy against the heat, and Surya gives him an umbrella and sandals, which he declares an inflexible custom for rites. Bhishma closes by praising these gifts as meritorious in the three worlds and urges Yudhishthira to give them to Brahmanas.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for the duties of the householder and the way to prosperity. Bhishma recounts how Vasudeva asked the goddess Earth the same question. She lists the worship of Rishis, deities, Pitris and men, the daily fire rites and offerings, hospitality to guests, and food for dogs and outcasts, and says following these duties brings fame and heaven.

Yudhishthira asks about the gift of light, and Bhishma recounts how Manu explained to the ascetic Suvarna why flowers and incense are offered to the deities. Sukra, teaching the Asura Vali, classifies the herbs and flowers, names the incenses each kind of being prefers, and explains that lamps give energy and are best made of ghee. The discourse ends with the Vali offerings to deities and household gods, and the teaching is handed down to Narada and then to Bhishma.

Yudhishthira asks why householders place their Vali offerings on the ground, and Bhishma tells how Nahusha, having won the sovereignty of heaven through merit, grew proud and made the Rishis carry his palanquin. Bhrigu comes to Agastya to complain, and Agastya explains that Brahma's boon shields Nahusha from being cursed by the Rishis. Bhrigu resolves to pull Nahusha down himself.

Yudhishthira asks how Nahusha fell from the sovereignty of the gods. Bhishma recounts how Nahusha, while pious, performed his rites, but later grew arrogant and yoked Agastya to his car. When Nahusha kicked Agastya's head, Bhrigu, who had hidden in the sage's matted hair, cursed him to become a snake, and Bhrigu then promised that Yudhishthira would one day free him. Indra was restored to heaven, and the chapter closes by urging householders to give lamps at evening.

Yudhishthira asks where those who steal or misappropriate Brahmanas' property end up. Bhishma tells of a Chandala, once a learned Brahmana, who was outcast after eating food sprinkled with milk from stolen kine, and who explains that the thieving king and everyone who drank the milk or the Soma fell into hell. A Kshatriya tells him that only giving up his life in battle to protect a Brahmana's wealth will free him, and the Chandala does so and wins a good end. Bhishma concludes that Brahmanas' property must always be guarded.

Yudhishthira asks whether all pious men reach the same region. Bhishma tells of the sage Gautama, who raised an orphan elephant that the king Dhritarashtra, really Indra in disguise, seizes. Gautama refuses the king's gifts and follows him through each heaven the king names, until Indra reveals himself and returns the elephant. The tale ends with the promise that reciting it leads to Brahma's region.

Yudhishthira asks which penance is the highest. Bhishma says fasting is the highest, and tells how King Bhagiratha reached Brahma's realm: not through his vast gifts and sacrifices, which he lists at length, but through the fast revealed by Usanas. Bhishma then urges Yudhishthira to keep the fast and to honor Brahmanas with gifts.

Yudhishthira asks what makes people live long and gain fame and wealth, and whether it is penance, celibacy, recitation, medicine, deeds or speech. Bhishma answers that conduct decides all of these, and then gives a long run of daily rules. They cover rising early, prayers, cleanliness, eating, speech, sleep, sexual conduct, marriage, respect for elders and avoiding harm to others. The chapter ends by stating that conduct brings long life, fame and heaven.

Yudhishthira asks how the eldest brother should treat his younger brothers, and how they should treat him. Bhishma says the eldest should guide them as a good teacher guides pupils, correcting faults gently and keeping the family united. He adds that the teacher, father and mother rank in increasing reverence, and that after the father's death the eldest brother stands in his place.

Yudhishthira asks why people of every class observe fasts, and what merit and heaven the fasts bring. Bhishma repeats the teaching that Angiras gave him: Brahmanas and Kshatriyas may fast up to three nights, Vaisyas and Sudras only one, and monthly fasts bring wealth, long life and progeny. Long fasts are said to earn the merit of great sacrifices and heaven, and Angiras declares that no penance surpasses fasting, which is how the sages Viswamitra, Vasishtha and others reached heaven.

Yudhishthira points out that sacrifices need wealth, so poor people cannot earn their merit, and asks for a substitute. Bhishma answers that the fasts taught by Angiras yield the same fruit as sacrifices, and then sets out a long sequence of fasts, each matched to a sacrifice and a heavenly reward. He concludes that even a poor man can reach the highest end through fasting and worship.

Yudhishthira asks which sacred bathing place brings the greatest purity. Bhishma says the best is the inner Tirtha called Manasa, whose waters are truth and whose lake is understanding, and that its cleansing fruits are freedom from greed, truth, compassion and self-restraint. He adds that outer sacred places also cleanse, and that purity from both sources is the most complete.

Yudhishthira asks which fasts bring the highest and surest fruit. Bhishma gives a yearly cycle of twelfth-day fasts, each paired with worship of Krishna under a different name and the merit of a particular sacrifice. The cycle is said to culminate in the merit of all sacrifices, and the vow closes with gifts to Brahmanas, a practice that Vishnu himself declared to be unsurpassed.

Vaisampayana introduces Yudhishthira, who approaches Bhishma lying on his bed of arrows and asks how to gain beauty, prosperity, merit, wealth and happiness. Bhishma names the Chandravrata vow, which begins in Margasirsha when the moon stands in a set sequence of constellations matched to the parts of the body. It ends with gifts of ghee to Vedic Brahmanas and brings knowledge and fullness like the full moon.

Yudhishthira asks Vrihaspati what truly follows a person after death, and Vrihaspati answers that no relative goes along, only righteousness does, so one should earn wealth lawfully and live by piety. He then explains how the elements witness each deed, how the vital seed forms and how the soul enters a new body. The chapter closes with a long list of animal rebirths that follow particular sins, such as theft, betrayal, injury to teachers and parents, and adultery, and urges Yudhishthira to hold to righteousness.

Yudhishthira asks what good end awaits those who have sinned. Vrihaspati answers that repentance and open confession before learned Brahmanas wash away sin, and that gifts of lawfully earned food are the greatest merit. Food is called the life of all beings, and giving it to deserving Brahmanas, according to one's own class and means, is said to free a person from hell.

Yudhishthira asks which of six practices, from non-injury and Vedic rites to service of teachers, brings the most merit. Vrihaspati says all six are doors to piety, but the highest good comes from universal compassion and treating all creatures as oneself, never doing to others what one would not wish done to oneself. Vaisampayana then tells that Vrihaspati rose into heaven before their eyes.

Vaisampayana says Yudhishthira asks Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, how a person who has harmed others in word, thought and deed can cleanse himself of misery. Bhishma says compassion has four parts that must all be kept, and that injury arises from action, word and thought. He argues against eating meat, since its taste enslaves the mind, and recalls righteous men who gave their own flesh to save others.

Yudhishthira asks how meat offerings at Sraddhas fit with the rule against harm, and what merit or sin attaches to killing, buying and eating meat. Bhishma says abstaining from meat brings long life, strength and the goodwill of all creatures, and that the sin is shared by all who kill, buy, cook, approve or eat. He allows only meat sanctified by mantras in the Pitri rites, and closes by listing kings who abstained in Karttika and the merit of hearing this teaching.

Yudhishthira is dismayed that people crave meat above every other food, and asks what merit comes from abstaining and what is edible. Bhishma admits that meat is tasty and strengthening, but says abstaining brings great merit, that flesh is for sacrifice, and that the slayer is in turn slain. He ends by naming abstention from cruelty as the highest religion, gift, penance and truth.

Yudhishthira asks what fate awaits those who die in battle, whether they wish to die or live. Bhishma tells of Vyasa, who came upon a worm fleeing a passing cart, and asked why it was so afraid. The worm replies that every creature clings to life, and reveals that it was once a cruel Sudra usurer whose memory survives through a single act of honoring a Brahmana guest.

Vyasa tells the worm that its memory survives because of one good deed and that it may rise again through merit. The worm stays on the road, is crushed by the cart, and after many animal births is reborn a Kshatriya through Vyasa's grace. Vyasa reminds him of his past sin and says that dying bravely in battle for kine or Brahmanas will lift him, step by step, toward the status of a Brahmana.

The reborn Kshatriya, recalling his earlier births, undertakes severe austerities, and Vyasa tells him that protecting all creatures is the penance of his order. He rules his subjects righteously, becomes a Brahmana, and Vyasa consoles him that only the loss of righteousness, not death, is to be feared. The former worm then reaches Brahma's realm, and Bhishma says the Kshatriyas who fell at Kurukshetra also attained a good end, so Yudhishthira should not mourn them.

Yudhishthira asks which is superior, knowledge, penance or gifts. Bhishma tells how Vyasa, travelling in disguise, was fed by the sage Maitreya at Varanasi and laughed in delight, and Maitreya asked why. Vyasa explains that gifts surpass ablutions and sacrifices, names non-injury, truth and giving as the three best vows, and urges Yudhishthira to give freely and rejoice.

Maitreya, a learned sage of a wealthy line, replies to Vyasa's teaching on gifts. He praises Vyasa's purity, and argues that learned, pure-born Brahmanas are the field in which gifts bear fruit. A gift to an unworthy receiver ruins both giver and taker, while the merit of a gift to a worthy one is shared equally.

Vyasa replies that penance is greater than gifts, since it destroys sins and wins the Vedas and heaven, though gifts and learning are also praised. He advises Maitreya on the duties of a householder, including contentment between husband and wife. He then blesses Maitreya and departs, and Maitreya returns the blessing.

Yudhishthira asks how good and faithful women behave. Bhishma tells of the heavenly woman Sumana, who asks Sandili how she reached heaven, and Sandili answers that she did not win it through outward signs, but through devoted service to husband, in-laws, guests and gods, with careful and discreet household conduct. Bhishma adds that reading this tale at full and new moons leads to heaven.

Yudhishthira asks whether conciliation or gifts is more effective. Bhishma tells how a Brahmana seized by a Rakshasa stayed calm and used conciliation, asking why the Rakshasa was so pale and lean. The Brahmana then flattered him with a long list of reasons, each a kindly account of his troubles, and the pleased Rakshasa made him a friend, gave him wealth and let him go.

Yudhishthira asks how a poor man should act, and which gift is best and when. Bhishma prefaces his answer with the mysteries of duty taught by Vyasa, then recounts a heavenly messenger's question to the Pitris about the three rice-balls of the Sraddha and the ban on sexual relations on Sraddha days. The chapter continues with rites of purification, the sins against the sun, wind, fire and cows, and gifts such as blue bulls, sesame and lamps that free a man from his debt to his ancestors.

Indra asks Vishnu what acts please him, and Vishnu says that honoring Brahmanas, hospitality, and worship of the Aswattha tree and the cow are his favored worship. Baladeva, the deities, Dharma, Agni and Viswamitra then give rules on sacred vessels, the unfit recipients of Sraddha offerings, the sin of kicking cows, fire or Brahmanas, and a prayer to the cow. The chapter closes with Brahma's answer to the seven Rishis: drinking moonlight after a bath on the Pausha full moon under Rohini earns the merit of great sacrifices, for those who lack wealth.

A run of short teachings, each given by a different sage or deity, on ritual conduct: offerings on lunar days, household objects and habits that drive away the gods and ancestors, and rules of hospitality. The last teaching, from Jamadagni, says a pure heart counts for more than costly sacrifice. The section treats ritual merit as depending on both correct practice and inner purity.

Vayu gives duties for the four rainy months and for ancestral rites, and names faults that bring sin, such as letting a Sudra kindle the sacred fire or letting unqualified women take part in rites. He gives an expiation of three days of fasting and fire offerings made with a mixture of cow's urine, dung, milk and ghee. He ends by saying that those who avoid these faults or expiate them reach heaven.

Lomasa warns that men who seek other men's wives, have intercourse with barren women, or take what belongs to a Brahmana are cut off by their ancestors, and their offerings fail. He then praises gifts of ghee, Akshata, sesame-filled vessels, water, lamps and Krisara food on lunar days. He says these gifts earn great merit from the gods and ancestors, and that gifts of cows, land or an Agnishtoma sacrifice count as equal merit.

The sages ask Arundhati, wife of Vasishtha, to reveal a high mystery of duty. She says it should be taught only to faithful or pure-hearted listeners, and describes washing a cow's horns and letting the water fall on one's head as bathing in all sacred waters. Brahman, Yama and Surya then speak in turn, praising gifts of water, lamps, Kapila cows, sandals and umbrellas and naming five kinds of sinners to avoid.

The gods, ancestors and sages ask the Pramathas, night-wandering spirits, why they harm some men and what stops them. The Pramathas list unclean acts that leave men open to attack, such as neglecting purification after intercourse, insulting elders and spitting into water. They also name protections for a home, such as sacred marks, Akshata grain, a fire that never goes out, and certain animal skins, animals or sacrificial smoke.

Brahman sends the naga Renuka to ask the eight elephants that hold up the world about the mysteries of duty. The elephants prescribe Vali offerings of treacle and rice at an ant-hill on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in Karttika, saying the rite gives merit and eases their burden of holding up the earth. The gods, ancestors and sages applaud Renuka.

Maheswara closes this run of teachings by praising cows. He says feeding cows each day for a month while eating one meal a day brings great merit, and he notes the bull on his standard as a sign of his favour for them. Even one day's feeding of cows, he says, gives a fourth part of the merit of a person's good deeds in life, so cows should be worshipped by all.

Skanda and Vishnu each teach a further duty and promise great rewards for hearing, reciting or performing it. Bhishma then says this knowledge is worth more than the whole earth. He adds that it must be withheld from the faithless, atheists, the unkind, and those who see other creatures as separate from themselves.

Yudhishthira asks from whom each of the four classes may accept food. Bhishma says Brahmanas may eat with Brahmanas, Kshatriyas and Vaisyas but never accept food from a Sudra, and he sets out the rules for the other classes. He names sources that defile, such as physicians, harlots and mechanics, and lists givers whose food must be refused, including killers of cows or Brahmanas and drunkards.

Yudhishthira asks what expiation a Brahmana must make after accepting various foods and gifts, especially those used for the gods and ancestors. Bhishma gives a long list of purification rites, each tied to the kind of food or gift and the setting, such as funerals, eclipses and a dead person's house. He ends by saying that eating food partly eaten by another class is cleansed by smearing the body with auspicious substances.

Yudhishthira asks whether charity or devotion is the greater merit. Bhishma answers with a list of kings and sages who reached heaven through their gifts, teaching or penance, such as Sivi, Pratardana and Rantideva. He says their fame will last and that he will answer further doubts in the morning, as night has come.

Yudhishthira asks how many kinds of gift there are, what each brings, and to whom each should be given. Bhishma answers that gifts are made for five motives: a wish for merit, a wish for profit, fear, free choice, and pity. He gives an example for each and says gifts raise the giver's merit and fame, and that Brahman advised giving according to one's power.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to teach on religion and profit, and Bhishma agrees to tell of Vishnu's power and a doubt that troubled Rudra and his spouse. He describes how Krishna, during a long vow, received sages at his hermitage, where fire from his mouth burned a mountain and then was called back and the mountain restored. When the sages ask about it, Krishna says the fire is his own energy and asks them to tell him something wonderful, and they choose Narada to recount a story.

Narada tells of Shiva (Mahadeva) resting on the Himavat mountains, surrounded by gods, ghostly beings and sages. Uma playfully covers his eyes, plunging the world into darkness, and a third eye then opens on his forehead and burns the mountain until Shiva restores it at her plea. Uma asks why he has the third eye, why he burned and restored the mountain, and why his faces, hair and throat look as they do. Shiva agrees to explain.

Uma asks Shiva about his four faces, his blue throat, his bull mount and his fondness for the crematorium, and he answers with stories of Tilottama, Indra and Surabhi's kine. She then asks what marks true religion, and Shiva lays out the duties of householders and of each class: Brahmanas, Kshatriyas, Vaisyas and Sudras. He goes on to describe the householder's path (Pravritti), the path of renunciation (Nivritti) and the kinds of wandering mendicants, and the chapter closes with a survey of ascetic groups such as the Phenapas and Valkhilyas.

Uma asks Shiva what duties forest recluses follow and what rewards different austerities bring. Shiva describes the daily rites, plain diet, hard postures and bodily hardships of these recluses, and says the married and unmarried kinds differ in their rules but share virtues such as harmlessness and sincerity. He then lists the heavenly and royal rewards for various fasts, vows and deaths, including dying in the manner of heroes.

Uma asks how people fall from their caste into a lower order and how lower-born men can rise to Brahmanhood. Shiva says birth gives the first order, but conduct decides whether a man keeps or loses it, so a Brahmana who neglects his duties or eats forbidden food sinks to a lower status. He lists the faults that cost a Brahmana his standing, and the good conduct by which Sudras and Vaisyas can rise, and says conduct, not birth alone, makes a Brahmana.

Uma asks what deeds, words and thoughts bind men and what frees them, and what lets them reach heaven. Shiva lists righteous conduct, honest wealth, harmlessness, faithfulness to one's spouse, truthful and gentle speech, and good mental habits such as not coveting what belongs to others. Uma then asks what makes life long or short, and Shiva says cruelty brings hell and a short life, while compassion brings long life and a divine state.

Uma asks which dispositions and gifts lead a man to heaven. Shiva says generous giving, honouring Brahmanas and the needy, and building wells, halls and tanks win heaven and a rich human birth, while miserliness, arrogance and cruelty lead to hell and humble rebirth. Uma then asks why some people are wise and others foolish, or born blind or diseased, and Shiva ties these to the deeds of learning, lust and cruelty. The chapter closes by contrasting conduct guided by the Vedas with conduct led by folly.

Mahadeva asks Uma to set out the duties of women, and she first consults the sacred rivers, led by Ganga, who praises her for asking. Uma then describes the wife's ideal: she should honour her husband as a god, serve him cheerfully, keep the household and its guests and dependants cared for, and share in his merit. The text adds that a wife should comply even with an improper command in a time of distress. The gods and rivers then depart.

The Rishis ask Shiva to describe the glory of Vasudeva, and Shiva answers with a long praise of Hari. He calls Vishnu the eternal supreme being, the source of Brahma, Shiva and all creatures, and traces his coming birth through the royal lines of Manu and Yadu. He foretells that Vasudeva will defeat Jarasandha and rule from Dwaraka, and urges all to worship him. He also describes an elder brother, who carries a plough and is identified with the infinite serpent Ananta, and ends by urging the ascetics to worship Krishna.

After Shiva's discourse, the Rishis see a storm, the ghostly host vanish, and then leave, praising Krishna as Brahma. Krishna returns to Dwaraka, where Rukmini bears him a son. Bhishma then extols Krishna at length, credits him with the Pandavas' victory, and tells Yudhishthira not to grieve, since Time, which is Krishna, has slain the fallen. Yudhishthira stays silent until Bhishma rests, and then he asks a further question.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma which god is the sole refuge, which religion is foremost, and which hymn frees a living being from birth and death. Bhishma answers that Vasudeva, the Lord of the universe, is the highest refuge, and recites his thousand names, grouped in sets and explained as the god's attributes. He says that reciting the names daily brings success, protection and prosperity by caste and, in the end, liberation, and he presents the hymn as composed by Vyasa.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma for a silent recitation that brings daily merit and success at journeys, new buildings and sacrifices. Bhishma gives the Savitri mantra, said to have been taught by Vyasa and recited by royal sages. He says it should be used with the names of Vishnu, the Rudras, Adityas, Vasus, Aswins, Rishis and the guardians of the quarters, and promises protection from fire, theft, disease and enemies. The chapter ends with Bhishma offering to answer further questions.

Yudhishthira asks whom people should worship and how they should treat others. Bhishma says Brahmanas deserve honour, since humiliating them humiliates the gods, and he describes their virtues and their role in upholding the world. He says a learned Brahmana is worthier still, but even an unlearned one is a god, just as fire and ghee stay sacred wherever they are, so a Brahmana of wicked conduct still deserves honour.

Yudhishthira asks what reward comes from honouring Brahmanas, and Bhishma tells of an old quarrel between the king Arjuna, also called Kartavirya, and the wind god. Kartavirya wins boons from the sage Dattatreya, then grows proud and scorns Brahmanas. The wind god warns him that the Brahmanas can cast him down, and the king asks what a Brahmana is like. The chapter ends with his question.

The wind god goes on answering Arjuna's boast that Kshatriyas outrank Brahmanas. He lists the power of Brahmanas: Kasyapa paralysed the Earth, Angiras drank the waters, Gautama cursed Indra, the Brahmanas cursed the ocean and Agni, and Kapila reduced Sagara's sons to ashes. He then argues that Arjuna should honour Brahmanas and reflects on the creation of Brahman, saying Brahman was not born from an egg, and Arjuna remains silent.

The wind god tells how the king of Anga wished to give the whole earth to the Brahmanas, and how Kasyapa entered and saved the earth. He then tells of Utathya, whose wife was carried off by Varuna, the lord of waters. Angiras dried up the waters, Utathya made the land barren until Varuna returned the wife, and the wind god asks whether any Kshatriya is greater than Utathya.

Bhishma reports that the wind god told Arjuna of two Brahmanas whose powers exceeded any Kshatriya's. Agastya burned the Danavas who had seized the sacrifices, but refused to destroy the Asuras hidden underground, because that would cost him penance. Vasishtha burned the Khalins who had attacked the gods, and brought the Ganga to the spot to protect them. Each time the wind god asks Arjuna whether any Kshatriya can surpass these Brahmanas.

The wind god offers two more tales of Brahmanas. Atri takes the forms of the sun and moon to dispel darkness caused by Rahu and to defeat the Asuras who attacked the gods. Chyavana then makes Indra accept the Aswins as Soma drinkers, creating the terrible Mada to threaten him when Indra refuses, and sends Mada to dwell in dice, hunting, drink and women. The wind god again asks whether Arjuna can name a Kshatriya higher than Chyavana.

The wind god tells how Chyavana took the earth from the gods and the Kapas took heaven, so the gods sought Brahman's help. Brahman sent them to the Brahmanas, who burned the Kapas with sacred fires after refusing a messenger's plea, and Narada told the gods that the Brahmanas had won. Arjuna thanks the wind god and credits Dattatreya for his might, and the wind god urges him to protect the Brahmanas and warns of future danger from the race of Bhrigu.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what reward comes from honouring Brahmanas. Bhishma says he is nearing death and that Krishna should answer, and he then praises Krishna at length. He describes Krishna as the source of the earth, the sky and the gods, who takes birth in each age to uphold righteousness and who lifted Govardhana and raised the earth as a boar. He calls Krishna the one called Vishwaksena, in whom the seasons, Vedas, elements and the four forms of Vasudeva are all contained.

Yudhishthira asks Krishna what prosperity comes from honouring Brahmanas, and Krishna recounts how his son Pradyumna once put the same question to him. Krishna tells how the sage Durvasa stayed in his house, wrecked his goods, humiliated Rukmini, and then blessed the couple and restored everything he had broken. Krishna concludes that his own prosperity comes from the grace of Brahmanas, and he urges Yudhishthira to honour them daily.

Yudhishthira asks Krishna to explain the knowledge he gained through Durvasa's grace. Krishna recites the Sata-rudriya hymn, which he says Brahman composed, and praises Mahadeva as the highest of beings. He recounts Rudra's fierce deeds, from piercing Daksha's sacrifice to burning the three cities of the Asuras, and then says Durvasa was Mahadeva himself, whose merits cannot be exhausted.

Krishna lists the many names of Rudra and explains their meanings, drawing on his greatness, his wrath, his care for creatures and his acts. He says Rudra has a fierce form and a mild form, and that he dwells in crematoria, gives and takes away life, and is the Lord of all. Brahmanas are said to recite the Sata-rudriya in his honour.

Yudhishthira asks whether direct perception or scripture is the true authority. Bhishma says that claiming perception alone is authoritative is foolish, that Brahman is understood only through long study and yoga, and that Righteousness is one though seen through three supports: the Vedas, observed practice and purity of conduct. He lists the virtues of the righteous, sets out the fates of those who love or hate Righteousness, and gives a long set of rules on conduct, purity and confession of sin.

Yudhishthira asks why effort and luck seem to fall unevenly, so that the fortunate prosper and the learned sometimes do not. Bhishma replies that when fortune fails, one should practise austerity and generosity, which bring rewards in later lives, and that a life free from cruelty brings long life. He ends by urging Yudhishthira to be tranquil, since the fates of even insects and ants follow their acts and nature.

Bhishma says that Time moves creatures towards righteousness or sin, and that a righteous soul stays pure, since sin cannot overcome Righteousness, which is eternal. He explains that the four orders share the same elements but have different duties, and that heaven as a reward is temporary while Righteousness is not. He ends by saying that unequal lots among men follow from their past acts.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, what brings happiness and cleanses sins. Bhishma recites a long list of gods, sages, sacred waters and mountains, Rishis of each quarter, and kings, and says that naming them morning, noon and evening cleanses a person of sin. He ends with a prayer that these lords will bring growth, long life and victory.

Janamejaya asks what Yudhishthira did after hearing Bhishma's teachings. Vaisampayana says that Vyasa tells Bhishma that Yudhishthira is ready to leave, and Bhishma sends him back to the city. Bhishma urges him to rule well, honour the gods and gladden his subjects, and to return when Bhishma's departure is near, at the sun's turn north.

Yudhishthira rules his kingdom and, after fifty nights, returns to Bhishma with funeral materials, finding him still on the bed of arrows. Bhishma notes that the sun has begun its northward course and that Magha has come, consoles Dhritarashtra, and praises Krishna as the eternal soul. Krishna grants leave to depart, and Bhishma bids his kin farewell, urging them to seek truth and honour Brahmanas, preceptors and priests.

Chapter 168 is the translator's footnote section that follows the Anushasana Parva. Its only narrative scene, S01, closes the Parva with Bhishma's death and funeral, Ganga's lament and Krishna's consolation. The numbered footnotes that follow, running to 631, gloss Sanskrit words, identify plants and animals, correct readings, criticise earlier translations and comment on gifts, marriage, rites and duties.

After the great war, Yudhishthira collapses in grief on the bank of the Ganga, and his brothers gather around him. Dhritarashtra tries to comfort him, admitting that he and Gandhari have the greater cause to mourn because he ignored Vidura's warnings about Duryodhana. The chapter opens the Aswamedhika Parva by setting Yudhishthira's despair at the centre of the story.

Krishna urges Yudhishthira to put aside grief, honour the dead with sacrifices and gifts, and carry out his duties as a king. Yudhishthira answers that he wants to leave for the forest because he feels guilty for killing Bhishma and Karna. Vyasa rebukes him for clinging to confused sorrow and reminds him of the teachings he has already received.

Vyasa tells Yudhishthira that no one acts by his own power and that sins can be cleansed through sacrifice, penance and gifts. He urges him to prepare the Rajasuya and the horse sacrifice. Yudhishthira objects that the war has left him with no wealth for gifts, and that Duryodhana emptied the treasury, so Vyasa points to a hidden store of gold left by Brahmanas at Marutta's sacrifice.

Yudhishthira asks Vyasa to tell him about the royal sage Marutta. Vyasa traces the royal line from Manu through Ikshvaku, Vinsa and Vivinsa to Karandhama, Avikshit and finally Marutta, who held a great sacrifice on Mount Meru. The chapter gives the family background needed to explain where Marutta's gold came from.

Yudhishthira asks how Marutta grew so powerful and so rich. Vyasa describes the rivalry between Vrihaspati, Indra's priest, and his brother Samvarta, and how Marutta's growing power angered Indra. Indra asks Vrihaspati to stop serving Marutta, but Vrihaspati refuses to serve a mortal king, and Indra's envy is set aside.

Marutta asks Vrihaspati to serve as his priest, but Vrihaspati refuses because he serves only the gods. Marutta despairs until Narada tells him to find Samvarta, who wanders near Varanasi in the guise of a madman. Following Narada's instructions, Marutta sets a corpse at the city gate, pursues Samvarta, endures his abuse and at last wins his attention under a fig tree, which sets up Samvarta's acceptance of the sacrifice.

Marutta finds Samvarta, who questions him and then, raving like a madman, refuses to perform the sacrifice until Marutta first asks Vrihaspati's permission. Marutta explains that Vrihaspati turned him away because Indra forbade it, and that he now wants Samvarta's help even at great cost. Samvarta agrees on condition that Marutta stays steadfast, so the sacrifice goes ahead with a new priest.

Samvarta sends Marutta to Mount Munjaban in the Himalayas, where Shiva dwells with Uma and his followers, and where gold mines are guarded by Kubera's attendants. Marutta is told to propitiate Shiva by his many names to obtain the gold. Marutta follows this advice and prepares a lavish sacrifice, but Vrihaspati grows sick with envy as he hears of it and Indra goes to comfort him.

Indra finds Vrihaspati pale and distressed, and Vrihaspati blames Marutta's sacrifice, with Samvarta as its priest, and asks Indra to stop it. Indra sends Agni to present Vrihaspati to Marutta, but Marutta insists on Samvarta, and Samvarta threatens to burn Agni with his eyes if he comes again. Indra orders Agni back with a threat of his thunderbolt, but Agni refuses and recalls how Chyavana once overpowered Indra, so the conflict escalates.

Indra threatens Marutta with his thunderbolt unless he accepts Vrihaspati as priest, and sends the Gandharva Dhritarashtra to carry the message. Marutta refuses, saying it would be a sin to break faith with Samvarta and that Vrihaspati should serve Indra instead. Samvarta calms the storm with incantations and summons Indra, who arrives, drinks the Soma, and is reconciled. Marutta gives away the gold, and Vyasa tells Yudhishthira that he should gather the same kind of gold for his own sacrifice.

Vasudeva (Krishna) sees Yudhishthira crushed by grief and tells him an old story. Vritra seized the earth's smell, the waters' liquid, light's colour, air's touch and ether's sound, and finally entered Indra's own body, leaving him confused until Vasishtha comforted him and Indra slew Vritra from within. Krishna presents the tale as a warning that the real enemies lie within, which prepares the ground for his teaching on the inner struggle.

Vasudeva (Krishna) explains that bodily and mental ailments both arise from the interplay of body and mind, and that the three qualities of the mind must stay in balance for health. He reminds Yudhishthira of past hardships, including the insult to Draupadi, the exile, and the fights with Drona and Bhishma, and says that Yudhishthira must now fight a battle alone against his own mind. The chapter moves from medicine to a call to self-discipline and to ruling well.

Vasudeva (Krishna) teaches that salvation comes from giving up attachment to the body's pleasures, not from merely renouncing external possessions. He sets death against the eternal Brahman and describes desire as the root of worldly attachment. He then recites the Kamagita, in which Desire itself explains that it cannot be destroyed by prayer, sacrifice, learning, truth or asceticism, since it takes many disguises. Krishna concludes that Yudhishthira should turn his desires toward virtue, perform the horse sacrifice, and stop grieving for the dead.
