Yudhishthira is consoled by the sages, including Vyasa and Narada, and by his brothers, Draupadi and Arjuna, and his grief lifts. He performs funeral rites for Bhishma, Karna and the other fallen Kauravas, gives gifts to the Brahmanas, and asks the sages to guide him to the Himalayas for the sacrifice. The sages vanish, and Yudhishthira returns to Hastinapura with Dhritarashtra and continues to rule with his brothers.

Janamejaya asks what Vasudeva and Arjuna did after the Pandavas regained their kingdom. Vaisampayana says the two travel happily and talk in the assembly hall at Indraprastha, and that Krishna comforts the grieving Arjuna. Krishna then says his work is done and asks Arjuna to tell Yudhishthira that he must return to Dwaravati, and Arjuna sorrowfully agrees, which marks the close of their time together.

Janamejaya asks what Krishna and Arjuna discussed after the victory, and Arjuna admits he has forgotten much of Krishna's earlier teaching from the battlefield and asks to hear it again. Krishna says the teaching cannot be repeated in full and instead tells an older tale of a sage named Kasyapa, who visited an emancipated Brahmana and served him. That Brahmana recounts his many lives of sorrow and how he took refuge in the Formless, which set up the Anugita's account of liberation.

Kasyapa asks the emancipated sage how the body dissolves, how the soul moves on to another body, and how it may be freed. The sage explains that harmful habits wear the body down, that heat and wind drive the vital breaths out, and that the soul leaves in pain carrying the record of its deeds. He also describes the heavens and the sufferings of hell that await the soul, which sets up the teaching on rebirth that follows.

The sage explains that a soul's deeds persist through rebirths and bear fruit in each new body, and that the soul enters the womb carrying its past. He lists the conduct of the good, such as gifts, truthfulness, restraint, compassion and reverence for parents and teachers, as the basis of righteousness. He then describes Brahma creating the worlds and the primal matter Pradhana, and says that the wise who see pleasure as impermanent cross the ocean of rebirth.

The sage describes the marks of a liberated person: one who is free from attachment, desire, and the pull of opposites, and who sees the soul as separate from the body. He then teaches Yoga, in which the senses are withdrawn and the soul is seen within the body, and the disciple asks about digestion and breath before leaving. Vasudeva concludes that this teaching is secret and hard to grasp, but that practising it for six months brings release.

Vasudeva tells the story of a learned Brahmana and his wife. She asks what fate awaits her, since her husband has abandoned rites, and he answers that action cannot be wholly escaped and describes the soul's seat in the body. He explains the breaths and an inner fire with seven flames, seven fuels and seven priests, which he presents as an inner sacrifice that creates the world. The story gives a teaching on the inward sacrifice that follows.

The Brahmana describes an inner sacrifice with ten priests, ten libations and ten fires, in which the mind serves as the ladle. His wife asks why Word arose after Mind and how breath works in sleep, and he explains that Prana is governed by Apana and that Mind rests on Prana. He then recounts a dispute in which Word yields to Mind, and concludes that the mind is the unmoving part and speech the moving one.

The Brahmana describes seven inner priests, the five senses plus mind and understanding, which cannot perceive one another's qualities, since each senses only its own object. His wife asks why, and he recounts a dispute in which the Mind claims that the senses cannot work without it. The senses reply that the mind relies on them and that pleasure comes only through the objects they grasp, so the mind is not superior.

The Brahmana names the five life-breaths (Prana, Apana, Udana, Samana and Vyana) as five inner priests and tells how each breath in turn claims to be the foremost, saying that its departure would end all the others. The breaths then argue until Brahma rules that none is superior, that each has its own role and sphere, and that they should live together in harmony. The story teaches that the inner powers are equal partners.

Narada explains to the Rishi Devamata how a creature's life-breaths arise and come in pairs, moving across, upward and downward, from wish, sensation and the union of seed and blood. He ties the breaths to fire and to the pairs of opposites, and ends by saying that the calm breath, Vyana, reaches the eternal Brahman. The teaching presents the breaths as the first steps toward that calm.

The Brahmana describes a four-part inner sacrifice in which the agent, the instrument, the action and release are the four priests of the universe. He says that the breaths are the chants and rites of an inner sacrifice of Yoga, that renunciation is the fee, and that Narayana is the soul of all. The chapter widens the inner-sacrifice teaching into a full ritual picture.

The Brahmana says there is one ruler, one preceptor, one kinsman, one dispeller and one enemy, and each of them lives in the heart. He tells a story in which the Lord of creatures answers the gods, snakes, sages, Asuras and Danavas with the single word Om, and each group takes a different path. He ends by describing the brahmacharin who lives in Brahman, teaching that the inner guide shapes a person's conduct.

The Brahmana describes the world as a dangerous forest full of desires, grief and passions, and says that he has crossed it into a greater forest of Brahman. His wife asks what that forest is like, and he describes its sevenfold trees, fruits, guests, hermitages and streams, with intelligence as the tree and liberation as the fruit. The passage is a metaphor for the inner path toward Brahman.

The Brahmana says that he is free of desire and aversion, which belong to Nature, and offers as an illustration a debate between a Yati, an ascetic who opposes harm, and an Adhwaryu, a priest who is about to sacrifice a goat. The Yati argues that taking life is wrong and that the soul cannot be destroyed, and the Adhwaryu admits the force of the argument. The Brahmana concludes that the priest completed the sacrifice free of delusion, which shows how the wise live.

The Brahmana tells of Kartaviryarjuna, the thousand-armed king, who angers the ocean by shooting arrows into it. He challenges anyone to match him, and the ocean sends him to Rama, the son of Jamadagni. Rama kills the king in battle, and then turns against the Kshatriyas over and over until a heavenly voice and his ancestors order him to stop, since a Brahmana should not slay kings.

The Pitris tell Rama the story of the royal sage Alarka, who conquered the earth and then turned to the inner conquest of the senses. He aims arrows at the mind, nose, tongue, skin, ear, eye and understanding, and each in turn warns him the arrows will only harm him. He then finds that Yoga alone wins, slays the senses in concentration, and sings that nothing is happier than Yoga. The Pitris urge Rama to stop killing Kshatriyas and take up penance, and he does so and succeeds.

The Brahmana names the three sets of three qualities (goodness, passion and darkness) as the threefold foes within, and says a steady man conquers them with his senses under control. He then quotes King Amvarisha, who had conquered many faults but not craving, which keeps the living bound to rebirth. Amvarisha concludes that the true sovereignty is rule over the soul.

The Brahmana recounts how King Janaka, angry at a guilty Brahmana, orders him banished, and the Brahmana asks where he may go. Janaka is struck speechless, then says he cannot find anything that is truly his, not on earth, in Mithila or among his children. He explains that he is indifferent to the pleasures of the senses, so the world is his in one sense and nothing in another. The Brahmana then reveals that he is Dharma, who came to test the king, and praises Janaka's understanding.

The Brahmana tells his wife that he is a learned, liberated man who lives as a householder and as a forest recluse, and that the knowledge of his identity with the universe is his wealth. He says there is one path for Brahmanas that leads to the same goal whatever their station, and that actions bind the body but understanding carries a person along the path. He reassures his wife that she need not fear the world to come, since she will reach his soul.

The Brahmana's wife asks how knowledge can be gained, and her husband answers with the image of two fire-sticks: devotion to Brahman as the lower stick and the teacher as the upper, rubbed by austerity and study to kindle the fire of knowledge. The Kshetrajna, the knower of the field, is without qualities, but can be grasped by an understanding cleansed through action. When the wife grasps this, she moves beyond the knower. Arjuna then asks Krishna where that Brahmana and his wife are, and Krishna replies that he himself is the Kshetrajna.

Arjuna asks Krishna to explain Brahma, the highest object of knowledge. Krishna recounts a dialogue in which a devoted disciple asks his preceptor what the highest good is, and the preceptor answers that knowledge is the highest goal and renunciation the best penance. The preceptor then tells how the great sages went to Brahma to ask the same questions, which leads into Brahma's teaching on truth, the stages of life and the elements.

Brahma describes the quality of Darkness, which binds the body's city of nine gates and its three inner ducts, and lists the faults it brings, such as delusion, sloth, anger and hostility. People ruled by Darkness sink into lower births, such as animals, insects or the afflicted, but those born in such states can rise again through the rites of Brahmanas. The chapter closes by naming the five great afflictions and urging that Darkness be understood and left behind.

Brahma turns to the quality of Passion, which drives people to action, desire, pride, quarrel and worldly ambition. He lists many forms of this quality, from war and trade to ritual and charity, and says that people caught in it seek pleasure and reward in this world and the next. Understanding these qualities frees a person from their hold.

Brahma describes the quality of Goodness, which brings joy, truth, forgiveness, courage, and freedom from anger, malice and the sense of mine. Those who practise it, free from egoism and expectation and treating all with an equal eye, rise upward and gain the power to enjoy whatever they desire without being attached to it. Understanding these qualities is the path to such a state.

Brahma explains that the three qualities cannot be fully separated, and that one or another predominates in each creature, with Darkness strongest in the lower creatures, Passion in the middle, and Goodness in the higher. These qualities are said to govern the castes, the times of day, the seasons and the elements of the body, and all of them act in the unmanifest. Those who understand the qualities and their workings are freed from the body and gain lasting happiness.

Brahma says that from the unmanifest first arose Mahat, the Great Soul, which is the source of all the qualities and the first creation. He lists its many names and describes it as the Being dwelling in the heart of all things. Those who understand this Great Soul are freed from delusion and live above the understanding.

Brahma says that the Great Soul gives rise to Egoism, which he calls the second creation, from which all beings come and which feels the thought I am all this. Those who are content with knowledge of the self, and who have won success through study and sacrifice, enjoy the eternal world. The passage links the self-sense to the enjoyment of the qualities and to the creation of the worlds.

Brahma explains how the five great elements arise from Egoism and how creation and dissolution run in reverse order. He lists the five life-breaths and the eleven organs, which include the senses, the organs of action and the mind, and assigns each a presiding deity, as well as the four modes of birth. He then describes the path of renunciation in which the senses are withdrawn and the self is seen in all beings, and ends by praising the Highest that is seen this way.

Brahma names the foremost of each class of beings and things, such as the royal Kshatriya among men, the elephant among vehicles, and Vishnu and Shiva among the gods, and he says that kings must protect the Brahmanas and good men. He then teaches non-injury as the highest duty and gives the characteristic of each element, sense and mental faculty, along with the powers that govern them. He concludes that the Kshetrajna, the knower of the field, is pure knowledge and is not seized by any symbol.

Brahma lists the first of many things, including the day, Om among the Vedas, gold among precious things, the householder's mode of life, Meru among mountains and the Ganga among rivers. He then teaches that all things created end in destruction and that only knowledge has no end. A person who is calm, restrained, free of possession and self-regard is released from sin by pure knowledge.

Brahma describes the wheel of life, which turns through grief, passion and time, with understanding as its strength, the mind as its hub and the senses as its spokes. One who understands its motion and stopping is free from delusion and from sin. Brahma then sets out the rules for the householder, who supports the other three stages of life, including the five sacrifices, teaching and receiving gifts from the pure, and says that faithful observance of these duties wins heaven.

Brahma lays out a graded way of life: the student who serves his teacher, the forest dweller who gives up his village, and the wandering renouncer who owns nothing, begs for his food and keeps eight vows of harmlessness, truth, restraint and freedom from backbiting. He describes the self as beyond the senses and the qualities, and says that one who knows it escapes death. The chapter ends with the mind fixed on that self at the time of death, and release follows.

Brahma says that renunciation is the best penance and that knowledge is the highest, and he describes Brahman as beyond opposites and qualities. He uses the image of an eternal tree of Brahman, cut down with the sword of knowledge, and of two birds, one unintelligent and one intelligent. The one who understands the field and transcends the qualities is freed from every sin.

Brahma explains that different thinkers regard Brahman as a tree, a forest, the unmanifest, or beyond all distress, and that a moment of inner peace, or breath control, leads to immortality. He ties Purusha, the self, to the quality of Goodness and says that some who claim that Nature and the self are one are mistaken, since they differ, like a fish and the water it lives in. The learned sages, still uncertain, then ask the Grandsire again, as the preceptor reports.

The Rishis complain that the many contradictory teachings on duty leave them confused, with some saying the soul survives death and others that it does not, and different people praising action, tranquillity, sacrifice, knowledge or renunciation. They ask Brahma to say which duty is most worthy and what links the knower of the field with Nature. Brahma prepares to answer their questions, which opens the next stage of the teaching.

Brahma explains that harmlessness is the highest duty and that pure knowledge frees one from sin. He sets out the relation between the knower, Purusha, who enjoys, and Nature, the enjoyed, which is like a lotus leaf and water, and traces Nature's order from the unmanifest through Mahat, Egoism and the five elements. Each element is given its qualities in detail, such as the ten kinds of smell and the twelve kinds of colour, and the chapter ends by placing Purusha above all of these as the Unfading Soul.

Brahma says that the mind governs the senses and the elements, and describes the body as a chariot driven by the mind, with understanding as reins. He teaches that penance accomplishes all things, that attachment is death and detachment eternal, and that understanding the immortal self brings tranquillity. Vasudeva then reveals that he was the preceptor and Arjuna's mind the pupil, urges Arjuna to practise the teaching, and asks leave to visit his father. Arjuna agrees to go to the elephant-named city to meet Yudhishthira and report Krishna's intention.

Krishna and Arjuna drive to the city named after the elephant, where Arjuna praises Krishna as the soul of the universe who won the war for the Pandavas. They are received by Dhritarashtra and the family, and in the morning they tell Yudhishthira that Krishna wishes to visit his kin in Dvaraka. Yudhishthira grants leave and offers gems and wealth, and Krishna sets out with his kinsmen and attendants, so the bond between the two heroes is marked by a formal parting.

On the road home, Krishna meets the ascetic Utanka in a dry desert and asks about the Kuru war. Krishna explains that he tried to make peace, but that fate and the Kauravas' own folly led to the total destruction of their side, with only the five Pandavas left. Utanka, angry that Krishna did not stop the war, threatens a curse, and Krishna pleads that the ascetic listen to him first and not lose the penance he has built up.

Utanka asks Krishna to teach him the Adhyatma, the teaching on the self. Krishna declares that the three qualities, the gods, the Vedas, the sacrifices and Dharma all rest on him, that he takes many forms to uphold righteousness, and that the Kauravas were destroyed by their own wrongdoing and the power of Time. He concludes that the Pandavas have won great fame. The teaching explains to Utanka why Krishna did not prevent the war.

Utanka is moved by Krishna's teaching and says his anger has gone, asking to see Krishna's sovereign form. Krishna shows him a vast cosmic form, which overwhelms Utanka, who then asks to see the human form again. Krishna grants a boon: whenever Utanka thirsts in the desert, he may call on him. Later, Utanka is refused a proffered water by a hunter, who turns out to be Indra in disguise, offering nectar. Krishna promises that clouds will bring water to the desert, which become known as the Utanka-clouds.

Janamejaya asks what penance gave Utanka the nerve to threaten Vishnu. Vaisampayana explains that Utanka served his teacher Gautama with unmatched devotion, so Gautama would not let him leave, and in old age Utanka breaks down in tears after his load of wood breaks and his white hair falls. Gautama rewards him with his daughter in marriage and restores his youth, and then Utanka, at the request of Ahalya, the teacher's wife, sets out to fetch the celestial ear-rings of Saudasa's queen. Gautama warns that the cursed king Saudasa may kill him, and Utanka meets the king in the forest.

Utanka meets Saudasa, now a man-eater under a curse, who is about to take food and claims the right to eat him. Utanka asks for the queen's ear-rings for his teacher's wife, and Saudasa replies that they belong to his wife and sends him to her. The queen Madayanti demands a sign from her husband, and describes the ear-rings' wonderful powers before she will hand them over.

Saudasa gives Utanka a sign, and Madayanti hands over the ear-rings, after which Saudasa explains that a king hostile to Brahmanas cannot prosper and asks Utanka to keep his promise. Utanka sets out, ties the ear-rings in his deer-skin, and hangs it on a tree while he picks fruit; the fruit knocks the knot loose, and a Naga takes the ear-rings into an anthill. Utanka digs with his staff for thirty-five days until Indra appears in disguise and warns him, and when Utanka insists, Indra opens the way to the Naga world. A fire-steed fills the Naga realm with smoke, the Nagas return the ear-rings with honour, and Utanka delivers them to Ahalya.

After granting the boon to Utanka, Krishna goes with Satyaki to Dvaraka, arriving during the festival of Raivataka hill, which is lit and filled with song and generous gifts. The Vrishnis and their allies greet him, and he honours his kin and then his parents. He sits among the Vrishnis and recounts the great battle to his father, which closes the account of this episode.

Vasudeva asks Krishna to describe the great battle, since Krishna witnessed it, and Krishna recounts how the commanders fell one by one: Bhishma, Drona, Karna, Salya, Sakuni and finally Duryodhana. He ends with the night slaughter of the Pandava camp by Drona's son, which left only the five Pandavas and a few allies alive. The Vrishnis are shaken by the account, which closes the war's narrative in the Aswamedhika Parva.

Krishna has left out the death of Abhimanyu from his account, so that Vasudeva would not be grieved, but Subhadra asks to hear of her son and faints. Vasudeva, too, falls senseless with grief, and when he recovers he asks how Abhimanyu died. Krishna describes how the boy fought bravely, was surrounded by the Kaurava heroes, and fell to the son of Dussasana. Subhadra mourns with Draupadi and Uttara, and Kunti comforts them and arranges the funeral rites for Abhimanyu.

Vasudeva performs the funeral rites for Abhimanyu and feeds many thousands of Brahmanas, but his kin, the Pandavas and Uttara remain grieving. Vyasa appears, promises that Uttara will bear a son who will rule after the Pandavas, and tells Arjuna that his grandson will be a great king. He then urges Yudhishthira to hold the horse sacrifice, and the king turns his mind to gathering the wealth needed for it.

Janamejaya asks how Yudhishthira obtained the wealth that Marutta buried in the earth. Yudhishthira calls his brothers together and asks how they can bring the wealth home, and Bhima proposes that they worship Shiva, whose Kinnara guardians would give up the treasure if the god is pleased. The brothers agree, and the Pandavas set out on the day of the favourable constellation after making offerings to Maheshvara.

The Pandavas set out with a cheerful army, their praises sung by bards, and cross lakes, rivers, forests and mountains until they reach the place where the wealth is buried. Yudhishthira makes camp in a level, auspicious place, placing learned Brahmanas and his priest Agnivesya in the front. The Brahmanas advise a day of fasting and drinking only water, so the brothers spend the night on kusa grass and listen to learned talk until morning.

The Brahmanas advise offerings to Mahadeva before the excavation, and the priest Dhaumya performs rites with cakes, flowers and food for Shiva, his attendants, Kubera and the Yakshas. The king gives away cattle, prays to the lord of treasures and his gems, and has the ground dug, and the buried vessels and coins are carried away on camels, horses, elephants and carts. The Pandavas then return toward Hastinapura with the wealth, marching a short distance each day and gladdening the Kurus.

Vasudeva returns to the Kuru capital with the Vrishnis, as Yudhishthira asked, for the horse sacrifice. There he finds that Uttara's child, Abhimanyu's son, has been born dead after Ashvatthama's Brahma-weapon struck the womb. Kunti begs Krishna to revive the boy, recalling his earlier promise and Abhimanyu's wish that his son be raised among the Vrishnis, and she falls to the ground in grief until Krishna lifts her up.

Subhadra, Krishna's sister, joins the lament and says that the child's death will make the Pandavas feel cheated, and that she will die if Krishna does not keep his earlier vow. She recalls how Krishna once promised to revive the child of Kiritin's son when Ashvatthama sought to destroy the unborn child, and asks him to fulfil that vow.

Krishna agrees to revive the child, and enters the lying-in room, which has been prepared with protective rites and fires. Draupadi brings Uttara to him, and Uttara laments that her child is dead, wishes that she had died instead, and asks Krishna to revive him. The chapter sets the scene for Krishna's act of restoring the child.

Uttara faints in grief, and the palace becomes a house of mourning. When she revives, she addresses her child and then bows to Krishna, begging him to save the boy. Krishna withdraws the Brahma-weapon and vows, by his own truth and by his friendship with Arjuna, that the child will live, and the child begins to stir.

When Krishna withdraws the Brahma-weapon, the birth chamber is lit by the child's father's energy, the Rakshasas flee, and a heavenly voice praises Krishna. The child revives, and Krishna gives gifts and names him Parikshit, because he was born when the race was nearly extinct. When the infant is a month old, the Pandavas return to the capital with great wealth, and the city is decked out in celebration.

Vasudeva goes out to meet the Pandavas, who return to Hastinapura with the treasure in their van and pay their respects to Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, Vidura and Yuyutsu. Vyasa visits, and Yudhishthira asks his leave to spend the treasure on the horse sacrifice, which Vyasa grants. Yudhishthira then asks Krishna to take up the rites of initiation and lead the sacrifice, and Krishna accepts, pledging to do whatever is asked, with the brothers to take part.

Yudhishthira asks Vyasa to perform his initiation, and Vyasa fixes the full moon of Chaitra for the rite and tells him to choose a horse and let it roam freely. The necessary articles are prepared, some of them of gold. Krishna names Arjuna as the one to guard the horse, while Bhima and Nakula guard the city and Sahadeva looks after the invited guests, and Yudhishthira tells Arjuna to avoid battle where he can and invite the kings to the sacrifice.

The initiation is performed, and Yudhishthira shines in his sacrificial garb. The horse is released by Vyasa, and Arjuna follows it on his white-horsed chariot with Gandiva, while the crowds and Brahmanas bless him. The horse roams from the north toward the east, and Arjuna fights many kings, from the Kiratas and Yavanas to other tribes, who have lost kinsmen in the war.

Sons and grandsons of the Trigartas, enemies of the Pandavas, surround Arjuna and try to seize the horse. Arjuna first asks them to desist, recalling Yudhishthira's order not to kill kings whose kin fell at Kurukshetra, but they attack. Arjuna defeats their leader Suryavarman and his brothers, and Dhritavarman wounds him so that Gandiva falls, but he recovers and drives them off. The Trigartas then submit, and Arjuna accepts their surrender.

The horse enters the realm of Pragjyotisha, where Vajradatta, son of Bhagadatta, seizes it and carries it back toward his city. Arjuna's arrows make him release the horse and flee, but he returns on his war elephant and challenges Arjuna. Arjuna cuts down his arrows, wounds him, and the elephant is pierced and bleeds heavily as the battle goes on.

The battle with Vajradatta lasts three days, and on the fourth day Vajradatta taunts Arjuna about killing his old father Bhagadatta, and charges him on the elephant. Arjuna brings the elephant down with an arrow and, recalling Yudhishthira's order not to slay kings who yield, spares Vajradatta. Vajradatta submits and agrees to attend the sacrifice on the full moon of Chaitra.

Arjuna is attacked by hundreds of Saindhavas, who surround him in a cage of cars and shower him with arrows, recalling his slaying of Jayadratha. Omens of disaster appear in heaven and earth, and Arjuna falls stupefied, dropping Gandiva. The gods and sages pray for him, and when his power returns he draws the bow again, scatters the Saindhavas, and drives them off in fear and grief.

Arjuna faces the Saindhavas, but recalls Yudhishthira's order not to kill warriors who come against him, so he tells them to yield and spares whoever admits defeat. As the battle wears on, Dussala, Dhritarashtra's daughter and queen of the Saindhavas, brings her grandson, Suratha's son, to Arjuna, and explains that Suratha died of grief on hearing that Arjuna had slain Jayadratha. Arjuna censures Duryodhana, makes peace, and sends Dussala home, and then follows the horse on to the realm of Manipura.

Vabhruvahana, the ruler of Manipura and Arjuna's son, comes out humbly with gifts to welcome his father, but Arjuna rebukes him for not meeting him as a warrior. The prince is goaded by his mother Ulupi, a Naga princess, into fighting. He wounds Arjuna, who falls senseless, then wakes and praises his son, and their battle continues until the prince pierces his father and the two fall together. Chitrangada, the prince's mother and Arjuna's wife, goes to the field and finds her husband dead.

Chitrangada blames Ulupi for the death and begs her to revive Arjuna, and then the grieving prince Vabhruvahana, who has killed his father, vows to starve himself or seek expiation. Ulupi then brings a gem that revives the dead and tells the prince that the fight was an illusion she made, for Arjuna's benefit, and that Arjuna cannot truly be defeated. The prince places the gem on his father's chest, and Arjuna revives to the praise of the gods, then asks why the women have come to the field.

Arjuna asks Ulupi why she and Chitrangada have come to the battlefield. Ulupi explains that Arjuna had won Bhishma's fall unfairly while Bhishma was fighting Sikhandin, so the Vasus cursed him, and she arranged for his son to defeat him, which freed him from the curse. Arjuna thanks her and tells Vabhruvahana to attend the sacrifice; the prince asks his father to rest in the city first, but Arjuna declines, since his vow keeps him with the wandering horse.

The horse turns toward Hastinapura and then to Rajagriha, where Meghasandhi, king of Magadha, challenges Arjuna. Arjuna disarms him, cuts down his chariot and weapons, and spares him, since Yudhishthira ordered that kings who oppose him should not be slain. Meghasandhi submits and promises to attend the sacrifice. The horse then travels along the sea coast into Banga, Pundra and Kosala, where Arjuna defeats many Mlechchha armies.

The horse passes through the southern lands, including the Chedi city, where Sarabha, son of Shishupala, welcomes Arjuna, and then through the Kasi, Anga, Kosala and Kirata realms, and the country of the Dasarnas, whose king Chitrangada Arjuna subdues. Arjuna defeats the Nishada king, son of Ekalavya, and then the Dravidas, Andhras and other southern peoples, before passing through Surashtra and Prabhasa to Dwaravati. There Ugrasena and Vasudeva greet him with honour, and the horse continues along the western coast toward Gandhara, where a fierce battle with the son of Sakuni begins.

The son of Sakuni leads a large Gandhara army against Arjuna, angry at his father's death and at the old feud with the Pandavas. Arjuna first asks the Gandharas to desist, but they surround the horse, and he cuts down many of them. He spares their king, who is unnerved by the defeat, and the king's mother comes out with a welcome and begs her son to stop fighting. Arjuna urges the Gandhara prince to stop the hostility and attend the sacrifice in Chaitra.

Yudhishthira learns that the horse is returning and that Arjuna is well, and sets the time for the sacrifice in the month of Magha. Bhima builds a vast sacrificial ground with golden halls, arches, lodgings for kings and Brahmanas, and sends messengers to invite kings, who bring gifts and attend. Yudhishthira feeds the guests and assigns them food, beds and stables for their animals, and when all is ready, the sacrifice begins. The second part of the chapter describes the crowds of disputants, the splendour of the grounds, and the great feeding of Brahmanas.

Yudhishthira asks Bhima to honour the arriving kings, and Krishna comes with the Vrishnis and their leaders. Krishna then reports that a messenger from Arjuna has come, saying that Arjuna is near and worn by many battles. Arjuna's message asks that the kings be honoured, that no massacre like the one at the Rajasuya be allowed, and that Vabhruvahana, his son, be welcomed. Yudhishthira agrees to all of it.

Yudhishthira asks why Arjuna always suffers hardship, and Krishna says the only fault he sees is a small feature of his face that keeps him always on the road. Draupadi is angered by the remark, since she cannot bear any fault being found in Arjuna. Arjuna's envoy then arrives with news of his return, and the king, Krishna and Dhritarashtra go out to meet him. Arjuna is welcomed by the citizens, the kings and his brothers, and Vabhruvahana comes to the city with his mothers and goes to Kunti.

Vabhruvahana greets his kin and is given gifts and a golden car by Krishna. Vyasa urges Yudhishthira to begin the sacrifice and to pay three times the usual Dakshina, and Yudhishthira takes the vow and performs the Horse-sacrifice, with the priests carrying out each rite carefully. The stakes and the golden fire altar are set up, and about three hundred animals, including the horse, are bound to them, while celestial beings, sages and musicians attend the sacrifice.

The priests sacrifice the horse, Draupadi sits beside its body, and its marrow is cooked and offered, completing the rite. Yudhishthira gives away a vast amount of gold and the whole earth to Vyasa, who returns it for a price, and Yudhishthira declares that the Brahmanas should divide the earth. Krishna then gives the earth back to Yudhishthira, who pays millions of coins and triples the Dakshina. The priests divide the wealth, Yudhishthira sends Vabhruvahana home with gifts, and the Vrishnis depart. The great sacrifice is celebrated as a festival, and Yudhishthira returns to his capital cleansed of sin.

Janamejaya asks for any wonderful incident from his ancestors' sacrifice. At the height of the feasting, a mongoose with half its body turned to gold declares that the great sacrifice is worth less than a small measure of barley given by a poor Brahmana of Kurukshetra. He tells how that Brahmana, his wife, son and daughter-in-law, in a famine, each gave up their share of their last barley to a hungry guest, who turned out to be the god of righteousness and took the family to heaven. The mongoose says that the dust of that barley is what turned half its body to gold, and the Brahmanas return home; Vaisampayana closes by saying that gifts, penance and harmlessness are as meritorious as sacrifice.

Janamejaya asks why the mongoose belittled the great Horse-sacrifice, when sacrifices are known to win heaven. Vaisampayana recounts an early sacrifice of Indra, where the sages objected to killing animals and proposed grain offerings instead, but the dispute was settled by King Vasu, who gave a false judgment and was sent to the nether world. Vaisampayana concludes that gifts from unrighteous wealth carry no merit, while modest gifts of lawfully gathered food or water, made with a pure heart, win heaven, as examples of ancient kings show.

Janamejaya asks how lawful wealth can win heaven, and Vaisampayana tells of Agastya's twelve-year sacrifice, in which Indra withheld rain until Agastya's penance and the sages' request brought it back. The story then explains that the golden mongoose was Anger, cursed by the Pitris after it spoiled a sage's milk, and that it disparaged Yudhishthira's sacrifice to be freed. The Parva closes here, and the translator's notes follow.

Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana how the Pandavas treated the defeated old king Dhritarashtra and Gandhari after recovering their kingdom, and how many years they ruled. Vaisampayana answers that the Pandavas governed with Dhritarashtra as their elder, consulting him, serving him with honour and giving him every comfort, while Bhima alone could not forget the dice match. The chapter sets the stage for the elders' later retirement to the forest.

Vaisampayana describes how the Pandavas, led by Yudhishthira, kept honouring Dhritarashtra and Gandhari and carried out their wishes, including funeral offerings for the dead sons. Yudhishthira forgave old wrongs and would punish anyone who spoke against the old king, and Dhritarashtra came to trust him. Bhima, however, could only show respect outwardly, which hints at trouble to come.

Bhima's bitter outburst before Dhritarashtra and Gandhari deepens the old king's grief, and after fifteen years he admits his past folly and asks leave to retire to the forest with Gandhari. Yudhishthira is stricken, offers the throne to someone else and says he will follow the old king into the woods if he goes. When Dhritarashtra insists, Yudhishthira collapses into grief, and the old king is revived only by his touch, so the departure is delayed until the sage Vyasa arrives.

Vyasa tells Yudhishthira not to stand in the way of the old king's retirement, since going to the forest in old age is the path royal sages take. Yudhishthira honours Vyasa as his father and teacher and accepts his advice. Vyasa then leaves, and Yudhishthira asks the old king to eat before he goes to his forest retreat.

Dhritarashtra returns to his palace with Gandhari, Vidura, Sanjaya and Kripa, and after the meal he calls Yudhishthira to his side. He then gives a long set of counsels on ruling a kingdom: honour the learned elders, choose loyal ministers, rely on well-tested spies, guard the city, the king's person and the royal household, punish offenders fairly, and keep a fixed daily routine. The chapter is the old king passing on his experience of statecraft to the new ruler.

Dhritarashtra goes on with his lessons in statecraft, explaining the circles of friends, enemies and neutral powers and the six policies of peace, war, marching, halting, sowing dissension and conciliation. He advises Yudhishthira when to fight and when to seek peace, how to give up land, wealth or troops in a way that costs least, and to protect the helpless. He ends by advising a weaker king to resist strong invaders and, if that fails, to fall fighting.

Dhritarashtra tells Yudhishthira to weigh his own strength against an enemy's before going to war, and to march only when his troops are healthy and cheerful. He lists the kinds of power a king should gather, such as allies, wealth, forest tribes, paid soldiers, the trading classes and spies, and names some battle formations. He closes by saying Bhishma, Krishna and Vidura have already taught Yudhishthira these duties, and that a righteous king earns merit equal to that of a hundred horse-sacrifices.

Yudhishthira agrees to follow his uncle's advice and asks him to keep teaching him, since Bhishma has gone to heaven and Krishna has gone to Dwaraka. Dhritarashtra then sends for Gandhari and tells her he will leave once Yudhishthira grants leave, but first he wants to make gifts in memory of his dead sons. He summons the people of the realm and the Brahmins, and tells them he means to retire to the forest.

Dhritarashtra speaks to the assembled people, recalling how earlier rulers, including Santanu, Vichitraviryya and his brother Pandu, governed them well. He admits that his son's pride and his own poor judgment led to the great slaughter of royalty, asks forgiveness for himself and Gandhari, and entrusts Yudhishthira to their care. The citizens and countryfolk are moved to tears and say nothing, only looking at one another.

The citizens stand silent in grief until Dhritarashtra asks them again for permission to leave. A Brahmin named Samba answers on the assembly's behalf, approving the old king's departure, praising Yudhishthira's rule and absolving Duryodhana and Dhritarashtra of blame for the war, which he attributes to fate. The assembly approves, and the old king dismisses it and goes home with Gandhari.

The next day Dhritarashtra sends Vidura to Yudhishthira, asking for wealth to hold funeral offerings for Bhishma, Drona, Somadatta, Valhika, his sons and Jayadratha, and announcing that he will leave on the Kartika full moon. Yudhishthira and Arjuna welcome the request, but Bhima angrily objects, recalling the dice match and the hardships of exile. Arjuna urges him to accept, and Yudhishthira silences Bhima when his anger threatens to say more.

Arjuna tells Bhima that Dhritarashtra deserves honour and that good men forget the wrongs done to them. Yudhishthira then tells Vidura to say to the old king that he may take as much wealth from the royal treasury as he wishes, and that Bhima should not be made unhappy. Yudhishthira also offers the king everything he and Arjuna own, to show his goodwill.

Vidura returns and reports to Dhritarashtra that Yudhishthira and Arjuna agree to his plan, and that Bhima accepted only reluctantly. Yudhishthira offers his kingdom, his life and all his wealth, and asks the king to forgive Bhima's outburst. The brothers also suggest charitable gifts to Brahmins, the poor and the blind, along with pavilions of food and water for cattle, and Dhritarashtra resolves to hold the great gift-giving on the Kartika full moon.

Pleased with the Pandavas, Dhritarashtra invites many Brahmins and sages and gives away wealth for the spirits of Bhishma, his sons, friends and kinsmen, naming each recipient as the gifts go out. Yudhishthira approves, and the gifts are lavish in cars, clothes, gold, livestock, slaves, elephants and horses, along with food and drink, music and dancing. The text says the ten-day gift-giving frees the old king from the debts he owed his sons and grandsons.

On the Kartika full moon Dhritarashtra completes the final rites, takes the sacred fire, puts on deer-skin and bark, and leaves his palace with Gandhari, Kunti and his daughters-in-law. Yudhishthira faints in grief and the Pandavas, Vidura, Sanjaya, Kripa and Dhaumya follow, while the women and citizens lament as they once did when the Pandavas were exiled after the dice match. The chapter closes the palace phase of the old king's life and begins his journey to the forest.

Dhritarashtra leaves the city amid a great crowd and sends the citizens home, keeping Vidura and Sanjaya with him but handing Kripa and Yuyutsu back to Yudhishthira. Yudhishthira tries to hold his mother Kunti back, and she answers with a speech of regret and farewell, recalling Karna and asking the brothers to care for their wives and one another. Yudhishthira, Bhima and the others plead with her in vain, and she goes on with Gandhari toward the forest.

Kunti explains that she spurred her sons to courage after the loss at dice, so they would not be disgraced or lose their fame, and that she acted to protect Draupadi from Dussasana's insults. She tells them that she does not want the kingdom they won and will spend her days in penance and service to her in-laws. She asks Yudhishthira and his brothers to stop following her and to keep to righteousness.

The Pandavas are ashamed and turn back, and Dhritarashtra asks Gandhari to make Kunti return, but Kunti will not be moved. The Kuru ladies wail, the Pandavas go back to a mourning city, and the old king's party camps by the Bhagirathi, where they perform their rites and rest for the night. Their first day in the forest is painful, both for them and for the grieving people they have left behind.

Following Vidura's advice, Dhritarashtra settles on the banks of the Bhagirathi, where visiting Brahmins and common folk see him, and then moves to Kurukshetra. There the former Kekaya king Satayupa welcomes him and takes him to Vyasa, who initiates him into the forest way of life. Dhritarashtra, Gandhari, Kunti, Vidura and Sanjaya then take up barks and skins and practise severe penance.

The sages Narada, Parvata, Devala and Vyasa visit the old king and gladden him with talk of religion. Narada tells of earlier royal ascetics who reached heaven through penance in the forest, and says Dhritarashtra and Gandhari will reach a high goal, with Vidura and Sanjaya also going on. Asked by Satayupa for the particulars, Narada says he has heard from Indra that Dhritarashtra has three years of life left, after which he will go to Kuvera's realm, and the company departs well pleased.

With the elders gone to the forest, the Pandavas and the citizens of Hastinapura grieve, worrying how the old king, Gandhari, Kunti, Vidura and Sanjaya will manage in the wilds. The Pandavas lose interest in rule and in study, dwelling on the deaths of Abhimanyu, Karna and Draupadi's sons. They are only partly comforted by the survival of Parikshit, the son of Virata's daughter.

The Pandavas, lost in grief, neglect the affairs of the capital and think constantly of their mother and the blind old couple in the forest. Sahadeva proposes going to see them, and Draupadi agrees and asks for the visit. Yudhishthira orders the army, carts, treasuries and kitchens made ready, and after waiting five days for citizens who wish to come, he sets out for the forest.

The Pandavas set out with a great procession of troops, chariots, elephants, camels and litter-borne women, with Yudhishthira under a white umbrella and his brothers and Draupadi around him. Kripa leads the army ahead toward the retreat, while Yuyutsu and Dhaumya stay behind to guard the city. Crossing the Yamuna, Yudhishthira sees the old king's hermitage in the distance, and the crowd rushes in with joy.

The Pandavas walk the last stretch on foot in humility, and the hermit community tells them the old king has gone to bathe in the Yamuna. Sahadeva runs ahead to Kunti, who rushes toward the blind couple, and the brothers fall to the ground before their father. Dhritarashtra recognises them by voice and touch, and Yudhishthira introduces the women and people of the court to him. The old king feels as if he is back in Hastinapura, and he returns to his forest hermitage with a crowd of visitors.

The visiting ascetics ask which of the newcomers is Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, the twins and Draupadi, and Sanjaya names each of them by their looks. He then names the other women of the household, including Subhadra, Ulupi, Chitrangada, Jarasandha's daughter, Virata's daughter who was Abhimanyu's wife, and the widows of Dhritarashtra's sons, who are dressed in white. Afterwards the old king makes courteous enquiries of the whole company.

Dhritarashtra asks Yudhishthira a long series of questions about his kingdom, justice, treasury, priests and ministers, and the duties of his subjects. Yudhishthira asks after the old king's peace and his mother's welfare, and then wonders where Vidura is. Vidura appears, emaciated and naked, and Yudhishthira chases him into the forest. Vidura enters Yudhishthira's body by Yoga and dies, and a voice tells Yudhishthira not to cremate the body, since Vidura was Dharma and goes to a heavenly region. The brothers are fed by the old king and sleep under a tree.

The Pandavas spend the night on the bare ground beside their mother and eat the food of the hermitage. The next morning Yudhishthira tours the surrounding retreats with his brothers, giving gifts to the ascetics, and then returns to his uncle, who is seated with Gandhari. Satayupa and the other sages of Kurukshetra arrive, followed by Vyasa, who is given an honoured seat and bids the assembly be seated.

Once the Pandavas are seated, Vyasa asks Dhritarashtra how his penances are going and whether his grief has eased, and asks after Gandhari, Kunti and the brothers. He then explains that Vidura was Dharma himself, born through a curse and Vyasa's own power, and that Yudhishthira is also a son of Dharma, and that Vidura has entered Yudhishthira's person. Vyasa offers to show the old king some wonder, and asks what he wants to see or hear.

Janamejaya asks what wonder Vyasa performed, and how long the Pandavas stayed in the forest and what they ate. Vaisampayana says they lived there about a month on the food they could find, and that sages gathered round, including Narada, Parvata and Devala. Vyasa offers Dhritarashtra any boon, and the old king speaks at length of his grief for his sons and his fear for his own end. Gandhari, whose grief is renewed, asks Vyasa to let the dead be seen, and Vyasa then turns to Kunti to ask what is on her mind.

Kunti confesses to Vyasa the secret of Karna's birth. As a girl she had served the wrathful sage Durvasas, who gave her a mantra, and she summoned the sun god, who fathered Karna and restored her maidenhood. Fearing shame to her father, she set the infant adrift in water and never acknowledged him, and she asks Vyasa to grant her wish to see her son, and the king his. Vyasa tells her she is blameless, since gods can beget children in several ways.

Vyasa promises that the king, Gandhari and Kunti will see their dead that night, and explains that the fallen heroes were portions of gods, celestial beings and sages who came to earth for a purpose and have now returned. He names several of them, including Dhritarashtra as the Gandharva king, Pandu as one of the Maruts, Yudhishthira and Vidura as Dharma, Duryodhana as Kali and Karna as a portion of the sun. He tells the company to go to the Bhagirathi, where they will see the dead, and they set out with joy.

At night the company gathers by the Bhagirathi and Vyasa bathes in its waters and calls up the dead. Warriors from both sides rise from the river in celestial robes and jewels, free of anger and pride, and Gandhari sees her sons and others with divine sight that Vyasa grants. Dhritarashtra also receives the sight, and the whole scene looks like a festival, and he is filled with joy at seeing the heroes.

The reunited dead and living meet with joy, and the Pandavas are reconciled with Karna, so that old enmities are set aside for one night. Vyasa then dismisses the crowd, the warriors go off to their heavenly realms, and the widows enter the Bhagirathi to join their husbands. The chapter ends with Vyasa's promise of rewards for those who hear or recite this account.

Janamejaya asks how bodies that have been destroyed can appear again in the same form, and Vaisampayana answers with a long philosophical reply. He says deeds are never lost without their consequences, that the body arises from deeds while the soul is unaffected by pleasure and pain, and that the sorrow of separation comes from confusing the body with the self. The discourse makes the apparition a matter of how the soul and deeds persist.

Dhritarashtra, who had never seen his sons, gains sight through Vyasa's grace and sees them as they were. Janamejaya asks to see his own father in the same form, and Vyasa brings Parikshit back from the other world, along with Samika and Sringin. Astika, a learned Brahmin, praises the sacrifice and the wondrous history, and Janamejaya asks Vaisampayana what followed for Dhritarashtra in the forest.

Janamejaya asks what Dhritarashtra and Yudhishthira did after the vision. Vyasa tells Dhritarashtra that the Pandavas should return to Hastinapura to rule, since more than a month has passed. Dhritarashtra agrees and, though Yudhishthira begs to stay and Gandhari insists he go, the brothers and women take their leave, and Yudhishthira sets out for the capital.

Two years after the Pandavas return to Hastinapura, the sage Narada visits Yudhishthira and asks about his father's fate. Narada reports that Dhritarashtra, with Gandhari, Kunti and Sanjaya, went to the Ganga and lived by severe penance, reduced to skin and bones. When a forest fire spread, Sanjaya urged escape, but the old king sat in meditation with the two queens and all three were burned, which the sage later confirmed from the bodies. The narrative thus reports the old king's death by fire, which the Pandavas then mourn.

Yudhishthira laments the death of his father in the forest fire, reflecting that fate is hard to predict for even a powerful king with a hundred sons. He mourns Kunti most, calls the fire-god ungrateful for burning the mother of Arjuna, whom he had once served at Khandava, and wishes that Bhima or Sahadeva had saved her. The sorrow of the brothers and the household is so great that the wails fill the palace and seem to reach the sky.

Narada corrects the account: Dhritarashtra did not die in an unsanctified fire but in his own sacred fire, which the attending priests had abandoned in the forest and which spread into a blaze. Yudhishthira and the whole household then perform the water offerings and cremation rites, and on the twelfth day make lavish gifts in memory of the old king and his queens. The section closes with a benediction on hearing the Asramavasika Parva, followed by the translator's notes on the text.

In the thirty-sixth year after the great war, Yudhishthira sees many bad omens and hears that the Vrishnis have been wiped out by an iron bolt. Janamejaya asks who brought this about, and Vaishampayana explains that Time drove the clan to ruin through a curse. The curse came after some Vrishni youths tricked visiting sages with Samva disguised as a pregnant woman. This opening sets up the cause of the Yadava downfall, which the rest of the parva describes.

The Vrishnis and Andhakas try to avert their fate, but Time appears in their houses and omens multiply. Animals and nature behave in unnatural ways, and people lose their sense of shame and respect. Krishna sees that the thirty-sixth year has come and that Gandhari's earlier words are about to come true. He orders the clan to make a pilgrimage to the sea-coast, which sets up the final gathering at Prabhasa.

Before leaving, the Vrishni women and men dream of portents, and their weapons and chariots vanish. The clan travels to Prabhasa, where Uddhava departs and the men start a drinking feast. A drunken quarrel between Yuyudhana and Kritavarma leads to Satyaki killing Kritavarma, and a wider brawl breaks out in which Satyaki and Pradyumna die. Krishna picks up a blade of grass that turns into an iron bolt, and the clan destroys itself, with Krishna and Daruka then turning toward Rama.

Krishna sends Daruka to bring Arjuna, then tells Vabhru to guard the women before a hunter's iron bolt kills Vabhru. Krishna goes to find Rama, who has died in yoga and whose serpent soul has gone to the ocean. Krishna thinks over the curses and his own fate, then lies down in yoga, where a hunter named Jara mistakes him for a deer and wounds him. Krishna then ascends to heaven, where the gods honour him.

Daruka reaches the Pandavas and reports that the Vrishnis have destroyed one another. Arjuna sets out for Dwaraka and finds the city empty of its heroes, with the widows and wives of Krishna overcome with grief. Arjuna weeps, is comforted by the women, and then goes on to see his maternal uncle. The scene marks the arrival of the Pandavas' sorrow at the fall of Dwaraka.

Arjuna finds his uncle Anakadundubhi, who is grieving for his dead sons and kinsmen. The old man tells him how Krishna left before he died, asking Arjuna to take the women and the kingdom and to perform the funeral rites. He says he has stopped eating and will not go on living. The chapter shows Arjuna taking on the responsibility for the surviving Yadavas.

Arjuna orders the Vrishni survivors to prepare for departure, since the sea will soon swallow Dwaraka. Krishna is cremated with his wives, and the dead Vrishnis are given their rites before the procession leaves the city. On the road, Abhira robbers attack the widows, and Arjuna cannot use his bow or weapons well enough to stop them, losing many women. He settles the rest at new places, and then he goes to see Vyasa, marking the end of the Yadava story for Arjuna.

Arjuna visits the hermitage of Vyasa, who notices his despair and asks what has happened. Arjuna describes the Vrishni destruction at Prabhasa, the robbery of the women, his lost strength, and Krishna's departure, and he says he no longer wishes to live. Vyasa explains that all this was fated and that Time governs rise and fall, and that the Pandavas' work is finished. He tells Arjuna that it is time for them all to depart.

After hearing of the slaughter of the Vrishnis and Krishna's ascent to heaven, Yudhishthira decides to give up the world, and his brothers agree. He hands the kingdom to Yuyutsu, places Parikshit on the throne under Kripa's teaching, and makes offerings for the dead. The Pandavas, Draupadi and a dog then set out eastward, and the fire god makes Arjuna give up his bow Gandiva before they head west and north to circle the earth.

The Pandavas climb north toward the Himalayas and Meru, and one by one they fall. Draupadi falls first, then Sahadeva, Nakula, Arjuna and Bhima, and Bhima asks Yudhishthira the cause of each fall. Yudhishthira names a fault in each, and he walks on alone with the dog, never looking back.

Shakra arrives with a chariot and invites Yudhishthira to heaven, but he refuses to go without his brothers and Draupadi. When Shakra insists he abandon the dog that has followed him, Yudhishthira refuses, arguing that abandoning one devoted to him is as sinful as killing a Brahmana. The dog then reveals itself as Dharma, who praises him, and Yudhishthira goes to heaven, where he insists on joining his brothers and Draupadi, closing the Mahaprasthanika section.

Janamejaya asks what heavenly regions his ancestors, the Pandavas and Kauravas, reached. Yudhishthira sees Duryodhana honored in heaven and refuses to share it, but Narada reminds him that enmities end in heaven. Yudhishthira then asks where his fallen brothers and allies are, showing that his grief is not yet settled.

Yudhishthira says heaven means nothing without his brothers and allies, and the messenger leads him down a foul, hellish road. Pleading voices from the suffering halt him, and when he asks who they are, they answer with the names of his dead kin, Karna, the Pandavas and Draupadi. Yudhishthira is bewildered, then angrily resolves to stay with them.

The gods arrive, and the hellish sights and smells vanish. Indra and Dharma explain that the whole hell scene was an illusion and a test, and that Yudhishthira's time there was linked to his earlier deception of Drona. Yudhishthira bathes in the Ganga, sheds his human body, and is freed of enmity and grief.

Praised by the gods, Yudhishthira goes to where his relatives and allies dwell in heaven. He sees Govinda, Phalguna, Karna, Bhima, the twins, and Draupadi, and Indra explains who each one is and where each now lives. The chapter shows the dead heroes reunited in heaven.

Janamejaya asks how long his heroic ancestors stayed in heaven and whether their place there is lasting. Vaishampayana answers by naming where each great warrior was absorbed after death, and the narrator then closes the whole work with praise of its virtues and of who recites it. The chapter ends the Svargarohana Parva and the frame of the Mahabharata's telling.

Janamejaya asks how a learned listener should hear the Bharata, what rites apply, and what rewards follow. Vaishampayana describes the work's scope, the qualities of a good reciter and listener, the heavenly rewards for hearing each portion, and the gifts due at each parva. The chapter closes with praise of the Mahabharata and the note that its eighteen parvas are complete, and it ends with a Project Gutenberg license notice that is not part of the epic.
